Feedback therefore connects classical control, optimization, planning, and learning-based autonomy rather than belonging to any one of them. The following subsections introduce feedback, control methods, and hierarchical autonomy. They also analyze stability, robustness, adaptation, and safety.

2.2.1 Foundations of Cybernetics: Feedback and Steady State

A feedback control system uses measurements of a physical system’s behavior to adjust its control inputs toward a desired target, which forms a feedback loop of measurement and correction. This section first introduces this feedback loop, and then discusses its transient and steady-state behavior, to assess how effectively a system approaches and maintains that target.

Negative Feedback Principle

Wiener1948 introduces cybernetics as a framework for studying control and communication in systems whose actions affect the conditions they subsequently observe. In this framework, a plant receives a control input $u(t)$ , evolves under its own dynamics and external disturbances, and produces an output $y(t)$ . For output tracking, a controller compares the measured output with a reference $r(t)$ and uses the tracking error to determine the next control command. The error, and the control input in the simplest case of proportional control with gain $K_{\mathrm{P}}$ , are defined as

 $e_{\mathrm{track}}(t)=r(t)-y(t),\qquad u(t)=K_{\mathrm{P}}e_{\mathrm{track}}(t),$ 

(2.16)

where the proportional law is the simplest instance of feedback. Integral and derivative action extend this relation in the proportional-integral-derivative controller introduced below.

Controllers may also use an estimate of the underlying state when the relevant variables are not directly measured. The loop is called negative feedback when the controller acts so as to reduce the measured deviation, as when a thermostat increases heating below its set point or a balancing vehicle generates torque opposing body tilt. Feedback is most valuable when the model is incomplete. If an actuator delivers less torque than commanded, or a manipulator grasps an object of unknown mass, a precomputed input cannot detect the resulting error. Feedback uses observations of the changed motion to compensate within the limits of sensing, actuation, and closed-loop bandwidth. Feedback thereby converts certain forms of uncertainty into observable error and permits repeatable behavior from imperfect components.

Negative feedback is not synonymous with stability. A correction whose sign is appropriate at low frequency may destabilize the loop once sensing, computation, or actuation introduces sufficient delay. Excessive gain has the same effect, and strong reaction to high-frequency measurement noise may excite unmodeled flexible modes. Feedback design must therefore shape the magnitude and phase of the loop response, not merely reverse the sign of the error (Åström and Murray, 2008). The signals entering the loop must also be distinguished. A reference describes intended behavior, a disturbance acts on the plant from outside, measurement noise corrupts the information available to the controller, and model uncertainty denotes the discrepancy between representation and mechanism. These signals can produce similar visible effects yet require different remedies, so an embodied controller is a negotiated balance among tracking, disturbance rejection, noise attenuation, actuator effort, and robustness. Feedback further depends on what is measured. Because the full state is rarely available, practical loops incorporate an estimator that fuses a dynamic model with sensor streams. Estimation and control become coupled processes in which actions determine which future observations become available.

Figure 2.1: Open-loop and closed-loop control. (a) In open-loop control, the controller maps the reference $r(t)$ directly to the plant input $u(t)$ , so an output disturbance $d(t)$ passes to the output $y(t)$ uncorrected. (b) In closed-loop control, the measured output is fed back and compared with the reference, and the controller acts on the error $e_{\mathrm{track}}(t)=r(t)-y(t)$ . For a stable closed loop, the feedback attenuates the output-disturbance response over frequencies at which the loop-gain magnitude $|L(\mathrm{j}\omega)|$ is sufficiently large. $C(s)$ and $P(s)$ denote the controller and plant transfer functions, respectively

Open-Loop and Closed-Loop Control

Two basic control arrangements are open-loop and closed-loop control, illustrated in Figure 2.1 (FranklinPowellEmamiNaeini2019; DorfBishop2017; Åström and Murray, 2008). An open-loop controller selects its input without measurements of the controlled outcome during execution. Such control is appropriate when the plant and environment are sufficiently repeatable, when feedback is unavailable, or when the maneuver is too fast for a sensor-to-actuator loop, but it cannot correct errors that become observable only after execution begins. Closed-loop control uses observations to revise action, and its advantage is made precise by the sensitivity functions. For a single-input, single-output linear system in the standard negative unity-feedback configuration with plant $P(s)$ and controller $C(s)$ , the loop transfer function $L(s)=P(s)C(s)$ yields

 $S(s)=\frac{1}{1+L(s)},\qquad T(s)=\frac{L(s)}{1+L(s)},\qquad S(s)+T(s)=1,$ 

(2.17)

where $T$ maps the reference to the output, $S$ maps an additive output disturbance to the output, and measurement noise reaches the output through $-T$ . Where $|L|$ is large and the loop is stable, $|S|$ is generally small, whereas noise is transmitted through $T$ . The multivariable case is analogous, with multiplication order significant. Feedback thus does not erase uncertainty but redistributes sensitivity across frequencies, subject to stability margins, delay, and unmodeled dynamics (SkogestadPostlethwaite2005).

Capable robotic systems combine feedback with feedforward. Inverse dynamics, for example, predicts the torques required for a desired motion, while feedback corrects residual errors caused by inaccurate parameters, friction, contact, or estimation error. This two-degree-of-freedom structure also clarifies the role of learned models, which improve the nominal action while the conventional loop rejects deviations within a known operating envelope. The open-loop/closed-loop distinction is therefore a design spectrum rather than a dichotomy. Feedforward motion may be embedded within a slower feedback loop, and symbolic goals may be issued to feedback controllers with local termination conditions. Physical feedback also carries costs. Sensors consume power and bandwidth, estimation and communication add latency, and a loop may regulate the wrong variable with high precision, as when position control damages a fragile object because contact force is unmonitored (RaibertCraig1981; Hogan1985).

Steady-State Error and Integral Action

Transient performance describes behavior while a system approaches its target. For a system that converges to a steady state, steady-state performance characterizes the residual behavior after transients have decayed (Ogata2010; FranklinPowellEmamiNaeini2019). For a constant reference $r(t)$ , with the tracking error $e_{\mathrm{track}}(t)=r(t)-y(t)$ as defined above, the steady-state error is

 $e_{\mathrm{ss}}=\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}e_{\mathrm{track}}(t),$ 

(2.18)

provided that the limit exists and the closed loop is stable. A proportional controller may fail to eliminate this error when a constant input is needed to balance a persistent load. For instance, a mobile robot ascending a slope requires a constant drive force to balance gravity, and because proportional action generates its command solely in proportion to the present error, such a nonzero force can be produced only while a nonzero error persists, so the vehicle settles into a steady climb at a speed below the reference. Integral action instead accumulates the error in an integrator state $\eta_{\mathrm{I}}(t)$ and adds an integral term $u_{\mathrm{I}}(t)$ to the control input,

 $\eta_{\mathrm{I}}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}e_{\mathrm{track}}(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau,\qquad u_{\mathrm{I}}(t)=K_{\mathrm{I}}\eta_{\mathrm{I}}(t),$ 

(2.19)

where $K_{\mathrm{I}}$ is the integral gain. A persistent deviation therefore continues to modify the command and, subject to closed-loop stability and sufficient control authority, is driven to zero. The internal model principle formalizes this mechanism. Under closed-loop stability and the solvability conditions of output regulation, exact asymptotic tracking or rejection that is robust to small plant-parameter variations requires a model capable of generating the reference or disturbance signal within the feedback path (FrancisWonham1976). The integral action discussed above is the simplest instance of this principle. An integrator generates constant signals, and a loop containing an integrator can therefore track a constant reference or reject a constant disturbance exactly. Robust tracking of sinusoidal references likewise requires the controller to contain a corresponding oscillatory model at the reference frequency.

Integral action has its own failure mode under actuator saturation. An actuator, such as an electric motor or a hydraulic drive, delivers only bounded torque or force, so the applied control input $u(t)$ stops following the command whenever the requested value exceeds this physical limit. During saturation, the integrator may continue accumulating error although additional command cannot affect the plant, and the stored term produces a large overshoot when the system re-enters the controllable range. Anti-windup schemes limit or discharge this accumulation by clamping the integrator, feeding back the difference between requested and applied input, or conditioning integration on the actuator state (KothareEtAl1994; TarbouriechTurner2009). For embodied systems, saturation must be treated as part of the model rather than as a rare implementation detail. Note that the significance of zero steady-state error is task-dependent. Contact tasks often tolerate deliberate pose error in exchange for regulated force, and legged robots accept bounded periodic error in exchange for lower impact and energy consumption.

2.2.2 Classical and Modern Control Methods

One of the most widely used control systems is proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control. It maps three interpretable features of the error into control action. In its ideal continuous-time form,

 $u(t)=K_{\mathrm{P}}e_{\mathrm{track}}(t)+K_{\mathrm{I}}\int_{0}^{t}e_{\mathrm{track}}(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau+K_{\mathrm{D}}\frac{\mathrm{d}e_{\mathrm{track}}(t)}{\mathrm{d}t},$ 

(2.20)

where $K_{\mathrm{P}}$ , $K_{\mathrm{I}}$ , and $K_{\mathrm{D}}$ are the proportional, integral, and derivative gains, and $e_{\mathrm{track}}(t)$ is the tracking error defined above. The proportional term $K_{\mathrm{P}}e_{\mathrm{track}}(t)$ responds to the present error, the integral term $K_{\mathrm{I}}\int_{0}^{t}e_{\mathrm{track}}(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau$ to its accumulated history, and the derivative term $K_{\mathrm{D}}\,\mathrm{d}e_{\mathrm{track}}/\mathrm{d}t$ to its local trend. For position or angle error with force or torque output, proportional action resembles a virtual spring, derivative action resembles a virtual damper, and integral action resembles a slowly adjusting bias that offsets gravity or friction. In a torque-controlled robot this analogy connects PID directly to impedance design. It also exposes the hazard of aggressive tuning. A stiff virtual spring improves free-space positioning while generating unsafe forces after unexpected contact, so that gains encode a physical interaction policy rather than a numerical convergence rate alone.

In practice, PID implementations modify the ideal equation in several ways. First, the derivative term is filtered against measurement noise and applied to the output rather than the reference to avoid derivative kick. Integral action also requires anti-windup. Additionally, actuator dead zones, quantization, rate limits, and computation delay can dominate performance if ignored (Åström and Hägglund, 2005). Tuning rules such as Ziegler-Nichols (ZieglerNichols1942) provide useful initial gains, but they do not replace validation on hardware. Practical implementations typically nest current, velocity, and position loops of decreasing bandwidth. When this bandwidth separation is weak, the independently tuned loops interact and may destabilize the mechanism. PID control is best suited to regulation tasks with few variables and nearly constant dynamics. Multivariable coupling, nonminimum-phase behavior, hard constraints, and large changes in the operating range call for model-based methods instead. Even then, PID often persists at the actuator interface, because its failure modes are familiar and its behavior is inspectable.

State Space and Optimal Control

Another model is the state-space model, which represents the internal configuration required to predict future evolution. A linear time-invariant model has the form

 $\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t)=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}(t)+\mathbf{B}\mathbf{u}(t)+\mathbf{E}\mathbf{w}(t),\qquad\mathbf{y}(t)=\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{obs}}\mathbf{x}(t)+\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{noise}}(t),$ 

(2.21)

where $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the state, $\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ the control input, $\mathbf{w}$ a process disturbance, $\mathbf{y}$ the measurement, $\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{noise}}$ measurement noise, and $\mathbf{A}$ , $\mathbf{B}$ , $\mathbf{E}$ , $\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{obs}}$ are matrices of compatible dimensions. A nonlinear system $\dot{\mathbf{x}}=f_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{u},\mathbf{w})$ can be linearized about an equilibrium or nominal trajectory. Controllability describes whether the input can move every state direction over a finite interval, and observability describes whether the initial state can be recovered from the input-output history. The weaker properties of stabilizability and detectability suffice for stabilization and estimator convergence, requiring only that every uncontrollable or unobservable mode already be stable. As a result, no controller compensates for an actuator lacking authority over an unstable direction, and no model complexity recovers a contact state invisible to the measurements (Åström and Murray, 2008). When the full state is not measured, an observer estimates it. For a linear model with zero-mean white process and measurement noises of known covariance, the Kalman filter is the minimum-mean-square-error estimator among linear estimators, and it is the optimal estimator without that restriction when the initial state and the noises are jointly Gaussian (Kalman1960). Because estimation error enters the loop as a dynamic signal, estimator bandwidth, outlier handling, and covariance calibration are part of controller design rather than preprocessing details.

The linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) (Kalman1960LQR) renders the trade-off between regulation and control effort explicit. For the system $\dot{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{B}\mathbf{u}$ , it minimizes

 $J_{\mathrm{cost}}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\left(\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{u}}\mathbf{u}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t,$ 

(2.22)

with $\mathbf{Q}\succeq 0$ and $\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{u}}\succ 0$ . Assuming $(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B})$ stabilizable11
 1

 A pair $(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B})$ is stabilizable when every eigenmode of $\mathbf{A}$ that cannot be influenced by the input is already asymptotically stable. Likewise, $(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{Q}^{1/2})$ is detectable when every eigenmode of $\mathbf{A}$ that is unobservable through $\mathbf{Q}^{1/2}\mathbf{x}$ is already asymptotically stable. These are necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of stabilizing linear state feedback and a linear observer with asymptotically stable error dynamics, respectively. Here detectability refers to the cost output $\mathbf{Q}^{1/2}\mathbf{x}$ . and $(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{Q}^{1/2})$ detectable, the unique stabilizing positive-semidefinite solution $\boldsymbol{\Pi}$ of

 $\mathbf{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Pi}+\boldsymbol{\Pi}\mathbf{A}-\boldsymbol{\Pi}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{u}}^{-1}\mathbf{B}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Pi}+\mathbf{Q}=0,$ 

(2.23)

yields $\mathbf{K}=\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{u}}^{-1}\mathbf{B}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Pi}$ and the state-feedback law $\mathbf{u}=-\mathbf{K}\mathbf{x}$ (LewisVrabieSyrmos2012). The optimum is conditional on the specified model, cost, horizon, and information pattern. $\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{u}}\mathbf{u}$ is an effort surrogate that equals physical energy consumption only under appropriate modeling. Trajectory tracking applies time-varying LQR to deviations linearized along a nominal trajectory, and applying the gain to a Kalman estimate yields the linear-quadratic-Gaussian controller under the separation principle. The principal limitation is constraint handling. LQR does not natively enforce joint limits, contact, collision avoidance, or torque saturation, and clipping an optimal command after computation alters the closed-loop dynamics and can invalidate the nominal analysis. Constrained quadratic programs impose instantaneous limits, while model predictive control extends the optimization across future steps.

Model Predictive Control

Model predictive control (MPC) is also commonly used and repeatedly solves a finite-horizon optimal control problem using the latest state estimate. A representative nominal discrete-time formulation is

 $\displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{u}_{0},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{H_{\mathrm{MPC}}-1}}$ 
 $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{H_{\mathrm{MPC}}-1}\ell(\mathbf{x}_{k},\mathbf{u}_{k})+V_{\mathrm{f}}(\mathbf{x}_{H_{\mathrm{MPC}}})$ 

(2.24)

 $\displaystyle\text{subject to}$ 
 $\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{0}=\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{now}},$ 

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{k+1}=f_{\mathrm{d}}(\mathbf{x}_{k},\mathbf{u}_{k}),$ 

 $\displaystyle k=0,\ldots,H_{\mathrm{MPC}}-1,$ 

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{k}\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{adm}},\quad\mathbf{u}_{k}\in\mathcal{U},$ 

 $\displaystyle k=0,\ldots,H_{\mathrm{MPC}}-1,$ 

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{H_{\mathrm{MPC}}}\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{term}}\subseteq\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{adm}},$ 

where $\ell(\mathbf{x}_{k},\mathbf{u}_{k})$ and $V_{\mathrm{f}}(\mathbf{x}_{H_{\mathrm{MPC}}})$ are the stage and terminal costs, $f_{\mathrm{d}}$ is the discrete-time plant dynamics, $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{now}}$ is the most recent state estimate, $\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{adm}}$ and $\mathcal{U}$ are the admissible state and input sets, and $\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{term}}$ is a terminal constraint set. Only the first optimized input is applied. The horizon then shifts forward, a new estimate is obtained, and the problem is solved again. When the optimization remains feasible and is solved as specified, this receding-horizon procedure induces a feedback law on the current state estimate.

MPC is attractive for embodied systems because constraints are part of the decision problem. A manipulator can bound joint angles, velocities, torques, or predicted collision distances, and a legged robot can also consider friction and feasible contact forces. For nominal regulation, recursive feasibility and asymptotic stability can be established through a positive-definite stage cost, a terminal controller that respects the constraints, a positively invariant terminal set, and a terminal cost decrease condition, provided that the initial problem is feasible (mayne2000constrained). Design choices are consequential. Short horizons reduce computation but limit how far ahead the controller predicts. Hard constraints declare violations inadmissible, whereas selected constraints may be softened with slack variables when requirements conflict. With linear dynamics, linear constraints, and convex quadratic costs, MPC is a convex quadratic program. Nonlinear MPC typically uses iterative numerical optimization, often with warm starts and sparse solvers.

Prediction does not eliminate the need for feedback or robustness. Model mismatch grows along the horizon, particularly during impacts, slip, or deformable contact. Tube MPC, stochastic MPC, chance constraints, or min-max formulations reserve margins against possible deviations. The system must define the response to infeasibility or solver timeout, whether retaining the previous command, switching to a stabilizing backup, or braking. Controller selection should follow the structure of the task, and the methods are frequently composed. MPC supplies whole-body references, an intermediate controller stabilizes deviations, and embedded PID loops realize actuator commands.

2.2.3 Hierarchical Architectures of Autonomous Systems

The Classical Sense-Plan-Act Pipeline

Sense-Plan-Act decomposes autonomous behavior into perception, planning, and control. Perception converts sensor data into estimates of robot and environment state. Planning selects goals, actions, or trajectories. Control converts plans into actuator commands while correcting deviations (Gat1998). The decomposition is misleading when read as a one-shot sequence. By the end of a long perception-and-planning cycle, the environment may have changed and localization uncertainty may have grown. Autonomous operation therefore requires repeated sensing and replanning, with components running concurrently under explicit latency budgets, because an accurate estimate of an old state can be less useful than a coarser estimate of the present one.

One design requirement for this pipeline is that information passed between the perception, planning, and control stages should include uncertainty and validity, not only nominal values (SicilianoKhatib2016). For example, a pose estimate without covariance encourages downstream modules to treat perception as certain, and a path without timing assumptions leaves control unable to distinguish acceptable tracking error from an obsolete plan. Interfaces should include reference frames, units, update rates, tolerances, and failure conditions, particularly when learned components are integrated with model-based control (BrugaliScandurra2009). Feedback paths should also cross stage boundaries. Control influences perception through active sensing, and a geometrically valid path may be dynamically infeasible. Finally, real-time performance is governed by worst-case timing rather than average throughput. Occasionally, a planner that requires 2 seconds may be unacceptable for collision avoidance. A predesigned degradation behavior provides a backup solution. Also, scheduling priorities must follow physical urgency, because motor stabilization and contact protection cannot wait for task-level planning.

Behavior Trees and Finite-State Machines

Finite-state machines (FSMs) can also formalize task execution as discrete modes and transitions triggered by events or conditions, with each state activating corresponding controllers or planners. Hybrid automata extend the representation by associating continuous dynamics with each mode (Henzinger1996), a natural description of systems that alternate among free motion, contact, and impact. However, a limitation of a flat FSM is combinatorial growth. As recovery cases and task variants accumulate, transitions proliferate and behavior becomes difficult to inspect. Hierarchical state machines mitigate this growth, but their interrupt, priority, and concurrency semantics must be specified explicitly. A logically valid transition may be physically unsafe if it switches references discontinuously or transfers control without resetting estimator and integrator states.

Behavior trees organize task logic through a rooted tree that is evaluated, or “ticked,” repeatedly. Internal control-flow nodes implement sequences, fallbacks, and parallel combinations. Leaf nodes evaluate conditions or execute actions. Every node returns one of the three statuses Success, Failure, or Running to its parent. A sequence ticks its children until one returns Running or Failure. A fallback ticks its children until one returns Running or Success. Because a subtree exposes a small status interface, it can be reused across tasks, and repeated evaluation supports reactive switching (ColledanchiseOgren2018; IovinoEtAl2022). Behavior trees do not themselves solve planning or control. A leaf labeled grasp object still requires perception, control, and recovery logic, and apparent modularity can conceal resource conflicts between branches. The choice between the representations should follow execution semantics. FSMs suit a small number of modes with well-defined transitions and admit formal verification, whereas behavior trees favor hierarchical composition and reusable recovery strategies, with an independent monitor retaining override authority for safety-related functions. Task-level switching also interacts with continuous control. Stability of each mode does not imply stability under arbitrary switching. Common and multiple Lyapunov functions, dwell-time conditions, guards, and reset maps address different classes of switched and hybrid systems (Liberzon2003), and the task executive and the low-level controller must share explicit entry, exit, and state-transfer rules.

Coordinating Reactive and Deliberative Systems

Reactive control maps current observations directly to actions, with little or no explicit look-ahead, whereas deliberative control constructs and evaluates possible futures. Neither is sufficient alone. Pure deliberation becomes slow or brittle once its world model is stale. Pure reaction may cycle, become trapped, or sacrifice a long-term goal. Layered architectures therefore emerged to combine the two (Brooks1986; Gat1998). A useful architecture separates time scales while preserving channels for intervention. Its layers range from actuator limits, balance, and contact stability through short-horizon motion generation and skill selection to mission-level reasoning over goals and resources. Each layer has a characteristic update rate, abstraction, authority, and failure response. Higher layers parameterize lower layers, and lower layers report feasibility, progress, and exceptions rather than merely accepting commands.

Coordination can be expressed through references and invariant sets. A local controller accepts a high-level goal only if it lies within a verified operating envelope, and it modifies or rejects commands that approach limits of balance, collision distance, or actuator temperature, reporting the reason. Learned policies fit naturally into this view. A policy may propose task choices, waypoints, residual torques, or complete actions, and its placement determines the consequences of error, because a high-level proposal can be checked by planning and constrained control whereas an end-to-end torque policy admits little downstream correction. When layers disagree, summing commands can produce an action intended by neither. Priority arbitration, constrained optimization, and supervisory switching provide explicit alternatives, and hysteresis and minimum dwell times prevent chattering. The resulting system is a hierarchy of closed loops rather than a linear pipeline. Each layer monitors variables appropriate to its horizon and receives feedback from below and from the environment, and autonomy arises when these loops maintain short-term viability while advancing long-term objectives.

2.2.4 Stability and Robustness Theory

Feedback enables a controller to respond to deviations from a reference, while stability and robustness analysis establishes the closed-loop guarantees under specified conditions. This subsection reviews Lyapunov methods, barrier functions, and robust and adaptive control as formal tools for making such guarantees explicit.

Lyapunov Stability

The stability of a closed-loop system depends on the specified equilibrium, trajectory, set, or orbit. For an equilibrium $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ , Lyapunov stability requires that trajectories starting sufficiently close remain close, asymptotic stability additionally requires convergence, and exponential stability specifies a convergence-rate bound (khalil2002nonlinear). These statements are not interchangeable, and a local certificate asserts nothing about initial conditions outside its certified region of attraction. Lyapunov’s direct method establishes stability without solving the differential equation. Let $f$ be locally Lipschitz on a neighborhood $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{Lyap}}$ of the equilibrium, with $f(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{0}$ . If a continuously differentiable function $V:\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{Lyap}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ , called a Lyapunov function candidate and distinct from the terminal cost $V_{\mathrm{f}}$ used in model predictive control above, satisfies

 $V(\mathbf{0})=0,\qquad V(\mathbf{x})>0,\qquad\dot{V}(\mathbf{x})=\nabla V(\mathbf{x})^{\top}f(\mathbf{x})<0,\quad\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{Lyap}}\setminus\{\mathbf{0}\},$ 

(2.25)

then the equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable. If these conditions hold on all of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $V$ is proper and radially unbounded, the equilibrium is globally asymptotically stable. If $\dot{V}$ is only negative semidefinite, stability follows, but asymptotic convergence requires additional reasoning such as LaSalle’s invariance principle (khalil2002nonlinear). Every stability claim should be paired with its domain, assumptions, and convergence notion.

For control-affine dynamics $\dot{\mathbf{x}}=f(\mathbf{x})+g_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}$ , a control Lyapunov function identifies inputs that render the derivative sufficiently negative and can be imposed as a constraint in an online optimization that remains close to a nominal command. This construction bridges nonlinear control and learning. A neural network may propose a command that a model-based filter modifies when the constraint would otherwise be violated. Claims that a learned certificate renders a neural controller unconditionally stable are nevertheless too broad. The positivity and decrease conditions must hold over a stated domain, not merely on sampled training points, and verification may require analytic bounds, interval methods, mixed-integer formulations, sum-of-squares relaxations, or reachability analysis. Neural representation changes the parameterization of the candidate, not the logical requirements of the theorem.

Stability also differs from safety. An asymptotically stable robot may pass through an obstacle on its way to the goal. Safety is commonly formulated as forward invariance of a set $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{safe}}=\{\mathbf{x}:h_{\mathrm{safe}}(\mathbf{x})\geq 0\}$ . For a differentiable relative-degree-one constraint and control-affine dynamics, a zeroing control barrier function requires an admissible input $\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{U}$ satisfying

 $L_{f}h_{\mathrm{safe}}(\mathbf{x})+L_{g_{\mathrm{in}}}h_{\mathrm{safe}}(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}+\alpha_{\mathrm{safe}}(h_{\mathrm{safe}}(\mathbf{x}))\geq 0,$ 

(2.26)

where $L_{f}h_{\mathrm{safe}}=\nabla h_{\mathrm{safe}}^{\top}f$ , $L_{g_{\mathrm{in}}}h_{\mathrm{safe}}=\nabla h_{\mathrm{safe}}^{\top}g_{\mathrm{in}}$ , and $\alpha_{\mathrm{safe}}$ is a locally Lipschitz extended class- $\mathcal{K}$ function. If a well-posed feedback law selects such an input and the regularity assumptions of the barrier theorem hold, trajectories starting in $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{safe}}$ remain in $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{safe}}$ (Ames et al., 2017). Feasibility can fail under input limits or conflicting barriers, so the inequality is not an unconditional safety guarantee. Lyapunov and barrier constraints can be combined in a quadratic program, with safety taking priority over convergence when relaxation is necessary. Formal claims must finally encompass computation and implementation. A continuous-time proof may not survive slow sampling, solver timeout, communication delay, or state-estimation error. A credible assurance case therefore connects the theorem to timing tests, uncertainty bounds, fault handling, and a validated operating domain, with formal analysis and empirical stress testing supporting one another.

Robust Control

Robust control studies whether stability and performance persist across a specified family of plants and disturbances. The uncertainty set is the central object. It may represent bounded parameter variation, neglected high-frequency dynamics, or uncertain contact stiffness, and no controller is robust to unspecified uncertainty of arbitrary magnitude. A common objective bounds the induced gain from a disturbance $\mathbf{w}$ to a performance output $\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{perf}}$ . In $H_{\infty}$ control, the closed-loop transfer matrix $\mathbf{T}_{zw}$ from the disturbance $\mathbf{w}$ to the performance output $\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{perf}}$ is designed so that

 $\lVert\mathbf{T}_{zw}\rVert_{\infty}=\sup_{\omega\in\mathbb{R}}\bar{\sigma}\!\left(\mathbf{T}_{zw}(\mathrm{j}\omega)\right)<\gamma_{\mathrm{gain}},$ 

(2.27)

where $\bar{\sigma}$ denotes maximum singular value. For a stable proper linear time-invariant interconnection with zero initial condition, this is the induced $L_{2}$ -gain bound $\lVert\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{perf}}\rVert_{2}<\gamma_{\mathrm{gain}}\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_{2}$ for nonzero $\mathbf{w}\in L_{2}$ . Weighting functions specify which signals and frequency ranges matter, and $\gamma_{\mathrm{gain}}$ is a certified performance bound for the chosen interconnection, not a probability of success in an arbitrary environment (ZhouDoyleGlover1996).

Frequency-domain concepts clarify why high nominal performance can erode tolerance to uncertainty. Gain and phase margins describe only particular scalar perturbations in a single loop, singular values generalize sensitivity analysis to multivariable systems, and structured singular-value methods distinguish repeated, real, complex, and dynamic uncertainties. Finer uncertainty models reduce conservatism but demand stronger plant knowledge. The guarantee covers only the uncertainty that analysis has identified and bounded. Robust performance also trades against nominal agility, and excessive conservatism is itself hazardous when a vehicle cannot maneuver quickly enough to avoid a collision. Learning reduces model error but introduces new uncertainty. A residual dynamics model may improve tracking in familiar conditions while extrapolating poorly after a payload or surface change. A practical pattern lets the learned component improve performance inside a confidence region while a robust backup or safety filter limits consequences outside it, preserving the separation between empirical performance and a separately justified safety mechanism (Brunke2022).

Adaptive Control

Adaptive control changes controller parameters online in response to observed behavior (Åström and Wittenmark, 1995). It is useful when the dynamics vary beyond what fixed gains can tolerate, as when a manipulator grasps an unknown payload or tire forces change with road conditions. A canonical analysis considers dynamics linearly parameterized by an unknown constant vector $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ . The controller maintains an estimate $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ , updated from tracking errors and measured regressors. The control and update laws are designed together so that a Lyapunov argument establishes boundedness and, under stated assumptions, tracking convergence. This structure is more specific than unconstrained online learning, because the form of uncertainty, the update signal, and the stability objective are stated in advance (Åström and Wittenmark, 1995). Gain scheduling selects among precomputed controllers, direct adaptive control updates controller parameters, and indirect adaptive control estimates plant parameters and redesigns the controller. Guarantees proved for constant $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ do not transfer unchanged to time-varying parameters, where bounded rates of variation yield ultimate bounds rather than exact asymptotic convergence.

Accurate tracking does not imply parameter convergence. For a regressor $\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\mathrm{PE}}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{reg}}}$ , a standard persistent-excitation condition requires constants $T_{0}>0$ and $\mu_{\mathrm{PE}}>0$ such that

 $\int_{t}^{t+T_{0}}\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\mathrm{PE}}(\tau)\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\mathrm{PE}}(\tau)^{\top}\,\mathrm{d}\tau\succeq\mu_{\mathrm{PE}}\mathbf{I}_{d_{\mathrm{reg}}}\qquad\text{for all }t\geq 0.$ 

(2.28)

Under the assumptions of a given adaptive law, such excitation supports convergence because the data distinguish all parameter directions. A robot holding a constant pose may regulate successfully while learning almost nothing about inertial coupling, whereas deliberate excitation improves identification but may conflict with task performance, comfort, or safety. Actions in adaptive control therefore influence both immediate regulation and future knowledge (Bar-Shalom and Tse, 1974).

Classical adaptive laws can drift when disturbances, unmodeled dynamics, or sensor bias violate their assumptions. Projection operators confine estimates to plausible bounds, dead zones prevent adaptation to noise-dominated errors, and leakage or $\sigma$ -modification discourages unbounded parameter growth, typically replacing exact asymptotic tracking with uniform ultimate boundedness. Modern learned adaptation extends beyond low-dimensional parameter estimation to latent-context identification, dynamics-model updating, and policy adaptation, but stability does not follow from low prediction loss alone. A conservative architecture confines adaptation to a nominal model or policy inside an envelope maintained by independent constraints, monitoring, and fallback behavior. Stability, robustness, adaptation, and safety answer distinct questions about what trajectories do, whether that behavior persists over a bounded uncertainty set, how the controller changes as information is acquired, and whether forbidden states are avoided. Dependable autonomy requires an explicit argument for each property, and it requires every feedback loop to declare what it regulates, what uncertainty it tolerates, and where its guarantees end.

## 2.3 Embodied Cognition and the Development of Intelligence

Embodied cognition examines how intelligence depends on the interaction between an agent’s body and its environment. Perception and action shape one another, and concepts gain meaning through sensory and motor experience. For Physical AI, this view calls for models and representations that are developed and tested through physical interaction.

2.3.1 Core Claims of Embodied Cognition

Embodied cognition is not a single theory but a family of claims about the unit of analysis for intelligence. Classical accounts often separate sensing, internal reasoning, and actuation. Embodied accounts emphasize that perception depends on possible movement, bodily dynamics change the control problem, and action alters the observations available next. Embodied, embedded, enactive, and extended cognition make distinct claims about bodily realization, real-time environmental dependence, autonomous sense-making, and the possible inclusion of external resources in a cognitive system (wilson2002sixviews; clark1997beingthere; varela1991embodied; clark1998extended). For Physical AI, the common methodological lesson is to analyze the coupled agent-body-environment system. Merely attaching sensors and actuators is not enough. The body and interaction history must materially organize the capability being explained.

Gibson’s ecological approach shifts perception from recovering detached object properties to detecting information relevant to an acting organism (gibson1979ecological). Its central concept, the affordance, is relational rather than a fixed label. The same ledge may afford stepping, climbing, or no safe action for bodies with different abilities (chemero2003affordances). An affordance-centered robot must therefore ask not only “What is this?” but also “What can this body do here under its current kinematic, dynamic, and safety constraints?” Sensorimotor theories complement this view by treating perception as mastery of action-dependent sensory regularities (oregan2001sensorimotor). Camera motion can reveal depth, wrist rotation can disambiguate shape, and tactile exploration can reveal compliance. Brooks’s situated robotics work in 1991 and subsequent dynamical analyses show how robust behavior can arise from such tight real-time coupling without an exhaustive central reconstruction (brooks1991intelligence; beer2000dynamical). These results challenge mandatory complete world models, but they do not show that long-horizon planning or reasoning about absent events can dispense with internal state.

Intelligence also requires the ability to combine learned concepts and apply them to new situations (fodor1988connectionism). However, these concepts must be connected to real-world experience. Harnad’s symbol-grounding problem highlights that symbols cannot obtain meaning only from relations to other symbols (harnad1990symbol). Barsalou’s perceptual-symbol theory suggests that concepts are grounded in perceptual and motor experiences (barsalou1999perceptual; barsalou2008grounded). For example, the concept of “heavy” can be associated with the effort required to lift an object and the adjustments needed to maintain a stable grip. Thus, intelligent systems need representations that support reasoning and generalization while remaining connected to perception and action.

A robot’s physical structure can simplify certain movements, while interaction with the environment provides information that helps it make better decisions (PfeiferBongard2006; wilson2013embodied). Rather than replacing internal models, physical interaction can complement them by providing feedback and helping robots adapt their behavior. This raises the question of how robots acquire and improve their knowledge and skills through repeated interactions with the physical world.

2.3.2 Perception-Action Coupling and Development

Action does more than follow perception. It can also improve perception. Action can help to select viewpoints, create contacts, and determine which perceptual signals may covary. Bajcsy (1988) formalizes active perception by proposing that sensing strategies be chosen jointly with task goals. Held and Hein’s 1963 yoked-control experiment further distinguishes receiving visual stimulation from causing it, supporting a developmental role for action-contingent experience under its controlled conditions (held1963movement). In robotics, an observation paired with the agent’s command, proprioception, and resulting state transition contains information absent from passive video. New motor skills also create developmental cascades. Reaching, locomotion, and tool use change what can be observed and manipulated, thereby changing the data distribution for later learning (Adolph and Hoch, 2019).

One aspect of development is learning sensorimotor coordinates and a body schema. Hand-eye coordination requires image displacement, head pose, arm configuration, joint motion, and contact to become mutually predictive. metta1999reaching show that an artificial system can refine a visuomotor reaching map through experience without a fully specified prior kinematic calibration. Body-schema research generalizes this result to revisable relations among commands, configurations, contacts, and sensory consequences (hoffmann2010bodyschema). The exploration policy matters. Uniform motor babbling may oversample redundant regions, whereas goal babbling selects desired outcomes and learns the inverse mapping needed to reach them (rolf2010goalbabbling). Internal models and sensorimotor coupling are therefore complementary. A model compactly predicts bodily contingencies, while intervention and feedback recalibrate it after tool use, wear, damage, or payload change.

The morphology of the physical body can also serve as a dynamical prior for learning and control. Morphological computation describes how geometry, inertia, and compliance reduce or transform what a controller must compute (paul2006morphological). McGeer’s passive walkers generate gait structure from gravity and mechanics under restricted conditions, and minimally actuated descendants in later work extend the principle to level-ground walking (mcgeer1990; collins2005efficient). Compliant bodies can likewise absorb impacts and provide fading-memory dynamics, although formal results apply only under specific assumptions (hauser2011morphological). These examples show how a task-matched body supplies a dynamical prior that learning can exploit. The gain is also task-specific, so morphology and learned control must be co-designed rather than treated as alternatives.

Lastly, self-generated experience creates a final selection problem concerning what the agent should practice next. Early curiosity systems reward expected improvement of a predictive model, while learning-progress methods direct attention toward activities that are neither mastered nor irreducibly unpredictable (schmidhuber1991curious; oudeyer2007intrinsic). Deep curiosity methods extend action-conditioned prediction error to high-dimensional observations, but evidence from video games does not resolve physical safety, wear, or stochastic “noisy-TV” effects (pathak2017curiosity). Taken together, active sensing determines what to observe, the body determines how action unfolds, body schemas relate commands to consequences, and intrinsic motivation allocates practice. These mechanisms explain how a learning trajectory can become structured. Developmental robotics asks how they can be integrated across an embodied lifetime.

2.3.3 Developmental Robotics

Developmental robotics studies how robots acquire and reorganize their abilities through experience over time. This subsection examines developmental constraints, lifelong and open-ended learning, imitation, and social interaction as complementary ways to guide that process.

Developmental robotics views intelligence as a gradual learning process rather than a collection of independently designed abilities. Autonomous mental development and cognitive developmental robotics study how robots are used both as constructive tests of developmental hypotheses and as systems that may benefit from developmental constraints (weng2001autonomous; Asada et al., 2001; lungarella2003survey). Development entails more than ordering examples by difficulty. The learner’s body, reachable goals, representations, and social relations can all change. Morphological growth or progressively released degrees of freedom can therefore structure exploration by temporarily reducing the search space (lungarella2002interplay). Infant development is valuable here as a source of mechanisms such as self-calibration, staged constraints, and skill reuse, rather than as a schedule robots must literally reproduce.

Another important research direction is lifelong robot learning, which focuses on how robots continuously learn new tasks while retaining and reusing previously acquired knowledge and skills (thrun1995lifelong; parisi2019continual). Robotics adds active data collection, temporally correlated experience, and simultaneous change in platform and environment, which static-dataset protocols often omit (lesort2020continual). Also, retention is only one component of development. An agent may preserve old task performance without inventing goals, composing skills, or changing its state and action representations. Open-ended learning therefore adds representational redescription and goal discovery (doncieux2018openended). Progress-based goal exploration offers one operational mechanism. Agents generate and order goals according to current learning progress, allowing acquired skills to become stepping stones for more complex behavior (oudeyer2007intrinsic; forestier2022imgep). A developmental architecture must consequently balance plasticity, consolidation, and expansion rather than optimize only final reward.

Additionally, individual exploration is expensive in the high-dimensional spaces of humanoid manipulators. Imitation learning is introduced to reduce this cost by directing attention toward actions another agent has made relevant. Still, it introduces a correspondence problem between different bodies, viewpoints, and intentions (schaal1999imitation). Demonstrations should therefore be treated as priors over goals and action structure, not as trajectories to copy blindly, and embodiment-specific practice remains necessary.

Lastly, social learning also requires shared reference. Constructive models show how saliency and sensorimotor regularities can scaffold joint attention (nagai2003jointattention), while sociable-robot studies show that timing, gaze, and expression shape the feedback humans provide (breazeal2003sociable). Language games with AIBO further demonstrate that social feedback can participate in forming shared perceptual categories and words (steels2001aibo). The resulting relation is reciprocal. Language directs attention and decomposes goals, while action constrains linguistic meaning (cangelosi2010roadmap). Developmental robotics thus integrates autonomous exploration, continual retention, and social scaffolding over one trajectory. In the studies reviewed here, however, these mechanisms are typically demonstrated separately and over short periods. Evaluation should measure skill diversity, retention, compositional reuse, adaptation to bodily change, safety cost, and tutor effort. This social-developmental account also provides the transition to symbols. Language becomes meaningful when shared expressions are connected to the learner’s evolving perceptual and action repertoire.

Figure 2.2: Grounding and multimodal pretraining

2.3.4 Embodied Grounding and Multimodal Pretraining

For robots to operate effectively in the physical world, they need both broad knowledge of the world and the ability to perform physical actions. Multimodal pretraining on images, text, and videos provides useful semantic knowledge and motion priors, but this knowledge alone is not sufficient for reliable robot control (bisk2020experience). Robots also need embodied experience to understand which actions are feasible and what consequences they may produce. Embodied grounding aims to connect these two sources of knowledge, linking what robots perceive and understand to what they can actually do. As illustrated in Figure 2.2, this perspective helps explain the roles of different embodied AI approaches, including vision-language-action (VLA) models, world-action models (WAMs), and multimodal agents.

Multimodal pretraining provides a scalable source of prior knowledge. Early systems explicitly connect speech to visual objects and compositional instructions to executable robot plans (roy2002words; tellex2011commands). At greater scale, CLIP learns broad image-language correspondences, while R3M extracts temporally informative representations from human video for downstream robot learning (radford2021clip; nair2023r3m). Image-text data primarily contribute semantic and referential knowledge. Human video additionally conveys motion patterns and likely object interactions. However, neither directly specifies a particular robot’s reachability, actuation limits, contact dynamics, or action costs. Such data therefore provide valuable semantic and motion priors, rather than sufficient evidence of executable competence.

Embodied experience supplies complementary evidence by connecting an agent’s actions with observed outcomes. Robot demonstrations illustrate how tasks can be accomplished with a particular embodiment, while self-generated interactions reveal feasible actions and their consequences. Work on intuitive physical prediction, robotic poking, and action-conditioned visual foresight exemplifies the transition from observation toward intervention-based learning (battaglia2013simulation; Agrawal et al., 2016; finn2017foresight). Modular systems also make the division between meaning and feasibility explicit. CLIPort combines pretrained visual-language semantics with spatial manipulation, and SayCan evaluates language-model skill proposals using embodiment-specific value functions (shridhar2022cliport; ichter2023saycan). Yet successful skill selection is not equivalent to learning new affordances or revising semantic beliefs after failure. Robust grounding requires both physically informed action and feedback that can improve subsequent decisions.

Recent embodied models increasingly integrate these complementary sources. VLA models learn language-conditioned control, progressing from RT-1 and RT-2 through heterogeneous cross-robot training to systems such as $\pi_{0.5}$ (pi2025pi05), which co-trains on robot actions, web data, and semantic subtasks for open-world generalization. EgoScale further explores human egocentric video as scalable motor supervision (brohan2023rt1; brohan2023rt2; openx2024; pi2025pi05; zheng2026egoscale). WAMs, including DreamZero and Cosmos Policy, extend action learning by predicting future observations alongside actions, potentially supporting consequence-aware planning (wang2026wamsurvey; ye2026dreamzero; kim2026cosmospolicy). General-purpose multimodal agents, as explored in preliminary evaluations of GPT-6 Astra, may instead contribute task-level reasoning, failure diagnosis, and replanning, but are not established substitutes for reliable low-level control (openai2026astra; su2026astra; zhang2026unexpected). These are complementary modeling emphases rather than successive stages. The shared challenge is to turn broad multimodal priors and embodiment-specific experience into reliable, adaptive behavior.

## 2.4 Learning and Reasoning in the Physical World

Physical AI requires more than representing the physical world. A learning-based physical AI agent must learn the underlying regularities of physical processes, reason about possible future states, and acquire effective behaviors through interaction. Unlike learning methods that primarily exploit statistical correlations in static data, Physical AI requires models that respect geometric constraints, dynamical laws, and causal consequences of actions.

Modern approaches therefore combine three complementary principles. Physical knowledge provides inductive biases, machine learning extracts unknown structures from experience, and reinforcement learning enables agents to improve through interaction. Together, these components provide the foundation for learning and reasoning in physical environments.

2.4.1 Physics-Informed Learning Architectures

Physical Inductive Biases

Physical environments contain strong structural regularities, including symmetry, conservation laws, locality, and relational interactions. Incorporating these properties into machine learning models reduces the hypothesis space and improves data efficiency.

A fundamental example is equivariant learning. Physical predictions should transform consistently under changes of coordinate systems. For a transformation $g_{\mathrm{group}}$ from a symmetry group, an equivariant model satisfies

 $f(T_{g_{\mathrm{group}}}(x))=T^{\prime}_{g_{\mathrm{group}}}(f(x)).$ 

(2.29)

For 3D physical systems, SE(3)-equivariant networks preserve rotational and translational consistency and have been widely applied to molecular modeling, geometric reasoning, and robotics (thomas2018tensor; satorras2021e3nn).

Graph Neural Networks for Physical Systems

Many physical environments naturally consist of interacting entities. Particles, objects, robot links, and articulated components can be represented as graphs of the form

 $G=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}),$ 

(2.30)

where nodes describe physical entities and edges represent interactions.

Graph neural networks learn system evolution through message passing of the form

 $\mathbf{h}_{i}^{\mathrm{node},t+1}=\phi_{\mathrm{node}}\left(\mathbf{h}_{i}^{\mathrm{node},t},\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)}\psi_{\mathrm{msg}}(\mathbf{h}_{i}^{\mathrm{node},t},\mathbf{h}_{j}^{\mathrm{node},t},\mathbf{e}_{ij}^{\mathrm{edge}})\right),$ 

(2.31)

where $\mathbf{h}_{i}^{\mathrm{node},t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{node}}}$ is a node-feature vector and $\mathbf{e}_{ij}^{\mathrm{edge}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{edge}}}$ is an edge-feature vector. The message function is $\psi_{\mathrm{msg}}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{node}}}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{node}}}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{edge}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{msg}}}$ , and the update function is $\phi_{\mathrm{node}}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{node}}}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{msg}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{node}}}$ . The positive integer dimensions $d_{\mathrm{node}}$ , $d_{\mathrm{edge}}$ , and $d_{\mathrm{msg}}$ need not be equal.

This representation preserves relational structures and enables learning of complex physical dynamics, including particle simulation and object interaction modeling (sanchezgonzalez2020learning).

Physics-Informed Neural Networks

When governing equations are partially known, physical laws can be directly incorporated into the learning objective. Given a differential equation

 $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{PDE}}[u^{\mathrm{field}}](x,t)=0,$ 

(2.32)

a neural approximation $u_{\theta}^{\mathrm{field}}(x,t)$ can be trained by minimizing both data error and physical inconsistency:

 $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{data}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{physics}}.$ 

(2.33)

The physical constraint is enforced through

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{physics}}=\sum_{i}\|\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{PDE}}[u_{\theta}^{\mathrm{field}}](x_{i},t_{i})\|^{2}.$ 

(2.34)

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a framework for combining sparse observations with known physical principles and have been widely used for solving and learning differential equations (raissi2019physics).

Neural Differential Equations

Instead of manually specifying analytical dynamics, neural differential equations use neural networks to parameterize continuous-time evolution as

 $\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}}{\mathrm{d}t}=\mathbf{f}_{\theta}^{\mathrm{drift}}(\mathbf{x},t).$ 

(2.35)

Neural ordinary differential equations (Neural ODEs) provide a flexible framework for learning continuous latent dynamics (chen2018neural). Stochastic extensions further model uncertainty through

 $\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{t}=\mathbf{f}_{\theta}^{\mathrm{drift}}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)\,\mathrm{d}t+\mathbf{G}_{\theta}^{\mathrm{diff}}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{W}_{t}^{\mathrm{Wiener}},$ 

(2.36)

where $\mathbf{x}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{state}}}$ is the state and $\mathbf{W}_{t}^{\mathrm{Wiener}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{noise}}}$ is a standard Wiener process. For the deterministic and stochastic dynamics above, $\mathbf{f}_{\theta}^{\mathrm{drift}}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{state}}}\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{state}}}$ is the drift mapping. The diffusion mapping is $\mathbf{G}_{\theta}^{\mathrm{diff}}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{state}}}\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{state}}\times d_{\mathrm{noise}}}$ . The positive integers $d_{\mathrm{state}}$ and $d_{\mathrm{noise}}$ need not be equal, and $\mathrm{d}\mathbf{W}_{t}^{\mathrm{Wiener}}$ denotes the Wiener increment.

These approaches bridge classical dynamical systems and modern representation learning by allowing models to learn unknown physical processes while preserving temporal structure.

2.4.2 Reinforcement Learning for Physical Interaction

Markov Decision Processes and Physical Interaction

Learning Physical AI requires not only predicting the world but also selecting actions that influence future states. Reinforcement learning formulates this process as sequential decision-making.

A Markov decision process (MDP) is defined as

 $(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P^{\mathrm{tr}},R,\gamma),$ 

(2.37)

where $\mathcal{S}$ represents states, $\mathcal{A}$ represents actions, $P^{\mathrm{tr}}$ represents transition dynamics, and $R$ represents rewards.

The goal of an agent is to learn a policy

 $\pi(a|s)$ 

(2.38)

that maximizes cumulative reward:

 $J(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\sum_{t}\gamma^{t}r_{t}].$ 

(2.39)

However, physical agents rarely observe complete states. A robot may observe an object’s appearance and motion without directly knowing its mass, friction coefficient, or contact condition. Sensor noise, occlusion, and delayed measurements further limit the information available for decision-making.

A partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) extends the MDP with an observation space $\mathcal{O}$ and an observation model:

 $(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P^{\mathrm{tr}},R,\mathcal{O},O,\gamma),$ 

(2.40)

where $O(o_{t+1}\mid s_{t+1},a_{t})$ specifies the probability of receiving observation $o_{t+1}$ after action $a_{t}$ leads to state $s_{t+1}$ , and $\gamma\in[0,1)$ is the discount factor. The physical state remains Markovian, but an individual observation need not contain enough information to predict future outcomes.

Decisions therefore depend on both past observations and past actions:

 $h_{t}=(o_{0},a_{0},o_{1},\ldots,a_{t-1},o_{t}),\qquad h_{0}=(o_{0}),\qquad\pi(a_{t}\mid h_{t}).$ 

(2.41)

Past actions matter because they help explain subsequent measurements. A change in an object’s position may result from the robot’s own push or from an external disturbance.

The history can be summarized by a belief state

 $b_{t}(s)=P(s_{t}=s\mid h_{t}),$ 

(2.42)

which represents uncertainty about the current physical state. With a known transition and observation model, the belief is a sufficient statistic of the history for decision-making, allowing a policy to be written as $\pi(a_{t}\mid b_{t})$ . Belief updates combine predictions from the previous action with evidence from new observations.

Practical systems may approximate this inference using state estimators, recurrent networks, or policies conditioned on a recent interaction history. For example, lifting an object provides force measurements that help infer its weight and guide subsequent control. POMDPs thus make explicit how uncertain perception, memory, and action jointly shape physical decision-making (sutton2018reinforcement).

Reward Design and Task Specification

The reward function defines the objective of an embodied agent. Designing appropriate rewards is challenging because physical tasks often involve long horizons and complex constraints.

Sparse rewards provide feedback at infrequent events, such as successful grasping or completion of a navigation task. Although simple, they create exploration difficulties.

Dense rewards introduce intermediate objectives, such as distance reduction, energy efficiency, or trajectory smoothness. However, poorly designed dense rewards may lead to unintended behaviors.

Curriculum learning gradually increases task complexity and allows agents to acquire complex physical skills from simpler subtasks.

Policy Optimization

Policy-gradient methods improve a parameterized policy using the outcomes of its actions. With the history-conditioned policy introduced above, a trajectory-based expression is

 $\nabla_{\theta}J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{\mathrm{ep}}\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})A^{\mathrm{adv},\pi_{\theta}}(h_{t},a_{t})\right],$ 

(2.43)

where $\tau_{\mathrm{ep}}$ is a sampled interaction trajectory and $A^{\mathrm{adv},\pi_{\theta}}(h_{t},a_{t})=Q^{\pi_{\theta}}(h_{t},a_{t})-V^{\pi_{\theta}}(h_{t})$ is the advantage, defined as the expected return of the selected action relative to the policy’s average return at that history. For fully observed systems, the current state $s_{t}$ can replace $h_{t}$ . Actor-critic methods use a learned value estimator to approximate the advantage while updating the policy.

Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) uses a clipped surrogate objective to limit the incentive for large policy changes:

 $\displaystyle L^{\mathrm{CLIP}}(\theta)$ 
 $\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t}\left[\min\left(\rho_{t}^{\mathrm{PPO}}(\theta)\widehat{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{adv}},\operatorname{clip}\bigl(\rho_{t}^{\mathrm{PPO}}(\theta),1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip}},1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}\bigr)\widehat{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{adv}}\right)\right],$ 

(2.44)

 $\displaystyle\rho_{t}^{\mathrm{PPO}}(\theta)$ 
 $\displaystyle=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})},$ 

where $\theta_{\mathrm{old}}$ denotes the policy parameters used to collect the batch, $\widehat{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{adv}}$ is an estimated advantage, $\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}>0$ controls clipping, and $\mathbb{E}_{t}$ denotes averaging over sampled steps. The symbol $\rho_{t}^{\mathrm{PPO}}$ distinguishes the policy probability ratio from the reward $r_{t}$ . These methods are widely used for locomotion and manipulation (schulman2017ppo). Optimization stability and the physical closed-loop guarantees discussed in Section 2.2 remain separate questions.

Offline Reinforcement Learning

Unlike simulation environments, real physical systems cannot collect unlimited interaction data. Offline reinforcement learning addresses this limitation by learning policies from previously collected datasets, including demonstrations and robot trajectories.

This paradigm is particularly important for Physical AI because large-scale datasets can provide diverse physical experiences without requiring unsafe exploration on real hardware.

2.4.3 Predictive Learning and World Models

This subsection develops the predictive-learning mechanisms underlying the action-consequence relation discussed in Section 2.3. The focus is on constructing internal states, learning how they evolve under actions, and using predicted outcomes for decision-making. The mathematical notion of state and the motivation for latent representations are introduced in Section 2.1.3.

Learning Latent Physical Dynamics

Under partial observability, an observation feature and an internal predictive state serve different purposes. An encoder extracts features from the current measurement, while a state-update model integrates them with past actions and the previous internal state:

 $e_{t}^{\mathrm{enc}}=f_{\theta}(o_{t}),\qquad\mathbf{z}_{t}=H_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t-1},a_{t-1},e_{t}^{\mathrm{enc}}),$ 

(2.45)

where $e_{t}^{\mathrm{enc}}$ denotes an observation feature, $\mathbf{z}_{t}$ an internal state, and $H_{\theta}$ a learned update function. This recurrent form is one way to summarize the interaction history $h_{t}$ used in the POMDP formulation of Section 2.4.2. The internal state should retain task-relevant information about hidden properties and contact conditions. A learned latent vector does not automatically constitute a calibrated belief distribution.

An action-conditioned dynamics model then predicts the next internal state as

 $\mathbf{z}_{t+1}\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{z}_{t},a_{t}),$ 

(2.46)

where $p_{\theta}$ is a learned transition distribution. A deterministic predictor, $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{t+1}=F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},a_{t})$ , is a simplified alternative. Training uses recorded observations, actions, and outcomes to learn useful state updates and transitions. Known physical structure can constrain these models through the architectural and loss-based approaches in Section 2.4.1. Their adequacy depends on preserving the distinctions that affect future outcomes, including uncertainty that remains after observing the interaction history.

Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures

The Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) approach learns representations by predicting target features from context features. I-JEPA predicts representations of masked image regions from visible context (Assran et al., 2023), while V-JEPA extends feature prediction to masked spatiotemporal regions in video (Bardes et al., 2024). A schematic prediction is

 $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{\mathrm{target}}=g_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{context}},m_{\mathrm{target}}),$ 

(2.47)

where $\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{context}}$ represents the visible context, $m_{\mathrm{target}}$ specifies target positions, and $g_{\phi}$ is the predictor. Predictions are matched to features produced by a target encoder. In these implementations, a stop-gradient target and an exponentially averaged target encoder help prevent representation collapse.

Such representations can supply observation features for a predictive world model. Learning from passive images or videos, however, does not by itself identify the effects of executable robot actions. An action-conditioned dynamics model additionally requires experience linking the agent’s commands to resulting changes. This distinction separates predictive representation learning from the action-grounded models needed for physical planning and policy improvement.

World Models, Imagination, and Decision-Making

Given a current internal state, a dynamics model can roll forward candidate actions. For a deterministic model and an action sequence $a_{t:t+H_{\mathrm{roll}}-1}$ of length $H_{\mathrm{roll}}$ , the rollout is

 $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{t}=\mathbf{z}_{t},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{t+i+1}=F_{\theta}(\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{t+i},a_{t+i}),\quad i=0,\ldots,H_{\mathrm{roll}}-1.$ 

(2.48)

A stochastic model instead produces a distribution of possible rollouts. A planner evaluates predicted outcomes against the task objective and constraints, executes a selected action, and updates the internal state from new observations. The receding-horizon control principle is developed in Section 2.2.2.

Model-based reinforcement learning can also use imagined trajectories to improve a policy. Dreamer learns behavior through rollouts in a learned latent world model (hafner2019dreamer), and DayDreamer applies world-model-based learning to physical robots (wu2023daydreamer). Prediction thus supports both selecting actions and learning better action policies. Model errors can accumulate over long rollouts, and a policy may exploit inaccurate predictions, so useful imagination requires validation against observed physical outcomes.

These mechanisms connect state representation, physical priors, and reinforcement learning through prediction of action consequences. Chapter 5 develops world-model architectures, training objectives, uncertainty, and validation in detail. Chapter 6 and Chapter 7 examine their relationship to learned manipulation and motor capabilities.

## Part II Methodology

"The world is its own best model."

— Rodney Brooks

## 3 Perception and Cognition

This chapter dives deeply into perception and cognition. One of the primary differences between normal AI systems and physical AI systems is that physical AI uses perception and cognition to bridge the physical environment with the actual AI system. The key part for that bridge is the multimodal sensing, which brings information about this complex and diverse world into digital form, and produces a compressed representation.

Therefore, the perception and cognition module aims to obtain a coherent and comprehensive understanding of the physical environment from raw sensor observations. This understanding grounds world models in sensory evidence and supports prediction, planning, and action. This chapter traces that pipeline from low-level multimodal sensing and sensor fusion, 3D spatial and four-dimensional (4D) spatiotemporal perception, to high-level semantic and interaction reasoning.

## 3.1 Tasks and Characteristics of Physical Perception

Figure 3.1: Embodied perception from multimodal observations. A complex physical environment is sampled through multiple sensors, producing a compressed and incomplete digital representation. Perception and cognition integrate these observations to infer the environment state relevant to an embodied agent’s task

Perception provides the fundamental interface between the physical world and embodied intelligence. Unlike symbolic or language-based environments, where information is already presented to a model in discrete and machine-readable forms, the physical world does not directly expose its underlying state. It is continuous, high-dimensional, dynamic, and only partially observable. As illustrated in Fig. 3.1, an embodied agent can access this world only through sensors that transform physical signals into digital observations. Before reasoning, prediction, planning, or action can take place, these observations must therefore be organized into representations that a computational model can interpret and use.

This transformation is inherently incomplete. Cameras have finite resolution and fields of view, depth sensors contain missing or uncertain measurements, force and tactile sensors observe only local contacts, and all sensing modalities operate with finite sampling rates and measurement noise. Occlusion further prevents parts of the environment from being observed at a given time. Consequently, the digital observations available to an embodied agent constitute only a partial and compressed representation of the underlying physical world. Perception must infer task-relevant structure from this incomplete evidence rather than assuming direct access to the true physical state.

This distinction makes perception particularly important for Physical AI. Downstream models reason and act on the basis of what has been observed and represented, rather than on the physical world itself. Errors or missing information in perception can therefore propagate to state estimation, prediction, reasoning, planning, and ultimately physical action. A missed obstacle may lead to a collision. An incorrect depth estimate may produce an invalid grasp. An incorrect estimate of object or material state may cause an otherwise reasonable plan to fail. Reliable Physical AI thus depends not only on the capability of downstream models, but also on the accuracy, completeness, consistency, and uncertainty of the perceptual representations on which they operate.

Physical perception addresses this problem by acquiring multimodal observations and progressively transforming them into representations of the environment that are useful for embodied tasks. Beyond recognizing what is present, a physical perception system must determine where entities are, how they move and change over time, what physical and semantic states they are in, and how they can be interacted with. Perception is therefore not merely a preprocessing stage for downstream intelligence, but a continuous process of constructing and updating an internal representation of the physical world.

Physical perception can be broadly organized into three levels. Low-level perception acquires observations through sensory modalities. These include color cameras using red, green, and blue (RGB) channels, together with depth sensors, LiDAR, infrared and event cameras, tactile and force sensors, and proprioception. These modalities capture complementary aspects of appearance, geometry, motion, temperature, contact, and the agent’s own physical state. Mid-level perception organizes these observations into spatially and temporally consistent representations, including 3D geometry, motion, and dynamic 3D/4D scene structure. High-level perception and cognition further associates these representations with semantic entities, physical properties and states, functional relationships, affordances, and interaction possibilities, enabling task-dependent interpretation and reasoning.

Across these levels, physical perception is characterized by multimodality, spatiotemporal consistency, physical grounding, uncertainty, and interaction-oriented understanding. Multimodal observations compensate for the limitations of individual sensors, while spatiotemporal modeling connects partial observations across viewpoints and time. Physical grounding associates semantic interpretation with measurable geometry, state, and physical evidence, and explicit treatment of uncertainty reflects the unavoidable incompleteness of sensing. Interaction-oriented understanding further focuses perception on the information that matters for action, including contact regions, object states, material conditions, and possible state transitions.

These requirements drive physical perception beyond isolated single-modality recognition toward integrated systems that continuously combine multimodal sensing, 3D/4D spatial modeling, semantic understanding, physical measurement, and interaction feedback. From this perspective, perception extends beyond recognition to make the physical world observable, representable, and actionable to an embodied intelligent system.

## 3.2 Multimodal Perception and Fusion

3.2.1 Multimodal Sensing and Data Acquisition

Multimodal sensing and data acquisition refer to the processes by which an embodied system measures the physical state of itself and its environment and converts heterogeneous measurements into digital observations. Perceiving and interacting with a physical environment require information about several complementary properties, including appearance, geometry, motion, temperature, and contact state. No single sensing modality can reliably and completely observe all of these properties. Embodied systems therefore commonly combine RGB cameras, depth cameras, LiDAR, force and tactile sensors, and proprioceptive sensors. Exteroceptive sensors observe the external environment, proprioceptive sensors measure the internal configuration and motion of the robot, and contact sensors characterize physical interaction at the robot-environment interface. Together, these measurements form the observational basis for subsequent perception, state estimation, reasoning, planning, and control. Section 9.2 provides additional details.

RGB Cameras

RGB cameras are the most widely used exteroceptive sensors in embodied intelligence. They measure visible optical radiation and provide dense observations of scene color, texture, boundaries, and appearance. These observations contain rich semantic cues but do not directly encode metric depth or contact state.

To describe how an RGB camera converts incident light into image measurements, this chapter first considers its radiometric image-formation model (healey1994radiometric; bhuyan2019computer; holst2007cmos). During an exposure, each photosite integrates the incident light according to its wavelength-dependent response. For a photosite associated with color channel $i_{\mathrm{rgb}}\in\{\mathrm{R},\mathrm{G},\mathrm{B}\}$ and spatial location $\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{pix}}=(u_{\mathrm{pix}},v_{\mathrm{pix}})$ , the resulting raw measurement can be expressed as

 $y_{i_{\mathrm{rgb}}}^{\mathrm{raw}}(\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{pix}},t)=Q_{i_{\mathrm{rgb}}}^{\mathrm{quant}}\!\left(\int_{t}^{t+\Delta t}\int_{\Lambda_{\mathrm{vis}}}S_{i_{\mathrm{rgb}}}(\lambda)E_{\lambda}(\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{pix}},\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda\,\mathrm{d}\tau+\varepsilon_{i_{\mathrm{rgb}}}(\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{pix}},t)\right),$ 

(3.1)

where $y_{i_{\mathrm{rgb}}}^{\mathrm{raw}}(\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{pix}},t)$ is the raw measurement of an individual photosite, $E_{\lambda}(\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{pix}},\tau)$ denotes the spectral irradiance incident on the sensor, $\Delta t$ is the exposure duration, and $S_{i_{\mathrm{rgb}}}(\lambda)$ is the effective spectral responsivity of channel $i_{\mathrm{rgb}}$ , incorporating wavelength-dependent optical transmission, color-filter response, quantum efficiency, and photoelectric conversion.
