The term $\varepsilon_{i_{\mathrm{rgb}}}(\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{pix}},t)$ represents sensor noise, while $Q_{i_{\mathrm{rgb}}}^{\mathrm{quant}}(\cdot)$ summarizes electronic amplification, analog-to-digital conversion, and quantization. A camera image is therefore an exposure-time integral rather than an instantaneous sample.

The collection of photosite measurements forms a raw mosaic image $Y_{\mathrm{C}}^{\mathrm{raw}}$ , which is subsequently transformed by an image signal processor (ISP) into an RGB image

 $I^{\mathrm{RGB}}=F_{\mathrm{ISP}}\!\left(Y_{\mathrm{C}}^{\mathrm{raw}}\right),$ 

(3.2)

where $I^{\mathrm{RGB}}$ denotes the output RGB image and $F_{\mathrm{ISP}}(\cdot)$ denotes the camera-specific processing pipeline, which may include demosaicing, white balancing, denoising, color correction, tone mapping, gamma encoding, and compression. Consequently, the final RGB values are not generally proportional to scene radiance, and their photometric interpretation depends on both the camera response and the processing pipeline (debevec2023recovering; brooks2019unprocessing).

Complementary to the radiometric model, which describes how pixel values are formed, a geometric image-formation model specifies how 3D scene points are projected onto the two-dimensional (2D) image plane (hartley2003multiple; szeliski2011computer; torralba2024foundations). Under the pinhole camera model, the projection of a point $\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{C}}=(X_{\mathrm{C}},Y_{\mathrm{C}},Z_{\mathrm{C}})^{\top}$ expressed in the camera coordinate frame is represented in homogeneous coordinates as

 $\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathrm{pix}}\propto\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{cam}}\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{C}},\qquad\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathrm{pix}}=(u_{\mathrm{pix}},v_{\mathrm{pix}},1)^{\top},$ 

(3.3)

where $\propto$ denotes equality up to a nonzero scale and $\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{cam}}$ is the camera intrinsic matrix, conventionally written as

 $\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{cam}}=\begin{bmatrix}f_{\mathrm{x}}&\gamma_{\mathrm{cam}}&c_{\mathrm{x}}\\
0&f_{\mathrm{y}}&c_{\mathrm{y}}\\
0&0&1\end{bmatrix},$ 

(3.4)

where $f_{\mathrm{x}}$ and $f_{\mathrm{y}}$ are the effective focal lengths measured in pixels, $(c_{\mathrm{x}},c_{\mathrm{y}})$ is the principal point, and $\gamma_{\mathrm{cam}}$ is the skew parameter between the image axes, which is commonly assumed to be zero in modern digital cameras. The intrinsic matrix maps normalized camera coordinates to pixel coordinates. Lens distortion is modeled separately. Its parameters are estimated during camera calibration and subsequently used to undistort or rectify the captured images (zhang2000flexible).

Within embodied systems, RGB cameras are commonly mounted on the head or torso to provide egocentric observations, on the wrist or end effector to capture close-range interactions, or in the environment to provide a global view of the robot and workspace. These visual streams constitute a primary source of exteroceptive information for semantic scene understanding, object localization, visual navigation, and visuomotor control. Visual navigation models such as ViNT use camera observations to learn navigational affordances under a general goal-reaching objective (shah2023vint), while large-scale manipulation datasets and policies increasingly combine synchronized multi-view imagery with language and proprioceptive state. DROID, for example, records three synchronized stereo RGB camera streams, together with robot states and actions, exterior-camera calibration, and natural-language instructions across 86 manipulation tasks (khazatsky2024droid). Generalist VLA models such as $\pi_{0}$ and $\pi_{0.5}$ similarly combine camera observations with language instructions and robot state to generate actions across diverse tasks and robot embodiments (black2024pi0; pi2025pi05). Despite their low cost and semantic richness, RGB cameras do not directly measure metric geometry or physical contact, and their reliability remains sensitive to illumination changes, saturation, specular reflections, motion blur, and occlusion.

Depth Cameras and LiDAR

Depth cameras and LiDAR provide metric observations of scene geometry, but their measurement principles and sampling patterns are not determined by the device category alone. Some depth cameras employ stereo triangulation, whereas others use time-of-flight principles closely related to LiDAR. A useful distinction is therefore made between axial depth $Z_{\mathrm{depth}}$ , defined as the coordinate of a scene point along the camera optical axis, and ray range $r$ , defined as the Euclidean distance from the sensing origin along a viewing or emission ray. The systems considered here are organized by how distance is inferred, distinguishing triangulation-based depth sensing from propagation-based optical ranging.

Triangulation-based systems infer depth from correspondences between calibrated rays originating from spatially separated camera or projector centers. For a rectified stereo pair with baseline $B_{\mathrm{stereo}}$ , common horizontal focal length $f_{\mathrm{x}}$ , and aligned principal points, the horizontal disparity $d_{\mathrm{stereo}}(\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{pix}})=u_{\mathrm{pix},\mathrm{L}}-u_{\mathrm{pix},\mathrm{R}}$ determines the axial depth. The resulting depth can then be back-projected into the reference-camera coordinate frame using

 $\displaystyle Z_{\mathrm{depth}}(\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{pix}})$ 
 $\displaystyle=\frac{f_{\mathrm{x}}B_{\mathrm{stereo}}}{d_{\mathrm{stereo}}(\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{pix}})},$ 

(3.5)

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{C}}(\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{pix}})$ 
 $\displaystyle=Z_{\mathrm{depth}}(\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{pix}})\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{cam}}^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathrm{pix}},$ 

where $f_{\mathrm{x}}$ and $d_{\mathrm{stereo}}(\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{pix}})$ are expressed in pixels, $\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{cam}}$ is the intrinsic matrix of the reference camera, and $\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathrm{pix}}=(u_{\mathrm{pix}},v_{\mathrm{pix}},1)^{\top}$ is the homogeneous image coordinate (hartley2003multiple). The second relation assumes that the depth image stores axial depth rather than distance along the viewing ray. Passive stereo relies on naturally occurring scene texture to establish correspondence. Active-stereo systems retain the same binocular geometry but project an unstructured infrared pattern to add texture in weakly textured regions. The pattern assists left-right image matching and need not be decoded into projector coordinates. The Intel RealSense D400 series is a representative example (keselman2017intel). Structured-light systems also recover depth by triangulation, but use a calibrated camera-projector pair and establish correspondences between observed image locations and encoded projector coordinates (zanuttigh2016time). Thus, although active stereo and structured light employ active illumination, both remain triangulation-based because depth is inferred from spatial correspondence rather than optical propagation time.

Propagation-based sensors emit optical signals and infer distance from temporal or phase properties of the returned signal rather than from spatial disparity. For a pulsed time-of-flight LiDAR, the measured round-trip propagation delay $\Delta t_{i}$ determines the range of the $i$ th return. Combining this range with the calibrated beam direction gives its three-dimensional position as

 $\displaystyle r_{i}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\frac{c_{\mathrm{light}}\,\Delta t_{i}}{2},$ 

(3.6)

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{p}_{i}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\mathbf{o}+r_{i}\mathbf{d}_{i},$ 

where $c_{\mathrm{light}}$ is the speed of light, $\mathbf{o}$ is the sensing origin, and $\mathbf{d}_{i}$ is a unit vector specifying the calibrated beam direction (royo2019overview). A return may additionally include a measure of return strength or intensity $a_{i}^{\mathrm{lidar}}$ and an acquisition timestamp $t_{i}$ . Per-return timing is important for compensating motion distortion, or deskewing, when a scanning LiDAR assembles a point cloud over a nonzero time interval. Time-of-flight depth cameras apply a related propagation-based principle at many pixels over a two-dimensional detector array. Depending on the sensor design, they estimate distance from the direct time of flight of optical pulses or from the phase shift of modulated illumination (horaud2016overview). The stored value may represent ray range or may be converted into axial depth according to the sensor’s calibration and output convention.

The native measurements of these sensors induce different spatial structures. A camera depth image can be back-projected into an organized point cloud whose samples preserve the image lattice, whereas LiDAR measurements generally form an irregular, sparse point cloud indexed by beam direction and acquisition time. After calibration and coordinate transformation, either representation may be converted into voxels, signed-distance fields, or continuous neural implicit fields for downstream perception and planning.

In embodied systems, depth observations are particularly useful for close-range geometry, including object-pose estimation, grasping, and workspace reconstruction. PerAct, RVT, and Act3D, for example, demonstrate how calibrated RGB and depth (RGB-D) observations can be transformed into volumetric, multi-view, or continuous three-dimensional representations for robotic manipulation (shridhar2023perceiver; goyal2023rvt; gervet2023act3d). LiDAR is more commonly employed on mobile and field robots, where its typically longer sensing range and direct metric measurements support localization, mapping, obstacle avoidance, and exploration. CERBERUS provides a representative example in subterranean environments (tranzatto2022cerberus). These modalities nevertheless exhibit different failure modes. Passive stereo correspondence becomes unreliable in textureless, repetitive, or occluded regions. Active stereo and structured light reduce texture ambiguity but remain limited by projector range, strong ambient illumination, interference, and transparent or specular surfaces. Propagation-based ranging can likewise be degraded by low-return surfaces, strong ambient illumination, multipath interference, and adverse atmospheric conditions.

Force and Tactile Sensors

Force and tactile sensors provide measurements of physical interaction that cannot be obtained directly from conventional vision. Force and torque sensors measure the resultant loads transmitted through a robot component, whereas tactile sensors measure local contact conditions over a sensing surface. This distinction concerns the spatial support and physical interpretation of the measurements rather than the transduction material alone. Resistive, capacitive, piezoelectric, optical, and magnetic mechanisms may be used in different sensor configurations.

A multi-axis force/torque sensor measures the resultant force and moment acting on a robot component, commonly at the wrist, ankle, or end effector. A six-axis sensor reports the wrench, expressed in a declared sensor coordinate frame, as

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{S}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=[\,\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{S}}^{\top},\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{S}}^{\top}\,]^{\top},$ 

(3.7)

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{S}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{cal}}(\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{sens}}-\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{sens},0}),$ 

where $\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{S}}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{S}}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ are the measured force and torque, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{sens}}$ denotes the raw electrical outputs, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{sens},0}$ is the zero-load offset, and $\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{cal}}$ is a calibration and decoupling matrix. The second relation is a common linear approximation for strain-based sensors, which infer applied loads from the deformation of an elastic structure (cao2021six). Such sensors provide accurate aggregate interaction loads but do not resolve how those loads are distributed across multiple contact points. Joint-torque sensors and motor currents can also support external-force estimation through a robot dynamics model, but these indirect estimates should not be treated as equivalent to a directly measured endpoint wrench.

Tactile sensors measure contact locally at the robot surface. Their outputs may describe contact location, surface deformation, normal and tangential loading, or slip. According to their dominant sensing and readout mechanisms, tactile sensors commonly used in embodied systems can be broadly organized into vision-based tactile sensors and taxel-based tactile arrays.

Vision-based tactile sensors illuminate a compliant elastomer and use an internal camera to observe its deformation during contact. Their native digital observation is an image rather than a direct force measurement:

 $I_{\mathrm{tac}}(\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{pix}},t)=\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{opt}}\!\left(\boldsymbol{\delta}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{pos}},t);\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{tac}}\right)+\varepsilon_{I}(\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{pix}},t),\qquad\widehat{\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{tac}}}_{t}=G_{\mathrm{tac}}\!\left(I_{\mathrm{tac}}\right),$ 

(3.8)

where $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ denotes the elastomer deformation, $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{opt}}$ summarizes the illumination and imaging process with sensor parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{tac}}$ , and $G_{\mathrm{tac}}(\cdot)$ is a calibrated or learned estimator of contact quantities $\widehat{\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{tac}}}_{t}$ , such as contact geometry, force, shear, or slip. The GelSight study establishes high-resolution optical measurement of contact geometry and force-related deformation (yuan2017gelsight), while the DIGIT study demonstrates a compact, lower-cost design suitable for robotic hands (lambeta2020digit). Because their output is image-like, these sensors also support visual representation learning. Sparsh, for example, learns transferable representations from unlabeled tactile images (higuera2024sparsh).

Taxel-based sensors use arrays of discrete tactile elements distributed over a compliant surface. A pressure-sensitive taxel primarily measures normal contact stress, whereas more general taxels may also respond to tangential stress or local deformation. For taxel $i$ with sensitive region $\mathcal{A}_{i}$ and area $A_{i}=\int_{\mathcal{A}_{i}}\mathrm{d}A$ , a generic calibrated measurement model is

 $\displaystyle\overline{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{i}(t)$ 
 $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{A_{i}}\int_{\mathcal{A}_{i}}\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{pos}},t)\,\mathrm{d}A,$ 

(3.9)

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{y}_{i}(t)$ 
 $\displaystyle=g_{i}^{\mathrm{taxel}}\!\left(\overline{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{i}(t),T_{\mathrm{temp}}(t)\right)+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{i}(t),$ 

where $\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\mathrm{c}}=[p_{\mathrm{press}},s_{1}^{\mathrm{shear}},s_{2}^{\mathrm{shear}}]^{\top}$ contains normal pressure $p_{\mathrm{press}}$ and two tangential stress components, and $g_{i}^{\mathrm{taxel}}(\cdot)$ represents the sensor-specific transduction and calibration. Resistive, piezoresistive, and capacitive arrays are widely used for compact quasi-static contact sensing. Piezoelectric elements are particularly responsive to changes in load and vibration. Magnetic or inductive designs can provide compliant multi-axis measurements. These mechanisms differ in sensitivity, bandwidth, hysteresis, drift, wiring complexity, and spatial resolution (dahiya2009tactile; meribout2024tactile).

Some specialized tactile devices additionally measure vibration, acoustic emission, or temperature. High-bandwidth vibration and acoustic signals can reveal impact, sliding, texture, and incipient slip, while thermal measurements can contribute to material recognition. These signals are less commonly used as standalone tactile modalities in embodied systems and are often incorporated as complementary channels in multimodal tactile sensors.

The appropriate sensor depends on the spatial scale and information required by the task. Six-axis force/torque sensors are mature choices for aggregate load feedback in compliant control, insertion, assembly, and human-robot interaction. Vision-based tactile sensors are particularly attractive in current robot-learning research because they provide dense contact geometry and can be processed with image-based models, whereas electrical or magnetic taxel arrays can be integrated into compact fingertips, finger links, palms, and larger-area robotic skin. Force and tactile measurements support contact detection, grasp stabilization, slip detection, texture recognition, object reorientation, and dexterous manipulation. RH20T illustrates their role in multimodal robot learning by recording force together with visual, audio, robot-state, action, and language information across diverse manipulation skills (fang2024rh20t).

These sensing families also have distinct limitations. Force/torque sensors do not localize individual contacts without additional geometric assumptions. Taxel arrays may exhibit hysteresis, drift, cross-talk, and limited spatial resolution. Vision-based tactile sensors are sensitive to illumination and camera-calibration errors, as well as elastomer wear and viscoelastic effects such as hysteresis and stress relaxation. Their physical estimates additionally depend on calibrated or learned mappings from deformation to contact quantities. All tactile modalities have a local field of view and become informative primarily after contact. They are therefore commonly combined with vision and proprioception. Vision estimates where interaction should occur, proprioception supplies the robot configuration, and force or tactile feedback verifies the resulting physical interaction.

Proprioceptive Sensors

Proprioceptive sensors measure the internal state and motion of the embodied platform. For an articulated robot, a representative proprioceptive observation is

 $\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{prop}}(t)=[\,\mathbf{q}^{\top},\dot{\mathbf{q}}^{\top},\boldsymbol{\tau}^{\top},\mathbf{i}^{\top},\mathbf{a}_{\mathrm{imu}}^{\top},\boldsymbol{\omega}_{\mathrm{imu}}^{\top}\,]^{\top},$ 

(3.10)

where $\mathbf{q}$ and $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$ are joint positions and velocities, $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ denotes measured or estimated joint torque, $\mathbf{i}$ is motor current, and $\mathbf{a}_{\mathrm{imu}}$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_{\mathrm{imu}}$ are specific force and angular velocity from an inertial measurement unit. Depending on the platform, proprioception may additionally include wheel odometry, base orientation, gripper aperture, actuator temperature, or foot-contact switches.

These signals support forward kinematics, state estimation, trajectory tracking, balance, and body-aware control. They also provide the configuration needed to transform head-, wrist-, and body-mounted sensor data into a common coordinate system. Joint torque and motor current can support external-force estimation through an explicit robot dynamics model, but the resulting estimate remains sensitive to transmission, friction, and model error. In learning-based embodied systems, proprioceptive state is commonly combined with visual and language inputs so that action generation is conditioned on both the external scene and the current robot configuration (black2024pi0; khazatsky2024droid).

Multisensor Acquisition, Calibration, and Time Synchronization

Combining sensors requires more than recording their outputs. Different devices use different coordinate frames, sampling rates, exposure intervals, clock domains, communication paths, and latency conventions. Reliable fusion therefore depends on calibrated spatial and temporal relationships between measurements.

Spatial calibration comprises intrinsic calibration of each imaging or ranging sensor and extrinsic calibration between sensor frames. If a point measured in sensor frame $\mathrm{S}_{m}$ is to be expressed in a reference frame $\mathrm{S}_{0}$ , the homogeneous-coordinate transformation is

 $\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathrm{S}_{0}}={}^{\mathrm{S}_{0}}\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{S}_{m}}\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathrm{S}_{m}},\qquad{}^{\mathrm{S}_{0}}\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{S}_{m}}\in\mathrm{SE}(3).$ 

(3.11)

For moving sensors, this transform is composed with the robot kinematic state at the measurement time. Calibration may also include image rectification, depth-to-color registration, tactile-frame localization, force-sensor bias estimation, and calibration of the transformation from sensor output to physical units.

Temporal alignment requires a model of each sensor clock. A common affine approximation relates sensor time $t_{m}$ to a reference time $t_{0}$ as

 $t_{m}=\alpha_{m}^{\mathrm{clk}}t_{0}+\beta_{m}^{\mathrm{clk}},$ 

(3.12)

where $\beta_{m}^{\mathrm{clk}}$ is the clock offset and $\alpha_{m}^{\mathrm{clk}}$ represents the relative clock rate. A timestamp must also be associated with a clearly defined event. For a camera, that event may be the beginning, midpoint, or end of exposure. For a ranging pulse, it may be emission or reception. A timestamp may also mark the arrival of a sample at the host computer. Joint estimation of spatial and temporal calibration is often necessary because an unmodeled time offset during robot motion can be mistaken for an extrinsic-calibration error (furgale2013unified).

Software synchronization aligns independently acquired streams through timestamps, buffering, interpolation, and nearest-neighbor association. It is flexible but cannot recover information lost through inaccurate timestamps or variable transport delay. Hardware synchronization distributes a common clock, trigger, or pulse-per-second signal and is preferable when the platform undergoes rapid motion or contact transitions. Even with hardware triggering, an acquisition system should account for exposure duration, rolling-shutter readout, sensor processing delay, network latency, and the time required to assemble scanning measurements.

The final synchronized record should preserve the raw measurements, calibrated measurements, timestamps, coordinate-frame definitions, calibration parameters, and validity indicators. An RGB image, depth frame, LiDAR return, tactile image, wrench sample, and joint state should either refer to the same physical instant or carry sufficient timing information to be transformed or interpolated to a common instant. This requirement is particularly important for visual-tactile learning, force-guided manipulation, and high-speed navigation, where small temporal errors can associate observations with different robot poses or contact regimes. Careful acquisition and calibration are thus integral to perception and determine the reliability of all subsequent multimodal fusion.

3.2.2 Multimodal Fusion for Joint Perception

Multimodal fusion combines complementary observations to estimate the state of the robot, its surroundings, and their interactions. RGB images describe appearance. Depth and LiDAR provide geometric measurements. Force, tactile, and proprioceptive signals supply information about contact and robot motion. A useful organizing principle is the stage at which information is combined, whether at the level of observations, intermediate features, or task-level estimates. These levels describe possible operations rather than mutually exclusive architectures (hall1997introduction; Baltrušaitis et al., 2019).

Observation-Level Integration and Cross-Modal Enhancement

When measurements have been spatially registered and temporally aligned, they can be associated in a common coordinate frame. For example, a registered RGB image and depth map associate appearance with measured distance at corresponding image locations. RGB-guided depth completion additionally uses image information to infer depth where measurements are sparse or missing (ma2018sparse). Such estimates must remain distinguishable from measured depth. An appearance edge need not coincide with a geometric boundary. Validity masks, calibration, and timestamps are therefore part of the fused observation, especially near occlusions or when the sensors move.

Feature-Level Fusion for Joint Perception

Modality-specific encoders can extract representations that are then combined through concatenation, learned weighting, or attention. The features may be aligned on an image grid or mapped into a shared three-dimensional or bird’s-eye-view space. FuseNet combines color and depth features for semantic segmentation (hazirbas2016fusenet). BEVFusion combines camera and LiDAR features in a bird’s-eye-view representation for three-dimensional perception (liu2023bevfusion). In embodied systems, visual, tactile, and proprioceptive features can likewise be related through robot kinematics and contact geometry, even when pixelwise correspondence is unavailable. Feature fusion allows task-dependent interactions but can be sensitive to missing modalities and errors in spatial or temporal alignment.

Estimate-Level Fusion

Alternatively, each sensor stream can produce an estimate, such as object pose, occupancy, or contact state, before the estimates are combined. This approach permits modality-specific processing and can accommodate different sampling rates, provided that the estimates refer to compatible states and their uncertainties and dependencies are accounted for (hall1997introduction). Because high-level estimates discard some measurement detail, they may offer less opportunity to exploit fine cross-modal correspondences. In practice, the fusion level is chosen according to the perceptual task, available calibration, measurement reliability, and computational constraints. A system may combine several levels.

## 3.3 3D/4D Spatial Perception

Three-dimensional spatial perception estimates scene geometry, object locations, and spatial relationships. 4D perception additionally represents changes over time, including object motion and deformation. Figure 3.2 illustrates alternative 3D representations of the same object. For an embodied agent, these estimates should support interaction with the physical environment, not only recognition or novel-view rendering. Because sensors observe only limited, noisy projections of the world, spatial perception maintains a task-relevant estimate rather than a complete copy of physical reality.

Figure 3.2: Schematic illustration of different 3D representations of the same object. The 3D visualizations are illustrative and are not ground-truth reconstructions or outputs computed from the source data. The scene image is from suresh2022shapemap

3.3.1 3D/4D Scene Representation and Modeling

Scene representations differ in the properties they encode and the queries they support. In a calibrated pinhole camera, a world point $\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{W}}$ projects to image coordinates according to

 $\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{C}}=\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{CW}}\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{W}}+\mathbf{t}_{\mathrm{CW}},\qquad\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathrm{pix}}\propto\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{cam}}\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{C}},$ 

(3.13)

where $\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{CW}}$ and $\mathbf{t}_{\mathrm{CW}}$ define the transform from world to camera coordinates, and $\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{cam}}$ is the intrinsic matrix (hartley2003multiple). Given axial depth $Z_{\mathrm{depth}}(u_{\mathrm{pix}},v_{\mathrm{pix}})$ , the corresponding camera-frame point is $\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{C}}=Z_{\mathrm{depth}}(u_{\mathrm{pix}},v_{\mathrm{pix}})\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{cam}}^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathrm{pix}}$ . Thus, RGB-D data can be lifted into 3D and registered to robot or world coordinates, subject to calibration, depth error, and temporal alignment.

Point clouds retain measured or predicted surface samples, but do not by themselves define continuous surfaces, object interiors, or free space. Occupancy grids represent cells as occupied, free, or unknown, often with probabilistic occupancy. OctoMap is a probabilistic octree-based example (hornung2013octomap). Signed-distance fields encode distance to a surface, with the zero level set representing that surface under a chosen sign convention. They support geometric queries such as clearance and collision checking. Voxblox incrementally constructs Euclidean SDFs for planning (oleynikova2017voxblox). Meshes explicitly represent surfaces and can support rendering or collision queries when constructed for that purpose. None of these representations alone supplies all physical properties required for interaction, such as friction, mass, articulation, or contact dynamics. Their coverage is also limited by sensor visibility and spatial resolution.

NeRFs represent a scene by mapping 3D position and viewing direction to volume density and view-dependent radiance, $(\sigma_{\mathrm{rad}},\mathbf{c}_{\mathrm{rgb}})=F_{\theta}^{\mathrm{NeRF}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{pos}},\mathbf{d})$ (mildenhall2020nerf). 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) represents a scene using anisotropic Gaussian primitives optimized for efficient rendering (kerbl20233d). These appearance-oriented representations can support high-quality novel-view synthesis, but rendering quality alone does not establish accurate metric geometry or collision-ready surfaces.

For dynamic scenes, the representation must also describe temporal change. Time-dependent radiance fields and Gaussian models can reconstruct or render scenes at different times. 4D Gaussian Splatting is one example that models dynamic scenes with Gaussian primitives and learned deformations (wu20244d). When motion estimation or interaction prediction is required, the system must additionally maintain quantities such as object identity, pose or shape trajectories, and correspondences over time. A temporally plausible rendering does not by itself guarantee physically valid motion.

Learning-based reconstruction has reduced the need to optimize a separate model from scratch for every scene. For example, VGGT directly predicts camera parameters as well as geometric attributes such as depth maps, point maps, and point tracks from one or more images (wang2025vggt). pixelSplat predicts a Gaussian radiance-field representation from image pairs (charatan2024pixelsplat). These predictions can complement geometric reconstruction, but scale, coordinate-frame alignment, calibration, and task-specific accuracy still require attention. Geometry in regions not constrained by observations is inferred rather than measured.

World models can combine scene representation with prediction or generation, but these functions should be distinguished. A renderer that generates plausible views is not necessarily a model that predicts physically valid outcomes under robot actions. Atlas, for example, is described by its developers as producing point-cloud or Gaussian-splat outputs from images and generating novel views. Its developers also state that unseen regions may be inferred to fill gaps (worldlabs2026atlas). A related but distinct capability is tool-assisted 3D authoring. OpenAI reports that GPT-6 Astra can generate computer-aided design (CAD) models from multi-view renders with tools and, in the reported demonstration, is used to create an editable house scene in Blender and a walk-through version in Unreal Engine (openai2026astra).22
 2

 Thomas Ricouard, OpenAI Developers Blog, Architectural Visualization with Astra, September 4, 2026. These developer-reported examples demonstrate 3D generation and software-mediated modeling. Their use for robot interaction requires distinguishing generated content from sensor-supported estimates and validating geometry and motion against physical constraints.

3.3.2 Model-Driven Spatial Perception and Reasoning

Learned models can associate geometric representations with semantic concepts and use these associations to answer spatial queries or guide actions. The approaches below differ mainly in where spatial information is retained and how it is grounded in observations.

Models Using Explicit Spatial Representations

An explicit map can associate semantic features or object labels with points, surfaces, or regions in a common coordinate frame. OpenScene, for instance, co-embeds features of 3D scene points with image and text features, enabling open-vocabulary queries about observed space (peng2023openscene). Such maps allow geometric grounding and repeated queries, although their coverage and semantic accuracy depend on observation quality, registration, and the underlying visual features.

Spatial Perception with Vision-Language Models

Vision-language models can infer object relations and answer spatial questions directly from images and text without necessarily maintaining a persistent 3D map. SpatialVLM shows that spatially grounded training can improve qualitative and quantitative spatial question answering (chen2024spatialvlm). These outputs can help interpret instructions and propose likely relationships, but a linguistic answer should not be treated as a verified metric measurement or reachability judgment, particularly when viewpoint, occlusion, or unknown scale creates ambiguity.

Agent-Based Spatial Perception and Reasoning

An agent can couple perception to action. It maintains a spatial state, chooses where to look or move, and revises its estimates as new observations arrive. SayNav incrementally builds a 3D scene graph to ground language-model plans for navigation in unfamiliar environments (rajvanshi2024saynav). VoxPoser grounds language instructions in 3D value maps and uses model-based planning to generate closed-loop manipulation trajectories (huang2023voxposer). These examples illustrate how spatial representations and learned knowledge can inform action. Reliable operation still requires checking proposed plans against current geometry, robot configuration, collision constraints, and physical limits, and updating the estimate from feedback during execution.

## 3.4 High-Level Perception and Cognition

High-level perception organizes sensory observations and spatial representations into entities, attributes, states, and relations that are relevant to a task. Cognition builds on these representations by integrating prior knowledge, retaining relevant history, reasoning about spatial and physical relationships, and identifying what additional evidence is needed when current observations are insufficient.

For example, picking up a cup requires more than detecting and localizing it. The system may need to estimate its contents and physical state, identify an appropriate contact region, and determine whether the intended interaction is feasible. Similarly, monitoring an automated experiment requires associating a vessel with the correct sample, interpreting changes in material state, and relating visual observations to instrument measurements and experimental history. Both cases require representations that connect semantic understanding with physical evidence and persist beyond a single observation. This section develops a progression from object- and scene-level semantic perception to the understanding of physical properties, states, and interaction possibilities. It finally addresses grounded reasoning with vision-language models, memory, measurements, and active perception.

3.4.1 Object Recognition and Scene Semantic Understanding

Object- and scene-level semantic perception provides the foundation for high-level physical understanding. It identifies the entities present in an environment, localizes them in observations, maintains their identities over time, and organizes their semantic and spatial relationships. These representations provide the targets and contextual structure required for subsequent state estimation, interaction perception, and task-level reasoning.

Figure 3.3: Illustration of object detection and instance segmentation.
Bounding boxes indicate the locations and categories of detected objects,
while colored masks delineate individual object instances at the pixel level

Object Detection, Segmentation, and Tracking

Object detection predicts object categories and locations, typically represented as bounding boxes. Semantic segmentation assigns category labels at the pixel level, whereas instance segmentation distinguishes individual object instances within each category, as illustrated in Fig. 3.3. Mask R-CNN jointly predicts object categories, bounding boxes, and instance masks (he2017mask), while DETR formulates object detection as Transformer-based set prediction (carion2020end). Tracking extends recognition across time by maintaining object identities using appearance, motion, and geometric information. ByteTrack, for example, incorporates lower-confidence detections during association to recover partially occluded objects (zhang2022bytetrack). Together, detection, segmentation, and tracking provide object categories, spatial regions, and persistent identities that support target selection and state estimation. A cup temporarily occluded by a gripper, for example, should remain associated with the same contents, physical state, and interaction history after it becomes visible again.

Open-vocabulary recognition extends this capability beyond a predefined set of object categories. Grounding DINO localizes objects specified through textual descriptions (liu2024grounding), while the Segment Anything Model (SAM) generates segmentation masks from spatial prompts such as points and bounding boxes (kirillov2023segment). Combining language-grounded detection with promptable segmentation connects task descriptions to observable image regions, allowing a system to identify and segment relevant targets without requiring an exhaustive task-specific label set.

Scene-Level Semantic Perception and Understanding

Recognizing individual objects is only the first step toward understanding a physical environment. Scene-level perception organizes entities according to their spatial, semantic, and functional relationships. Scene graphs, for example, represent objects or regions as nodes and relationships such as support, containment, proximity, or attachment as edges. These structured relationships provide context for interpreting both individual objects and the overall scene. For example, cups and a kettle located on the same countertop may jointly indicate a beverage-preparation area. In a laboratory, scene relationships may associate a sample with its vessel, a vessel with an instrument, and an observation with the experimental stage at which acquisition occurs. Such associations make isolated sensor observations interpretable within the context of an ongoing task or physical process.

Context can also help resolve ambiguous observations. An object that appears partially behind a drawer may be contained inside it or merely occluded by it, while a visible liquid region may belong to one of several overlapping transparent vessels. Scene representations should therefore retain not only predicted relationships but also the evidence and uncertainty associated with them. New observations can then confirm, reject, or revise previously inferred relationships.

These semantic representations answer questions about what entities are present, where they are, and how they are related. Physical interaction, however, requires additional information about what properties they have, what states they are in, and what actions they afford. These aspects are considered next.

3.4.2 Object Properties, States, and Interaction Perception

High-level physical perception extends object recognition beyond identifying what an object is toward understanding what properties it has, what state it is in, and how it can be interacted with. Such understanding requires connecting semantic observations with physical properties, functional structures, interaction possibilities, and feedback from the environment.

Observable Attributes and Latent Physical Properties

Objects exhibit directly observable attributes, such as color, texture, shape, and visible geometry, as well as physical properties that are only indirectly observable, including mass, friction, stiffness, compliance, and fragility. Visual appearance provides useful cues for these properties but is often insufficient for reliable estimation. Visually similar objects, for example, may differ substantially in mass because of their contents or internal structure.

Multimodal sensing and physical interaction provide complementary evidence for resolving such ambiguities. Deformation under load can reveal compliance, object motion during controlled contact can constrain friction estimates, and force measurements during lifting can provide evidence about mass. These estimates remain dependent on contact conditions, sensing quality, and dynamical assumptions, and should therefore retain uncertainty. Their primary role in physical perception is not necessarily to recover exact physical parameters, but to provide sufficient information for selecting appropriate contact regions, forces, and interaction strategies.

States, Functional Parts, and Affordances

Recognizing an object category alone does not determine how the object should be used or manipulated. Object function describes its typical role, while functional parts identify regions that support particular interactions. A cup, for example, may function as a container, while its handle provides a functional region for grasping.

Affordances further describe the actions that are possible for a particular agent under the current physical and task conditions. Unlike object categories or intrinsic properties, affordances are relational. They depend jointly on object geometry, physical state, environmental context, agent capabilities, and task requirements. A handle may be graspable by one gripper but inaccessible to another, and an otherwise graspable cup may be unsuitable for lifting when its contents are likely to spill. In an automated laboratory, relevant affordances may instead concern access to a vessel opening, available capacity, or whether a valve can be operated in its current state.

Interaction perception connects these semantic and physical descriptions to possible actions and state transitions. It estimates discrete conditions such as open, closed, grasped, or slipping, as well as continuous quantities such as deformation and contact force. It also associates functional parts with candidate interactions and evaluates whether an observed response is consistent with the intended action. Methods such as Where2Act demonstrate how actionable regions and interaction proposals can be inferred for articulated objects (mo2021where2act). Such proposals nevertheless remain candidates rather than executable actions and must be checked against reachability, collision, object state, and task constraints.

Physical interaction also reveals information that may be unavailable from external vision. During contact, relevant regions can become occluded, while incipient slip, local deformation, and contact loading may be difficult to infer visually. Tactile and force sensing provide complementary observations of these conditions. GelSight, for example, demonstrates how vision-based tactile sensing can capture local contact geometry and deformation (yuan2017gelsight). Observed slip, deformation, or unexpected resistance can then update the estimated interaction state and support adjustments to contact location, grasp force, or subsequent actions.

Material and Process-State Perception

High-level physical perception is not limited to robot-object contact. In autonomous laboratories and other process-oriented environments, the target of perception may instead be a material state or a process variable. Relevant observations include liquid levels, phase boundaries, precipitates, vessel contents, and changes occurring during an experiment. Distinguishing the container from its contents is particularly important because material regions may lie within, overlap with, or be partially occluded by the surrounding vessel. Reflections, refraction, foam, transparency, and occlusion can further make visible boundaries ambiguous.

Visual observations should therefore be connected to calibrated measurements and process context. Estimating a liquid level may require vessel geometry, camera calibration, or a visible scale, while determining material identity may require sample metadata or analytical measurements. Other quantities, including temperature, pressure, mass, and spectral measurements, may be obtained directly from instruments or extracted from their displays. Regardless of the acquisition mechanism, observations should retain their units, timestamps, sample associations, and measurement quality. Maintaining these relationships allows semantic interpretation to remain grounded in the physical process being observed.

3.4.3 Grounded Perception and Cognition with Vision-Language Models

Vision-language models (VLMs) provide a flexible semantic interface between visual observations, task instructions, and prior knowledge. In Physical AI, however, semantic interpretation alone is insufficient. Model predictions must ultimately be grounded in specific entities, physical states, spatial geometry, measurements, and interaction history. VLMs should therefore be viewed as one component of a broader perception and cognition system rather than as a replacement for geometric estimation, physical sensing, memory, or measurement.

Semantic, Property, and Affordance Understanding

VLMs can associate visual appearance with semantic concepts, material cues, object functions, and typical interactions. This capability is particularly useful when a system encounters unfamiliar objects or must interpret them in the context of a task. Given an image and an instruction to move a cup, for example, a ceramic appearance may suggest fragility and careful handling, while a visible handle may indicate a candidate interaction region. PhysObjects illustrates the use of physical-concept annotations to improve the understanding of properties relevant to manipulation (gao2024physically).

Such predictions should be interpreted as hypotheses rather than direct physical measurements. A visual model may suggest that an object is heavy, fragile, or slippery, but quantitative or safety-critical judgments generally require additional sensing or interaction evidence. Semantic knowledge therefore provides useful priors that can guide subsequent observation and interaction without replacing physical verification.

Semantic knowledge must also be grounded in specific locations in the current environment. RoboPoint, for example, predicts image-space affordance points from visual observations and language instructions, linking semantic requests to candidate interaction regions (yuan2024robopoint). These predictions help identify where an interaction may occur but do not by themselves specify a feasible physical action. Depth, geometry, object state, collision constraints, and robot kinematics are still required to convert semantic interaction targets into executable contact poses and motions.

Reasoning with Geometry, Memory, and Measurements

High-level physical reasoning frequently requires information beyond the current image. Spatial questions may require calibrated geometry, questions about change require previous observations, and process-state interpretation may depend on event history or instrument measurements. A grounded cognition system therefore combines semantic reasoning with explicit geometric representations, persistent memory, and quantitative measurements.

Relevant information can be retrieved through object, sample, or task identity and associated with the current observation. Geometry provides spatial structure, memory provides temporal context, and sensors or instruments provide quantitative physical evidence. VLMs can integrate these sources to interpret a request, relate observations to the intended task, and identify missing or inconsistent evidence. Memory management, geometric computation, and numerical measurement remain explicit system functions even when their outputs are consumed by a multimodal model.

PaLM-E demonstrates one architecture for incorporating visual observations, continuous state estimates, and textual representations into an embodied language model (driess2023palme). More generally, physical information may be provided to a reasoning model through structured records, tool outputs, or textual representations. Regardless of the interface, physical semantics should be preserved, including units, timestamps, coordinate frames, object identities, and measurement uncertainty.

Consider determining whether a vessel has reached a target fill level. Visual perception first identifies the vessel and candidate liquid boundary, while calibration or vessel geometry converts image evidence into a physical estimate. Memory provides the target level and relevant filling history, and complementary measurements can be consulted when the visual evidence is ambiguous. The VLM helps interpret the task and associate the available evidence with the correct sample, while geometric and measurement tools support the quantitative comparison. This division of roles prevents semantic plausibility from being mistaken for physical certainty.

Active Perception and Feedback-Based Updating

Physical cognition becomes particularly important when the available observations do not uniquely determine the current state. Rather than forcing a decision from incomplete evidence, a high-level reasoning module, potentially implemented with a VLM, can maintain competing hypotheses, identify unresolved variables, and propose additional observations or controlled interactions that reduce uncertainty.

The resulting process forms a perception-cognition loop. The system observes the environment, interprets the available evidence, identifies relevant uncertainty, acquires additional evidence, and updates its internal state. Additional evidence may come from a new camera viewpoint, a different sensing modality, an instrument measurement, or a controlled physical probe. The choice of observation should consider expected information gain, acquisition cost, execution risk, and potential disturbance to the physical process.

For example, when observing unfamiliar storage furniture, a change in viewpoint may reveal hinges or rails and help distinguish rotational from translational motion. If ambiguity remains, a gentle probe with measured motion and force can provide further evidence about the underlying mechanism. In a laboratory, an apparent liquid boundary may instead correspond to a reflection or foam edge. A different viewpoint or illumination condition can test the visual hypothesis, while a mass measurement may provide independent evidence. In both cases, active perception should target the specific uncertainty rather than simply acquire more observations.

Feedback from execution provides another source of evidence. A failed grasp, unexpected resistance, observed slip, or inconsistent measurement can revise the estimated object state, interaction hypothesis, or process interpretation. Perception and cognition are therefore not restricted to a single observation-decision sequence. They continuously update their representation of the physical environment as new evidence becomes available.

Limitations, Multiple Time Scales, and Outlook

High-level semantic reasoning remains vulnerable when model outputs become detached from geometry, measurement, or physical history. Plausible semantic predictions do not guarantee correct localization, physical feasibility, or accurate state estimation. Evaluation should therefore extend beyond language quality to include entity grounding, spatial relations, physical-property judgments, state estimation, affordance prediction, and the appropriate use of new evidence. Occlusion, viewpoint changes, ambiguous material boundaries, and conflicting instrument readings provide useful settings for testing whether a system can recognize uncertainty and request additional evidence rather than produce an unsupported conclusion.

Another challenge arises from the multiple time scales of physical perception. Contact and force measurements may change rapidly, visual observations arrive at another rate, and material, thermal, or experimental processes may evolve over much longer intervals. A shared physical state should therefore preserve acquisition time, validity, uncertainty, and evidence provenance. High-level semantic reasoning can query this state when needed without requiring every sensor update to pass through a language model. This separation enables high-frequency physical sensing and lower-frequency semantic reasoning to coexist within the same perception architecture.

Looking forward, a research direction is the development of persistent and grounded physical cognition that combines multimodal memory, 3D spatial reasoning, quantitative measurements, and active perception. Such systems should not only recognize objects and describe scenes, but also maintain up-to-date estimates of physical states, identify missing evidence, and select informative observations or interactions when uncertainty matters. For autonomous laboratories, this requires connecting sample identity, material observations, instrument measurements, and experimental history. For robotic manipulation, it requires linking semantic targets to geometry, physical properties, interaction states, and execution feedback.

Progress should ultimately be assessed by whether these capabilities improve the interpretation and control of physical systems. The assessment should determine whether a system can correctly identify relevant entities, maintain their evolving states, recognize when its evidence is insufficient, acquire information that resolves the ambiguity, and revise its interpretation under real feedback. From this perspective, VLMs provide a flexible semantic and reasoning interface within a broader physical perception and cognition system, while grounded sensing, geometry, memory, and interaction provide the evidence that keeps such reasoning connected to the physical world.

## 4 Data for Physical AI

Perception and cognition are only passive to understand our physical world. Still, to build an active embodiment, interaction data in the real world is critical, as it provides the empirical foundation for AI systems to understand the actual physical dynamic environment and how to interact with it. Since this data records how actions alter physical states under known operating conditions, one can learn a control policy, calibrate a simulation pipeline, or build a validation benchmark. This chapter focuses on how to build a robust data collection pipeline for these purposes. It first introduces the data formats, curation pipelines, and real-world collection strategies spanning human teleoperation, autonomous exploration, and interactive feedback. It then examines how physics engines and generative world simulators expand data coverage, and how sim-to-real transfer aligns synthetic trajectories with physical hardware. Finally, it analyzes physical data scaling laws, the role of heterogeneous cross-embodiment datasets, and closed-loop data flywheels driven by deployment feedback.

## 4.1 Data Foundations for Physical AI

Physical data link observations, actions, and their consequences under specified operating conditions. A drawer image may support recognition. Learning to open it also requires the applied commands, contact events, and resulting motion. The same distinction applies to industrial processes, traffic control, and automated experiments. This section defines the evidence and record structure needed to interpret such data. Subsequent sections address its collection, generation, alignment, and growth.

4.1.1 The Spectrum of Physical Data

Data sources differ in how directly they support physical execution. The Data Pyramid for Embodied Manipulation organizes real-robot data, Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI)-style demonstrations, egocentric and exocentric observations, simulation data, and general vision-language data around the tension between scalability and robot alignment (ye2026pyramid). Here, the complementary question is what each record actually establishes. Video can reveal an object’s motion without identifying the force or command that caused it. A simulated trajectory can include exact action labels without establishing the corresponding real-world response.

Table 4.1 distinguishes these forms of evidence. They can coexist within one dataset and do not constitute a ranking of quality. In particular, reconstructed poses and latent actions are action proxies. Converting them into executable supervision requires a mapping to the target embodiment and controller. Representative released datasets spanning robot execution, portable demonstrations, and human observation are cataloged in Table 4.3 in Section 4.2.

Table 4.1: Evidence levels in physical data and their limits

Evidence

Provides

Does not establish

Observation

Appearance, scene context, visible motion

Executable commands or contact forces

Action proxies

Reconstructed poses, trajectories, or latent actions

Feasibility on the target embodiment

Execution

Recorded commands and measured responses

Coverage of unfamiliar states or failures

Closed-loop experience

Policy-induced states, interventions, and outcomes

Correct behavior or reliable annotations

Synthetic evidence

Controlled variation, scalable trajectories, dense model-derived labels

Real-world dynamics or sensor behavior

For interaction data, let $s_{t}$ denote the underlying physical state, $o_{t}$ the observation, and $a_{t}$ the action. A useful conceptual record is

 $\tau_{\mathrm{ep}}=\left(c,g,\left\{\left(o_{t},\zeta_{t}^{\mathrm{state}},a_{t}^{\mathrm{cmd}},a_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}},e_{t}^{\mathrm{event}},\Delta t_{t}\right)\right\}_{t=0}^{T},y\right),$ 

(4.1)

where $c$ records the embodiment, environment, and collection conditions, and $g$ is the goal. The optional field $\zeta_{t}^{\mathrm{state}}$ is a state estimate or belief, while $e_{t}^{\mathrm{event}}$ records events such as contact or intervention. The field $\Delta t_{t}$ gives elapsed time, and $y$ records the outcome. The command $a_{t}^{\mathrm{cmd}}$ is distinguished from $a_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}}$ , which denotes the measured execution response rather than a second command. The available fields vary by source. Missing measurements require validity masks, and inferred values require provenance.

4.1.2 Unified Representation

A common schema must preserve the meaning of its fields. In the RT-X experiments, Open X-Embodiment converts actions into a common seven-dimensional end-effector representation, but retains differences in coordinate frames and in absolute, relative, or velocity control. The same vector can therefore induce different motions on different robots (openx2024). Matching dimensions enables shared processing but does not establish physical equivalence.

Each record should retain the embodiment, tool geometry, control interface, and calibration needed to interpret it. Coordinate transforms must specify their direction and reference frames. Sensor acquisition, command issue, and physical response times must also remain distinguishable. Pairing an image with a command issued before its exposure can change the supervision target. Sampling rate, action duration, and controller update rate should be recorded separately.

Measured, estimated, and generated quantities require distinct provenance. A reconstructed wrist pose is an estimate, and a simulator’s contact force is a model output. Neither should silently replace a physical measurement. Derived fields should identify their source records, generating method and version, and any available uncertainty or validity bounds. A shared coordinate frame resolves geometric ambiguity but leaves embodiment-dependent limits and dynamics to be accounted for.

Minimum Action Specification

An action field should identify its issuer and target, control mode, reference frame and tool point, units, duration and effective time, applicable limits or saturation, controller gains where relevant, and the associated execution feedback.

4.1.3 Data Organization

Physical records are organized into steps, transitions, segments, and episodes. These boundaries carry learning semantics. Reinforcement Learning Datasets (RLDS), for example, distinguishes the last recorded step from an environment terminal state. A truncated episode does not establish that the task terminated, and its final observation need not have a valid outgoing action. Training views must preserve these distinctions instead of treating every stored row as a complete transition.

Raw records, standardized records, and training views serve different purposes. Raw records preserve the original signals and metadata. Standardized records make units, timestamps, coordinates, and episode boundaries explicit. Training views specify selection, segmentation, annotation, and augmentation. Keeping these stages traceable allows a calibration or labeling error to be corrected without repeating collection.

Every episode should retain a stable identifier and links to its source, embodiment, operator or policy version, calibration, and processing history. Segments and generated variants should retain their parent identifiers. Dataset splits can then keep related records together and hold out the task, scene, object, or embodiment relevant to the generalization claim. Splitting adjacent frames at random cannot establish transfer to unseen physical conditions.

4.1.4 Annotation Framework and Workflow

A recording may show an object moving, a temperature rising, or a machine stopping. The signals are recorded, but what happened? Annotations identify the objects and materials involved, the operating conditions, the actions taken, and their consequences. They may mark an object in an image, contact during a motion, stages of a production process, or the outcome of an experiment. The same record can then support different learning tasks, including recognizing a material, predicting its response, choosing an action, or judging whether the outcome meets a goal.

Annotation starts with rules that different people and tools can apply consistently. A small trial reveals unclear definitions and disputed boundaries before labeling expands. Automated tools can propose labels, while reviewers examine uncertain cases and spot-check the rest against the recordings. Each label keeps a link to its evidence and records whether it comes from measurement, human judgment, inference, or simulation. Uncertainty remains visible, and corrections update the labels without rewriting the underlying evidence.

4.1.5 Quality Governance

Quality checks should distinguish recording defects from difficult but valid experience. A force spike may indicate contact. A stalled gripper may reveal an execution failure. Neither warrants deletion solely because the signal is irregular. Checks should cover signal integrity, consistency across timestamps and coordinate frames, correspondence between commands and responses, and agreement between event annotations and outcomes.

Learning utility also depends on the learner and the intended supervision. The robomimic study systematically varies demonstration quality, observations, and learning algorithms, showing that these choices materially affect policy performance (mandlekar2022matters). A valid failure trajectory can support outcome prediction while providing unsuitable actions for nominal behavior cloning. Data validity, task outcome, and suitability as an imitation target should therefore be recorded separately.

Dataset documentation makes these judgments inspectable. Following Datasheets for Datasets, a release should describe its composition, collection process, intended uses, and limitations (pi12_gebru2021). For physical data, this should include embodiment and control specifications, calibration history, missing modalities, outcome definitions, and known recording defects. A versioned manifest should link released samples to their processing code and access or reuse conditions. These records provide the basis for the collection procedures in Section 4.2 and the synthetic-data validation developed in Section 4.3 and Section 4.4.

## 4.2 Data Collection and Interaction

Data collection and interaction proceed through collection design, human demonstrations, autonomous collection, and interactive feedback in four linked steps. In this view, producing data means actively sampling the physical world. The emphasis is on distributions, supervision, efficiency, and safety. Implementation details of individual devices are addressed only where they constrain the evidence that can be collected.

4.2.1 Collection Design

Collecting physical data is not indiscriminate recording of real-world processes. It is an active sampling of the space of reachable states, possible actions, and actual outcomes. Initial states, task goals, acting agents, control constraints, disturbances, and termination conditions all shape the resulting distribution. The collection policy is therefore part of the data-generating mechanism. A sound design first identifies the capability to be developed or the hypothesis to be tested, and then determines what to collect.

Design typically starts with the intended deployment distribution and works backward to define task families. A coverage matrix can span objects, scenes, initial states, goals, disturbances, embodiments, operators or policies, outcomes, and risks. Frequent states require sufficient density to establish basic competence. Rare but consequential states require targeted collection. Matched comparison cases can weaken spurious correlations with backgrounds, positions, or operator styles. The number of task names is not a measure of coverage. “Tidy the desk” can probe very different capabilities as object combinations, occlusion, starting poses, and time pressure change.

The variable specification should distinguish controlled factors, observable quantities, and potential confounders. In robotic manipulation, one can vary object positions and materials, container states, illumination, and disturbances. Traffic and industrial systems also require records of topology, load, shifts, operating rules, and decisions by multiple actors. Intelligent laboratory systems should retain reagent batches, instrument states, step dependencies, and measurement uncertainty. These conditions must be represented in task templates and metadata if performance differences are to be attributed to plausible causes rather than described merely as isolated successes or failures.

Sensor configuration further bounds what can be observed. Measurement principles, mounting locations, and coverage determine which quantities can be measured directly. Range, noise, and calibration determine how trustworthy those measurements are. An uninstalled or uncovered channel should be marked as missing, rather than represented by a zero reading. Contact forces inferred from images or a dynamics model must likewise be distinguished from directly measured forces. Temporal resolution depends jointly on sensor bandwidth, sampling rate, filtering, and the transmission path. A higher logging rate does not necessarily provide more usable information.

Force and tactile sensing illustrate these constraints. A six-axis wrist force/torque sensor measures the net force and moment, not the distribution of fingertip contacts. A tactile array covers only its sensitive surface. Some force sensors support sampling at kilohertz rates (ATI Industrial Automation, n.d.), whereas vision-based tactile sensors are limited by camera frame rate. The DIGIT prototype, for example, operates at 60 frames/s (lambeta2020digit). Directly reducing a high-rate force stream to the video frame rate can hide collision peaks and transient slip. The raw time series should therefore be retained, with a separately aligned stream generated after antialiasing. Collection also requires calibration and zeroing, together with compensation of wrist readings for tool weight and inertial effects. Quality checks are also required for thermal drift, hysteresis, saturation, and dropped frames. Calibration versions, filter settings, and anomaly flags should accompany the data. The confidence assigned to contact labels should account for both synchronization error and measurement uncertainty.

Success criteria, failure categories, safety limits, and reset rules must be defined before collection. Success should be expressed in verifiable object states, process conditions, or operational metrics rather than left to an operator’s impression. Failures should distinguish perception errors, planning errors, control deviations, unstable contact, timeouts, safety aborts, and external disturbances. An incomplete reset, or physical traces left by a previous trial, can also compromise the independence of subsequent data. When an outcome is difficult to determine automatically, sensor-based rules can be combined with visual checks and human review in a staged assessment.

Temporal segmentation is likewise part of collection design. An episode should start at a verifiable initialization or reset and end in success, failure, timeout, or an abort. Skill segments and action chunks should have explicit temporal meanings. The acquisition system must distinguish the rates of sensor sampling, model decisions, action updates, and low-level servo control. It should record the issue, delivery, and actual effective time of each command. Source timestamps, coordinate-frame calibration, latency measurement, and completeness monitoring are minimum requirements. Detailed hardware and software implementation belongs in Chapter 9.

Recent large-scale real-world datasets illustrate different organizational approaches. DROID shows how relatively uniform hardware and protocols can support distributed collection across sites. RoboMIND brings multiple embodiments, task protocols, and demonstrations of failure with recorded causes into one platform. AgiBot World scales trajectories through centralized facilities, standard procedures, and human-in-the-loop verification. Humanoid Everyday further includes whole-body locomotion, manipulation, and human-robot interaction (khazatsky2024droid; wu2025robomind; AgiBot-World-Contributors et al., 2025; zhao2025humanoideveryday). Together, these efforts show that scaling requires reproducible task definitions, staffing procedures, equipment states, and quality judgments, as well as more devices.

Collection performance should be measured by effective data yield. Beyond raw hours and trajectory counts, useful measures include minutes of meaningful interaction, the share of recordings that pass training quality checks, incremental coverage after deduplication, the yield of rare events, equipment availability, human and machine time, time spent resetting, and the final retention rate from raw records to the training release. Consecutive stationary frames, repeated successes, and multiple derived versions of the same behavior inflate volume without necessarily adding new experience. Efficient collection uses limited physical interaction to close identifiable capability gaps.

The output of collection design is thus an executable data-collection protocol, not merely a task list. It specifies the target distribution, variable combinations, episode boundaries, success and failure definitions, safety constraints, data schema, quality gates, and cost metrics. Human demonstrations, autonomous execution, and interactive corrections are different ways of gathering evidence under this plan.

4.2.2 Human Demonstrations

Figure 4.1: Human-demonstration data collection paradigms, arranged by their
distance from executable robot actions.
(a) Teleoperation drives the target robot through leader-follower
mechanisms and records robot observations, actions, and outcomes directly
(Mobile ALOHA, photo from Stanford News).
(b) Portable interfaces such as UMI record retargetable end-effector motion
in natural environments using a hand-held gripper, a wrist-mounted camera,
and visual-inertial tracking (photo from the UMI project).
(c) Egocentric human data capture natural activity at scale with
head-mounted devices, providing broad behavioral priors without native
robot states (photo from ABC News)

Human demonstration converts human intent into behavioral evidence that a machine can learn from and, ideally, execute on the target embodiment. Methods can be arranged by their distance from executable robot actions (Figure 4.1). Teleoperation and kinesthetic teaching with the target robot in the loop directly produce embodied actions. Portable tools, motion capture, and wearable systems record motions that can be retargeted. Egocentric and Internet videos provide broad observations and behavioral priors. These sources complement one another in action fidelity, coverage of natural settings, equipment occupancy, and processing cost.

Master-slave robot arms, spatial controllers, and immersive teleoperation operating on the target embodiment can record robot observations, control commands, embodiment states, contacts, and outcomes together. ALOHA uses matched leader and follower mechanisms for fine-grained bimanual demonstrations (zhao2023). GELLO provides a low-cost, kinematically matched interface that helps an operator perceive joint limits (wu2023gello). Open-TeleVision incorporates stereoscopic views and active head motion into the teleoperation loop (cheng2024tv). The collection interface is therefore not a neutral accessory. Its mapping, feedback delay, viewpoint strategy, and operator burden systematically shape trajectories.

Portable, robot-independent interfaces bring demonstrations into natural environments. UMI records relative end-effector motion with a handheld gripper, wrist-mounted cameras, and visual-inertial tracking, then accounts for target-robot reachability and latency at deployment (chi2024umi_ch6). DexWild uses a portable, human-centered system to extend dexterous demonstrations in everyday settings (tao2025dexwild). FreeTacMan synchronizes visual and tactile collection, so that contact feedback can support both the operator and supervision of contact phases (wu2025freetacman). These methods reduce occupancy of the target robot and expand scene coverage, but still have to address tracking errors, scale, action retargeting, and the target embodiment’s dynamics.

Humanoid and mobile manipulation extend demonstration beyond tabletop end-effector motion to whole-body coordination. TWIST2 uses portable full-body teleoperation without external motion capture to bring legged locomotion, torso, both arms, hands, and head-mounted views into one loop (ze2025twist2). The central requirement is not simply more degrees of freedom. Navigation, support, manipulation, and active vision must remain temporally consistent. A recording should also distinguish actions supplied by the operator from compensation supplied by a stabilizer or whole-body controller. Otherwise, high-level intent and low-level control corrections become conflated.

Egocentric human data offer natural behavior at greater scale. EgoDex synchronizes egocentric images with three-dimensional head, upper-body, and hand poses, turning video into a more calibratable behavioral record (hoque2025egodex). AoE explores sustained collection of natural egocentric experience and joint training with a smaller amount of robot teleoperation data (yang2026aoe). ActiveMimic jointly recovers camera and wrist trajectories from single-camera in-the-wild egocentric video, emphasizing the relationship between active viewpoints and manipulation motion (lin2026activemimic). These approaches broaden the range of objects, scenes, behavioral phases, and viewpoint priors. Human-video records themselves, however, do not natively supply robot joint states, gripper signals, tactile measurements, or feedback from actual robot execution.

Turning human or Internet videos into robot supervision requires alignment of camera frames, recovery of scale, mapping from hands or bodies to tools, correction for kinematic reachability, temporal alignment, contact assumptions, and confidence assessment. Point tracks, wrist poses, body poses, and latent actions are action proxies with different levels of reliability. They should not all be labeled as ground-truth robot actions. Table 4.2 compares the supervision, executability, and limitations of interaction data sources. More defensible training strategies include learning visual and temporal representations first and then post-training on robot data, using separate loss heads for human and robot data, weighting examples by confidence, or restricting explicit action supervision to reliable channels.

Table 4.2: Supervisory value and principal limitations of interaction data sources

Warning signs, takeovers, corrections, recovery, and consequences

High

Selected by intervention triggers. Supports correction, recovery, and safety-oriented post-training

Demonstration quality also depends on how people are organized. A collection plan should retain anonymized operator identifiers, levels of training, interface configurations, and work periods. Task rotation, fatigue monitoring, spot checks of replays, and coverage across operators can reduce style bias. Expert demonstrations may not visit the error states encountered by novices, while natural human movements may violate a robot’s safety constraints. The value of a demonstration lies in how clearly it conveys intent, constraints, and an executable path.

Human data thus form a gradient from rich semantics to reliable executable actions. A sound combination uses observational data to broaden tasks and scenes, wearable and tool-based data to reduce the gap in action semantics, and interactions on the target embodiment to calibrate execution. Whether cross-domain data actually help must ultimately be established through closed-loop evaluation on robots or other real systems. Section 9.6.4 follows these collection choices into a dexterous-hand system, where wrist tracking, finger capture, and contact sensing supply different parts of the demonstration.

Table 4.3 makes this spectrum concrete through representative publicly available datasets. Its focus is real-world manipulation and human activity relevant to the collection methods above. Reading the scale together with the supervision distinguishes robot execution records from tool-mediated demonstrations and human behavioral observations. The official resource links provide entry points for inspecting each release.
