4.2.3 Autonomous Data Collection

Autonomous data collection should be understood as an agent actively sampling the space of possible experiences, rather than a robot repeating its current policy indefinitely. Passive production logs reflect the natural frequency of events but are often dominated by routine states. An active system can instead select tasks and initial conditions according to novelty, uncertainty, prediction error, failure density, gaps in coverage, or risk priority. If a collection policy repeatedly succeeds only in familiar regions, the sample count may grow while behavioral diversity and the boundaries of competence remain unchanged.

AutoRT illustrates an early use of foundation models to orchestrate collection. A vision-language model describes the scene, a language model proposes and filters tasks, and the system schedules their execution using existing policies or human operators (Ahn et al., 2024). Its contribution in this context is not to replace physical control with a language model, but to bring scene understanding, task discovery, safety rules, and available policy resources into a common orchestration process. A high-level model may likewise identify gaps in coverage for factories, traffic systems, mines, or laboratories, while concrete actions remain subject to control authority, real-time constraints, and safety interlocks.

A systematic study of scaling autonomous robot data collection finds that environment instrumentation, reliable object resets, success detection, and maintaining stable conditions remain major costs. In some tasks, adding a small number of human demonstrations is more effective than adding many autonomous episodes (mirchandani2025autonomous). These findings show how autonomous collection shifts some labor from episode-by-episode teleoperation to environment interfaces, online assessment, and risk control. If that infrastructure is unreliable, scaling up may merely accumulate repetitive, mislabeled, or dangerous data.

The distinctive value of autonomous interaction is its access to states rarely covered by successful human demonstrations. PlayWorld uses autonomous play to collect contact-rich and long-tail robot-object interactions for learning action-conditioned changes in the world (yin2026playworld). The lesson for the present section concerns data production. Open-ended play can complement demonstrations with failures, slips, precursors to collisions, and nonexpert trajectories. The use of such data to train generative world models is discussed in Section 4.3 and Chapter 5.

Effective active sampling must balance information gain with representativeness. A collection budget can be divided into three parts. One maintains a baseline density for states common in deployment, another targets regions where the current model is uncertain or incurs high loss, and the third explores rare risks and new tasks. A task selector should also suppress near-duplicate trajectories and avoid favoring short tasks merely because success is easy to detect. For high-risk states, constrained environments, low-speed operation, safe proxy tasks, or simulation-based prescreening should take priority over deliberately inducing accidents.

A complete autonomous episode should retain the policy version, model inputs, raw outputs, commands after safety filtering, actual execution, random seed, initial state, reset method, termination reason, success-detector version, and any human involvement. In particular, a policy-initiated abort, a safety-system intervention, a human emergency stop, and an equipment failure must be distinguished because they carry different training semantics. Continuous operation also requires monitoring for clock drift, frozen sensors, saturated actions, repeated tasks, degradation of the scene, and failed resets, so that the pipeline does not continue blindly accumulating data after the physical system has ceased to behave as intended.

Multiple robots can collect data in parallel, but the number of concurrent robots is not the only measure of efficiency. As fleets grow, task scheduling, spare parts, networks, storage, calibration, and on-site supervision become more complex. Drift and maintenance history across devices may also introduce hidden domain differences. A more mature system coordinates equipment health, task queues, risk levels, gains in coverage, and human workload, and admits each new data batch into training only after it passes a quality gate rather than adding every operating log directly to the model.

The scope of autonomous collection should be clear. This section concerns the selection and execution of interactions in the real world. Scaling simulated agents and generative scenes belongs to Section 4.3, the simulation-reality gap to Section 4.4, and the longer-term deployment and retraining flywheel to Section 4.5. Autonomy is, first, a means of collecting informative experience and, second, a means of reducing the human cost of each individual data point.

4.2.4 The Interactive Feedback Loop

The most valuable supervision often lies at the boundary of a policy’s competence. Complete, successful demonstrations describe a manifold of nominal behavior, whereas autonomous deployment exposes the distribution of states induced by the current policy itself. Interactive supervision connects the two. A failed episode, the warning signs before failure, the instant of human takeover, corrective actions after takeover, and the recovery segment that returns the system to a feasible state have different learning semantics. They should not be collapsed into a single “failure” label.

The collection system should retain the policy’s original actions, commands after safety filtering, the human’s modifications, and the actual execution results, together with the reasons for intervention, its start and end times, and the subsequent outcome. If only the smooth trajectory after takeover is saved, a model may incorrectly attribute the human’s behavior to the policy. If only the segment before failure is retained, it cannot learn how to recover. Linking warning, trigger, takeover, correction, recovery, and outcome within one event chain supports risk prediction, corrective policies, and recovery skills.

Human-in-the-Loop Sample-Efficient Robotic Reinforcement Learning (HIL-SERL) connects initial demonstrations and online human interventions with reinforcement learning on real robots, showing that human-in-the-loop data can provide continued supervision on the policy’s execution distribution, beyond offline imitation (luo2025hilserl). Hi-ORS further combines online rejection sampling with flexible human correction, exploiting recovery segments under comparatively stable supervision targets (lu2025hiors). Together these works point to a shift from a single sequence of “collect, then train” to a short-cycle loop among execution, evaluation, and updating.

HELP further organizes human-in-the-loop involvement as a scarce supervision resource. Different staff members undertake multi-robot monitoring, physical resets, and high-value remote takeovers, while rollout segmentation distinguishes progress-making, idle, failure-inducing, and recovery segments (zhai2026help). This exploration suggests that a scalable loop need not assign one person to continuously control each robot. One person can monitor several robots, intervene when risk warrants it, and concentrate limited human effort on states with the greatest learning value. The results still depend on the platform and task. No particular ratio of people to robots should be treated as a universal rule.

The quality gate is an intermediate layer of the loop. Before each round of data enters training, it should undergo completeness checks, physical-consistency checks, event segmentation, review of successes and failures, near-duplicate suppression, and provenance audits. After training, improvements must also be verified on held-out scenes, objects, operators, and embodiments. A new version that improves only on the collection distribution, or raises average success at the cost of safety and recovery, does not establish an effective feedback loop.

Safety is a system variable that determines what may be collected, when to intervene, and how the resulting data may be used. Task rules, policy uncertainty, kinematic and dynamic constraints, low-level monitoring, software and hardware interlocks, and human oversight should provide protection together. New policies should progress from offline checks through constrained environments and low-speed operation without a payload before normal operation. In settings involving people, hazardous materials, public roads, or critical infrastructure, near misses, controlled perturbations, and safe proxy tasks should take priority. Long-tail data should not be sought by causing real accidents.

Interactive feedback loops also apply to Physical AI systems that do not have a single robot body. Human takeover in a traffic system may mean reverting to a previous signal plan. Recovery in a factory may mean degrading process parameters and isolating equipment. Correction in a laboratory may mean stopping a procedure, recalibrating, or changing experimental conditions. Whatever the system, its recommendations, authorization decisions, issued commands, actual process, alarms, human interventions, and final results should remain linked in the same event chain.

The efficiency of the loop should be measured by capability gains per human-hour or robot-hour, alongside effective minutes of interaction, the fraction of usable episodes, rare-event yield, takeover frequency, recovery success, gains in coverage, and safety incidents. Raw operating time is merely a proxy for cost and cannot stand in for data value. The output of a short-cycle loop consists of training batches that pass quality gates and traceable model versions. The longer-cycle flywheel of deployment, failure discovery, renewed collection, and retraining is developed in Section 4.5.

## 4.3 Physics Engines and Generative Worlds

Section 4.1 defines physical data as records that link observations and actions to their consequences. Among these records, failures and the recoveries that follow them are the most informative and also the hardest to obtain (Section 4.2). A policy that must recover when a grasped object starts to slip needs to experience many slips, and a legged robot that must get up after a fall needs to fall, yet physical systems cannot be reset cheaply (Section 1.1). In simulation, a slip can be staged 1,000 times, and a simulated fall causes no physical damage to robot hardware. A model computes the recorded consequences, so their physical consistency has to be tested before the data can be trusted.

Table 4.4: Sources of synthetic experience and what must be checked before use

Every synthetic trajectory depends on three choices. The world in which it unfolds may be authored by hand, reconstructed from scans, or generated. The consequences of each action may be computed by a physics engine or by a network trained on data. The actions may come from planners, reinforcement-learning experts, or adapted human demonstrations. The section first considers what simulation adds to a dataset and then takes the three choices in turn. Table 4.4 summarizes the sources involved and what must be checked before their output is used. In what follows, synthetic data are any data produced by a model. Simulated data come from a physics engine, and generated data from a learned model. Most examples are drawn from manipulation and locomotion, where the evidence is richest, but the same questions arise for the simulators and digital twins of process plants, traffic systems, and laboratories.

4.3.1 What Simulation Adds to a Dataset

In the notation of Section 4.1, a simulator turns chosen actions into trajectories through two conditional distributions,

 $s_{t+1}\sim P_{\xi_{\mathrm{sim}}}^{\mathrm{tr}}(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t}),\qquad o_{t}\sim O_{\psi_{\mathrm{render}}}(\cdot\mid s_{t}),$ 

(4.2)

where the physical and numerical parameters $\xi_{\mathrm{sim}}$ (masses, friction coefficients, time step, solver tolerance) govern the dynamics and the observation parameters $\psi_{\mathrm{render}}$ (camera models, lighting, sensor noise) govern what is sensed. Delays in the real system, such as actuator response time or sensor latency, have to be represented in $s_{t}$ or in an explicit history buffer. Otherwise the simulator assumes that commands act instantly and that sensors report the present. Two further ingredients complete a simulated dataset, namely the distribution of initial states and tasks from which episodes start and the predicate that decides whether an episode meets the success criterion. The dynamics, the observation model, the initial conditions, and the success predicate can each differ from reality, and Section 4.4 classifies the reality gap along these four lines.

The most visible gain is access to the full state. Object poses, contact forces, and material parameters can be recorded at every step, even though a deployed policy cannot observe them directly. This privileged information is valuable for training teachers, critics, and state estimators (Section 7.2 and Section 7.3), provided it never leaks into the deployed policy’s inputs. Each synthetic field should therefore be tagged as simulator state, rendered observation, or inferred quantity.

A deeper gain is the exact and inexpensive reset, which physical systems lack. Episodes restart from saved states, thousands of environments run in parallel, and the same initial state can be replayed under different actions, friction coefficients, or disturbances to see what changes the outcome. Counterfactual replay of this kind supports curricula, failure diagnosis, and targeted generation. Its findings concern the model, however. A policy’s sensitivity to a simulated friction coefficient says something about a real material only after the simulator has been checked against measurements.

Simulated episodes need the same conventions as real trajectories and the same care in task design. An action vector means different things under torque, position, and Cartesian control, so the action specification of Section 4.1 belongs with every episode. Favorable starting poses hide difficult approaches, and a reset triggered as soon as an object slips ends the episode before the recovery that a deployed policy will need to learn. Success is best defined by the physical outcome of interest, such as a plug that is fully seated or a lid that stays closed, instead of by whatever the simulator makes easy to check.

4.3.2 Scenes from Scans and from Generators

Hand-built scenes are slow to author and tend to be few and tidy, so the training data available to policies cover a narrow range of environments. Reconstruction from real scans and automatic generation both widen that slice. Reconstruction has considerably reduced the appearance gap for visual policies. Neural radiance fields and Gaussian splatting (Section 3.3) recover geometry and appearance, although collision geometry, articulation, and physical parameters must still be added before a scene can be simulated. With these additions, reconstructed scenes can largely stand in for real ones. RGB manipulation policies trained entirely on data from SplatSim, which renders a simulator’s scenes with Gaussian splats, achieve 86.25% average success in the reported SplatSim experiments zero-shot on real hardware, against 97.5% for policies trained on real data (qureshi2024splatsim). RialTo fine-tunes policies with reinforcement learning inside a reconstructed replica of the deployment scene itself, reporting an average improvement of 67% in success over baselines under perturbed object poses, distractors, and disturbances (torne2024rialto).

Some pipelines use reconstruction without simulating dynamics at all. Real2Render2Real turns a phone scan of an object and a single video of a person manipulating it into thousands of rendered robot demonstrations (yu2025r2r2r). The object’s motion is copied from the human and collision modeling is switched off, so no model computes the consequences of the robot’s actions. Even so, in the reported Real2Render2Real experiments, policies trained on data rendered from one human video match policies trained on 150 teleoperated demonstrations. The approach works when the object’s path alone defines the task, and it cannot handle tasks that depend on force.

Reconstruction also raises the question of how faithful a training scene needs to be. A digital twin is tied to one physical site and kept up to date with it. A digital cousin, by contrast, is a generated environment that preserves what matters for interaction in a real scene, such as where objects are and how they can be grasped or opened, without copying it exactly. In the reported digital-cousin experiments, policies trained across a set of cousins achieve 90% zero-shot success in the original real scene, whereas policies trained on a single faithful twin achieve 25% (dai2024acdc).

Generating scenes at scale requires assets, and a training asset must be a physical specification as well as a shape. It needs consistent scale, collision geometry, mass and inertia, joint axes and limits, and material parameters. A photorealistic cabinet with a misplaced hinge axis adds visual variety but nothing a policy can practice on. Articulation is particularly hard to produce automatically. Articulate-Anything has a vision-language model write articulation code from text, images, or video and revise it after inspecting the result. On the PartNet-Mobility benchmark, the reported Articulate-Anything evaluation shows that this raises the success rate of reconstructed articulations from 8.7 to 11.6% for earlier methods to 75% (le2025articulate).

Generative models can supply tasks as well as assets. GenSim and RoboGen prompt a language model to generate tasks, write the code that builds their scenes, and produce the supervision needed to learn them (wang2024gensim; wang2024robogen). RoboCasa populates kitchens with assets from text-to-3D and text-to-image models, and RoboCasa365 scales the approach to 365 tasks across 2,500 kitchen layouts (nasiriany2024robocasa; nasiriany2026robocasa365). A generated task is usable only if it resolves to identifiable objects, admissible actions, and a success predicate that can be checked, so generation pipelines usually execute each proposed task and discard those that a solver cannot complete.

4.3.3 Agent-Built Scenes and Simulations

The methods above use a language model for one part of a scene at a time. Agents built on language and vision-language models now assemble whole scenes, and increasingly whole simulations, by writing code, running it, and inspecting the result. Early systems focus on layout. Holodeck asks GPT-4 which objects a described room should contain and how they relate spatially, then places Objaverse assets with a constraint solver (yang2024holodeck). Fine-tuning on Holodeck scenes raises a navigation agent’s success in unfamiliar room types, such as music rooms and gyms, from 4.1% to 20.4%, against 17.0% for scenes with the same assets in procedural layouts.

Later systems also supply physical properties. In SceneSmith, designer and critic agents build a room in stages, from the floor plan to furniture to small objects, while a vision-language model estimates each object’s mass and material from rendered views and articulated furniture is drawn from a library (pfaff2026scenesmith). The generated rooms contain about 71 objects, against 11 to 23 for earlier generators, and 95.6% of the objects stay in place under simulation. SAGE uses a similar generate-and-critique loop to build scenes for a given task (xia2026sage). Parameters inferred from appearance are enough to keep a scene standing, but contact-sensitive tasks still need them calibrated.

General-purpose models released in 2026 can carry out the whole real-to-sim process. In its 2026 release materials, OpenAI presents 3D world and asset generation as a main capability of GPT-6 Astra (openai2026astra), and reports published within weeks of release describe several groups using it to build simulation scenes (li2026agenticrsr).33
 3

 Max Bickley and Ashley Goldstein, NVIDIA Technical Blog, How to Use AI Agents to Prepare 3D Scenes for Simulation, September 16, 2026. In Agentic RSR, a Codex agent running GPT-6 Astra turns an RGB video of a robot workspace into a MuJoCo scene with collision geometry and joints, then develops a policy program by running it there (li2026agenticrsr). Across 18 tasks on 2 robot arms, 10 succeed in simulation and 8 of those also succeed on the real robots. The authors find that the agent behaves differently across interfaces and runs, so the model version belongs in the record of any data it generates.

Benchmarks show where such agents still fall short. In Video2World, agents rebuild a simulated world and the demonstrated behavior from a video of a robot or a person performing a task (tang2026video2world). The best of 9 agent systems achieves 25.5% task success over 222 instances, against 58.8% for human-assisted reconstructions, and GPT-6 Astra achieves only 10.7% although it recovers object shapes more accurately than any other agent. On indoor scans, the reported LiteReality-Agent evaluation shows 24 interpenetrating furniture pairs for GPT-6 Astra and none for the specialized LiteReality-Agent pipeline (huang2026literealityagent), and on 4DCodeBench good static reconstruction does not carry over to deformation, fluids, or fracture (shen2026fourdcodebench). Accurate geometry does not guarantee a scene in which the task can be performed.

Two recent systems close part of this gap by adding structure around the model. Text2Sim splits the writing of a Genesis simulation among planner, writer, and critic agents, and the writers consult Debug Cards, short notes distilled from 99 demonstrations in graphics papers on how simulations of a given kind fail and how to repair them (xiong2026text2sim). On 42 held-out prompts, its automatic physical-quality score is 95.3, against 86.6 for direct use of its own underlying model (GPT-5.6-Sol). Without the cards, the score falls to 91.3. WorldAgent instead verifies every construction and simulation step in Blender, checking interpenetration, support, numerical stability, and causal order against scene geometry and simulator states, so it also catches overlaps hidden from the camera (wang2026worldagent). With GPT-6 Astra as the underlying model, WorldAgent reduces the worst interpenetration during simulation to about 1/5 of that from direct prompting. In these evaluations, neither system is checked against measured behavior, and both infer physical parameters instead of measuring them.

World generators skip the agent altogether. Marble turns text, images, or video into Gaussian splats with a collision mesh, and such worlds have been imported into MuJoCo and Isaac Sim. The mesh is a single static surface, so the robot and the objects it manipulated were added from asset libraries (wmWorldLabs2025Marble).44
 4

 World Labs, Scaling Robotic Simulation with Marble, 2025. Genie 3 generates an interactive environment from a prompt in real time and keeps it consistent for several minutes, and DeepMind’s SIMA agent has pursued goals inside such worlds.55
 5

 Jack Parker-Holder and Shlomi Fruchter, Google DeepMind, Genie 3: A New Frontier for World Models, August 5, 2025. A world of this kind has no explicit state or parameters to inspect, so, like the video world models discussed later in this section, it can be judged only by the consequences it predicts.

4.3.4 Contact, Fidelity, and Throughput

Once a world is built, a model must compute what happens in it, and the accuracy required depends on the task. Articulated rigid-body dynamics suffice for most legged locomotion and for pick-and-place with rigid objects, whereas cloth, cables, food, and soft tissue need deformable or continuum models. A useful test is whether the model reproduces the events that change the correct action, such as a grasp that slips, a peg that jams, or a support that gives way.

Most such events happen at contact. Section 2.1 describes contact through non-penetration and Coulomb friction, and engines differ mainly in how they enforce these two conditions. Classical time-stepping schemes pose them as a complementarity problem, in which two bodies at a contact either separate or push on each other, never both at once (stewart1996). MuJoCo relaxes them into soft constraints and solves a convex optimization problem at each step, obtaining smooth, well-posed dynamics at the price of small interpenetrations and some compliance (todorov2012mujoco). For many tasks the relaxation does no harm, and a calibrated compliance can even describe a rubber fingertip better than a perfectly rigid model. In tight-tolerance insertion or stacking, however, a soft contact model can let a part slide into place where the corresponding real part would bind.

Deformable objects make non-penetration harder to enforce. Incremental Potential Contact guarantees, under its algorithmic assumptions, that simulated deformable bodies never pass through each other and that mesh elements never turn inside out (li2020ipc). Trajectories computed with it are free of interpenetration artifacts, but the method says nothing about the stiffness, damping, or friction of a particular sponge or garment, and these values must be measured before the recorded forces and deformations can be trusted.

Numerical artifacts are a separate hazard, because reinforcement learning can favor policies that exploit them. A policy can learn to exploit interpenetration, spurious impulses from numerical jitter, or contacts that stick when they should slide, and the time step, collision geometry, solver tolerance, and constraint softness determine which of these artifacts the optimizer can find. A cheap safeguard is to replay a sample of accepted trajectories with a smaller time step, tighter tolerances, or perturbed contact parameters, and to discard behaviors whose success does not survive. The check is best run before a large dataset is produced, since an artifact that goes unnoticed is copied into thousands of examples.

Throughput determines how much variation can be explored. Isaac Gym keeps physics simulation and policy training on the same graphics processing unit (GPU) and reports speedups of two to three orders of magnitude over pipelines that simulate on the central processing unit (CPU) (makoviychuk2021isaac), which makes it possible to train quadruped walking policies in minutes (rudin2022learning). For policies that use images, the bottleneck moves to rendering. ManiSkill3 parallelizes rendering on the GPU along with physics and reports that, with rendering enabled, it runs 10 to 1,000 times faster than other platforms on its benchmarks (tao2024maniskill3). Frame rates are nonetheless a poor guide to the cost of data. They vary with scene complexity and contact density, and they leave out resets, policy inference, filtering, and storage. A better measure is the simulated counterpart of the effective data yield of Section 4.2, which counts only trajectories that pass the quality gates and weighs their cost against how much they improve the policy.

4.3.5 Learned Simulators and Video World Models

Hand-written engines are limited to what their authors can model. Learned models trade explicit physical structure for coverage of phenomena that are hard to write down, and they can replace the solver, the renderer, or both. The price is that their errors are harder to diagnose. An error in an engine can usually be traced to a parameter, a missing mechanism, or a solver setting, whereas an error in a learned model is spread across its weights. Measurements on the physical system then become the main check on its physical consistency.

Learned simulators replace the solver but keep the state-based interface of Eq. (4.2). Graph Network-based Simulators and MeshGraphNets, for example, learn how particles and meshes evolve for fluids, granular media, cloth, and deformable solids (sanchezgonzalez2020learning; wmPfaff2021). In its evaluation, MeshGraphNets runs 1 to 2 orders of magnitude faster than the solvers used to produce its training data. Such models are reliable mainly within their training regime. Over long rollouts their errors accumulate, and conservation laws hold only approximately unless they are built into the architecture (Section 2.4).

Observation generators leave the physics to an engine and replace only the renderer, changing the lighting, textures, backgrounds, and clutter that the camera sees. Cosmos-Transfer, for instance, generates realistic video conditioned on segmentation, depth, and edge maps rendered by a simulator (nvidia2025cosmostransfer). The risk is that the generator alters something the labels depend on. If it shifts a handle by a few centimeters while restyling the scene, and the simulator keeps the original pose, a correct grasp label becomes wrong. Agreement between image and simulator state therefore needs checking near contacts, around thin structures, and under occlusion, where such errors are most likely.

Video world models replace both, learning the consequences of actions directly from recordings (Chapter 5) (bruce2024genie; yang2024unisim; nvidia2025cosmos). UniSim, an action-conditioned video simulator, learns from image, robot, and navigation data and is used to train policies that transfer to real robots. For generating data, the first question is which training data the model has received. A model trained on demonstrations rarely observes failures or unusual contact, so it tends to predict that actions succeed. Training on autonomous play, as in PlayWorld (Section 4.2), exposes a world model to the slips, collisions, and near misses that demonstrations omit (yin2026playworld).

Because video models produce pixels, actions have to be recovered before their output can train a policy. DreamGen fine-tunes an image-to-video model on the target embodiment and uses it to generate videos of familiar and new tasks (jang2025dreamgen). The videos are then labeled with actions, either by an inverse-dynamics model, which infers the action taken between consecutive frames, or by a latent-action model, which infers an abstract action code. Starting from teleoperation data for a single pick-and-place task in one environment, a humanoid trained on these generated trajectories acquires 22 new behaviors in seen and unseen environments. The recovered actions are action proxies in the sense of Section 4.1, and they can be screened by replaying them in a physics simulator and keeping those whose simulated motion matches the generated video (kim2026robocurate). A policy can also be fine-tuned inside a world model, on imagined successes or on rewards that a vision-language model assigns to imagined rollouts (guo2026ctrlworld; sharma2026worldgymnast), at the risk of learning to exploit the model’s errors (Section 5.4).

4.3.6 Synthetic Demonstrations and Pretraining Corpora

The third choice is the agent. Behavior can come from motion planners that use the simulator’s exact state, from reinforcement-learning experts trained with privileged observations and then distilled into policies that use deployable sensors (Section 7.2), from programs written by language models, or from a few human demonstrations adapted to new situations. Each source leaves its mark on the data. Planners produce smoother and more direct motions than an operator would produce, reinforcement learning may find strategies that a person would not demonstrate, and adapted demonstrations carry human habits along with human skill.

MimicGen shows how far a few demonstrations can be stretched. It splits each demonstration into segments defined relative to the objects involved, transforms the segments to new object poses, stitches them together, and keeps the results that succeed when executed in simulation. In MimicGen, about 200 human demonstrations yield more than 50,000 demonstrations across 18 tasks with varied scenes, objects, and robot arms. Policies trained on the synthesized demonstrations perform comparably to policies trained on additional human demonstrations (mandlekar2023mimicgen). Later systems extend the method to long-horizon skill sequences and to bimanual dexterous hands (garrett2024skillmimicgen; jiang2025dexmimicgen). MimicGen’s output, however, recombines the strategies in the seed demonstrations without adding new ones, and because failed executions are discarded, the resulting training data provide few examples of failure or recovery.

Synthetic demonstrations should pass the same quality gates that Section 4.2 applies to real batches, along with checks specific to synthesis. These checks cover action semantics that match the deployed controller, privileged fields that are marked, and outcomes that survive the solver checks described earlier. Rejected samples are worth keeping, sorted by the reason for rejection, because different reasons call for different responses. Invalid geometry, a mismatch between the rendered observation and the simulator state, and an infeasible task all point to defects in the generator. A valid execution that ends in failure is ordinary failure data, unsuitable as an imitation target but useful for learning to predict outcomes and to recover. If generator versions, parameter distributions, solver and renderer settings, and random seeds are kept on record, a problem found later can be fixed at its source before more data are produced from it.

Synthetic data have also moved beyond narrow skills into pretraining. Simulated trajectories make up a large part of the training mixture of the GR00T N1 humanoid model, and GraspVLA, pretrained on 1 billion frames of simulated grasping, transfers zero-shot to real objects (bjorck2025gr00t; deng2025graspvla). The most direct comparison comes from InternData-A1. In InternData-A1, a model with the $\pi_{0}$ architecture, pretrained only on its 630,000 simulated trajectories, matches the official $\pi_{0}$ on simulated, real, and long-horizon dexterous tasks. The official $\pi_{0}$ had been pretrained largely on real robot data (tian2025interndata). Results of this kind are strongest where outcomes depend mainly on geometry, as in grasping and pick-and-place. Where outcomes depend on contact dynamics, a synthetic corpus is only as useful as the calibration of the engine that produced it, and calibration requires real data.

## 4.4 Sim-to-Real Transfer and Real-World Alignment

A policy trained on synthetic data inherits the errors of its source, and how much those errors matter depends on the task. In legged locomotion, policies trained entirely in simulation with randomized dynamics and learned actuator models now routinely transfer without real-world fine-tuning. Manipulation is harder. Contact, deformation, and vision all differ between simulation and reality, and transfer there typically involves some real data. This section begins with what simulated and real data each contribute. It then follows the order in which the reality gap is commonly addressed. This sequence consists of finding where simulation and reality disagree, correcting the simulator with measurements, training policies that are robust to the remaining error, and checking the result in closed loop on the physical system.

4.4.1 What Simulated and Real Data Each Contribute

Table 4.5: Complementary strengths of simulated and real data

Aspect

Simulated data

Real data

Scale and cost

Millions of episodes, with cost dominated by building scenes and by compute

Limited by robots, operators, and resets, with cost growing with every episode

Perception and labels

Exact poses, contacts, masks, and depth, although rendering may look unrealistic

Sensor noise, calibration error, missing depth, with labels that must be estimated or annotated

Dynamics

Only as accurate as the contact, material, and actuator models

Real consequences, including effects that no model captures, though their causes may go unmeasured

Rare and dangerous states

Staged and replayed on demand

Rare, costly, and sometimes unsafe to collect

Main role

Breadth, privileged supervision, pretraining, stress tests

Training where dynamics matter, calibration of simulators and world models, validation

Choosing between simulated and real data means trading scale and label accuracy against the reliability of the dynamics (Table 4.5). Simulation offers scale, exact perception labels, and free resets (Section 4.3), but its dynamics, and therefore the consequences it computes, are only as accurate as its contact, material, and actuator models. Real data have the reverse profile. They are limited by robot time, operators, and the cost of resetting the world, and their observations are imperfect. Cameras add noise and blur, depth sensors drop out on shiny surfaces, calibration drifts, and object poses or contact forces must be estimated instead of read off. Their dynamics, on the other hand, are the real ones. A real trajectory reflects the actual friction, compliance, backlash, and delay of the system, including effects that no simulator models, even without direct measurements of those effects. Neither source dominates. Simulation is most useful where exact labels and broad coverage matter and the dynamics are easy to model, while real data are hard to replace where the outcome depends on contact, deformation, or actuation that simulators approximate poorly.

Because real data are scarce, how they are spent matters as much as how much is collected. They serve three purposes, namely training policies directly, calibrating the simulators and world models that generate synthetic data, and validating both the generators and the policies trained on their output. The three purposes compete for the same evidence, and evidence spent on one cannot serve as an independent check on another. Trajectories used to fit a simulator cannot show that the fit is accurate, and trials used to select a policy cannot certify it.

4.4.2 Where the Reality Gap Comes from

The four ingredients of a simulated dataset listed in Section 4.3 also give a natural way to classify the reality gap (Table 4.6). A dynamics gap means that $P_{\xi_{\mathrm{sim}}}^{\mathrm{tr}}$ in Eq. (4.2) is wrong, either because its parameters are off or because it lacks a mechanism. Errors in mass, inertia, friction, and compliance alter accelerations and contact outcomes, and actuators add discrepancies of their own through gains, torque limits, backlash, and delay. An observation gap means that $O_{\psi_{\mathrm{render}}}$ misrepresents what the sensors report, whether in appearance, camera calibration, depth dropouts on shiny or transparent surfaces, proprioceptive bias, or timing. Touch is a particular weak point, since many tactile sensors respond through elastomer deformation and internal optics that simulators capture only roughly. The remaining two gaps are easier to miss. A distribution gap arises when training does not cover the initial states, objects, and tasks the robot actually meets. An objective gap arises when simulated success is not real success, as when a success predicate credits an insertion that reaches the right depth but would not hold in a real fixture.

Table 4.6: Components of the reality gap and how they are diagnosed and addressed

Gap

Typical symptom

Diagnostic

Main remedies

Dynamics ( $P_{\xi_{\mathrm{sim}}}^{\mathrm{tr}}$ )

Overshoot, sluggish tracking, unexpected slip or jamming, wrong deformation

Replay identical command sequences in simulation and on hardware and compare the responses

System identification, actuator or residual models, dynamics randomization

Observation ( $O_{\psi_{\mathrm{render}}}$ )

A correct plan executed at the wrong place or time, and failures under particular lighting or materials

Compare sensor streams for matched states and measure end-to-end latency

Calibration, latency modeling, sensor noise models, visual randomization

Distribution (initial states and tasks)

Failures concentrated on unseen objects, layouts, or initial states

Stratify evaluation by condition

Targeted real or synthetic collection, broader scene and task generation

Objective (success predicate)

Episodes counted as successes in simulation that fail in reality

Audit success predicates against physical outcomes

Redefine success and reward and relabel data

Each gap calls for a different remedy, so the gap has to be identified before anything is changed. A delayed command is fixed by calibrating the interface, an unmodeled deformation needs a better model, and an action that is executed correctly but is wrong for the task needs new supervision. Telling these cases apart requires the commanded and executed actions, events, and outcomes in the trajectory record (Section 4.1), which a binary success flag does not provide.

A gap of any kind is amplified in closed loop. An early mistake moves the robot into a state that no demonstration covered, the policy’s next action there is worse, and errors snowball. For imitation learning, this intuition has a precise form. With per-step task costs bounded in $[0,1]$ , a cloned policy with error probability $\epsilon_{\mathrm{BC}}$ under the expert state distribution can incur an excess expected cost of order $T^{2}\epsilon_{\mathrm{BC}}$ over $T$ steps (ross2010efficient). Dataset Aggregation (DAgger) collects expert labels on states visited during rollouts that may mix expert and learner policies. Under the assumptions of its analysis and with sufficiently many iterations, some learned iterate has excess expected task cost relative to the expert bounded by $u_{\mathrm{dev}}T\epsilon_{\mathrm{DAgger},N_{\mathrm{iter}}}+O(1)$ . Here $\epsilon_{\mathrm{DAgger},N_{\mathrm{iter}}}$ is the minimum average surrogate loss achievable within the policy class over the state distributions induced by the rollout policies across $N_{\mathrm{iter}}$ iterations, and $u_{\mathrm{dev}}$ bounds the increase in the expert’s remaining cost after one deviating action (ross2011dagger). The constant $u_{\mathrm{dev}}$ is a measure of recoverability, the property that Section 1.1 argues planning must take into account when resets are not free.

The analysis assumes access to an expert policy that can label the states visited during data collection. A privileged teacher in simulation can supply such labels when its policy is defined on those states, and teacher-student distillation usually labels the states that the student visits. Human operators find it hard to say what the robot should have done in a state they are not controlling, which is why intervention-based collection (Section 4.2) lets them take over when the policy goes wrong. Either way, training data must include the states that the deployed policy actually reaches.

4.4.3 Calibrating Simulators and World Models with Real Data

Calibration adjusts a model’s parameters until it reproduces real measurements. With $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{r}}$ denoting a set of real trajectories, system identification can be written as Bayesian inference over the simulator parameters,

 $p(\xi_{\mathrm{sim}}\mid\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{r}})\propto p(\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{r}}\mid\xi_{\mathrm{sim}})\,p(\xi_{\mathrm{sim}}),$ 

(4.3)

where the prior $p(\xi_{\mathrm{sim}})$ encodes datasheet values and physical bounds and the likelihood measures how well the simulator with parameters $\xi_{\mathrm{sim}}$ reproduces the recorded observations. When states are only partially observed, the likelihood must also account for state and sensor uncertainty. A point estimate is often enough in practice, but the full posterior keeps track of ambiguities that matter later, for instance when randomization ranges are chosen.

The data used for identification must be informative. As Section 2.2 explains, accurate tracking alone does not imply parameter convergence. Persistent excitation of the regressor supports parameter convergence under the assumptions of the specified adaptive law. Identification likewise requires data that distinguish the relevant parameter directions. Slow motions in free space reveal little about actuator bandwidth, grasps that never slip reveal little about sliding friction, and different combinations of motor strength, payload, and gain can produce nearly identical trajectories. Calibration experiments should therefore excite the mechanisms the task depends on, for example with fast reversals for actuator response, controlled pushes for friction, and loaded lifts for inertia, while staying within safe limits.

Where first-principles models fall short, models learned from data often do better. Learned actuator networks, which map commanded positions and recent history to delivered torque, are central in the early legged-transfer study (Section 7.2) (hwangbo2019). ASAP applies data-driven correction to a whole humanoid. A motion-tracking policy trained in simulation is run on the real robot, and the recorded rollouts train a delta-action model, a network that adds a correction to each action inside the simulator so that simulated motion matches the recorded real-robot motion. The policy is then fine-tuned in the corrected simulator. In tests of transfer between two simulators and deployment on a real Unitree G1, the reported ASAP evaluation shows that the approach tracks agile whole-body motions more accurately than system identification, domain randomization, or a learned correction to the simulator’s dynamics (he2025asap).

Learned corrections can, however, fit the data for the wrong reason. A correction trained on one set of motions may absorb a calibration error elsewhere in the system, and testing at speeds, loads, and contact points outside the fitting data exposes such errors. The same tests separate parameter errors, which calibration can fix, from structural ones, which it cannot. No value of $\xi_{\mathrm{sim}}$ repairs a model that omits cable twisting or a compliant gripper pad.

Nor is a single best-fit simulator always necessary. SimOpt instead calibrates a distribution over parameters. It adjusts the distribution so that simulated rollouts of the current policy match real ones, retrains the policy under the updated distribution, and repeats. Policies trained in this way transfer to real swing-peg-in-hole and drawer-opening tasks (chebotar2019simopt). A simulator fitted to one policy’s behavior can remain wrong in regions that policy never visits, so calibration data should also cover the behaviors that later policies are likely to try.

Learned simulators can be calibrated more directly, because their parameters can be updated by gradient descent on real data. NeRD replaces the dynamics and contact solvers of a conventional simulator with a learned model that can be fine-tuned on real trajectories (xu2025nerd). For video world models, VLAW alternates between improving the model and improving the policy. Real rollouts of a vision-language-action policy refine the world model, and the refined model generates rollouts for training the policy (guo2026vlaw). On a real robot, the authors report that the method raises success by 39.2 percentage points over the pretrained policy and by 11.6% over fine-tuning on the same real rollouts filtered for success. In that evaluation, the refined world model thus adds value beyond the real data used to build it. Establishing the accuracy of the model would still require fresh trajectories from conditions outside the fitting data.

4.4.4 Randomization, Adaptation, and Co-Training

Calibration narrows the uncertainty that measurements can resolve, and the policy must tolerate whatever remains. Domain randomization trains it to do so across a distribution $p_{\eta_{\mathrm{sim}}}(\xi_{\mathrm{sim}})$ over simulator parameters, shaped by design parameters $\eta_{\mathrm{sim}}$ ,

 $\max_{\theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{\mathrm{sim}}\sim p_{\eta_{\mathrm{sim}}}}\bigl[J(\pi_{\theta};\xi_{\mathrm{sim}})\bigr],$ 

(4.4)

where $J(\pi_{\theta};\xi_{\mathrm{sim}})$ is the expected return of the policy in the world with parameters $\xi_{\mathrm{sim}}$ . Training across varied models aims to reduce reliance on any one exact model, and randomizing appearance and dynamics in this way underlies much of sim-to-real transfer in perception and control (tobin2017domain; peng2018).

Choosing $p_{\eta_{\mathrm{sim}}}$ in Eq. (4.4) is a data-design problem. Parameters should be resampled on the timescale at which they actually vary. An object’s mass is fixed within an episode, sensor noise changes with every reading, and actuator response drifts slowly with temperature and wear. Dependencies should be explicit, since appearance and friction are correlated for a given material.

Wide ranges are not enough by themselves. A range that contains the true value is of little use if the distribution places almost no probability near it, and ranges that are too broad produce cautious policies without fixing the failures seen in deployment. Moderate variation around a well-chosen nominal value often helps more than pinning each parameter to a single estimate, as the digital-cousin result of Section 4.3 suggests, and Section 4.5 reports a similar effect of diversity in real data. The posterior in Eq. (4.3) is a natural source for both the nominal values and their spread, and evaluation should report performance for groups of conditions as well as the average over the distribution.

Automatic domain randomization automates part of this design by widening each range as the policy meets the performance criterion within the current one, which turns randomization into a curriculum. OpenAI uses it to train a Shadow Dexterous Hand to solve a Rubik’s cube. In ten reported trials, the hand solves cubes needing 15 face rotations 6 times and solves the hardest cubes (which need 26 face rotations) 2 times (akkaya2019rubik). The result also depends on a cube instrumented with sensors, a classical solver that chooses the sequence of face rotations, and months of large-scale training.

Adaptive policies deal with the remaining uncertainty differently. Instead of performing well under every condition, they infer the current one from recent history and adjust to it, as in the teacher-student and rapid motor adaptation methods of Section 7.2 (kumar2021). Training them requires data that contain changes and transients, such as a payload added in the middle of a task or the onset of slip, as well as conditions that are unknown but fixed. When adaptive rollouts are later reused for training, the inferred context should be stored with each example, because an action that is correct for a heavy payload becomes a wrong label once the payload information is dropped.

In vision-based manipulation, where both the visual and the physical gap are large, a common alternative is to train on simulated and real data at once and let each cover the other’s weaknesses (Table 4.5). Co-training minimizes a weighted sum of losses over the two sources, the mixture objective of Eq. (9.1) with one simulated and one real component. Across tasks on a robot arm and a humanoid, the reported co-training study shows that adding simulation data improves real-world performance by an average of 38%, and the benefit persists when the real dataset grows to 400 demonstrations (maddukuri2025cotraining). A controlled study of planar pushing from pixels examines when and why the benefit appears (wei2025cotraining). In that study, simulation data raise success two- to sevenfold when real data are scarce, but the gains plateau unless real data grow too. Narrowing the physics gap matters more than improving visual fidelity. Unexpectedly, the best policies can distinguish simulated inputs from real ones, and a modest visual difference between the domains helps. A mechanistic analysis attributes this to a balance between aligning representations across domains, so that knowledge transfers, and keeping the domains distinguishable, so that the policy can apply the right dynamics to each (lei2026mechanistic).

The same pushing study finds that mixing the sources during training outperforms pretraining in simulation and then fine-tuning on real data, and that fine-tuning a co-trained policy does not consistently help. These comparisons involve single tasks and modest datasets. Whether broad multi-task pretraining followed by fine-tuning helps is a separate question, taken up in Section 4.5.

4.4.5 Validating Transfer and Closing the Loop

Most of the evaluation that guides development happens away from hardware, yet the criterion remains closed-loop performance on the physical system (Section 1.1), so every proxy evaluator has to be checked against it. SIMPLER builds simulated counterparts of real manipulation setups, matching camera views, appearance, and control. It compares policy rankings in simulation with their rankings on real robots (li2024simpler). Agreement is measured by the Pearson correlation between simulated and real success rates and by the mean maximum rank violation (MMRV), which penalizes the simulator for misordering two policies in proportion to the gap between their real success rates. By these measures, simulated evaluation tracks real results far better than offline metrics such as the error of predicted actions on held-out demonstrations. World models can serve the same purpose. In WorldGym, success rates measured inside an action-conditioned video model correlate with real success at $r=0.78$ on tasks from the BridgeData V2 tabletop setup (quevedo2026worldgym).

Simulated and real trials can also be combined statistically instead of merely compared. SureSim treats the problem as prediction-powered inference. A small number of paired real and simulated trials estimate the simulator’s bias, and that estimate corrects a large number of simulated trials (Badithela et al., 2025). The result is a valid confidence interval on real performance, which raw simulated success rates cannot provide, and an interval of similar width needs 20 to 25% fewer hardware trials than one estimated from hardware trials alone. Like any agreement between a proxy and reality, the correction holds for the policies and conditions for which it is measured and must be rechecked when either changes.

Consider a fleet of mobile manipulators that open drawers in office kitchens. At one site, pulls repeatedly stall after an approach and grasp that look correct in the logs. Engineers rebuild the scene in simulation from the logs and a scan, and the simulated robot reproduces the approach but opens the drawer without difficulty. Since the approach is reproduced and the stall is not, the discrepancy most likely lies in the simulated drawer rather than in perception or in the grasp. Pulls with a force-sensing gripper reveal a soft-close damper and a detent that the simulated drawer lacks. Once the damper and detent are modeled and their parameters fitted (Eq. (4.3)), randomization is restricted to damping and detent force around the identified values, and new scenes vary handle position and pull direction near the failure. The retrained policy is screened in simulation and then tested on held-out drawers at that site and at others, to confirm that the fix generalizes beyond the cabinet where the failure occurs.

The example also shows the many points at which real data enter a pipeline nominally trained in simulation, and claims of transfer should account for all of them. “Zero-shot” usually means that the policy was not fine-tuned on the target embodiment, yet real data may still have been used to identify parameters, reconstruct scenes, pretrain perception, or select checkpoints. Reporting these uses makes the contribution of simulation measurable. It also sharpens a question that co-training raises and that Section 4.5 takes up. The question concerns how many synthetic trajectories one real trajectory is worth.

## 4.5 Scaling Laws and the Data Flywheel for Physical AI

Language-model scaling studies show predictable improvements as data, parameters, and compute grow together, and progress in vision-language-action models now depends mainly on data (Section 6.2). Whether physical data will yield equally predictable gains is far from clear. Every trajectory comes from a particular body in a particular world and costs robot time and usually human time. The practical question concerns allocation. It covers which data to collect or generate and in what proportions. It also covers how to divide scarce physical interaction among training, calibration, and validation. A further aspect is when a robot system can collect what it needs through its own operation. Such a system, a data flywheel, is worth running only if the capability it adds outweighs its cost. Throughout, value is measured by closed-loop performance on the physical system, not by loss, frame counts, or simulated success.

4.5.1 The Data Pyramid

Figure 4.2: The data pyramid for Physical AI. For physically collected data, relevance to the target embodiment and cost per sample rise together toward the apex, where the target embodiment acts in the physical world. Lower layers are cheaper, larger, and more diverse but supervise physical execution less directly. Simulated and generated data are drawn separately because they supply robot actions at low cost while computing their consequences with a model, so their effective position depends on calibration. Adapted from bjorck2025gr00t and ye2026pyramid. The order of the layers reflects relevance and cost, not dataset quality

Section 4.2 describes human data as a gradient from rich semantics to executable actions. Figure 4.2 extends that gradient to all physically collected data and adds the dimension of scale, with layers widening toward the base as cost per sample falls. The trajectory record of Section 4.1 gives a way to judge relevance. Data are most relevant when they record the target embodiment issuing executable commands under deployment conditions, together with the measured consequences of those commands. Each layer below the apex gives up part of this record. Handheld and wearable devices capture real contact and robot-like actions without a robot, human video captures real physics without robot actions, and web data supply semantics without physical interaction. The most relevant data are also the most expensive, since every hour of them needs a robot, an operator, and resets, and they are correspondingly scarce. Goldberg estimates that the largest teleoperation datasets amount to about a year of robot experience, whereas the text and images used to train vision-language models would take a person some 100,000 years to read and view (goldberg2025datagap).

Simulation does not fit this ordering, which is why the figure draws it separately. It supplies executable actions on a model of the target embodiment at almost no marginal cost. The reported GR00T N1 study produces 780,000 simulated trajectories, equivalent to about 6,500 hours of human demonstration, in 11 hours (bjorck2025gr00t). Because its consequences are computed, its relevance depends on calibration (Section 4.4), and simulated corpora have so far done best where geometry decides the outcome (Section 4.3). Section 9.2 places simulation alongside handheld devices in a related pyramid organized by the kind of evidence each source provides.

A capable system needs both ends of the pyramid. The apex provides executable actions and real consequences on the system’s own body. The base provides diversity. Chen and colleagues argue that diversity sets the ceiling on how far a model can generalize and that, for now, only internet-scale data supply enough of it (wmChen2026Roadmap). Much of this chapter concerns lowering the cost of relevant data and raising the value of cheap data through calibration, retargeting, and filtering.

Within the physically collected layers, the collection method largely determines cost and yield. Section 4.2 describes how each method works. The paragraphs below compare their economics, including what an hour of collection costs, how much it yields, and what the resulting data lack.

Egocentric video is the cheapest to collect and the easiest to scale, since it needs only a head-mounted camera or glasses. Its drawback is the embodiment gap, since human hands differ from robot grippers and video records neither commands nor forces. The gap can be narrowed by design. If the robot is built to resemble the human and both are recorded with the same sensors, human data can be worth more per hour than robot data. In EgoMimic, the reported evaluation shows that an hour of egocentric recording yields about 1,400 demonstrations against 135 from teleoperation, and adding an hour of human data improves the co-trained policy more than adding an hour of robot data (kareer2025egomimic).

A handheld gripper costs a few hundred dollars and needs no robot. Using UMI, 3 people collect 1,400 demonstrations across 30 locations in 12 person-hours, and on 1 task collection runs more than 3 times faster than teleoperation with a 3D mouse (chi2024umi_ch6). Because the fingers match the robot’s, gripper-level actions transfer directly. The arm itself goes unrecorded, so its joint states and dynamics are missing and reachability has to be checked at deployment. Forces are also absent unless tactile sensors are added.

Teleoperation yields the most relevant data and the least of it. The hardware has become cheaper. A kinematically matched leader arm costs under $300, and a complete bimanual system, robots included, costs about $20,000 (wu2023gello; zhao2023). A robot and an operator, however, remain in the loop for every hour. The reported DROID data-collection effort involves 50 collectors at 13 institutions gathering 76,000 trajectories over one year (khazatsky2024droid). As Section 4.2 notes, the data also carry the imprint of the interface, since latency, limited haptic feedback, and operator style shape the trajectories.

Exoskeletons and hand trackers fall between the handheld gripper and teleoperation, both in cost and in how closely they match the robot. An exoskeleton with the same kinematics as the target arm records joint-level motion directly. AirExo-2 costs about $600 for a dual-arm rig, and in the reported user study its operators complete a task in 5.7 s on average against 17.3 s with joint-space teleoperation (fang2025airexo2). Gloves and motion-capture systems extend joint-level recording to dexterous hands, and the DexCap study reports collection 3 times faster than teleoperation (wang2024dexcap). In exchange, the operator has to wear the rig, the data must be retargeted whenever the human and robot hands differ, and force feedback is limited.

Across the four methods, the cheaper the source, the further its data sit from the target embodiment. How much each source is worth for a given task has to be measured. Scaling studies are the usual instrument, but in their standard form they rest on assumptions that physical data do not meet.

4.5.2 Scaling Laws and What They Assume

Scaling laws come from language modeling. kaplan2020scaling find that the test loss of language models falls as a power law in model size, dataset size, and training compute, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude. A common form separates the contributions of the parameter count $N_{\mathrm{par}}$ and the amount of training data $N_{\mathrm{data}}$ ,

 $L_{\mathrm{scale}}(N_{\mathrm{par}},N_{\mathrm{data}})=L_{\mathrm{floor}}+a_{\mathrm{scale}}N_{\mathrm{par}}^{-\alpha_{\mathrm{scale}}}+b_{\mathrm{scale}}N_{\mathrm{data}}^{-\beta_{\mathrm{scale}}},\qquad a_{\mathrm{scale}},b_{\mathrm{scale}},\alpha_{\mathrm{scale}},\beta_{\mathrm{scale}}>0,$ 

(4.5)

where $L_{\mathrm{scale}}$ is a held-out loss and $L_{\mathrm{floor}}$ an irreducible floor. With compute $C_{\mathrm{train}}\approx 6N_{\mathrm{par}}N_{\mathrm{data}}$ , about six floating-point operations per parameter per training token, minimizing Eq. (4.5) at fixed $C_{\mathrm{train}}$ makes the optimal $N_{\mathrm{par}}$ and $N_{\mathrm{data}}$ grow as powers of $C_{\mathrm{train}}$ . The exponents prove harder to pin down than the form. The original study concludes that most additional compute should go into parameters, whereas hoffmann2022compute find that parameters and data should grow in equal proportion as compute increases. Later work traces most of the difference to how parameters and compute are counted and to optimizer settings (pearce2024reconciling; porian2024resolving). An exponent, in other words, reflects the measurement protocol as well as the model family.

The allocation argument also rests on the three assumptions that every unit of data is equally informative, that compute is the only cost, and that lower loss means a better model. Physical data strain all three. Robot trajectories are highly correlated, so much of a robot dataset behaves like repeated data. Even in language modeling, repeating data for more than about 4 epochs yields rapidly diminishing returns (muennighoff2023scaling). Collecting robot data consumes robot time, operators, and resets that never appear in $C_{\mathrm{train}}$ . Section 12.1 calls this resource physical interaction capacity and argues that it must grow along with investment in compute. Held-out loss, finally, is a weak guide to closed-loop success. In the robomimic study, the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss performs significantly worse than the checkpoint with the highest rollout success (mandlekar2022matters).

Table 4.7: Selected evidence on scaling in robot learning and related domains

Study

Varied

Setting

Measured

4.5.3 What Robot-Learning Studies Show

Evidence for scaling in robot learning accumulates, but controlled studies remain rare. The cited meta-analysis of 327 papers finds that robot performance generally improves as a power law in data, model size, and compute, and that it improves faster than performance on language tasks (sartor2024neural). Because meta-analyses average over very different tasks and metrics, the clearest evidence comes from studies that vary one factor at a time, summarized in Table 4.7. Some of these studies measure loss rather than success. Pretraining studies of imitation policies and world models, for example, find language-like power laws in loss, with coefficients that depend on the tokenizer, task, and architecture (pearce2025agents).

The most consistent finding is that diversity matters more than volume. In a study of single-task imitation with handheld grippers, generalization to new environments and objects follows a rough power law in the number of environments and objects seen in training, while extra demonstrations in environments already covered stop helping beyond a threshold (lin2025datascaling). Guided by this finding, the study reports that 4 people collect enough data in one afternoon to train policies that succeed about 90% of the time on 2 tasks in new environments with unseen objects. Locomotion shows the same pattern across bodies. Adding procedurally generated embodiments to training improves generalization to unseen ones substantially more than adding data for a fixed set, and the best policy transfers zero-shot to real Unitree Go2 and H1 robots (Ai et al., 2025).

Broad pretraining pays off chiefly by making new tasks cheaper to learn. In the Toyota Research Institute’s study of large behavior models, evaluated in blind real and simulated trials, fine-tuning a pretrained model matches single-task training with 3 to 5 times less task data, and the advantage grows under distribution shift (Barreiros et al., 2026). Without fine-tuning, the pretrained model gives mixed results. Pretraining may also extend what a model can handle. In the first training phase of $\pi_{0.5}$ , 97.6% of the examples come from sources other than mobile manipulators working in homes, such as other robots and web data, yet the reported model controls mobile manipulators in homes that had not appeared in its training data (pi2025pi05).

The split of additional compute between model size and data has been measured directly in at least one physical domain. In motion forecasting and planning for driving, closed-loop metrics improve along with the loss as compute increases, and the compute-optimal model size grows 1.5 times as fast as the dataset (Baniodeh et al., 2025). Driving logs accumulate passively across a fleet and are far cheaper than manipulation data, so the result does not carry over directly, but it shows that the measurement can be made in a physical setting.

Industry now reports manipulation datasets far larger than academic ones. In a blog post, Generalist AI describes pretraining on more than 270,000 hours of real-world manipulation data (generalist2025gen0). It reports that the post-training validation error falls as a power law in the amount of pretraining data, and that roughly billion-parameter models stop improving with more data while seven-billion-parameter and larger models keep improving. These are prediction errors on the company’s own tasks rather than closed-loop success rates, and they have not been peer reviewed.

Precision imposes a different kind of limit. In the cited simulation study, the demonstration count $N_{\mathrm{demo}}$ needed for a fixed success rate is modeled by the empirical fit $\log N_{\mathrm{demo}}=m_{\mathrm{fit}}/(P_{\mathrm{tol}}-c_{\mathrm{lim}})+n_{\mathrm{fit}}$ , with fitted coefficients $m_{\mathrm{fit}}>0$ and $n_{\mathrm{fit}}$ . Here $P_{\mathrm{tol}}$ is the length tolerance and $c_{\mathrm{lim}}$ the fitted system limit. For $P_{\mathrm{tol}}>c_{\mathrm{lim}}$ , this fit predicts that $N_{\mathrm{demo}}$ diverges as $P_{\mathrm{tol}}$ approaches $c_{\mathrm{lim}}$ from above (xu2026precision). The limit depends on the whole system, and adding a wrist camera or using a better expert moves it toward finer precision. For such tasks, better sensing can pay off more than additional demonstrations.

All such curves are hard to measure precisely. Real-robot success rates are estimated from tens or hundreds of trials, so each point carries a wide confidence interval (Section 9.5) and a fitted exponent is loosely constrained. With that caveat, the evidence supports consistent gains from diversity across environments, objects, embodiments, and data sources, and from pretraining followed by fine-tuning. It does not yet establish universal exponents, compute-optimal model sizes for robot policies, or a dependable link between loss and closed-loop success.

Better evidence requires purpose-built experiments that vary the quantity and the diversity of data independently while keeping the training procedure fixed. Such experiments would report new trajectories apart from extra passes over old ones, evaluate on held-out conditions that stay the same between runs, and check predictions made from small runs against a larger run held in reserve. A plateau in such an experiment deserves attention in its own right, since it may point to missing sensing, an inadequate model, or an unsuitable objective instead of a shortage of data.
