4.5.4 Valuing and Curating Heterogeneous Data

Raw volume overstates what a dataset contains. Experience is nested, with frames inside trajectories, trajectories inside tasks and scenes, and scenes inside embodiments and sites, so counts of hours and frames treat many correlated samples as independent. This is why Section 4.2 measures collection by effective data yield, and scaling studies should likewise report growth in independent interactions and their spread over tasks, scenes, objects, and embodiments.

How many samples from one layer are worth one sample from another can be measured in specific settings. In the InternData-A1 study (Section 4.3), fewer than 1,600 simulated samples match the performance of 200 real ones on 4 tasks with closely aligned simulated and real setups, a ratio below 8:1 (tian2025interndata). EgoMimic’s hour-for-hour comparison, described above, gives a corresponding rate for human data. Both rates depend on how closely the source matches the task, on how much contact is involved, and on how the sources are weighted in training, and neither should be expected to hold elsewhere.

Curation can matter as much as collection. CUPID uses influence functions to estimate how a trained policy’s closed-loop return would change if a given demonstration were removed, and ranks every demonstration by its effect on performance (Agia et al., 2025a). On the simulated robomimic benchmark, training on less than a third of the data, selected in this way, produces diffusion policies that match the state of the art. Hardware experiments show similar gains. Related methods weight whole datasets, as Re-Mix does for Open X-Embodiment by choosing mixture weights that maximize worst-case performance across its constituent datasets (hejna2024remix), or score demonstrations by the mutual information between states and actions (hejna2025deminf). A scaling curve plotted against raw demonstration counts can therefore partly reflect how much harmful or redundant data a collection contains.

Knowing which kinds of diversity matter helps both collection and retrieval. A study using procedurally generated datasets with controlled composition identifies camera poses and the spatial arrangement of objects as the dimensions most relevant in that study, both for diversifying new collections and for retrieving relevant demonstrations from existing datasets. Retrieval guided by these findings raises the real-world performance of policies trained with DROID data by up to 70% (saxena2025matters).

Retrieval and curation presuppose that data can be found. A growing number of hubs collect robot datasets, and Table 4.8 lists some of the largest. Aggregators such as the LeRobot hub, Open X-Embodiment, and ARIO gather datasets in common formats, making cross-dataset training and retrieval practical, while large single-source collections offer consistent protocols at scale. Licenses and access conditions range from open to gated and non-commercial, and, as the documentation practices of Section 4.1 require, they should travel with any dataset derived from these sources.

4.5.5 Building a Data Flywheel

Flywheels have worked best where success can be detected cheaply, because the robot can then label its own experience. Large-scale autonomous collection on real robots therefore focuses on grasping in early studies, where a robot can tell by itself whether it is holding the object. One early study reports more than 800,000 grasp attempts on up to 14 robots (levine2018grasping), and the QT-Opt study uses more than 580,000 attempts to train a vision-based Q-function that grasps unseen objects with 96% success (kalashnikov2018qtopt). Where success is harder to judge, people or learned models have to supply the labels. Sirius-Fleet uses a visual world model to predict whether a robot’s upcoming actions are likely to fail and asks a human to intervene when they are. As the policy improves, the failure predictor adapts and requests for help become rarer (liu2024sirius).

Post-training has since moved to the fleet level. RECAP, used to train $\pi^{*}_{0.6}$ , combines demonstrations, autonomous experience, and expert corrections in batched offline reinforcement learning (Section 6.3) (Amin et al., 2026). SOP streams on-policy experience and intervention signals from a fleet to a central learner that runs either interactive imitation, in which humans correct the robot during execution, or RECAP (pan2026sop). In its experiments, the wall-clock time needed to reach 80% success falls from about 174 minutes with 1 robot to 127 with 2 and 72 with 4, a 2.4-fold speedup from 4 times as many robots. The human-in-the-loop methods of Section 4.2 are the short-cycle version of the same idea.

One iteration of such a loop can be written so that the three uses of real data become explicit. Let $\mathcal{D}_{k}$ be the accumulated training data at iteration $k$ , $\pi_{k}$ the current policy, $W_{k}^{\mathrm{sim}}$ the simulator or world model, and $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{eval}}$ a held-out evaluation set collected under conditions that training never sees. Then

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{k}^{\mathrm{data}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\operatorname{Collect}(\pi_{k},\mathcal{A}_{k}^{\mathrm{acq}}),$ 

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{k+1}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}_{k}\cup\operatorname{Curate}(\mathcal{B}_{k}^{\mathrm{data}}),$ 

 $\displaystyle(\tilde{\pi},W_{k+1}^{\mathrm{sim}})$ 
 $\displaystyle=\operatorname{TrainAndCalibrate}(\mathcal{D}_{k+1},W_{k}^{\mathrm{sim}}),$ 

 $\displaystyle\pi_{k+1}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\operatorname{Accept}(\tilde{\pi},\pi_{k};\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{eval}}),$ 

(4.6)

where $\mathcal{A}_{k}^{\mathrm{acq}}$ is the collection plan, $\operatorname{Curate}$ applies the quality gates of Section 4.2, and $\operatorname{Accept}$ keeps the candidate $\tilde{\pi}$ only if it outperforms $\pi_{k}$ in closed loop on $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{eval}}$ . Each batch $\mathcal{B}_{k}^{\mathrm{data}}$ feeds both policy training and, through the procedures of Section 4.4, the recalibration of $W_{k}^{\mathrm{sim}}$ , while $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{eval}}$ stays outside both. Even so, repeated acceptance decisions gradually fit the policy to $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{eval}}$ itself, so the evaluation set has to be refreshed from time to time, with a final set held back for reporting.

For the drawer fleet of Section 4.4, $\operatorname{Collect}$ in Eq. (4.6) uploads every operator takeover and every pull whose force profile leaves the expected envelope, while subsampling routine successes. $\operatorname{Curate}$ turns takeovers into recovery demonstrations attributed to the operator, $\operatorname{TrainAndCalibrate}$ retrains the policy and refits the drawer model, and $\operatorname{Accept}$ compares the result with the frozen previous version on held-out drawers at the failing site and at others. The release process that follows, including replay testing, staged deployment, and release gates, is described in Section 9.4.

4.5.6 Choosing What to Collect Next

Section 4.2 discusses how active sampling selects tasks and states within a collection campaign. At the level of the flywheel the choice is broader, because the next unit of effort may go to a new site, a calibration experiment, corrective demonstrations, a batch of simulated scenarios, or held-out trials for validation. A natural criterion is the expected improvement per unit cost,

 $x^{\star}=\argmax_{x}\;\frac{\mathbb{E}\bigl[\Delta J\mid x\bigr]}{c_{\mathrm{acq}}(x)},$ 

(4.7)

where $\Delta J$ is the resulting change in closed-loop performance on held-out conditions and $c_{\mathrm{acq}}(x)$ is the cost of collecting, curating, and learning from $x$ . Physical options are expensive, since resets take time and some trials carry risk. Synthetic options are cheaper but less certain to help. In practice, candidates are ranked with heuristic scores such as novelty, disagreement between models, gaps in coverage, and predicted failure (Agia et al., 2025b; xu2025faildetect). Each score can mislead. An unfamiliar background may look novel without adding any physical information, and persistent uncertainty may come from sensor noise instead of a gap the policy could learn to close (Section 10.5).

Since Eq. (4.7) can at best be approximated before training, a collection strategy has to be judged after the fact, by retraining on the selected data and testing the result. The comparison should be made at a matched budget against reasonable alternatives, in particular stratified sampling over known conditions. It should also include a frozen baseline evaluated under the same conditions (Section 12.1), so that a better strategy is not confused with a larger investment. All costs belong in the same account, from robot occupancy and resets to interventions, annotation, simulation, and training. For repeatable tasks, total cost per accepted output is a convenient summary. Flywheels complicate the comparison further, because each policy changes the data collected next and because hardware, sites, and operators drift between iterations.

The measurements that would settle the central questions of this chapter are still largely missing. Most published scaling curves for robot learning put demonstrations, hours, frames, or tokens on the horizontal axis. Few relate closed-loop capability to the total amount of real interaction, counting the simulation and human effort that come with it. Such curves would show whether the next robot-hour is better spent on training data, on calibration, or on evaluation. They would also show whether a flywheel is actually improving the system. Chapter 10 considers what it would take for loops of this kind to sustain open-ended growth in capability.

## 5 World Models

Previous chapters discuss how perception captures physical scenes at the current moment, and physical data record how it evolves over time (Chapter 4). With them, we can present a more comprehensive account of world modeling, which studies how an environment evolves over time and how external actions or interventions change that evolution. This is also an important step for the physical agent that will be discussed in the later section, as it helps a physical agent to predict, before acting, how the world will evolve and how its own action would change that evolution. Figure 5.1 illustrates this closed-loop interaction among the physical environment, the world model, and the querying agent. Within the technical stack of this book, world models build on the state-space formulations of Chapter 2, the perception of Chapter 3, and the data and simulation of Chapter 4 to provide action-conditioned predictions for the manipulation and whole-body control models in Chapters 6 to 7.

Figure 5.1: A world model as a compact, queryable description of how the environment can change. Solid arrows carry information available at deployment. The dashed arrow carries the observation correction that revises the internal state after each step. A particular model may expose only a subset of the four query interfaces

Based on this, this chapter frames physical world modeling in five parts. Section 5.1 establishes the conceptual framework (state, belief, query, and evidence) and clarifies what a world model is and is not. Section 5.2 surveys how the internal state is represented, ranging from generative observation-space models to latent dynamics, 3D and object-centric structures, and unified multimodal architectures. Section 5.3 develops training strategies, from self-supervised pretraining to action-conditioned and interaction-driven learning. Section 5.4 addresses how predictions are deployed and validated across forecast accuracy, physical consistency, and downstream decision utility. Section 5.5 concludes with open challenges and the long-term role of world models in Physical AI.

Additionally, A Definition and Roadmap for World Models organizes physical world modeling around finite-resource compression, local observation, asynchronous multimodal evidence, and the relationship between understanding and prediction (wmChen2026Roadmap). This perspective organizes the chapter’s discussion of current systems and future directions. The scope of the chapter includes robots, scientific instruments, and distributed physical processes rather than only visually observed manipulation.

## 5.1 Concepts and Theoretical Frameworks of World Models

World models are compact, queryable descriptions of how an environment can change. They are not required to reproduce every physical detail. Their purpose is to retain the distinctions needed by the questions that an agent must answer, including what is present, what is hidden, what will happen under an action, and which action is preferable. This section fixes the common vocabulary of state, transition, query, and evidence used throughout the chapter. A model is useful when these elements are connected and its claims can be checked against new observations.

5.1.1 Definition, Boundaries, and Basic Properties

Physical scenes contain objects, fields, energy, and interactions at many scales, while an agent has finite sensors, memory, and time. A world model therefore compresses observations into an internal state from which future states and task-relevant outputs can be queried. The compression is task-relative. A logo may be irrelevant when predicting whether a cup will spill, but essential when identifying a reagent. A lower-dimensional representation is not automatically a better one. It is better only when it preserves the distinctions needed by the intended queries.

The same visible image can correspond to different velocities, contact modes, temperatures, or internal masses. A stationary drawer can be unlocked or held by a latch, and the same pull then has different consequences. A world model must use history, interaction, and background conditions to maintain these hidden alternatives. Operationally, its functions include inference from evidence, conditional evolution over time, and readout of observations or physical and task quantities. These functions may be modular or share parameters. A particular model can expose only a subset of them, but its advertised interfaces should have testable meanings.

A Development Trajectory Organized by Underlying Problems

Three enduring questions explain the main technical lineages. First, how can an agent infer a sufficient state from incomplete measurements? State-space estimation and filtering make a distinction between an evolving state and its noisy observations. Kalman’s work provides a foundational linear formulation (Kalman1960). Second, how can an internal model improve action rather than merely fit observations? Dyna connects real experience, model learning, planning, and acting, so the learned model supplies additional experience for decision learning (wmSutton1991). Third, how can these functions operate on high-dimensional sensory data? Learned encoders and recurrent dynamics replace hand-specified state variables with representations shaped by prediction and control. The World Models architecture separates visual compression, temporal memory, and a controller. PlaNet performs planning through learned latent dynamics. Dreamer trains behavior using imagined latent trajectories (ha2018world; hafner2019planet; hafner2019dreamer).

These developments do not form a sequence in which each new architecture makes its predecessors obsolete. Explicit states remain useful when physical variables are measurable, generative models retain information for rich observation queries, and decision-oriented latent models can avoid reconstructing details that a task does not use. Recent multimodal and world-action models extend the same underlying questions to the sharing of semantic, predictive, and behavioral information. Their shared foundation is the connection among state inference, conditional prediction, and action learning. The discussion below compares implementations of these functions rather than presenting successive product generations.

Predictive Sufficiency Rather than a Miniature Copy of the World

The central abstraction is a state that preserves answers, not necessarily a state that reproduces every observation. Predictive state representations make this idea explicit by representing a controlled system through predictions of future observation tests rather than through a prescribed list of hidden variables (wmLittman2002). Learned embeddings, object states, and physical fields are different ways of approximating such predictive sufficiency. A useful idealized criterion is

 $p(y_{t+k}^{q_{\mathrm{query}}}\mid h_{t},A^{\mathrm{seq}},c)\approx p_{\Theta}(y_{t+k}^{q_{\mathrm{query}}}\mid E_{\phi}(h_{t},c),A^{\mathrm{seq}},c),\qquad q_{\mathrm{query}}\in\mathcal{Q},\;A^{\mathrm{seq}}\in\mathcal{A}_{H},$ 

(5.1)

where $\mathcal{Q}$ is the set of supported queries, $y_{t+k}^{q_{\mathrm{query}}}$ the outcome of query $q_{\mathrm{query}}$ at offset $k$ , $\mathcal{A}_{H}$ a declared set of input sequences over horizon $H$ , and $A^{\mathrm{seq}}$ one such externally supplied sequence. The history is $h_{t}$ , $c$ records known conditions, $E_{\phi}$ compresses history into an internal state, and $\Theta$ parameterizes the predictive distribution. The left side describes the environment under the specified experimental input protocol. The right side describes its learned approximation. This is a design criterion, not a guarantee of identifiability from passive recordings. Its tolerance, horizon, and query set must be stated.

The criterion explains why compression and generality trade off. A representation sufficient to decide whether a drawer opens can omit texture but must preserve the latch hypothesis. A representation intended to answer new visual questions may need much more detail. A state sufficient for ranking a particular policy’s actions need not be sufficient for estimating forces, synthesizing views, or optimizing a different objective. Broader query coverage therefore requires richer targets, retained evidence, or a mechanism for refining the representation on demand. Changes of latent coordinates do not change predictive capability when all interfaces transform consistently, so physically meaningful readouts matter more than requiring every latent coordinate to have a unique physical name.

Boundaries with Neighboring Systems

Several neighboring systems should be distinguished by their interfaces. A video generator can reproduce motion without correctly responding to a specified intervention. A physics engine advances a supplied state but need not infer that state from open-ended observations. A digital twin is tied to a particular physical counterpart, whereas a policy outputs actions without necessarily exposing conditional futures. Table 5.1 summarizes the distinctions used here. These are functional distinctions. One implementation may combine several rows, and a model’s name does not establish all the listed capabilities.

Table 5.1: Neighboring concepts and the capabilities their interfaces do not establish. The rows describe functions and may overlap within one system

System

Primary object

Typical interface

Not established by the interface alone

Video generator

Observations and temporal appearance

Images or videos under conditions

Correct interventions or physical quantities

Physics engine

Explicit state and physical dynamics

State propagation, contact, and forces

State inference from open observations

Digital twin

A specified physical counterpart

Monitoring, updating, and prediction

Transferable modeling across entities

Policy model

Goal-conditioned behavior

Actions, skills, or control targets

Independently queryable consequences

World model

Internal state and conditional evolution

Inference, prediction, and queries

A complete agent or controller

The state boundary must specify which variables are explicit, which are conditions, and which are unknown disturbances. Precision and horizon are part of this choice. A temperature interval can suffice for a safe-touch query but not for metrology. A short transport may treat material parameters as fixed while a long heating process cannot. Local boundaries also require attention to external inputs. A container can exchange heat and material with its surroundings. Missing measurements should remain marked as missing and should not create unjustified certainty. Claims of generality should state the tested state range, intervention interface, timescale, and query precision.

5.1.2 Internal State and Belief Updating Under Partial Observation

A POMDP distinguishes the environmental state, the actions applied to it, and the measurements available to an agent (Kaelbling1998). Let $s_{t}$ be the physical state at discrete index $t$ , $o_{t}$ a possibly multimodal observation, and $a_{t}$ the control input applied over the subsequent interval. Let $c$ denote the known embodiment, environment, and sensor conditions. Here a discrete index orders updates. It need not imply equally spaced measurements. The history $h_{t}=(o_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})$ contains observations and past inputs, with their timestamps and validity metadata understood. The belief over the hidden physical state is the conditional distribution

 $b_{t}(s)=p(s_{t}=s\mid h_{t},c).$ 

(5.2)

The argument $s$ is a possible state value. $b_{t}$ represents uncertainty about which value is current. A learned internal representation $z_{t}$ is distinct from $s_{t}$ . It may encode a point estimate, parameters of a distribution, or information sufficient for selected future queries. Calling a vector a belief does not by itself give it probabilistic semantics.

Belief maintenance alternates between prediction and correction. For a transition kernel $T$ and an observation likelihood $O$ , the Bayesian filtering recursion is

 $\displaystyle\widetilde{b}_{t+1}(s^{\prime})$ 
 $\displaystyle=\int T(s^{\prime}\mid s,a_{t},c,\Delta t)\,b_{t}(s)\,\mathrm{d}s,$ 

(5.3)

 $\displaystyle b_{t+1}(s^{\prime})$ 
 $\displaystyle=\frac{O(o_{t+1}\mid s^{\prime},c)\widetilde{b}_{t+1}(s^{\prime})}{\int O(o_{t+1}\mid u,c)\widetilde{b}_{t+1}(u)\,\mathrm{d}u},$ 

where $s^{\prime}$ is a candidate next state, $u$ a dummy integration variable, $\Delta t$ the elapsed physical time, and $\widetilde{b}_{t+1}$ the predictive prior before observing $o_{t+1}$ . The denominator normalizes the posterior when the observation has nonzero probability. Integrals become sums for discrete states. The recursion assumes a Markov state and an observation model conditionally independent of earlier history given that state and $c$ . Delays or actuator memory that violate these assumptions must be included in the state or conditioning record. Learned filters approximate this recursion rather than inheriting its correctness merely from architectural resemblance.

The distinction is concrete during grasping. If the gripper moves upward but the object remains on the table, the observation should revise the attachment hypothesis. If the camera is occluded, lack of visible motion need not mean a failed grasp. A delayed temperature reading belongs to its acquisition time, not its arrival time. Using it may require correcting an earlier state and propagating the correction through intervening actions. Asynchronous processing therefore requires temporal bookkeeping, not compulsory resampling of every sensor to one frequency.

Keeping alternatives separate can be more meaningful than averaging them. The mean of two possible object locations may lie inside an obstacle, and a mean of sticking and sliding contact is not a realizable contact mode. Partial-observation uncertainty concerns the current hidden state. Aleatoric uncertainty concerns variability unresolved at the chosen modeling level. Epistemic uncertainty concerns limited knowledge of model parameters or mechanisms (wmKendall2017). These categories can interact, and their decomposition depends on the state and sensor specification. Extra sensing may resolve a hidden contact, whereas collecting diverse interactions may reduce model error. Simply increasing the number of sampled futures addresses neither problem automatically.

5.1.3 Understanding-Oriented and Prediction-Oriented Objectives

Understanding is best stated as a set of testable abilities, including identifying entities and relations, recognizing operating modes, distinguishing variables that control subsequent change, and identifying what present evidence cannot determine. A fluent explanation is not sufficient. For example, a valve model must distinguish a command, the mechanical position, and the resulting flow. A grasp model must distinguish a closed gripper from a stable attachment. The understanding-prediction distinction in wmChen2026Roadmap provides a useful way to organize these requirements without treating them as mutually exclusive capabilities.

Prediction supplies a complementary pressure. Given a history and conditions, the model should produce a measurable future state, observation, or distribution. Copying a background and extrapolating smooth motion may solve short video prediction while ignoring contact. Longer horizons, action perturbations, and event-level targets test whether the state retains the missing distinctions. Distributional prediction matters when several qualitatively different outcomes remain possible. A single mean trajectory can represent none of them.

Reconstruction is a useful information diagnostic but not proof of understanding. DIAMOND demonstrates that visual detail can affect learned behavior in Atari, illustrating why discarding apparently minor observations may be harmful (Alonso et al., 2024). Conversely, a model can render a convincing container without connecting liquid level, acceleration, and spillage. Decision-oriented abstractions are legitimate when they preserve distinctions needed to compare actions. MuZero learns quantities needed for planning without requiring reconstruction of the original observation, showing that control sufficiency and observation reconstruction are different targets (wmSchrittwieser2020). Neither example establishes a universally preferred representation for physical modeling.

Understanding also requires separating reusable relations from accidental correlations. If every heavy training container is red, color may predict lifting success until the correlation changes. A useful representation should allow mass hypotheses to be revised after force feedback without having to change color identity. This example does not require every latent coordinate to have a human name. It requires an intervention-relevant distinction to remain available to downstream queries. Prediction and understanding can thus be mutual checks. An explanation proposes a testable consequence, while a prediction error exposes a missing variable or an inadequate transition.

Representation Learning, Forecasting, and Identification

These goals differ in the evidence they require. Representation learning can exploit correlations across regions or times. Forecasting must respect the observations available at its issue time. Identifying an intervention response additionally requires the action interface and relevant confounders to be accounted for. A passive video predictor can learn that a human usually opens a drawer after reaching toward it, while still being unable to distinguish a push from a pull applied by a robot. Likewise, fitting a trajectory does not uniquely identify mass and friction when several parameter combinations produce the same motion. An informative probe is one that makes these alternatives predict measurably different outcomes. This connects world modeling to state estimation and system identification, rather than treating physical knowledge as an automatic consequence of video scale.

Learning with a JEPA offers a complementary response to the information problem by predicting selected representations of observations rather than all their low-level details. LeCun’s architectural proposal places this idea within a larger system of perception, predictive modeling, memory, and action selection (lecun2022path). The reusable principle is selective prediction. Whether the selected information supports causal forecasting, planning, or physical explanation is determined by the conditioning, training data, and readout tests developed below.

5.1.4 Functional Roles, Query Interfaces, and System Positioning

The role of a world model is determined by the questions it answers. An observation query produces a sensor-like output. A state query returns objects, relations, or physical quantities. A transition query predicts an action’s consequences. And a decision-related query estimates reward, constraint violation, or task success. Figure 5.1 assembles these roles into a reference architecture. A compact conceptual implementation is

 $\displaystyle z_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=E_{\phi}(h_{t},c),\qquad\widehat{z}_{t+1}\sim T_{\theta}(\cdot\mid z_{t},a_{t},c,\Delta t),$ 

(5.4)

 $\displaystyle\widehat{o}_{t+1}$ 
 $\displaystyle\sim O_{\omega_{\mathrm{obs}}}(\cdot\mid\widehat{z}_{t+1},c),\qquad\widehat{y}_{t+1}=Q_{\psi}(\widehat{z}_{t+1},g,c),$ 

where $E_{\phi}$ is a history encoder, $T_{\theta}$ a learned transition, $O_{\omega_{\mathrm{obs}}}$ an observation decoder, and $Q_{\psi}$ a task readout. Their subscripts denote parameter sets, which may overlap in a shared network. The goal or query specification is $g$ , $y$ is the requested task quantity, a hat denotes a prediction, and $\sim$ denotes sampling. $Q_{\psi}$ is a generic query head, not necessarily an action-value function. Eq. (5.4) is an interface-level synthesis of state-space and learned-model formulations, not a requirement that these functions be separate networks (Kaelbling1998; hafner2019planet).

In the figure, the history encoder $E_{\phi}$ compresses the observation-action history $h_{t}$ and known conditions $c$ into the internal state $z_{t}$ , which approximates the belief $b_{t}(s)$ over the hidden physical state. The prediction-correction update keeps hidden alternatives separate. The learned transition $T_{\theta}$ then rolls out imagined latent states $\widehat{z}_{t+1},\ldots,\widehat{z}_{t+H}$ under a candidate action sequence, and the readouts $O_{\omega_{\mathrm{obs}}}$ and $Q_{\psi}$ answer observation, state, transition, and decision queries over the inferred state and the imagined rollout. Figure 5.1 also makes two boundaries explicit. The first separates inference from imagination. The internal state is updated from real observations only at the correction step, whereas the rollout is advanced by the learned transition alone and accumulates model error with horizon. The second separates the model from its consumer. Readouts answer queries over the inferred state and the imagined futures, but the scoring of candidate actions and the choice of the applied $a_{t}$ belong to the agent or planner. A model may support transition and decision queries without an observation decoder. Evaluation should follow the query interfaces it exposes.

This decomposition helps localize failure. A wrong rendered texture with a correct measured trajectory suggests a decoding problem. A wrong contact event suggests a state or dynamics problem. A correct prediction that never influences action suggests a decision-interface problem. Such diagnoses are hypotheses to test, since errors may also propagate across modules.

The world model can sit inside a model-predictive controller, provide training-time imagination to a policy, supply predictive features to an action model, or expose a shared state service to several agents. The surrounding loop remains perception, state inference, prediction, decision, execution, and feedback. Actions change both the world and the observations available next. This connects the chapter to physical data acquisition in Chapter 4 and to the foundation-model and motor-control interfaces in Chapters 6 to 7. World modeling is one component of Physical AI. Sensing, actuation, safety, and recovery do not follow automatically from a predictive network.

The remaining sections separate four questions concerning how information is represented, how parameters are learned, how predictions are used and verified, and how the full loop can improve. In particular, training with future observations, predicting future observations at runtime, and executing actions with real feedback are different operations. This chapter makes their information boundaries explicit throughout.

## 5.2 Representations and Architectures of World Models

No single representation dominates all physical queries. Observation generators retain visible detail, latent dynamics can reduce imagination cost, and structured three-dimensional or object-centric states make entities and relations explicit. These are composable design routes rather than disjoint model classes. Following the distinction between functional and architectural taxonomies in wmChen2026Roadmap, it is useful to ask separately what is predicted, how dynamics are represented, which functions share computation, and which modules run at deployment. A diffusion model can operate over pixels, compressed video latents, or object states. A geometric representation can support both rendering and planning. And any of these can be coupled to a policy.

Figure 5.2 organizes representative world models along two complementary dimensions of functional role and architectural representation. The functional axis distinguishes rendering observations, simulating state evolution, and generating actions for decision making. The architectural axis distinguishes observation-level generation, structured world representations, and latent-space dynamics. These categories are not mutually exclusive. A model family may span several functions, and a system may combine multiple representational choices.

Figure 5.2: Two-dimensional taxonomy of representative world models. The vertical axis distinguishes functional roles. Renderers produce observations, simulators predict states, and planners produce actions. The horizontal axis distinguishes architectural routes, including observation-level generative models, 3D or structured world representations, and latent-space dynamics models. Spanning regions indicate model families or systems that support multiple roles or combine representational choices. World-action models (WAMs) couple predictive modeling with action generation. Placement is schematic rather than a performance ranking. Planning capability may depend on additional policy or search components

5.2.1 Generative Architectures in Observation Space

An observation-oriented model predicts images, video, audio, or other sensor streams. For an externally specified action sequence, a causal autoregressive factorization is

 $p_{\theta}(o_{1:N_{\mathrm{step}}}\mid o_{0},a_{0:N_{\mathrm{step}}-1},c)=\prod_{t=0}^{N_{\mathrm{step}}-1}p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid o_{0:t},a_{0:t},c),$ 

(5.5)

where $N_{\mathrm{step}}$ is the final sequence index, $\theta$ the model parameters, and $i{:}j$ an inclusive sequence of indices. The elapsed times are included in $c$ for this expression. Each action is aligned to the interval in which it acts. The equation assumes that future prescribed actions do not affect earlier observations. With actions selected in response to future measurements, conditioning retrospectively on the entire executed action sequence can reveal additional information. Such observational conditioning is not automatically equivalent to an intervention.

Tokenization and Generative Mechanism

Autoregressive models predict a sequence of discrete or continuous tokens from preceding context. Their ordering makes causal rollout natural, but generating many spatial and temporal tokens can require substantial sequential computation. Diffusion and flow-based models instead generate a frame or chunk through iterative denoising or transport, enabling parallel updates within the chunk while requiring multiple network evaluations. Chunkwise generation combines these choices. Chunks advance causally in physical time, while tokens within each chunk can interact bidirectionally. Physical rollout time and the artificial denoising time are different axes. Section 5.3.1 defines the corresponding training objectives.

An observation-oriented generator need not perform all computation in pixel coordinates. A variational autoencoder (VAE) can compress observations, a generative model can predict the compressed variables, and a decoder can reconstruct the output. Latent diffusion demonstrates this division between perceptual compression and generative computation (wmRombach2022). It reduces the number of generated elements but does not, by itself, turn video latents into a sufficient physical state. The architectural distinction from an abstract latent-dynamics model concerns the representation’s role and supervision, not whether a tensor is called a latent.

Conditioning and Interaction

Genie learns latent controls from videos and uses them for interactive generation, whereas UniSim learns conditional real-world video simulation from heterogeneous data (bruce2024genie; yang2024unisim). These examples illustrate different intervention interfaces. A latent action inferred from visual changes is not automatically a robot command. Camera motion, actor motion, and object motion can be confounded. Executable control requires a mapping to an embodiment and verification of the resulting response. Language can specify desired behavior, but the same sentence may leave force, speed, contact, and timing unspecified.

Observation generation is useful when detail matters for perception, when imagined data will train a visual policy, or when a person must inspect a predicted future. Its limitations include high spatial cost, temporal drift, and the possibility of replacing a wrong state with a plausible texture. A video of a drawer opening should be checked for the commanded displacement, latch state, object identity, and occluded contents, not only visual sharpness. Multiple rendered views are valuable only when they describe a compatible underlying scene. These requirements motivate persistent latent states, geometric structure, and action-grounded supervision rather than ruling out generative prediction.

Broad Video Priors and Spatially Indexed Memory

Cosmos illustrates how pretrained video models, tokenizers, and data processing can form a reusable platform for physical-AI adaptation (nvidia2025cosmos). Such a prior can supply appearance and motion regularities before task-specific action data are available. Its contribution is different from learning the calibrated response of a particular actuator. Downstream conditioning and validation must establish that interface. This separation between broad pretraining and local grounding remains useful as individual video backbones change.

Persistent visual context can also be organized spatially rather than only as a recent temporal window. World Labs’ RTFM uses an autoregressive diffusion frame model with camera poses and retrieval of relevant posed frames as spatial memory (wmWorldLabs2025RTFM). It illustrates a learned rendering route that need not construct an explicit mesh at every update. Revisiting a place queries stored evidence about that place rather than forcing an ever-growing sequence through a fixed context window. Camera-conditioned view generation, however, primarily specifies how observation changes with viewpoint. Controlling a camera and predicting an object’s response to force are distinct interfaces. This distinction is important when a navigable generated world is later used for interaction.

5.2.2 Latent-Space Dynamics Architectures

Latent models encode observation history and propagate a compact state. A generic form is

 $\displaystyle z_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=E_{\phi}(h_{t},c),\qquad\widehat{z}_{t}=z_{t},$ 

(5.6)

 $\displaystyle\widehat{z}_{t+k+1}$ 
 $\displaystyle\sim T_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\widehat{z}_{t+k},a_{t+k},c,\Delta t_{k}),$ 

 $\displaystyle\widehat{y}_{t+k+1}$ 
 $\displaystyle=Q_{\psi}(\widehat{z}_{t+k+1},g,c),\quad k=0,\ldots,H-1,$ 

where $H$ is the rollout horizon, $\Delta t_{k}$ the duration of its $k$ th interval, $E_{\phi}$ the history encoder, and $Q_{\psi}$ the query readout. The symbols $z$ and $\widehat{z}$ distinguish inferred and imagined states. $y$ may be an observation, reward, physical variable, or event. The readout can be omitted during intermediate rollout steps. A useful state preserves the conditional distribution of the intended queries. Histories merged into one representation should not demand incompatible answers after the same future input. A recently heated vessel and a long-cooled one may look alike while requiring different temperature forecasts.

Generative State-Space Models

PlaNet combines deterministic recurrent memory with stochastic latent variables, while Dreamer uses learned latent dynamics to train an actor and critic through imagination (hafner2019planet; hafner2019dreamer). A recurrent component can retain predictable history, and stochastic variables can represent outcomes that remain uncertain. Training distinguishes a prior predicted without the next observation from an approximate posterior corrected by that observation. Reconstruction and auxiliary targets encourage informative states. Prior-posterior regularization makes them predictable. Overly strong regularization can suppress observation information, whereas a weakly trained prior can fail when real frames are absent. The loss and its multi-step extensions are developed in Section 5.3.

JEPA: Predicting in a Learned Target Space

A JEPA relates a context representation to a target representation through a predictor. Its defining choice is the prediction target, not a particular recurrent layer, transformer size, or policy head. I-JEPA learns image representations by predicting target-region embeddings from visible context. It is a spatial representation learner, not by itself an action-conditioned temporal simulator (Assran et al., 2023). V-JEPA extends feature prediction to masked spatiotemporal regions of video, using a predictor and a slowly updated target encoder rather than a pixel-reconstruction objective (Bardes et al., 2024). In both cases, what is hidden and what remains visible determine whether the task teaches spatial completion, temporal interpolation, or future anticipation.

V-JEPA 2 connects large-scale action-free representation learning to a separately post-trained action-conditioned latent predictor. Its planning variant uses robot observations, proprioception, and recorded actions to predict future features, then evaluates candidate actions against an image goal in representation space (Assran et al., 2025). Recorded interactions ground the predictor in robot actions. Self-supervision constructs targets from these records without task-success annotations or a hand-designed reward for each training example.

The architectural advantage is that a predictor can avoid synthesizing every unpredictable texture while retaining information useful for recognition or control. The corresponding obligation is to show that contacts, relative motion, object identity, and material cues have survived the target representation. A deterministic embedding forecast need not describe the distribution of possible futures, and its distance to a goal need not be a calibrated measure of physical reachability. Observation reconstruction and predictive embeddings are therefore complementary choices. A model can learn from both, or attach an optional decoder without making rendering a prerequisite for each decision. Section 5.3.1 develops the target update and loss, while Section 5.4.3 discusses tests that do not privilege models with a visual decoder.

Decision-Oriented Abstraction and State Maintenance

MuZero and TD-MPC-style systems emphasize reward, value, or latent consistency sufficient for decision making rather than unrestricted observation queries (wmSchrittwieser2020; wmHansen2024). DreamerV3 retains a generative latent model while improving robustness of model and behavior learning across different domains through normalization and loss balancing (wmHafner2023DreamerV3). These examples distinguish the choice of representation from the numerical techniques needed to train it reliably. A small state is efficient only if it preserves the distinctions required by the objective. Changing the goal or downstream query can expose previously harmless information loss.

Latent coordinates need not correspond one-to-one to physical quantities. A feature from which mass can be decoded may still entangle mass with shape, and an arbitrary coordinate edit need not realize a meaningful mass intervention. A history encoder should also distinguish an observation-corrected state from one propagated without new evidence. Its memory may be recurrent, attention-based, spatially retrieved, or hierarchically summarized. What matters is whether the representation preserves consequential hidden alternatives through occlusion and updates them when new evidence arrives. Tests should compare posterior updates, pure open-loop prediction, and feedback-interleaved prediction at the same physical horizons.

5.2.3 3D, 4D, and Object-Centric Architectures

Structured states make geometry, entities, and relations directly queryable. They can use occupancy or bird’s-eye grids, object slots, scene graphs, particles, meshes, or continuous fields. Their relation to world modeling depends on the associated transition. A static 3D reconstruction supports novel views but does not specify what a push will do. A 4D reconstruction describes temporal observations but may not predict a new intervention. The spatial perception methods in Chapter 3 become a world-model substrate when they are connected to evolving attributes, interactions, and conditional prediction.

Object-centric methods allocate separate representations to entities and model their interactions. Slot Attention provides a mechanism for learning object-centric representations from observations (wmLocatello2020). Graph-network simulators and MeshGraphNets illustrate dynamics expressed through local interactions among particles or mesh elements (sanchezgonzalez2020learning; wmPfaff2021). These structures can make interaction locality and changes in object count easier to express than an undifferentiated global vector. However, the structure is an inductive bias, not a guarantee. Learned slots may exchange identities, an object may split or merge, and contact can change the interaction graph discontinuously.

Geometry and physical attributes should be distinguished. Shape alone does not identify mass, friction, stiffness, temperature, or internal contents. A deformable state may need both configuration and a constitutive description. A liquid requires boundary conditions and appropriate conservation accounting. PhysGaussian couples Gaussian-based rendering with continuum-mechanics simulation, illustrating how visual representation and physical evolution can share a substrate within a specified regime (wmXie2024). The same representation must still be supplied with suitable physical parameters and verified against the intended materials and interactions.

Hybrid representations can assign different resolutions to different objects or processes. A rigid container may be represented as an object, while its contents are a field or a small set of effective variables. A coarse query could ask whether spilling is likely. A fine query might require the flow near an outlet. Expanding the representation only where the query requires it is a plausible way to balance cost and detail. The levels must share coordinate frames, identity, units, boundary fluxes, and physical time so that a coarse state is compatible with a refined prediction.

The structured route is attractive for metric queries, contact reasoning, and compositional changes. It introduces costs in reconstruction, correspondence, annotation, and numerical integration, and it may inherit a simulator’s modeling assumptions. A representation built around rigid objects can fail on cloth or fragmentation. A fixed field resolution can miss thin contacts. Validation should test identity through occlusion, changed topology, altered parameters, and action-dependent response. Structured models can be combined with learned latent residuals and generative observation heads, rather than being treated as alternatives to neural representation learning.

Hierarchies, Fields, and Physical-Prediction Structure

The Hierarchical Relation Network (HRN), developed by Mrowca and colleagues, represents bodies with hierarchies of particles and learns their interactions through graph-based computation (wmMrowca2018). Its lasting contribution is the separation of local interactions from larger-scale object structure, allowing rigid and deformable dynamics to share a representation without pretending that all objects are single rigid slots. Hierarchical modeling can reduce the distance over which information must propagate, but the useful grouping and coupling still depend on the physical process. The related Physion evaluation program tests future object contact across varied physical scenarios and distinguishes learning from images from prediction with privileged state (wmBear2021Physion). It provides an empirical counterpart to the architectural question of which state distinctions are needed to forecast an event.

Continuous-field models broaden the scope beyond articulated robots and discrete objects. Fourier neural operators learn mappings between parameter or input fields and solution fields for families of partial differential equations (wmLi2021FNO). They can serve as components for fluid, thermal, or other distributed-process predictions. A field-to-solution surrogate need not include perception, uncertainty, or an action policy. It supplies one transition or query component of a larger world model. Generalization across spatial resolution also differs from generalization across boundary conditions or physical regimes. Coupling a learned field solver to objects requires consistent interfaces for forces, fluxes, time, and units.

Persistent Spatial Generation and Multimodal Reconstruction

The spatial-intelligence route associated with World Labs should be distinguished from, rather than conflated with, the physical-dynamics work above. Marble generates persistent, editable 3D environments from multimodal prompts and supports explicit scene outputs (wmWorldLabs2025Marble). It illustrates the value of a scene that can be revisited and queried from different viewpoints, instead of a sequence whose geometry is reconstructed anew at every frame. The public Atlas description further combines text, posed images, and depth within a shared spatial context using an autoregressive diffusion architecture, with reconstruction and space-time generation interfaces (worldlabs2026atlas). These are developer-described systems. Their available interfaces should not be expanded into unsupported claims about arbitrary contact dynamics or physical precision.

The underlying distinction is between reconstructing evidence, completing unobserved regions, and evolving a state under interventions. A model may do all three, but their outputs carry different evidential status. Adding real views can constrain a previously imagined region. Creating a visually plausible hidden room does not measure that room. An explicit 3D scene can supply geometry for a simulator while leaving collision properties, mass, and material parameters to be assigned or identified. Conversely, an implicit renderer can maintain useful spatial consistency without exposing a simulation-ready mesh. The choice of explicit or implicit representation should therefore follow the required queries, not a blanket identification of 3D output with physical understanding.

5.2.4 Unified Multimodal and Cross-Paradigm Architectures

Unification concerns several different design decisions, including sharing an input interface, sharing a representation, learning multiple objectives together, and executing multiple functions in one runtime. A system may unify one level while retaining separate modules at another. Describing the level of unification is more informative than calling the entire architecture unified.

Multimodal Evidence and Representation Sharing

Vision, touch, proprioception, sound, temperature, and process readings can update a common state while retaining modality-specific noise and timing. Fusion can occur at the input, in intermediate state representations, or at query time. Early fusion preserves rich interactions but couples token budgets and preprocessing. Separate encoders with state-level exchange preserve sensor-specific processing while introducing alignment interfaces. Query-time fusion is modular but can lose information already discarded by each encoder. In a lifting task, disagreement between vision and torque may indicate an incorrect mass hypothesis, a grasp failure, or a sensor fault. Averaging the signals into an unexplained scalar is not a solution.

Understanding and generation also have different representational needs. Show-o combines autoregressive and diffusion-based modeling within a unified transformer. BAGEL studies shared multimodal understanding and generation with specialized representational pathways (wmXie2025Showo; wmDeng2025). These attempts show that shared processing need not require identical tokenizers or identical prediction targets. They motivate joint semantic and generative learning, but successful image understanding and synthesis do not independently verify a model’s response to physical interventions.

Coupling Future Prediction and Action Generation

Let $A_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}=a_{t:t+H_{\mathrm{a}}-1}$ denote an action chunk of length $H_{\mathrm{a}}$ , and let $F_{t}^{\mathrm{future}}=o_{t+1:t+H_{\mathrm{o}}}$ denote future observations over $H_{\mathrm{o}}$ observation steps. A statistical joint model admits the factorizations

 $\displaystyle p_{\Theta}(A_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}},F_{t}^{\mathrm{future}}\mid h_{t},g,c)$ 
 $\displaystyle=p_{\Theta}(A_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}\mid h_{t},g,c)\,p_{\Theta}(F_{t}^{\mathrm{future}}\mid A_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}},h_{t},g,c)$ 

(5.7)

 $\displaystyle=p_{\Theta}(F_{t}^{\mathrm{future}}\mid h_{t},g,c)\,p_{\Theta}(A_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}\mid F_{t}^{\mathrm{future}},h_{t},g,c),$ 

where $\Theta$ denotes the model’s parameters. The action and observation horizons must refer to compatible physical intervals even when their sample counts differ. The first factorization suggests action proposal followed by consequence prediction. The second suggests a future subgoal followed by inverse-dynamics action generation. An observed conditional distribution is not automatically an interventional model, and an attractive generated goal is not necessarily reachable.

Unified World Models (UWM) couples video and action diffusion with independent modality-specific noise levels, using the conditioning pattern to obtain policy, forward-dynamics, inverse-dynamics, and video-generation interfaces (zhu2025uwm). This illustrates how the same parameter set can support different queries when the training distribution and masks explicitly cover those queries. It does not imply that every joint generator reliably supports every conditional query. A cascaded design is easier to inspect but can compound errors and latency. A jointly sampled design enables stronger coupling but must control incompatible objectives and future-information leakage.

DreamZero supplies another representative use of a pretrained video prior for joint future-video and action modeling (ye2026dreamzero). Together with UWM, it illustrates a broad design axis in which action supervision can shape a model of anticipated observations instead of being added only to a static visual encoder. The systems need not share the same architecture, sampling procedure, or adaptation protocol. OpenWAM’s composable framework makes this distinction explicit by separating prediction, action generation, their interaction structure, and inference choices for controlled comparison (wang2026openwam). Its methodological lesson is to compare one interface choice at a time, rather than attributing every difference between complete systems to “world modeling.”

A third route uses future supervision to shape a representation available from present evidence, without generating future observations during deployment. InternVLA-A1.5 trains foresight tokens through a frozen video model and removes the video branch at inference (wmMa2026A15). InternW0- $\Delta$ combines a video expert, an action expert, frozen VLM semantics, and training-only 4D distillation. Causal Imprint connects future-derived supervision to observation-conditioned action features (wmMiao2026Delta). Such systems unify predictive learning with action generation without requiring a full future rollout for every policy call.

Expert Specialization and Runtime Organization

A mixture-of-transformers can retain separate parameters and token streams while allowing masked attention between experts. The mask specifies which observations, predicted variables, and action tokens can influence one another. Shared attention does not imply unrestricted bidirectional access. A cache can be reused across action-denoising steps only if its inputs and all upstream dependencies remain unchanged. Architectural independence, gradient isolation during training, and asynchronous execution are three distinct properties.

InternW0 illustrates a complementary runtime design in which slower video prediction supplies cached context, and a faster action expert adapts that context to recent observations through an observation-conditioned routing interface (wmCai2026InternW0). This differs from training away the future generator. In InternW0- $\Delta$ , future-video tokens are omitted at inference, but the video expert still processes observed context and Causal Imprint once before action-only denoising (wmMiao2026Delta). Neither arrangement should be summarized simply as “the video module is free.” Their evidence boundaries are taken up again when decision utility is evaluated in Section 5.4.4.

Comparative Strengths and Composable Choices

Table 5.2 compares the four routes by what they make convenient, what they cost, and what must be validated. The entries describe tendencies, not universal performance rankings. Actual cost depends on backbone size, representation resolution, number of sampling steps, and deployment implementation.

Table 5.2: Architectural routes, practical trade-offs, and principal validation questions. The routes are composable. Multimodal unification is also a cross-cutting organization choice

Route

Main cost or limitation

Critical validation

Observation generation

A design can therefore combine an object-centric state, latent stochastic transitions, an optional video decoder, and a policy trained from future supervision. The right combination is determined by the required queries and evidence. Cross-query consistency is useful. Rendering a state and re-estimating it should preserve relevant quantities. However, two heads can share the same bias, so their agreement is not independent physical validation. Section 5.5 returns to hierarchical, multi-timescale, and selectively activated architectures as future directions rather than treating a single fully shared backbone as inevitable.

Reading Representative Work Through Common Design Questions

Table 5.3 summarizes representative implementations of the preceding principles. It is a map of mechanisms, not an exhaustive catalog or a ranking. A new model can be located by its retained state, supervisory target, intervention interface, and deployed computation without adding a new supposedly disjoint category for every paper.
