The table also exposes missing interfaces. An image representation learner still needs a temporal, action-conditioned predictor to support control queries. A persistent scene generator still needs dynamics for manipulation. And a successful policy still needs separate tests before being used as a general predictive simulator. These are opportunities for composition, not reasons to exclude the corresponding lines of research from world modeling.

## 5.3 Training World Models

Training must make the internal state useful for future queries rather than merely reconstruct familiar observations. A complete account specifies the data available to each objective, the variables predicted, the parameters updated, the rollout horizon, and the information excluded from deployment. Representation learning, dynamics learning, policy learning, physical constraints, and uncertainty estimation solve related but different problems. Their combination is a design choice, not one mandatory loss shared by all world models.

A practical training program can start from scratch, adapt pretrained components in stages, or connect frozen specialists through learned interfaces. Broad observation pretraining supplies reusable visual and temporal structure. Action-conditioned training grounds intervention semantics. Downstream post-training adapts the model to a task or embodiment. Interaction-driven updates address the states reached by the deployed system. Some systems combine these stages, and some do not require all of them. PlaNet illustrates joint latent-model learning, V-JEPA 2 separates broad representation learning from action-conditioned post-training, and UWM combines predictive and behavioral supervision within a shared generative framework (hafner2019planet; Assran et al., 2025; zhu2025uwm). Figure 5.3 summarizes this landscape by showing the entry points along the top, the data sources on the left, the four training stages in the center, and the world-action interfaces on the right.

Figure 5.3: Training world models. Three entry points (top) lead into a staged training pipeline (center), fed by the data sources of Chapter 4 (left). Interaction-driven updates retrain on the states reached by the deployed system, closing the loop through new data. The right panel defines the world-action interfaces as attention masks over observed-context ( $\mathrm{C}$ ), action ( $\mathrm{A}$ ), and future-observation ( $\mathrm{F}$ ) tokens

The data foundations are developed in Chapter 4. Their training consequences differ. Action-free videos can supervise observation or representation prediction. Recorded controls can supervise action-conditioned transitions. Demonstrations can supervise a policy. And simulator states, force readings, or teacher features provide additional targets with distinct provenance. A valid failed trajectory can teach dynamics and outcomes without being an appropriate nominal imitation target. Missing channels must be masked rather than treated as measured zeros.

The four stages in the center of Figure 5.3 carry different objectives. Broad observation pretraining applies masked reconstruction, autoregressive likelihood, diffusion or flow, and feature-prediction targets, with an exponential-moving-average teacher where the target representation must stay stable. World-action learning adds forward, inverse, and behavioral targets on recorded interaction. Downstream post-training adapts the model to a task and embodiment. And interaction-driven updates retrain on the states the deployed system actually reaches. That last stage closes the loop only through new data, which is what distinguishes continual improvement from repeated fitting of a fixed corpus. In the right panel, the forward mode predicts $\widehat{\mathrm{F}}$ from $\mathrm{C}$ and $\mathrm{A}$ , the inverse mode predicts $\widehat{\mathrm{A}}$ from $\mathrm{C}$ and $\mathrm{F}$ , and the policy mode predicts $\widehat{\mathrm{A}}$ from $\mathrm{C}$ only, with the future-to-action path masked out as a leakage route (red cross). In all three modes the context rows are barred from reading $\mathrm{F}$ , so the context representation remains a pure function of observed evidence even when the action query may consult the future. These interfaces are reading modes over the same token groups, selected by attention masks, rather than three separate models. One network can be trained to serve all of them provided the masks are enforced exactly, as Section 5.3.2 discusses. The deployment-ready model is then an inference pass with all training-only branches absent.

5.3.1 Self-Supervised and Generative Representation Learning

Self-supervised objectives extract structure from observations without requiring every physical variable to be annotated. Temporal prediction, masked reconstruction, contrastive discrimination, and target-representation prediction impose different information bottlenecks. A reconstruction target retains observable detail. A feature target retains distinctions present in its encoder. A temporal target encourages information predictive over its selected horizon. None automatically identifies mass, contact, or causality when the observations do not distinguish them.

Autoregressive Likelihood and Masked Reconstruction

Let $x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N_{\mathrm{tok}}})$ be a target sequence of $N_{\mathrm{tok}}$ tokens, $\kappa$ the available conditioning information, and $\mathcal{D}$ the training distribution. A maximum-likelihood objective is

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AR}}=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,\kappa)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{tok}}}\log p_{\theta}(x_{i}\mid x_{<i},\kappa)\right].$ 

(5.8)

The index $i$ orders tokens, $x_{<i}$ contains preceding target tokens, and $\theta$ denotes trainable parameters. The conditioning can include past observations, a goal, and supplied actions, depending on the advertised query. Discrete tokens yield cross-entropy training. Continuous outputs require an explicit conditional density. During teacher-forced training, preceding targets are real tokens, whereas free generation conditions on the model’s own outputs. Thus a low teacher-forced loss does not establish stable recursive prediction.

Masked reconstruction instead withholds selected spatial or temporal observations and predicts them from visible context. A mask that reveals observations on both sides of a hidden frame trains interpolation or smoothing, not causal future prediction. Such supervision can still be valuable for representation pretraining, but a causal predictor needs a corresponding future-blind training or adaptation stage. The mask pattern, temporal window, and conditioning availability should be recorded alongside the loss.

Diffusion and Flow-Matching Objectives

For a clean continuous target $\mathbf{x}$ , a noise-prediction diffusion loss takes the form

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{x}^{(j)}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{j}}\,\mathbf{x}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{j}}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\qquad\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}),$ 

(5.9)

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{diff}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\kappa,j,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left[w_{j}\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(j)},j,\kappa)-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right],$ 

where $j$ indexes artificial noise levels, $\bar{\alpha}_{j}$ is the retained signal fraction, $\mathbf{I}$ the identity covariance, $w_{j}$ a nonnegative loss weight, and $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}$ the learned noise predictor. The expectation samples targets, conditions, noise levels, and Gaussian noise. This is a conditional adaptation of denoising diffusion training (wmHo2020). The physical timestep remains distinct from $j$ . Predicting clean data or a different noise-data combination changes the parameterization and weighting, not the underlying requirement to learn a conditional distribution.

A simple flow-matching construction uses the following linear data-to-noise path

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{x}^{\sigma_{\mathrm{flow}}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=(1-\sigma_{\mathrm{flow}})\mathbf{x}+\sigma_{\mathrm{flow}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\qquad\sigma_{\mathrm{flow}}\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1],$ 

(5.10)

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\kappa,\sigma_{\mathrm{flow}},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left[\left\|\mathbf{v}_{\theta}^{\mathrm{flow}}(\mathbf{x}^{\sigma_{\mathrm{flow}}},\sigma_{\mathrm{flow}},\kappa)-(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\mathbf{x})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right],$ 

where $\sigma_{\mathrm{flow}}$ is continuous artificial time, $\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]$ the uniform distribution, and $\mathbf{v}_{\theta}^{\mathrm{flow}}$ a learned velocity field in the target space. The target velocity is $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\mathbf{x}$ under this convention. Sampling starts at noise and integrates from $\sigma_{\mathrm{flow}}=1$ toward $0$ . Reversing the path convention reverses the velocity sign. This is a representative conditional flow-matching objective, not a unique choice of path or solver (wmLipman2023).

The target $\mathbf{x}$ can be a future-video latent, an action chunk, or a structured physical quantity. Video and action branches can have separate noise levels and masks, as in UWM (zhu2025uwm). This allows examples with missing action labels to train the video objective without fabricating control supervision. Tokenization and normalization determine how the squared loss weights different channels. An angular coordinate, translation, and contact force should not compete merely according to their raw numerical scales. Fewer inference steps lower cost but introduce a solver and approximation trade-off that must be measured at the task interface.

Stochastic State-Space Representation Learning

A generative latent model must learn both an observation-informed posterior and a prior that can advance without new observations. For clarity, consider a fixed initial latent $z_{0}$ , a Markov prior $p_{\theta}(z_{t}\mid z_{t-1},a_{t-1},c)$ , an observation likelihood $O_{\omega_{\mathrm{obs}}}(o_{t}\mid z_{t},c)$ , and a filtering variational distribution $q_{\phi}(z_{t}\mid z_{t-1},h_{t},c)$ . A representative sequence objective is

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SSM}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\sum_{t=1}^{N_{\mathrm{step}}}\Big[$ 
 $\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(z_{1:t}\mid h_{t},c,z_{0})}[-\log O_{\omega_{\mathrm{obs}}}(o_{t}\mid z_{t},c)]$ 

(5.11)

 $\displaystyle+\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}\,\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(z_{1:t-1}\mid h_{t-1},c,z_{0})}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_{\phi}(z_{t}\mid z_{t-1},h_{t},c)\,\|\,p_{\theta}(z_{t}\mid z_{t-1},a_{t-1},c)\right)\Big].$ 

The variational sequence distribution is the product of its filtering factors. $D_{\mathrm{KL}}$ is Kullback-Leibler divergence, and $\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}$ weights prior-posterior agreement. Elapsed times are suppressed in $c$ . With $\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}=1$ , this is the negative evidence lower bound for the stated model, conditional on $z_{0}$ . Learning an uncertain initial state adds its corresponding initial term. Other $\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}$ values yield a regularized objective rather than the same exact likelihood bound. The construction combines variational learning with sequential latent dynamics (wmKingma2014; hafner2019planet).

The reconstruction term trains the encoder and decoder to retain evidence. The divergence trains the prior to match the observation-informed posterior while limiting information that the prior cannot predict. Reparameterized sampling allows gradients through continuous latent variables. In practice, balancing or stopping selected gradient paths, protecting a minimum latent information budget, and adding reward or event targets can stabilize learning. Their details should be reported, because identical symbolic losses can optimize different parameters under different gradient rules. A deterministic recurrent memory may be included alongside the stochastic state, provided its dependencies are included in the model definition.

Predicting Target Representations

For a context encoder $E_{\phi}$ , predictor $P_{\theta}$ , and target encoder $E_{\bar{\phi}}$ , a generic joint-embedding objective is

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{repr}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D},\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{mask}}}\left[d_{\mathrm{feat}}\!\left(P_{\theta}(E_{\phi}(x_{\mathrm{vis}}),\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{mask}},\kappa),\operatorname{sg}[E_{\bar{\phi}}(x_{\mathrm{target}})]\right)\right],$ 

(5.12)

where $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{mask}}$ specifies target positions or masked regions, $x_{\mathrm{vis}}$ the visible context, $x_{\mathrm{target}}$ the withheld target, $d_{\mathrm{feat}}$ a feature distance, and $\operatorname{sg}$ the stop-gradient operator. The target parameters $\bar{\phi}$ can be frozen or updated by an exponential moving average of $\phi$ , rather than by backpropagation through this loss. I-JEPA and V-JEPA 2 instantiate related predictive-embedding mechanisms at different spatial and temporal scales (Assran et al., 2023; Assran et al., 2025).

The predictor and context encoder learn to make retained target information predictable. Stop-gradient alone is not a universal proof against collapse. The target update, masking, architecture, and representation statistics must work together. A collapsed representation can achieve a trivial small distance, and a semantic target can discard fine motion. Comparing downstream readouts, representation variation, and controlled physical predictions is therefore necessary. The main trade-off concerns which information is retained, how expensive the target is to produce, and which later queries the representation supports.

From Masked JEPA Pretraining to Causal Latent Dynamics

A typical training iteration first selects a clip and its visible and target regions. The context encoder receives only the visible content. The target encoder processes the target evidence, possibly with the wider context specified by the method, and produces the features to be matched. The predictor is conditioned on the target positions and, when the task requires them, actions and elapsed time. After the student update, an exponential-moving-average teacher can be updated as

 $\bar{\phi}\leftarrow m_{\mathrm{EMA}}\bar{\phi}+(1-m_{\mathrm{EMA}})\phi,\qquad 0\leq m_{\mathrm{EMA}}<1,$ 

(5.13)

where $\phi$ is the updated student-encoder parameter vector, $\bar{\phi}$ the teacher vector, and $m_{\mathrm{EMA}}$ the momentum coefficient. The teacher is not updated by the predictive-loss gradient. A larger $m_{\mathrm{EMA}}$ changes targets more slowly but can leave them behind a rapidly adapting student. This target-update mechanism is used in the JEPA lineage (Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024). Freezing an independent pretrained teacher is a different design.

For causal dynamics learning, the visible context must stop at the forecast origin, and the predictor must associate a proposed control sequence with later target features. V-JEPA 2’s action-conditioned post-training illustrates this additional step (Assran et al., 2025). Bidirectional pretraining remains useful, but its masked-completion score should not be relabeled as open-loop prediction accuracy. A goal-conditioned planner also needs a meaningful discrepancy between predicted and goal features and a valid action-search procedure. Representation quality, transition quality, and search quality are separately testable.

Feature regression has a statistical limit worth making explicit. With a fixed target representation and squared error, the population-optimal deterministic prediction is its conditional mean. With scalar absolute error, it is a conditional median. Neither objective by itself recovers multiple modes or assigns probabilities to them. A scene with two plausible future contact states can therefore require a stochastic latent predictor, multiple hypotheses, or a probabilistic event head. The appropriate objective depends on whether the downstream consumer needs a reusable feature, a most likely outcome, or a calibrated distribution. This applies to JEPA-style targets and to predictive-feature distillation in world-action models alike.

5.3.2 Action-Conditioned Dynamics and World-Action Learning

Actions connect prediction to intervention, but an action record must have a precise meaning. Distinguish a proposed command, the command actually applied after clipping or safety filtering, and the subsequent measured physical response. A deployable forward model can condition on the applied input or model the actuator transformation from a proposed command. It must not require the future measured response as an input to predict that same response. Controller mode, reference frame, units, duration, delays, and saturation belong in the record. The notation $a_{t}$ refers to the declared input interface, not an unspecified mixture of command and consequence.

Forward, Inverse, and Behavioral Targets

A forward model predicts the next observation or state from current evidence and an input. An inverse model predicts an input compatible with two states or observations. A policy predicts an input from current evidence and a goal. These targets are related by the joint distribution in Eq. (5.7), but they are not equivalent. Several actions can reach the same endpoint, and matching endpoints can hide different contact forces or unsafe intermediate states. Inverse-dynamics training therefore needs a multimodal output distribution or an explicit criterion for selecting among compatible actions.

The three targets correspond to the three world-action interfaces in the right panel of Figure 5.3, defined as attention masks over observed-context tokens $\mathrm{C}$ , action tokens $\mathrm{A}$ , and future-observation tokens $\mathrm{F}$ . A forward dynamics model (FDM) predicts $\widehat{\mathrm{F}}$ from $\mathrm{C}$ and $\mathrm{A}$ . Given what is observed and a candidate input, it forecasts the consequence, which is exactly the transition query of Figure 5.1 and the rollout mechanism used in planning and imagination. An inverse dynamics model (IDM) predicts $\widehat{\mathrm{A}}$ from $\mathrm{C}$ and $\mathrm{F}$ . It reads how the scene actually changed and infers a compatible input. An IDM that requires the realized future observation cannot use that observation to choose the preceding action online. In the training interface considered here, it labels recorded interaction with action estimates, recovers latent actions from action-free video, and shapes representations that encode how actions change the world. Even here, only the action query may read the future. The context rows of the inverse mask bar $\mathrm{C}$ from attending to $\mathrm{F}$ , so context features, which may be cached or shared with the policy mode, remain deployable summaries of observed evidence rather than carriers of future information. A policy mode predicts $\widehat{\mathrm{A}}$ from $\mathrm{C}$ alone, possibly with a goal encoded in the context. The future-to-action attention path is therefore masked out entirely (the crossed-out cell in Figure 5.3). A single leaky edge would let action tokens read future observations at training time and silently lose that input at test time.

Sharing one network across the three modes is attractive because the modes provide complementary supervision. The FDM grounds what actions do, the IDM grounds which actions produce observed change, and the policy converts both into executable behavior. The cost is discipline in the masks and in gradient routing. A stop-gradient blocks a parameter update but not a forward information path, so frozen and detached components must be distinguished from masked ones, and a deployment-mode forward pass with all training-only branches absent is the decisive test that the policy mode’s inputs are exactly those available at runtime.

Behavior cloning learns demonstrated actions, using a likelihood, regression, diffusion, or flow objective. Diffusion Policy exemplifies a conditional distribution over action sequences rather than a single independent action at each step (chi2023diffusion). A failed action can remain useful for a forward model and an outcome predictor while being excluded from a nominal imitation objective. Reward, termination, contact-event, and task-progress heads can make a state more useful for decisions, but they supervise different quantities. A progress label is not a value target unless its connection to future return has been established.

Multi-Source and Multi-Objective Optimization

A useful way to document joint training is

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{joint}}(\Theta)=\sum_{i_{\mathrm{src}}=1}^{N_{\mathrm{src}}}\rho_{i_{\mathrm{src}}}\,\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{\mathrm{sample}}\sim\mathcal{D}_{i_{\mathrm{src}}}}\left[\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\lambda_{j}\,m_{j}(\xi_{\mathrm{sample}})\,\ell_{j}(\Theta;\xi_{\mathrm{sample}})\right],$ 

(5.14)

where $N_{\mathrm{src}}$ is the number of data sources, $\mathcal{D}_{i_{\mathrm{src}}}$ the distribution of source $i_{\mathrm{src}}$ , $\rho_{i_{\mathrm{src}}}\geq 0$ its sampling weight with $\sum_{i_{\mathrm{src}}}\rho_{i_{\mathrm{src}}}=1$ , and $\xi_{\mathrm{sample}}$ a sampled training record. The set $\mathcal{J}$ indexes enabled objectives, $\ell_{j}$ their per-example losses, $\lambda_{j}\geq 0$ their weights, and $m_{j}(\xi_{\mathrm{sample}})\in\{0,1\}$ indicates whether the target exists and is appropriate. The parameter collection is $\Theta$ . Per-dimension masks and normalization by valid target counts are applied inside $\ell_{j}$ when needed. This equation is a bookkeeping template, not an assertion that the objectives have one common probabilistic interpretation.

The distinction between sampling weights and loss weights matters. Increasing a robot source’s sampling rate increases all of its enabled objectives, whereas increasing an action-loss coefficient changes the balance within sampled records. Loss scales also depend on token counts and units. A long video target can dominate a short action chunk unless normalization is deliberate. Joint training can share useful structure but can also let appearance gradients erase precise control information or let narrow action data degrade broad semantics. Freezing pretrained modules, staged unfreezing, separate experts, restricted gradient paths, and alternating updates offer different compromises between preservation and adaptation.

Future Supervision Without Future-Input Leakage

Future observations are legitimate training targets. The restriction is on the forward information available to the deployed policy. A predictive feature branch can map present history to future-relevant features and align them with a detached future teacher. Alternatively, a frozen generative model can receive learned conditioning and send a loss gradient back through that conditioning while its own weights remain fixed. Freezing weights is not the same as disabling the gradient with respect to the model’s input. InternVLA-A1.5 uses this latter mechanism to train foresight conditioning (wmMa2026A15).

InternW0- $\Delta$ uses latent-change supervision and detached future-feature alignment for Causal Imprint, alongside training-only 4D teacher targets (wmMiao2026Delta). The general lesson is to document every route by which future information could reach action activations, including shared attention, side conditioning, cached features, and preprocessing. A direct mask between future and action tokens is insufficient if an intermediate token first reads the future and then passes it onward. A detached target blocks a gradient path. A causal attention restriction blocks a forward information path. Both can be required, but they solve different problems. Temporal “causality” of a mask also does not by itself establish causal identification of the physical system.

A Worked Multi-Supervision Construction

World-action training becomes clearer when each auxiliary target is written separately. InternW0- $\Delta$ provides a concrete example with video and action flow losses, clean-latent change regression, future-feature alignment, and training-only 4D distillation (wmMiao2026Delta; wmInternW0DeltaProject). The following normalized formulation explains their roles using this chapter’s notation. It is not a prescription for the paper’s exact layer indices, tensor layout, or loss coefficients.

Let $u_{t}^{\mathrm{vid}}$ be a clean video-autoencoder latent for the current observation, and let $U_{t}^{+}=(u_{t+\tau_{\mathrm{stride}}}^{\mathrm{vid}},\ldots,u_{t+N_{\mathrm{slice}}\tau_{\mathrm{stride}}}^{\mathrm{vid}})$ contain $N_{\mathrm{slice}}$ future latent slices with sampling stride $\tau_{\mathrm{stride}}$ . The autoencoder is frozen in this construction. The action chunk is $A_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}$ . Let $q_{t}=P^{\mathrm{q}}_{\theta}(h_{t},g,c)$ denote predictive tokens computed only from observed history, instruction, and known conditions. A readout $\widehat{D}_{t}$ from these tokens is trained against consecutive clean-latent differences given by

 $\displaystyle D_{t,i}$ 
 $\displaystyle=u_{t+i\tau_{\mathrm{stride}}}^{\mathrm{vid}}-u_{t+(i-1)\tau_{\mathrm{stride}}}^{\mathrm{vid}},\qquad i=1,\ldots,N_{\mathrm{slice}},$ 

(5.15)

 $\displaystyle D_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=[D_{t,1};\ldots;D_{t,N_{\mathrm{slice}}}],\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{change}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\|\widehat{D}_{t}-\operatorname{sg}[D_{t}]\|_{2}^{2}}{d_{\mathrm{D}}}\right],$ 

where brackets denote stacking, $d_{\mathrm{D}}$ is the number of valid scalar target entries, and the expectation averages training records. The norm is the Euclidean norm of the concatenated valid scalar latent entries. The readout includes any output reshaping or projection needed to match dimensions. Padded entries are omitted. A latent difference emphasizes change rather than static appearance, but it is not a physical velocity. Its units are feature units, and the sampling interval still matters. Computing differences before noise injection avoids supervising independent diffusion noise as if it were motion. Camera changes and encoder instability can also create latent differences, so this objective needs complementary semantic or geometric checks.

A second target can transfer richer intermediate features. Let $\mathbf{q}_{t,i_{\mathrm{tok}}}^{(\ell_{\mathrm{s}})}$ be a predictive token at student layer $\ell_{\mathrm{s}}$ and spatial position $i_{\mathrm{tok}}$ , and let $\mathbf{f}_{t,i_{\mathrm{tok}}}^{+,\ell_{\mathrm{T}}}$ be a spatially corresponding feature of a future slice at target layer $\ell_{\mathrm{T}}$ . With compatible feature dimensions, a representative alignment objective is

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}=\mathbb{E}_{t,i_{\mathrm{tok}}}\!\left[1-\operatorname{cos}_{\mathrm{sim}}\!\left(\mathbf{q}_{t,i_{\mathrm{tok}}}^{(\ell_{\mathrm{s}})},\operatorname{sg}[\mathbf{f}_{t,i_{\mathrm{tok}}}^{+,\ell_{\mathrm{T}}}]\right)\right].$ 

(5.16)

The function $\operatorname{cos}_{\mathrm{sim}}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{v}/(\|\mathbf{u}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{v}\|_{2})$ measures direction similarity for nonzero feature vectors, with numerical stabilization used in implementation. Layer indices and spatial correspondence are part of the target definition. The future feature can come from another branch of the same trainable model. Detaching this target prevents this loss from updating it, while other objectives may still update its parameters. Such a target is not the same as a permanently frozen teacher. Compared with clean-latent regression, feature alignment transfers the target branch’s abstraction but inherits its biases and changes during training.

An external geometry-and-motion teacher supplies a third, complementary signal. Let $\mathbf{r}_{t}^{\mathrm{T}}=R_{\mathrm{T}}(o_{t:t+H_{\mathrm{o}}},c)$ be a descriptor extracted from a recorded clip and $\mathbf{r}_{t}^{\mathrm{S}}=R_{\theta}^{\mathrm{S}}(h_{t},g,c)$ the student descriptor predicted from available observations. The horizon $H_{\mathrm{o}}$ is the observation horizon. $R_{\mathrm{T}}$ is frozen and may access training-only future frames, while $R_{\theta}^{\mathrm{S}}$ may not. A corresponding objective is

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{geom}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{valid}}\!\left[\frac{\|\mathbf{r}_{t}^{\mathrm{S}}-\operatorname{sg}[\mathbf{r}_{t}^{\mathrm{T}}]\|_{2}^{2}}{d_{\mathrm{r}}}\right],$ 

(5.17)

where $d_{\mathrm{r}}$ is the descriptor dimension and the expectation includes only samples with valid teacher outputs. Descriptor components should be normalized according to their semantics. Unlike a hard physical constraint, this objective transfers an estimated geometric or motion prior. It does not establish exact metric geometry, correct forces, or conservation. The auxiliary student readout can be removed after training when its role was only to shape a representation already used by the policy.

The combined objective is then

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WAM}}={}$ 
 $\displaystyle\lambda_{\mathrm{v}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}^{\mathrm{v}}(U_{t}^{+})+\lambda_{\mathrm{a}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}^{\mathrm{a}}(A_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}})+\lambda_{\mathrm{ch}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{change}}$ 

(5.18)

 $\displaystyle+\lambda_{\mathrm{al}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{ge}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{geom}}.$ 

The superscripts $\mathrm{v}$ and $\mathrm{a}$ identify separately conditioned video and action flow objectives of Eq. (5.10). The nonnegative $\lambda$ coefficients balance their contributions. Source-specific weights and validity masks follow Eq. (5.14). This combination assigns distinct jobs to reconstructable future detail, executable behavior, change prediction, and teacher knowledge. Ablations should remove or vary these jobs independently, matching data and optimization budgets, rather than comparing only the total loss.

A limitation follows from the conditioning. When $q_{t}$ does not receive a candidate action sequence, it predicts future-relevant information under the behavior represented in its data, not the separate outcome of every possible intervention. Its value can be improved action features without a standalone counterfactual simulator. Joint video-action training should therefore declare whether its video branch sees supplied actions, generated actions, or neither. The behavioral benefit of future supervision and the correctness of action-conditioned physical prediction are different claims.

Parameters, Information Paths, and a Training Iteration

Table 5.4 distinguishes the pathways in this construction. Observation encoders, frozen semantic models, detached targets, and trainable world experts play different roles even when their outputs are all called features. A forward dependency restriction concerns the information available to activations. A stop-gradient concerns which parameters a loss updates. Freezing a module’s weights does not necessarily stop derivatives through its computation to an upstream trainable input.

Table 5.4: Information and optimization roles in predictive-feature world-action training. This is a general implementation checklist, not a claim that all world-action models use identical branches

One minibatch update proceeds as follows. Construct a time-consistent observed context, action chunk, future targets, and validity masks. Encode frozen inputs and retrieve any valid cached teacher descriptors. Noise the video and action targets according to their declared schedules, while keeping the observed conditioning and clean change targets separate. Run the experts with the intended directed dependencies, compute only the supported losses, normalize them by valid entries, and update the trainable parameter groups. If a moving-average teacher is used, update it after the student step. Finally, test an inference-mode forward pass with all training-only future and teacher branches absent. The policy must still have every input it requires.

This last test should inspect indirect as well as direct paths. An observed token that reads a future token at one layer can leak that future to the policy at a later layer even when future-to-action attention is masked. Temporal preprocessing can leak in the same way. Encoding an observed frame together with future frames through a noncausal video encoder can contaminate its latent. Cache reuse additionally requires independence from the evolving action and artificial-time inputs, not merely independence from future observations. These checks turn a verbal claim of “training-only supervision” into an auditable computation graph.

Learning a World Model Versus Learning Within One

Model-based reinforcement learning adds a second optimization problem in which a policy is improved using transitions generated by a learned model. In Dreamer, imagined trajectories train behavior while the learned dynamics provide the rollout mechanism (hafner2019dreamer). Model parameters can be held fixed during policy optimization even when derivatives through the model are used to update policy parameters. Conversely, updating the model to maximize its own predicted reward would not necessarily improve its physical accuracy.

Dyna-style alternation uses real experience to improve the model and model-generated experience to improve decisions (wmSutton1991). MBPO highlights a useful compromise by using short model rollouts branched from real states, limiting reliance on distant model predictions (wmJanner2019). Longer imagination expands possible credit assignment but exposes the policy to compounding errors and model exploitation. Offline data create an additional support problem. A proposed policy may select actions absent from the training distribution. Policy improvement should therefore be coupled to rollout-length selection, conservative use of uncertain predictions, renewed real data, and independent physical evaluation rather than judged only by imagined return.

5.3.3 Physical Constraints, Counterfactuals, and Uncertainty Modeling

Physical structure can enter through loss penalties, architectural restrictions, or a hybrid of known dynamics and learned corrections. Physics-informed neural networks demonstrate the use of governing-equation residuals as learning signals (raissi2019physics). Structured simulators illustrate complementary restrictions arising from a representation and its update rules (sanchezgonzalez2020learning; wmXie2024). The appropriate choice depends on which laws, parameters, and boundary conditions are actually known.

Soft Penalties and Structural Constraints

For a predicted physical trajectory $\widehat{S}=(\widehat{s}_{t},\ldots,\widehat{s}_{t+H})$ under actions $A_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}$ , a representative penalty is

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{phys}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{J_{\mathrm{eq}}}\alpha_{j}^{\mathrm{eq}}\|f_{j}^{\mathrm{eq}}(\widehat{S},A_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}},c)\|_{2}^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{J_{\mathrm{ineq}}}\beta_{j}^{\mathrm{ineq}}\|[g_{j}^{\mathrm{ineq}}(\widehat{S},A_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}},c)]_{+}\|_{2}^{2}\right].$ 

(5.19)

The residual $f_{j}^{\mathrm{eq}}=0$ specifies an equality, $g_{j}^{\mathrm{ineq}}\leq 0$ an inequality, $[u]_{+}=\max(u,0)$ applied componentwise, and $J_{\mathrm{eq}},J_{\mathrm{ineq}}$ the numbers of each constraint. The nonnegative coefficients $\alpha_{j}^{\mathrm{eq}},\beta_{j}^{\mathrm{ineq}}$ include suitable scaling by units and tolerances. The expectation averages training records and sampled predictions. These coefficients are local to this equation. Constraints must act on physical readouts or physically defined latent variables, not on arbitrary embedding coordinates without an interpretation.

Examples include joint limits, nonpenetration, contact consistency, and energy or mass balance under known boundary fluxes. A system exchanging heat or liquid with its surroundings should obey a balance equation, not an inappropriate constant-energy or constant-mass penalty. Tolerances should reflect measurement precision and modeling assumptions. A strong incorrect constraint biases the model. A weak penalty may leave violations large. Enforcing symmetries or integrating known mechanics can reduce violation by construction, but only for the constrained property and under the numerical method’s assumptions. It cannot identify an unmeasured friction coefficient or certify all downstream behavior.

Counterfactual and Intervention Supervision

Paired rollouts can compare different actions from matched initial conditions. A resettable simulator can hold state and external inputs fixed while varying an intervention. In a physical experiment, the same comparison requires reproducible initial conditions, controlled confounders, or a justified statistical design. Outcome diversity from an unconditioned video generator is not evidence that it learned how a particular action changes the outcome. Synthetic counterfactuals supervise the simulator’s mechanisms. Independent measurements are needed before transferring those conclusions to reality.

A useful training contrast varies the commanded magnitude, direction, or duration while keeping nonintervened conditions comparable. It can supervise the sign and scale of the response as well as which objects should remain unchanged. Care is required near discontinuities. A slightly larger force may change sticking to sliding rather than yield a slightly larger displacement. A smooth penalty that averages these modes can suppress the event the model is supposed to predict.

Predictive Distributions and Uncertainty Sources

Deterministic regression is cheap but cannot express multiple plausible outcomes. A conditional Gaussian supplies a mean and variance. Mixtures, stochastic latent states, diffusion, or flows can represent more complex distributions. For a scalar measured target $y$ and condition $\kappa$ , a Gaussian negative log-likelihood, omitting an additive constant, is

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Gauss}}=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\left[\frac{(y-\mu_{\theta}(\kappa))^{2}}{\sigma_{\theta}^{2}(\kappa)}+\log\sigma_{\theta}^{2}(\kappa)\right],$ 

(5.20)

where $\mu_{\theta}$ is the predicted conditional mean and $\sigma_{\theta}^{2}>0$ the variance. The residual term penalizes inaccurate concentrated predictions, while the logarithmic term discourages arbitrarily inflating variance. Positivity can be enforced through a log-variance parameterization with numerically appropriate bounds. This example illustrates heteroscedastic likelihood learning (wmKendall2017). Its Gaussian assumption is inadequate when distinct contact modes produce well-separated outcomes.

An ensemble adds variation across fitted models. For $M$ equally weighted scalar predictors with means $\mu_{m}$ and variances $\sigma_{m}^{2}$ at the same condition, the mixture variance obeys

 $\bar{\mu}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\mu_{m},\qquad\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid\kappa)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\sigma_{m}^{2}+\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}(\mu_{m}-\bar{\mu})^{2},$ 

(5.21)

where $Y$ is the predicted random quantity and $m$ the ensemble index. The identity separates within-model dispersion from between-model disagreement. Deep ensembles and probabilistic ensemble dynamics use this kind of diversity for predictive uncertainty and planning (wmLakshminarayanan2017; wmChua2018). However, disagreement is only a proxy for epistemic uncertainty, and the within-model term can include unresolved state ambiguity as well as observation and process noise. Correlated model errors can leave an ensemble confidently wrong.

Uncertainty must also propagate consistently across time. A hidden but fixed mass should be sampled once for a trajectory hypothesis rather than independently every step. Sensor noise may vary at each observation. More detailed distributions increase sampling and calibration costs. Deterministic models can still be useful when their operating range is narrow and externally monitored, but they should not be presented as calibrated probabilistic simulators. Section 5.4.3 explains how uncertainty is evaluated rather than inferred from the mere presence of stochastic layers.

5.3.4 Multi-Step Prediction, Multiple Time Scales, and Adaptation

One-step accuracy can hide recursive drift. A generic horizon-weighted objective is

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{multi}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{H}w_{k}\,\ell\!\left(\widehat{y}_{t+k\mid t},y_{t+k}\right)\right],\qquad w_{k}\geq 0.$ 

(5.22)

The prediction $\widehat{y}_{t+k\mid t}$ is generated from evidence available at $t$ , recursively applying the supplied actions without incorporating intermediate real observations. The target $y_{t+k}$ is a later measurement or explicitly identified teacher target. $w_{k}$ weights horizon $k$ , $H$ is the maximum horizon, and $\ell$ is a suitable regression or probabilistic loss. A probabilistic $\widehat{y}$ denotes a distribution, not necessarily one sampled value. Supervision should score that distribution appropriately rather than force every sample to match one realized future.

Teacher Forcing, Free Rollout, and Curriculum

Teacher forcing provides stable local supervision but exposes the model mainly to data states. Free rollout trains on its own evolving predictions and addresses the deployment distribution more directly, at the cost of unstable early trajectories and longer gradient paths. Scheduled sampling mixes real and generated preceding inputs (wmBengio2015). It is a training heuristic, not generally the original sequence-likelihood objective. A sensible comparison therefore includes teacher-forced error, open-loop error, and task behavior rather than assuming that mixed inputs always improve all three.

Latent overshooting in PlaNet extends consistency pressure beyond one transition by matching multi-step predictive distributions to observation-informed states (hafner2019planet). Related multi-step objectives can supervise physical readouts or future embeddings. Longer windows improve exposure to delayed effects, but require more memory and can overweight a particular target encoder’s errors. A curriculum can begin with short horizons and then include longer windows and contact-centered segments, while preserving enough ordinary motion to avoid a distorted training distribution. Truncating backpropagation lowers cost but changes which temporal dependencies receive direct gradient signals.

Multiple Timescales and Temporal Consistency

Different sensors and physical variables evolve at different rates. Training should include elapsed-time conditioning, modality-validity masks, and action durations rather than assuming one frame equals one control interval. Slow semantic context, faster visual dynamics, and high-rate force feedback can share state through explicit timing interfaces. Interpolation is appropriate only when its assumptions hold. Interpolating across an impact can erase the discontinuity.

For a Markov transition kernel under the same constant control input $a$ and conditions $c$ , time consistency takes the form

 $T_{\theta}(z^{\prime\prime}\mid z,a,c,\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2})\approx\int T_{\theta}(z^{\prime\prime}\mid u,a,c,\Delta_{2})T_{\theta}(u\mid z,a,c,\Delta_{1})\,\mathrm{d}u,$ 

(5.23)

where $z,z^{\prime\prime}$ are initial and final latent states, $u$ is an intermediate latent state, and $\Delta_{1},\Delta_{2}>0$ are physical durations. This is a distribution-level Chapman-Kolmogorov consistency condition under the stated Markov and fixed-input assumptions. It is not generally valid to replace the intermediate distribution by its mean in nonlinear dynamics. If actions or external conditions change, both sides must use the same time-varying input schedule. If the compressed state is not Markov, residual inconsistency may reveal missing memory rather than numerical error.

Post-Training, Distillation, and Continued Interaction

Task-specific post-training can refine action interfaces, contact targets, or selected dynamics. InternW0 adds available force and tactile histories and predicts future contact channels during contact-aware post-training (wmCai2026InternW0). Such adaptation requires valid contact supervision. Missing physical channels cannot be recovered simply by adding a new output head. Distillation can transfer an expensive teacher’s features or predictions to a smaller or less frequently executed branch, but the teacher’s uncertainty and errors should remain distinguishable from measured truth.

Local adaptation should separate belief correction, physical-parameter identification, and updates to learned network weights. A failed grasp may revise a contact hypothesis without changing the model. Repeated measured slip may justify identifying friction. Systematic errors across conditions may require a new training round. Replay, regularization, and selective parameter updates address the trade-off between new learning and retention. Elastic weight consolidation is one example of limiting changes to parameters important for previous tasks (kirkpatrick2017ewc), not a guarantee against forgetting in an arbitrary world model. New versions should be accepted only after tests of both new and retained capabilities.

Staging Auxiliary Supervision and Adapting the Deployed Interface

A multi-objective recipe can be organized around a stable behavioral and predictive baseline rather than enabling every target from the first update. InternW0- $\Delta$ first performs joint pretraining and subsequently adds cached 4D supervision during continued pretraining, before task- and embodiment-specific post-training (wmMiao2026Delta). The general choice is between early joint shaping and later auxiliary refinement. Early auxiliary losses can guide representation formation, but noisy or mismatched teachers can interfere before the action interface becomes useful. Later introduction reduces that early interference but may require a smaller learning rate or replay to avoid disturbing established behavior. Neither schedule is a universal optimum.

Post-training should match the actual deployment contract. A target robot may change valid action dimensions, normalization, camera configuration, actuation delay, or the relation between predicted and executed chunk lengths. Adapt the relevant input/output mappings and condition the model on these differences. Do not reinterpret an identical numerical vector as an identical physical action. If successive chunks overlap or part of a chunk has already been committed to execution, the training condition should identify that prefix and the loss should target the remaining controllable portion. Where online feedback is used to choose future actions, it must be separated from the fixed action sequence assumed by an open-loop dynamics objective.

Frozen-encoder and teacher caches can reduce repeated training work, but only while their dependencies remain fixed. Changing an encoder checkpoint, a crop, a view layout, an instruction, or the temporal window can invalidate a cached feature. Offline geometric descriptors should retain their source clip, teacher version, confidence, and normalization. Activation checkpointing trades extra computation for memory. Mixed precision reduces storage and arithmetic cost but needs checks for unstable losses and gradients. Report these implementation choices separately from reductions in the amount of training data or the number of optimization steps. A faster experiment pipeline is valuable, but it is not itself evidence of better learned dynamics.

For model selection, monitor the component losses alongside open-loop predictions and closed-loop behavior. A lower teacher-feature error can coexist with worse action accuracy if the representation discards contact detail. Likewise, a lower action loss on demonstration states can conceal failure on states visited by the policy. Compare a frozen baseline, a joint-training variant, and an auxiliary-supervision variant on fixed held-out conditions, with unchanged target preprocessing and comparable budgets. This distinguishes the contribution of predictive supervision from a larger backbone, a different data mixture, or additional optimization.

Training Trade-Offs and Reproducible Reporting

Table 5.5 summarizes choices that should be reported together rather than hidden inside a total loss. At minimum, an experiment should state its data mixture and splits, temporal sampling, target normalization, trainable and frozen modules, gradient paths, optimizer and learning-rate schedule, effective batch size, sequence length, number of updates, numerical precision, and training and inference budgets. No fixed recipe is optimal across video generation, latent planning, and multimodal control.

The common criterion is whether the resulting model answers the intended queries on evidence it could actually receive. Training losses are useful diagnostics, but the relationships among reconstruction, dynamics, uncertainty, and behavior must be established through the validation protocols below.

## 5.4 Using and Validating World Models

Using a world model means making a query under a declared information boundary and, when appropriate, using its answer to choose an intervention. Validation should separate the quality of a forecast from its physical consistency and from the utility of the decision it supports. A model can produce physically possible but inaccurate futures, accurate short-term forecasts that do not improve a policy, or useful actions without exposing a general-purpose predictive interface. This section develops protocols that make these distinctions measurable.

5.4.1 Interactive Simulation and Conditional Queries

An interactive call starts from an inferred state, belief, or observation history and returns one or more conditional futures. A query may request an image, object trajectory, contact event, temperature, boundary crossing, or task outcome. It should specify the available evidence, intervention interface, physical horizon, environment conditions, and required precision. For a partially known scene, the returned uncertainty should include unresolved state alternatives, not only randomness introduced during decoding.

State Posterior, Future Prediction, and Retrospective Checking

The state posterior summarizes evidence available up to the prediction time. A future forecast propagates that posterior without using the future measurements to be predicted. For an observation-generating latent model, a representative factorization is

 $\displaystyle p_{\theta,\phi,\omega_{\mathrm{obs}}}(o_{t+1:t+H}\mid h_{t},A_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}},c)$ 

(5.24)

 $\displaystyle=\int q_{\phi}(z_{t}\mid h_{t},c)\prod_{k=0}^{H-1}\Big[T_{\theta}(z_{t+k+1}\mid z_{t+k},a_{t+k},c,\Delta t_{k})O_{\omega_{\mathrm{obs}}}(o_{t+k+1}\mid z_{t+k+1},c)\Big]\,\mathrm{d}z_{t:t+H},$ 

where $h_{t}$ is the observed history, $A_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}=a_{t:t+H-1}$ a supplied action sequence of $H$ intervals, $q_{\phi}$ the inferred latent-state posterior, $T_{\theta}$ the learned transition, and $O_{\omega_{\mathrm{obs}}}$ the observation likelihood. The integration marginalizes the current and future latent states $z_{t:t+H}$ . $\Delta t_{k}$ specifies each physical interval. The symbols $\phi,\theta,\omega_{\mathrm{obs}}$ denote fixed fitted parameters in this expression. It is posterior prediction with respect to the current latent state, not necessarily a Bayesian average over uncertain network parameters. The Markov and observation assumptions are those introduced in Section 5.1.2. A model with additional dependencies must include them explicitly (Kaelbling1998; hafner2019planet).

After real execution, the withheld observations can be used to check the forecast and then update the state. This retrospective validation of an earlier prediction is different from reconstructing a future frame after that frame has already entered an inference network. Likewise, smoothing a past state using later evidence can be useful for diagnosis but cannot be reported as an online forecast made with less information. Evaluation logs should retain the prediction, model version, conditioning evidence, and issue time before the target outcome is revealed.

Eq. (5.24) describes a query interface, not a requirement that every architecture evaluate an explicit density. Sample-based models can approximate the predictive distribution. Deterministic models return a restricted point prediction. A latent-only model can answer a physical or task query through a readout rather than an observation decoder. In all cases, a goal specifies what is desired and should not be treated as evidence that the goal will occur. Scenario assumptions, such as a proposed payload or a fixed external temperature, must remain distinguishable from measured conditions.

Interactive Correction and Information Acquisition

Real feedback should update the inferred state before the next query. A prediction made before a grasp slips may no longer be a valid context for later actions even if its video remains visually coherent. Asynchronous systems should therefore expose the age and observation support of cached predictions, together with the conditions that trigger correction, regeneration, or rejection.

Predictions can also help choose what to observe next. If two action rankings differ mainly because contact is uncertain, an additional tactile measurement may be more useful than another distant camera frame. This is an information-acquisition decision within the partially observable control problem (Kaelbling1998). Its value depends on an observation model, the cost of sensing, and whether the proposed measurement can actually resolve the ambiguity. Querying the same model repeatedly does not create independent evidence about the physical state.

5.4.2 Imagination, Planning, and Decision Calls

Planning proposes candidate actions, predicts their consequences, and ranks them using task objectives and constraints. An imagined collection of branches can be written as

 $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{cand}}=\left\{\left[\left(a_{t+k}^{(b)},\widehat{z}_{t+k+1}^{(b)}\right)\right]_{k=0}^{K_{b}-1}:b=1,\ldots,N_{\mathrm{roll}}\right\},$ 

(5.25)

where $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{cand}}$ is a collection of ordered imagined paths, $N_{\mathrm{roll}}$ is the number of candidate branches, $b$ indexes a branch, and $K_{b}$ is its number of intervals. The action $a_{t+k}^{(b)}$ produces the imagined next state $\widehat{z}_{t+k+1}^{(b)}$ from the preceding state in that branch. Branches may also be repeated under different state hypotheses or stochastic outcomes. Increasing $N_{\mathrm{roll}}$ explores alternatives. Increasing $K_{b}$ reveals later consequences but also exposes more model error.

For candidates with a common horizon $H$ , a useful illustrative objective is

 $\displaystyle U(A_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}\mid b_{t},g,c)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{model}}\!\left[\sum_{k=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{k}\big(r_{t+k}-\lambda C_{t+k}^{\mathrm{run}}\big)-\eta_{\mathrm{pen}}\,\mathbf{1}\{\mathcal{V}_{t:t+H}^{\mathrm{viol}}\}\,\middle|\,b_{t},A_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}},g,c\right].$ 

(5.26)

The utility $U$ scores the action sequence $A_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}=a_{t:t+H-1}$ starting from current belief $b_{t}$ , goal $g$ , and conditions $c$ . The expectation averages the model’s predicted state and outcome uncertainty. The transition reward $r_{t+k}$ measures task benefit, $C_{t+k}^{\mathrm{run}}\geq 0$ a per-interval resource cost such as time or energy, and $\gamma\in(0,1]$ the discount factor for equally spaced intervals. The coefficient $\lambda\geq 0$ converts resource cost into utility units. The indicator $\mathbf{1}\{\mathcal{V}_{t:t+H}^{\mathrm{viol}}\}$ equals one when a specified violation occurs anywhere along the trajectory. $\eta_{\mathrm{pen}}\geq 0$ penalizes that trajectory-level event once. Both the reward and the per-step cost are inside the sum. For unequal durations, discounts and accumulated costs should instead follow physical time. This is a generic decision objective, not a world-model fitting loss or a safety certificate. Constrained MPC provides the broader control framework (mayne2000constrained).

A planner may optimize actions by sampling, tree expansion, or differentiating through a learned transition. PlaNet uses latent-space planning, while probabilistic ensemble methods such as PETS propagate alternative dynamics and state outcomes during action evaluation (hafner2019planet; wmChua2018). A separately trained actor may instead amortize this computation into direct action generation. The actor can be trained using imagined trajectories without running a planner at deployment, as in Dreamer (hafner2019dreamer). Planning at inference and policy learning through imagination therefore have different runtime costs and failure modes.

Receding-horizon execution applies only an initial portion of the selected sequence and replans from new real evidence. Without this correction, action optimization may deliberately enter regions where prediction errors create unrealistically high reward. Longer imagined rollouts are not automatically better. They can change action ranking for the wrong reason. Model-based policy optimization addresses this issue by controlling the use and length of imagined experience (wmJanner2019). Uncertainty-sensitive ranking can compare candidate outcomes across hidden-state hypotheses, but agreement among several copies of a biased model is not independent confirmation.

Hierarchical imagination can compare coarse routes or process phases before refining a selected interval. Candidates should terminate at a common physical horizon or comparable completion event, with appropriate terminal-value treatment. Otherwise a shorter trajectory can appear preferable merely because its later costs are omitted. Efficient execution can also reuse observation features or invoke detailed prediction only near consequential events. These savings must be evaluated together with the error introduced by stale context, reduced branching, or omitted detail, rather than by model throughput alone.

Table 5.6: Validation objects, suitable evidence, and common overclaims. The evaluation protocol must preserve the information available at the forecast issue time

Object

Evidence or protocol

Example readout

Overclaim to avoid

Observation forecast

Held-out, time-matched outcomes

Declared sample budget

Pixel or perceptual error, conditional and distribution checks

Overall realism establishes action correctness

Occlusion, reappearance, and history changes

Position, orientation, or attribute drift

Single-frame recognition establishes memory

Controlled changes and matched initial conditions

Any action sensitivity establishes a correct intervention model
