5.4.3 Prediction Quality and Physical-Consistency Tests

Prediction quality asks whether a forecast agrees with the subsequently observed outcome or its conditional distribution. Physical consistency asks whether the predicted trajectory respects relevant identities, mechanisms, and constraints. These are separate axes. Several trajectories may be physically possible, while only one occurs per trial. A visually similar output may still violate contact or respond incorrectly to an action. Table 5.6 organizes the evidence needed for each claim.

Prediction Quality at a Fixed Information Boundary

Report one-step prediction from newly observed context, open-loop multi-step prediction without future measurements, and feedback-interleaved prediction with explicitly scheduled observations separately. Also specify whether future controls were fixed before the forecast or recorded from a feedback policy. Conditioning retrospectively on a policy’s later actions can reveal information about later states. It is not equivalent to forecasting an independently supplied intervention sequence.

Observation forecasts can be compared using pixel errors, perceptual feature distances such as learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS), and distribution-level video measures such as Fréchet video distance (FVD) (wmZhang2018; wmUnterthiner2018). These answer different questions. Pixel error is sensitive to small spatial misalignment. Perceptual metrics inherit the features of their evaluator. A good aggregate distribution score does not establish that each sample follows its supplied action. Multimodal futures further complicate paired image error. A legitimate but unobserved outcome can be penalized even when the predicted distribution is appropriate. Report the sample budget and avoid presenting best-of-many selection as the performance of a single unselected prediction.

State and event queries require measurements matched to their meaning. Object positions and velocities can be evaluated in physical units. Orientations need an appropriate rotational distance. Contact or phase-change events require detection and timing errors. For a scalar physical quantity, a horizon-specific summary is

 $\operatorname{RMSE}(k)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{eval}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{eval}}}\left(\widehat{y}_{t_{i}+k\mid t_{i}}^{(i)}-y_{t_{i}+k}^{(i)}\right)^{2}},$ 

(5.27)

where $N_{\mathrm{eval}}$ is the number of independent evaluation trials, $i$ indexes a trial, $t_{i}$ is its forecast origin, $k$ the forecast offset on a declared sampling grid, $y$ the measured quantity, and $\widehat{y}_{t_{i}+k\mid t_{i}}$ the point forecast issued at $t_{i}$ . Root mean squared error has the same physical unit as $y$ . For multiple quantities, report errors separately or declare the normalization instead of adding meters, newtons, and temperatures without scaling. Plotting or tabulating the error against elapsed time exposes drift hidden by an average over horizons. A probabilistic forecast also needs a distributional score, not only error of its mean.

Physical Consistency and Intervention Response

Evaluate persistence of object identity and hidden attributes through occlusion, compatibility of geometry across views, non-penetration within measurement tolerance, contact creation and release, and agreement between predicted motion and known control changes. When forces, boundary fluxes, and physical parameters are available, check momentum, energy, or material balances under the corresponding assumptions. Conservation of an isolated system must not be imposed on an open or externally actuated process. These tests should use the physical quantities underlying the constraints of Section 5.3.3, not merely whether an auxiliary loss is small during training.

Contact and other mechanism changes deserve event-centered reporting. Most recorded frames may show easy steady motion, so an aggregate average can conceal incorrect impact timing, slip onset, or release. Partition errors into free motion, contact formation, sustained contact, release, and relevant process transitions. Controlled changes in action direction, magnitude, duration, or timing test whether the model predicts the right change, rather than merely any change. Where possible, paired trials should hold the initial conditions and non-intervened factors fixed. Simulation supports precise resets. Physical repeats require reporting reset variability and measurement uncertainty.

Physics judged only from rendered images remains an indirect test. A perception model used to extract trajectories can introduce correlated errors, and a language-model judge can prefer plausible-looking motion. Such evaluators should be validated against independent labels or measurements for the claimed quantity. A state predictor without a visual decoder can instead be assessed through its native physical outputs or a readout fitted only on training data. Requiring every architecture to produce a video would conflate query availability with dynamics quality.

Benchmark Tasks and Information Parity

Physion illustrates evaluation of a physical event by asking a model to predict, from an initial visible segment, whether specified objects will contact during the unseen continuation, rather than requiring every model to generate a video (wmBear2021Physion). The task permits comparisons among learned visual features, explicit states, and dynamical predictions, provided that their input privileges and readout training are reported. A model given simulator particle states has a different information budget from one given RGB observations. Their gap can help diagnose perception versus dynamics, but cannot be interpreted as a matched-input architectural ranking.

The same principle applies across model families. Spatial generators need held-out-view and revisit consistency tests with measured regions distinguished from completed regions. JEPA-style models need fixed, independently trained readouts or action-conditioned rollout tests, not only similarity to their own changing teacher. Joint world-action models need both policy evaluation and any separately claimed forecast evaluation. No single rendering metric, contact classifier, or robot success rate covers all these interfaces. A useful benchmark suite therefore combines common physical questions with native-interface tests and publishes what information each model receives.

Probability, Calibration, and Sharpness

A forecast distribution should place probability on outcomes in a way that is both accurate and informative. Proper scoring rules reward the predictive distribution rather than a conveniently selected sample (wmGneiting2007). For a binary event, a scalar observation, and its predictive distribution, two representative scores are

 $\operatorname{BS}=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{eval}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{eval}}}(p_{i}-e_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}})^{2},\qquad\operatorname{CRPS}(F_{\mathrm{CDF}},y)=\mathbb{E}|Y-y|-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}|Y-Y^{\prime}|,$ 

(5.28)

where BS is the Brier score, $p_{i}\in[0,1]$ the predicted probability of event $e_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}\in\{0,1\}$ , and $N_{\mathrm{eval}}$ the number of trials. CRPS is the continuous ranked probability score for a scalar measurement $y$ and predictive cumulative distribution $F_{\mathrm{CDF}}$ . $Y$ and $Y^{\prime}$ are independent draws from $F_{\mathrm{CDF}}$ , assumed to have finite first moments. Lower values are better. CRPS can be estimated from samples without evaluating a density. A log score is appropriate when a normalized predictive density or probability mass is available. A diffusion training loss is not itself the log likelihood of a deployed forecast.

Calibration asks whether probabilities or intervals agree with empirical frequencies. For example, cases assigned a contact probability near a specified value should exhibit contact at approximately that frequency. A nominal prediction interval should be assessed by empirical coverage and width, since an excessively broad interval can cover almost every outcome while being unhelpful. Calibration curves and post-hoc calibration techniques are useful diagnostics, but calibration on one distribution need not persist after a shift (wmGuo2017). Marginal coverage alone does not establish correctness within each task, contact mode, horizon, or material group. Sample diversity and ensemble disagreement should therefore be tested against realized outcomes rather than interpreted as uncertainty quality by construction.

Splits, Aggregation, and Reproducibility

Separate model fitting, calibration or threshold selection, and final testing. Group related frames and derived samples by trajectory, scene, object combination, and collection session as appropriate to the generalization claim. Report results by physical horizon, event type, and change of conditions before aggregating them. Confidence intervals should account for trajectory-level dependence. Treating adjacent frames as independent trials substantially overstates the amount of evidence. Include failure cases and invalid predictions in a declared accounting scheme rather than silently removing them from the denominator.

The rows in Table 5.6 are complementary, not interchangeable levels of one score. A model may pass state-persistence tests while failing intervention tests, or yield useful decisions while offering no calibrated probability interface. The evaluation report should identify supported claims and missing evidence separately. Decision-level evaluation is developed next.

5.4.4 Decision Utility and Applicability Boundaries

The operational question is whether model calls improve real outcomes. Compare systems with and without the relevant world-model function while matching the policy proposal mechanism, observation history, action interface, training data, and inference budget as closely as possible. For a specified real-task score $J_{\mathrm{real}}$ , define

 $\Delta J=J_{\mathrm{real}}(\pi_{\mathrm{with\ model}})-J_{\mathrm{real}}(\pi_{\mathrm{reference}}),$ 

(5.29)

where $\pi_{\mathrm{with\ model}}$ is the policy or complete decision procedure using the tested model function, $\pi_{\mathrm{reference}}$ the comparison procedure, and $\Delta J$ their difference under the same outcome definition and evaluation distribution. The score may be success rate, measured task quality, or another explicitly specified objective. It is not the model’s own predicted reward. Report initial conditions, repetitions, uncertainty intervals, failures, interventions, and resource costs. A positive average gain can conceal systematic failure on the very candidates the model ranks most confidently.

Ablations should replace one function at a time. A persistence predictor tests the value of temporal evolution beyond current state. An action-shuffled predictor tests sensitivity to the supplied control. Removing future supervision tests its contribution to the learned representation. Matched history and parameter budgets help separate predictive learning from a larger encoder or additional context. These controls diagnose mechanisms but do not individually prove a causal explanation for an entire system’s improvement.

Efficiency has several boundaries, including observation acquisition and transfer, encoding, predictive prefill, action or video sampling, communication, and physical execution. Report model-side action-update time separately from sensor-to-command latency, full query latency, and successful task throughput. Asynchronous prediction moves work off a critical path but does not remove its computation or the risk of stale predictions. Hardware, precision, batch size, context length, action horizon, denoising steps, and update rates should accompany timings. Neither the inverse of average inference time nor a high low-level servo rate establishes closed-loop responsiveness under all conditions.

Applicability boundaries should cover objects, materials, actions, temporal horizons, modalities, and embodiments. A model may generalize to new appearance while failing under new friction, or predict free motion while failing after a contact switch. Test combinations of mechanism changes as well as isolated shifts. Distinguish recovery through fresh observation, belief correction, physical-parameter identification, and network retraining. These require different resources and support different transfer claims. Uncertainty, modality disagreement, and residuals can trigger shorter horizons, additional sensing, or fallback, but their thresholds need validation against actual errors. Independent execution constraints and safety mechanisms remain system responsibilities.

Deployment validation should establish whether a world model improves outcomes under matched comparisons, within stated boundaries, and at a cost the system can afford. Its query interfaces must specify the limits of those claims.

## 5.5 Current Challenges and Future Outlook

The preceding sections suggest that progress should be described through capabilities and their evidence rather than a single architecture label. Broad pretrained priors, explicit physical structure, and efficient action interfaces contribute different strengths. Their integration raises questions about what can be learned from existing observations, what requires new intervention, and how a model can remain useful while its environment and operating conditions change.

5.5.1 Acquiring Physical Knowledge from Observation to Intervention

Videos provide rich evidence about appearance and motion but usually omit commanded forces, contact states, and other variables that determine the response to an intervention. Different mechanisms can explain the same observed trajectory. Larger observational datasets can improve coverage without resolving this ambiguity when the distinguishing variable is never measured or excited. The relevant challenge is to connect reusable visual and semantic priors with evidence that identifies executable action consequences.

Action-free pretraining followed by grounded interaction learning offers one division of labor, as illustrated by the separate representation and action-conditioned stages of V-JEPA 2 (Assran et al., 2025). Other systems can jointly train on several evidence types or transfer a prior through distillation. The choice should follow the gap to be closed. Unfamiliar object semantics, an unobserved material property, a new control interface, and a missing deformation mode are different problems. Transferring a representation does not remove the need to calibrate units, timing, and embodiment-dependent dynamics.

Multimodal measurements and targeted probes can expose distinctions that passive video leaves unresolved. A controlled lift with load measurements constrains mass. A slide under measured force constrains friction within a contact model. A thermal observation distinguishes visually identical process states. Such experiments should be chosen for their ability to separate plausible explanations, not merely to maximize visual novelty. Their cost and risk must be included in learning efficiency. For instruments and infrastructure, the intervention may be a process-setting change rather than a robot motion, but the same requirement holds. Predicted effects must be checked against the measurements relevant to the mechanism.

A further challenge is preserving uncertainty where evidence remains insufficient. A model should represent several compatible explanations instead of inventing a unique physical parameter from appearance. Uncertainty reduction through new sensing, identification through repeated interaction, and correction of structural model error should remain distinct. This distinction gives the closed loop a scientific role. Action tests an explanation, and the resulting discrepancy determines what knowledge should be revised.

5.5.2 Reliable Consequence Prediction in Complex and Long-Horizon Processes

Contact switches, non-rigid deformation, and coupled physical processes can turn small local errors into qualitatively different futures. Long-horizon prediction therefore requires more than a longer context window. It needs persistent state, representations of consequential events, appropriate time resolution, and uncertainty that remains useful as the forecast extends. A model may need to predict a phase boundary accurately without reproducing every intermediate texture.

The architectural routes in Table 5.2 are likely to be combined in several ways, but no single combination is established as universally preferable. One design direction connects compact predictive states to detailed generative readouts on demand. Another combines object- or field-based physical structure with learned residual dynamics. A third coordinates slower semantic and process models with faster contact or motion models. Each requires an interface that preserves identity, units, physical time, and uncertainty. A hierarchy is not useful when its levels describe incompatible worlds.

Combining routes along any of these directions raises a representation question. A shared substrate can support understanding, prediction, and action, while specialized encoders and heads preserve the information each function needs. Shared parameters are only one implementation. Aligned representations, directed cross-expert communication, and training-only predictive supervision offer alternatives, as discussed in Section 5.2.4. The roadmap’s distinction between functional roles and architectural choices is useful here. A common physical description should support compatible queries without forcing all modalities into one update frequency or every task into one decoding objective (wmChen2026Roadmap).

Future comparisons should therefore test composition rather than only larger monolithic models. Does adding structure improve held-out contact response? Does a generative head retain information needed by a new query? Does selective prediction save computation without making action ranking less reliable? Longer horizons and richer modalities should be assessed at matched resource budgets, with prediction errors decomposed by mechanism. These tests can reveal when an interface is missing information, when a transition is wrong, and when extra detail simply does not help the task.

A persistent challenge is deciding what must remain explicit across abstraction levels. A coarse state may encode that liquid will spill, while a fine field predicts where it flows. The two outputs should refer to the same container, contents, and boundary conditions. Learned refinement must recover detail compatible with the coarse state, not silently revise the initial condition until a preferred prediction becomes possible. The model may retain raw evidence or an external memory so that a new query can request information omitted from its current compact state. This makes memory retrieval and adaptive resolution part of world modeling, rather than equating longer token context with a sufficient physical state.

A second challenge is modular identification. If a prediction fails, the system should distinguish a wrong observation interpretation, an incorrect physical parameter, a missing interaction mechanism, and an inadequate decision objective. Composable models make these distinctions easier to test when their interfaces have clear semantics. A monolithic model can offer the same diagnostic access through controlled readouts and interventions. The long-term comparison is therefore not simply modular versus end-to-end. It is how reliably a system can localize error, acquire the evidence needed to correct it, and preserve previously valid knowledge at an acceptable cost.

5.5.3 Closing the Real-World Loop: Real-Time Operation, Transfer, and Continual Improvement

A deployed world model participates in a continuing loop among observation, understanding, prediction, action, and external feedback. It may help identify an uncertain state, propose informative experiments, screen candidate actions, or supply imagined experience for policy learning. The physical process then produces evidence that the model did not choose. This separation between internal imagination and external verification is essential. Repeated agreement between a generator and an evaluator sharing its assumptions does not establish improved knowledge of the world.

Real-time operation requires allocating computation while the environment continues to change. Cached context, asynchronous experts, selective decoding, and short action chunks can reduce particular costs, but each creates a responsibility for freshness and correction. Transfer adds another problem. A new body, tool, sensor, or process can change what an action means. Reusable physical knowledge should be separated from the local parameters and interfaces that require new evidence. Systems such as InternW0 and InternW0- $\Delta$ show concrete ways to separate training and runtime work, not a guarantee that one update schedule transfers unchanged to every physical system.

Continual improvement should use diagnosis to choose the scale of an update. Fresh evidence may be enough to correct the current belief. Repeated discrepancies may justify identifying a small set of physical parameters. A persistent missing mechanism may require new data and network retraining. These responses should be recorded separately, together with the amount of real interaction, human intervention, and computation required. Updating every model after every observation can be wasteful, while never updating parameters can leave systematic errors unresolved.

A practical improvement cycle retains real failures and corrections, selects data that target identified gaps, updates the relevant model or policy components, and evaluates the candidate version on both new conditions and a retained regression suite. Synthetic rollouts can broaden practice near a known weakness, but acceptance must include evidence not produced by the same model. Replay and parameter regularization can help retain previous skills. They must still be checked for interference and loss of adaptability. Chapter 4 treats the data-side loop, while the present chapter specifies the predictive interfaces whose validity must survive each update.

The long-term aim extends beyond more elaborate imagined worlds. It is a system in which better representations produce more informative forecasts, forecasts support better real interventions, and the resulting evidence produces measurable correction. Progress should be reported through predictive accuracy, physical consistency, calibrated uncertainty, and improved physical outcomes, together with the costs of training, adaptation, operation, and recovery. This closes the chapter’s organizing chain from state and transition to query and evidence.

These challenges converge on a single claim about priorities. Perception models tell an agent what is present. Policy models tell it what to do. A world model has the potential to help an agent understand what will happen, what would have happened instead, and why. In this sense the world model is one of the most important foundation models of Physical AI, providing a substrate on which perception, decision, and control can all stand. Its importance lies in the potential to connect testable predictions of the world with better decisions. More accurate predictions of task-relevant dynamics can support safer exploration, cheaper learning, and more reliable decisions across tasks and embodiments. For a world model to support decisions, its predictions need sufficient accuracy at the relevant resolution. Building machines that act in the world therefore depends, to a large extent, on building models of it and on making the limits of their evidence and predictions explicit.

## 6 Foundation Models for Robot Manipulation

Physical AI not only discusses how to perceive the world dynamics, but also instructs robots to actually interact with it. In robotics, manipulation is one of the important forms of physical action, which includes grasping, moving, assembling, and transforming objects through controlled contact, and beyond. This chapter examines foundation models for robot manipulation, which are the core of an embodied system that maps multimodal observations and task instructions to behavioral goals or low-level motor actions. Because open-ended environments present an unbounded variety of objects and tasks, engineering each manipulation skill individually is impractical. Instead, foundation models learn web-scale multimodal priors from physical robot trajectories, enabling a single pretrained model to be reused across tasks, environments and embodiments.

The chapter begins with the evolution of manipulation foundation models, focusing on the vision-language-action (VLA) architectures that dominate current practice. It then examines the pre-training and post-training that shape the model’s capabilities, the model’s adaptation across embodiments, and its deployment under real-time and resource constraints. It closes by applying these ideas to multi-fingered hands, where high-dimensional actuation, intricate contact transitions, and scarce demonstration data push every stage of the pipeline to its limits.

Figure 6.1: Foundation models for robot manipulation

## 6.1 Emergence and Taxonomy

An embodied agent should transform an instruction into a sequence of physically meaningful decisions. Recognizing a bottle is only one part of opening it. The agent must identify the requested outcome, choose a grasp and an opening strategy, interpret resistance during contact, and determine whether the cap has actually been released. Foundation models for robot manipulation aim to make these capabilities reusable across tasks, objects, environments and sometimes even bodies. They bring together multimodal representation learning, generalist robot policies and models of action consequences. Figure 6.1 provides an overview of foundation models for robot manipulation. The key question is how broadly acquired knowledge can guide ongoing physical interactions.

6.1.1 Conceptual Scope and Enabling Conditions

In this chapter, a foundation model for robot manipulation is a pretrained model that can adapt to new tasks. It draws on multimodal evidence and task context to make task-relevant decisions, set behavioral goals, or generate robot actions. The foundation model property concerns the reuse of learned structure. A single model should provide a useful starting point for many downstream tasks or operating conditions. Neither a large parameter count nor a natural-language interface establishes this property on its own.

Let $o_{t}$ denote exteroceptive observations, $\mathbf{q}_{t}$ denote proprioceptive measurements, $\mathbf{a}_{t}$ denote an action at the model’s declared control interface, $\ell_{\mathrm{lang}}$ denote a task instruction, and $e$ describe the embodiment. The interaction history is defined as follows.

 $h_{t}=(o_{0:t},\mathbf{q}_{0:t},\mathbf{a}_{0:t-1}),\qquad\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}=[\mathbf{a}_{t}^{\top};\ldots;\mathbf{a}_{t+H-1}^{\top}].$ 

(6.1)

An action-producing model implements $\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}\mid h_{t},\ell_{\mathrm{lang}},e)$ . A higher-level model may instead output a subgoal $g_{t}$ , a skill identifier, a program, or a constraint on the desired interaction. These outputs are different interfaces to physical behavior, and should not be treated as interchangeable. An instruction to “grasp the bottle” leaves substantially more work to downstream modules than a sequence of end-effector poses or joint targets.

Four developments have made this reuse practical. Vision-language pretraining supplies broad semantic representations. Increasingly diverse robot datasets provide action-grounded supervision. Sequence and generative models capture temporal and multimodal behavior. Training infrastructure and simulation make repeated optimization and controlled data variation feasible. These conditions are complementary. Additional computation cannot recover action semantics that were never recorded, and simulated diversity is useful only to the extent that learned behavior transfers to the target physical conditions.

The distinction from adjacent chapters follows these interfaces. The perception models of Chapter 3 extract task-relevant evidence from observations, while Chapter 4 addresses the data that support learning. The world models of Chapter 5 represent conditional evolution and answer questions about possible consequences. Foundation models for robot manipulation use evidence and predictive knowledge to decide what behavior to pursue. The foundation models for whole-body motor control discussed in Chapter 7 regulate the realization of that behavior under body dynamics and contact constraints. One network may implement several of these functions, and a VLA model may extend into motion generation. The distinction concerns the responsibility of an output, not the size, name, or location of a network. Chapter 8 then considers how these capabilities are assembled into agents that manage memory, tools, and extended activities.

For example, during cap opening, task reasoning first identifies which bottle to open and what the desired open state is. Prediction then estimates what will happen if the agent grasps and rotates it. Action generation proposes a motion, and local control adjusts that motion based on contact feedback. The same tactile event may cause either a local correction, such as reducing grip force, or a task-level revision, such as regrasping. Effective coordination therefore requires feedback in both directions.

6.1.2 From Specialized Policies to Reusable Embodied Models

Figure 6.2: Algorithm development framework

Figure 6.2 summarizes the transition from specialized visuomotor policies to reusable embodied models.

These early learned visuomotor policies often acquire one skill on one setup. Their representations are optimized for a narrow demonstration distribution, so even a change in camera, object, instruction, or robot can require substantial retraining. Multitask policies change the unit of learning from an isolated skill to a task-conditioned behavioral repertoire. RT-1 demonstrates instruction-conditioned robot control at scale, while the Open X-Embodiment study investigates the transfer available from pooling trajectories across robot platforms (brohan2023rt1; openx2024). These developments make data diversity and interface compatibility central modeling issues.

A second development is the transfer of semantic knowledge from language and vision-language pretraining. In modular systems, a language model can select grounded skills or generate programs that invoke perception and control functions. SayCan and Code as Policies illustrate these two approaches (ichter2023saycan; liang2023code). In direct action models, brohan2023rt2 incorporate robot action prediction into vision-language training with RT-2, and kim2024openvla release OpenVLA as a pretrained VLM-based policy available for adaptation. This kind of transfer can broaden object and instruction understanding, but it does not supply the missing dynamics or contact experience of an unfamiliar robot.

A third development focuses on temporal structure and continuous behavior. Diffusion Policy demonstrates multimodal action-sequence generation for visuomotor control, Octo combines a generalist policy with adaptable observation and action interfaces, and $\pi_{0}$ connects a pretrained VLM to a flow-based action expert (chi2023diffusion; octo2024; black2024pi0). These designs make a useful distinction between the representation needed to understand a scene and the computation needed to generate a coherent trajectory. They also show that a foundation model for robotics need not be an autoregressive language model throughout.

Finally, broad pretraining is increasingly connected with heterogeneous supervision and deployment experience. $\pi_{0.5}$ studies open-world generalization through heterogeneous co-training, while the RECAP approach underlying $\pi^{*}_{0.6}$ uses experience and corrections to improve a pretrained policy (pi2025pi05; Amin et al., 2026). The progression is consequently not a simple replacement of control by larger language models. It is the integration of semantic priors, physical action interfaces, predictive representations, and feedback-driven improvement. Each component addresses a different limitation of demonstration-only learning.

6.1.3 Major Model Lineages and Architectural Evolution

The main model lineages can be compared along the three axes of primary knowledge source, learning objective, and decision interface. Generalist policies emphasize reusable behavior learned from robot trajectories. VLAs introduce broad vision-language knowledge into action generation. And world-action models couple behavior with predictions of environmental change. Table 6.1 summarizes these emphases. The categories overlap. A generalist policy can be a VLA, and a VLA can contain a world model. Direct, hierarchical, and prediction-assisted execution are architectural choices that cut across all three lineages.

Table 6.1: Three model lineages compared by knowledge source, learning target, and decision interface. The categories are complementary rather than exclusive

Lineage

Knowledge source

Main learning target

Decision interface

Generalist robot policy

Diverse robot trajectories, task labels

Actions, chunks, or skills

RT-1, RT-X, Octo

Vision-language-action model

Vision-language pretraining plus robot interaction

Semantic grounding and conditioned action generation

Action tokens or continuous trajectories

RT-2, OpenVLA, $\pi_{0}$ 

World-action model

Video and interaction data with available action labels

Coupled action and future-state prediction

Actions with predicted outcomes, or prediction-assisted decisions

Unified World Models

Generalist Robot Policies

These policies learn primarily from collections of robot trajectories, usually conditioned on language, goal images, or task identifiers. Shared training allows reaching, grasping, placing, and other recurring structures to contribute to multiple tasks. RT-X explores such sharing across embodiments, and Octo provides a policy initialization that can be adapted to new observation and action spaces (openx2024; octo2024). Generality here comes from how broadly the behavior covers and transfers, not from conversational ability. Language may serve as a conditioning representation without making the policy itself a pretrained language model. The main limitation is coverage. Robot trajectories provide physically grounded actions but are costly to collect and can be concentrated in a few environments or control interfaces.

Vision-Language-Action Models

These models connect visual observations and linguistic goals with a declared action space. A prominent route initializes the policy from a pretrained VLM so that the policy does not have to learn object knowledge and instruction semantics entirely from robot demonstrations. Action supervision then grounds that knowledge in the robot’s control interface. The phrase VLA specifies a multimodal policy interface more clearly than it specifies a single architecture. Discrete autoregression, deterministic regression, diffusion, and flow matching are alternative ways of producing actions within this broad class. Their differences concern precision, multimodality, learning signals, and execution cost, as developed in Section 6.2. Semantic transfer is especially useful for interpreting an unfamiliar instruction, but successful interpretation still requires a motor repertoire capable of realizing it.

Predictive and Joint World-Action Models

A world model can choose actions in several ways, including evaluating proposed actions, generating subgoal observations, or sharing a representation with a policy. Joint video-action modeling, illustrated by Unified World Models, couples predictive and behavioral learning (zhu2025uwm). These couplings should be distinguished. A model that predicts a future image that appears to satisfy the task goal does not thereby show that the robot can reach that image. Likewise, predicting a future and an action together does not automatically provide a calibrated answer to every counterfactual action query. The benefit of prediction must be demonstrated through better decisions or more transferable representations.

One formulation models $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}},O_{t}^{+}\mid h_{t},\ell_{\mathrm{lang}},e)$ , where $O_{t}^{+}$ denotes future observations over a declared horizon. With appropriate conditioning and training, the model can relate a proposed behavior to its expected outcome, or use a desired outcome to help infer behavior. Action-free video can supervise the predictive component while action-labeled robot data ground executable decisions. This is a potential advantage of joint learning, but the missing robot actions in human video cannot be recovered merely by renaming visual motion as an action. Viewpoint, embodiment, and unobserved forces still constrain transfer.

Architectures for Organizing Decisions

A direct policy maps the current task context straight to actions. A hierarchical system exposes subgoals or skills between task reasoning and motion generation. A prediction-assisted system brings anticipated outcomes into learning or action selection. Language and program-mediated planners can compose existing behaviors, provided that their calls are grounded in perception, skill preconditions, and execution feedback. A higher-level process can also maintain context while a faster process updates motion using recent observations. GR00T N1 provides an example of tightly coupled vision-language and action-generation modules (bjorck2025gr00t). Gemini Robotics 1.5 illustrates the coordination of embodied reasoning with action capabilities (gemini2025robotics15). Architectural separation does not mean asynchronous execution. Whether modules run independently, share cached features, or wait at synchronization points is a deployment property that must be specified separately.

Connecting Policy, Prediction, and Evaluation

The relationships among these arrangements can be expressed with the following shared task representation and three possible output interfaces

 $\displaystyle z_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=f_{\theta}(h_{t},\ell_{\mathrm{lang}},e),$ 

(6.2)

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}$ 
 $\displaystyle\sim\pi_{\psi}(\cdot\mid z_{t},\ell_{\mathrm{lang}},e),$ 

 $\displaystyle\widehat{z}_{t+1:t+H}$ 
 $\displaystyle\sim p_{\phi}(\cdot\mid z_{t},\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}},e),$ 

 $\displaystyle\widehat{v}_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=V_{\omega_{\mathrm{critic}}}(z_{t},\ell_{\mathrm{lang}},e).$ 

Here $z_{t}$ summarizes available evidence, the policy proposes behavior, the transition model predicts its consequences, and the evaluator estimates a task-related quantity. Not every system contains all three heads, and the equations do not require shared parameters. They distinguish functions that are often conflated in discussion of unified models.

There are several ways to connect them. A policy may use a predicted subgoal as conditioning, a planner may score sampled action chunks through a world model, or predictive training may improve an encoder that is used without online rollout. In a joint generative model, what the model samples (an action, a future observation, or both) depends on how it is conditioned and masked. Each choice changes which questions can be asked at inference time and which computational costs lie on the control path.

Evaluation also requires precise semantics. A progress score estimates how far an observed process has advanced. A success classifier estimates whether a terminal criterion holds. A value function estimates future return under a specified policy and reward. A model trained for one of these tasks is not automatically a substitute for the others. During cap opening, observing rotation may indicate motion without demonstrating release. Outcome feedback must therefore be grounded in the property the task actually requires.

Interpreting Generalization Claims

Embodied generalization has several independent dimensions. A model may transfer to new object appearances while still relying on the same workspace and robot. It might understand a new composition of familiar instructions while lacking the corresponding motor skill. Or it might adapt to a new embodiment only after target demonstrations. Claims should specify which factors change and which remain fixed. In particular, zero-shot execution, few-shot adaptation, and large-scale fine-tuning are distinct capabilities.

Closed-loop evaluation should test the decisions that make reuse valuable, including selecting the intended object among distractors, completing unfamiliar combinations of known stages, revising behavior after a disturbance, and transferring with a stated amount of new data. A useful experimental design varies task, environment, and embodiment separately before testing their combination. Retaining performance on previously supported conditions matters as much as improvement on the new condition. Offline action prediction error alone cannot establish these properties because it does not measure the states visited by the executing policy.

The remainder of this chapter follows the resulting development path. Section 6.2 examines action representations and multimodal architectures. Section 6.3 explains how different supervision sources shape capabilities. Section 6.4 addresses the physical meaning of transfer between bodies. Section 6.5 then asks how these capabilities can be delivered within the timing and resource constraints of an actual robot.

## 6.2 Vision-Language-Action Model

Many current VLA models start from a pretrained VLM and extend it to output actions, a modality its pretraining never covered. This section begins with how actions are represented and generated, then turns to how they are combined with visual and linguistic inputs in a single sequence model, and closes with how this model is extended to sensory inputs beyond images and language.

6.2.1 Action Representation and Generation

Within a VLA, action is treated as a third modality alongside images and language, although it behaves quite differently from both. Actions are continuous rather than symbolic, their dimensionality and control rate vary with the embodiment, and consecutive actions are sampled at high frequency and are strongly correlated. Since action is also the model’s output, how it is represented decides both how demonstrations are encoded during training and how commands are decoded at run time. Writing $\mathbf{a}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ for the action at step $t$ and $\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}=[\mathbf{a}_{t}^{\top};\ldots;\mathbf{a}_{t+H-1}^{\top}]$ for an action chunk of horizon $H$ , modern VLAs predict a whole chunk at once instead of a single step (zhao2023; chi2023diffusion). Doing so limits the accumulation of errors over time, produces smoother motion, and spreads the cost of one forward pass over $H$ control steps. Existing methods fall into two families according to how $\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}$ is fed into the sequence model and how it is generated. The discrete route converts $\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}$ into tokens that the language backbone predicts, whereas the continuous route lets a dedicated head generate real-valued chunks directly. The two routes trade off training efficiency, inference speed and the preservation of the pre-trained VLM in opposite ways, which is why recent hybrid schemes combine discrete training with continuous execution.

Discrete Action Representations

Once a chunk is mapped to tokens $z_{1:N_{\mathrm{acttok}}}^{\mathrm{act}}$ , the VLA is trained with the ordinary next-token objective

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AR}}=-\sum_{k=1}^{N_{\mathrm{acttok}}}\log p_{\theta}\big(z_{k}^{\mathrm{act}}\,\big|\,z_{<k}^{\mathrm{act}},\,o_{t},\,\ell_{\mathrm{lang}}\big).$ 

(6.3)

This requires no change to the VLM architecture, and since robot data and web data are trained with the same loss, the backbone remains a language model shaped by both. The methods differ mainly in the tokenizer that produces $z_{1:N_{\mathrm{acttok}}}^{\mathrm{act}}$ . The simplest, per-dimension binning, splits each action dimension into a fixed number of uniform bins (256 in RT-1 (brohan2023rt1), RT-2 (brohan2023rt2) and OpenVLA (kim2024openvla)). RT-2 writes the bin indices as text, so the VLM outputs an action as a string of integers, while OpenVLA reassigns the least-used tokens of the Llama vocabulary to action bins. Binning is easy to implement but scales poorly, because a chunk becomes $H\cdot d$ tokens that must be decoded one after another, neighboring tokens at high control rates are nearly identical and therefore carry little learning signal, and precision can never exceed the bin width. Compression-based tokenization turns this redundancy into an advantage. FAST (pertsch2025fast_ch6) applies a discrete cosine transform to each action dimension, quantizes the coefficients so that most high-frequency ones become zero, and compresses the result with byte-pair encoding. The resulting sequences are much shorter than those produced by binning, the same tokenizer transfers across embodiments, and $\pi_{0}$ -FAST reaches the performance of the flow-matching $\pi_{0}$ with less training compute. Learned quantizers take a different approach and train a vector-quantized autoencoder (van2017neural) whose codebook entries act as short motion primitives. Residual vector quantization (RVQ) increases resolution by quantizing the remaining error over several stages, and VQ-VLA (wang2025vq) shows that training the tokenizer on more real and simulated trajectories improves both long-horizon success and smoothness. The price is an embodiment-specific decoder that has to be deployed together with the policy. Sequential autoregressive decoding of long action-token chunks through a billion-parameter backbone can incur substantial inference latency. Parallel decoding in OpenVLA-OFT (kim2025oft_ch6) predicts all action tokens in a single pass and thus raises throughput, but it no longer models the joint distribution over tokens explicitly.

Continuous Action Representations

On the continuous route, an output module produces $\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d}$ directly. A simple option is an $L_{1}$ action-regression head, as used in OpenVLA-OFT (kim2025oft_ch6). For direct point regression, expected elementwise $L_{1}$ loss is minimized by conditional coordinatewise medians. Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) uses an $L_{1}$ reconstruction term together with a weighted KL-divergence term within a conditional variational autoencoder (zhao2023). Such methods can perform well on benchmarks, but a single point prediction need not capture distinct valid action modes. Other generative heads model the full, possibly multimodal, action distribution. Diffusion Policy (chi2023diffusion) denoises action chunks conditioned on observations, and Octo (octo2024), RDT-1B (liu2025rdt) and GR00T N1 (bjorck2025gr00t) scale the idea up with diffusion transformers. Within VLAs, the reference design is $\pi_{0}$ (black2024pi0), in which a PaliGemma backbone encodes images and language and a separate, smaller action expert attends to the backbone tokens and is trained with conditional flow matching. With an interpolant $\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq},\tau_{\mathrm{flow}}}=\tau_{\mathrm{flow}}\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}+(1-\tau_{\mathrm{flow}})\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ , $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d}$ with independent entries $\varepsilon_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ , the expert learns the velocity field

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}=\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{\mathrm{flow}},\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}\big\|\,\mathbf{v}_{\theta}^{\mathrm{flow}}(\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq},\tau_{\mathrm{flow}}},\tau_{\mathrm{flow}},o_{t},\ell_{\mathrm{lang}})-(\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})\big\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2},$ 

(6.4)

where $\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}$ sums squared entries over the $H$ action steps and $d$ action coordinates. At inference the velocity field is integrated with a few Euler steps, and because the backbone prefix is cached, each step requires a forward pass through the expert only. Diffusion and flow-matching action heads avoid action-bin quantization and can represent multimodal action distributions. Compact action expert modules and a small number of sampling steps can make inference efficient. However, in the cited VLA comparisons, training with a continuous action expert converges more slowly than autoregressive action-token training, and gradients from a randomly initialized expert can interfere with the pretrained backbone. Gradient control and co-training with VLM data mitigate this interference in the reported settings (driess2025insulation_ch6). Co-training with web data, or interleaving actions with language reasoning, also requires additional machinery. It is therefore natural to use tokens for learning and continuous generation for execution, and several recent systems combine the two in this way. $\pi_{0.5}$ (pi2025pi05) pre-trains the whole model autoregressively on FAST tokens and adds a flow-matching expert only during post-training, where it optimizes $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AR}}+\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}$ with the two action representations masked from each other. At run time the model first decodes text and then runs a few denoising steps of the expert. Knowledge insulation (driess2025insulation_ch6) merges the two stages into one. The backbone is trained on FAST tokens and vision-language data while a stop-gradient prevents the flow-matching loss from reaching it. The reported model trains faster, runs faster, and generalizes better than either pure route. These systems point toward a division of labor in which discrete tokens shape the backbone’s representation and a lightweight continuous generator handles control. Which tokenizer shapes the backbone best, and how the two representations should be scheduled across pre-training, post-training and continual learning, are still open questions.

Figure 6.3: Two mainstream VLA structures. (a) In a mixture-of-transformers structure, the expert has its own weights but the same depth as the backbone, and in every layer its tokens attend to the backbone’s keys and values through a shared self-attention. The backbone can additionally generate reasoning text $r_{t}^{\mathrm{reason}}$ or FAST action tokens through an optional language-model head. (b) In a cross-attention structure, a separate diffusion transformer reads backbone token-feature matrix $\mathbf{H}_{t}^{\mathrm{VLM}}$ through cross-attention, so its depth, size and rate are independent of the backbone

6.2.2 Paradigm of Vision-Language-Action Models

The VLA paradigm starts from a simple observation. A policy $\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}\mid o_{t},\ell_{\mathrm{lang}})$ that maps images $o_{t}$ and an instruction $\ell_{\mathrm{lang}}$ to an action chunk $\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}$ takes the same inputs as a vision-language model, so a policy initialized from a VLM and fine-tuned on robot demonstrations can inherit knowledge that the VLM has learned from billions of web image-text pairs. Almost every current VLA pairs the vision encoder and language backbone of a VLM with an action output module and couples the two in one of two mainstream ways (Figure 6.3). This section first describes this common template before tracing its development.

Components

Both structures in Figure 6.3 share three components. The first is a vision encoder, usually the SigLIP or DINOv2 vision transformer (ViT) inherited from the VLM, which maps each camera image to a few hundred patch tokens. When there are several views, each is encoded separately and the tokens are concatenated. The second is a vision-language backbone, typically a decoder-only transformer with 2 to 7 billion parameters in open models (Llama 2, Qwen-VL, PaliGemma) and a frontier-scale model in closed systems, which processes the image tokens together with the tokenized instruction and produces the representation from which actions are read out. The third is an action output module, one of the heads described in Section 6.2.1, which turns this representation into an action chunk. Discrete action tokens need nothing beyond the backbone’s own language-model head, as in RT-2 and OpenVLA, whereas current generalist VLAs mostly follow the continuous route and add a smaller action expert trained with flow matching or diffusion. Proprioceptive state $\mathbf{q}_{t}$ enters alongside them, either as discretized tokens in the prefix or through a small embodiment-specific multilayer perceptron (MLP), and other sensing modalities are deferred to Section 6.2.3.

Two Mainstream Structures

With a continuous expert in place, the key architectural question becomes how the expert reads from the backbone, and current VLAs answer it in one of two ways (Figure 6.3). In a mixture-of-transformers (MoT) design ( $\pi_{0}$ (black2024pi0), $\pi_{0.5}$ (pi2025pi05), LingBot-VLA (wu2026pragmatic), InternVLA-A1 (cai2026internvla)), the expert is a narrower transformer with the same depth as the backbone. The two keep separate weights but share a single self-attention operation in every layer, so the action tokens simply form another block of the same sequence and read the backbone’s keys and values layer by layer (Figure 6.3a). This gives the tightest possible coupling, since the expert can draw on every level of the backbone’s representation and the backbone’s language-model head remains available for reasoning text or FAST tokens in the same sequence. The downside is that the expert is bound to the backbone’s depth and clock, and its gradients reach every backbone layer, which is what knowledge insulation (driess2025insulation_ch6) is designed to stop. In a cross-attention design (GR00T N1 (bjorck2025gr00t), SmolVLA (shukor2025smolvla), InternVLA-M1 (chen2025internvla)), the expert is a separate diffusion transformer (DiT) over state and action tokens that reads backbone token-feature matrix $\mathbf{H}_{t}^{\mathrm{VLM}}$ through cross-attention layers interleaved with self-attention (Figure 6.3b). The position and width of this interface are then free design choices, and published systems make them differently. GR00T N1 conditions its DiT on middle-layer rather than final-layer features of the VLM, and SmolVLA keeps only the lower half of a small VLM’s layers so that the whole model has just 0.45B parameters. InternVLA-M1 inserts a querying transformer whose learnable queries cross-attend to intermediate layers of a 3B VLM, passes the resulting fixed set of tokens to an 86M diffusion action expert, and attenuates the expert’s gradients before they reach the backbone. Decoupling allows the expert to be sized and clocked independently of the VLM, which dual-system layouts exploit by running a slow VLM above a fast expert, as GR00T N1 does. The price is a narrower channel, because the expert sees the backbone only through the features or queries it is given and does not take part in the backbone’s own attention. In practice, MoT is preferred when the expert and the backbone are trained jointly on one sequence, and cross-attention when the expert has to be small, fast or run at its own rate.

Sequence Organization

Whatever the structure, the inputs of one control step are organized as one ordered sequence, canonically

 $\underbrace{[\,\mathrm{img}(o_{t}^{1}),\ldots,\mathrm{img}(o_{t}^{N_{\mathrm{view}}}),\ \mathrm{txt}(\ell_{\mathrm{lang}})\,]}_{\text{prefix}}\;\underbrace{[\,\mathrm{txt}(r_{t}^{\mathrm{reason}})\,]}_{\text{reasoning}}\;\underbrace{[\,\mathrm{emb}(\mathbf{q}_{t}),\ \mathrm{emb}(\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq},\tau_{\mathrm{flow}}})\,]}_{\text{suffix}},$ 

(6.5)

where $N_{\mathrm{view}}$ is the number of views, $r_{t}^{\mathrm{reason}}$ is an optional intermediate text output (a subtask, plan or chain of thought), and $\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq},\tau_{\mathrm{flow}}}$ is the noised continuous action chunk at flow time $\tau_{\mathrm{flow}}$ . Discrete action tokens instead use $z_{1:N_{\mathrm{acttok}}}^{\mathrm{act}}$ as defined above. In an MoT the whole sequence passes through shared self-attention, which follows a block mask rather than a plain causal one. Prefix tokens attend to each other bidirectionally, as in prefix-LM training of PaliGemma-style VLMs, while the reasoning block is causal because it is generated token by token. The suffix attends to everything before it and bidirectionally within itself, since all $H$ actions are produced together, but no earlier block attends to the suffix. This keeps the prefix key-value cache independent of the actions, so that it can be reused across denoising steps. A cross-attention design arrives at the same structure by construction, because the backbone processes only the prefix and the reasoning block while the expert processes the suffix and reads the backbone through cross-attention. Here too the backbone features are computed once per observation and reused across denoising steps. When discrete and continuous representations coexist in training, as in $\pi_{0.5}$ (pi2025pi05) and knowledge insulation (driess2025insulation_ch6), the two suffixes are additionally masked from each other so that the flow expert cannot copy the FAST tokens.

Development

The template described above takes shape over several years. RT-1 (brohan2023rt1) predates the use of VLMs but sets conventions that later work retains. A transformer with 35 million parameters, trained on about 130,000 teleoperated episodes from 13 robots, learns to follow several hundred instructions. Its actions are discretized into 256 bins per dimension and emitted as tokens. Its generalization grows with the breadth of tasks and robots rather than with model size. RT-2 (brohan2023rt2) then co-fine-tunes internet-scale VLMs (PaLI-X 55B, PaLM-E 12B (driess2023palme)) on web data together with robot episodes whose actions are written as integer strings, and the resulting policy generalizes semantically in ways that no robot dataset could have taught it, for instance picking up the object “that could be used as a hammer”. RT-2, however, is neither open nor backed by shared data. Open X-Embodiment (openx2024) addresses the data gap by pooling 60 datasets from 22 embodiments into more than a million episodes and showing positive transfer across robots, and OpenVLA (kim2024openvla) addresses openness by releasing a 7B open-weight policy trained on this corpus.

The current generation keeps this foundation but adopts continuous action experts and trains on data far beyond public collections, and its progress has come on three fronts. The first front is scale, starting with $\pi_{0}$ (black2024pi0), which pairs a 3B PaliGemma backbone with a 300M flow-matching expert and trains it on roughly 10k hours of data from 7 robot configurations. $\pi_{0.5}$ (pi2025pi05) adds heterogeneous co-training and subtask prediction, which allows the same policy to work in homes that had not appeared in its training data, GR-3 (cheang2025gr) reproduces the template on a Qwen2.5-VL backbone, and LingBot-VLA (wu2026pragmatic) reports steady gains as its bimanual data grow from 3k to 20k hours, with no sign of saturation.

The second front is hierarchical control, motivated by whole-body and long-horizon tasks for which a single synchronous model is too slow. GR00T N1 (bjorck2025gr00t) establishes the open dual-system template for humanoids, with a 2B VLM feeding a diffusion transformer that runs at 120 Hz, and the Gemini Robotics series (gemini2025robotics15) pairs a frontier VLA with a separate embodied-reasoning model that plans in natural language and orchestrates the VLA.

On the third front, supervision has moved beyond imitation. $\pi^{*}_{0.6}$ (Amin et al., 2026) learns from its own deployment experience through reinforcement learning, while $\pi_{0.7}$ (intelligence2026pi) conditions on subgoal images generated by a world model and shows early signs of compositional generalization to tasks that have no demonstrations in its training data. InternVLA-A1 (cai2026internvla) unifies understanding, future-frame generation and action in one mixture-of-transformers, and its successor InternVLA-A1.5 (wmMa2026A15) replaces explicit future-frame generation with a small set of learnable foresight tokens supervised by a frozen pre-trained video generator, so that the policy inherits the generator’s dynamics priors while the video branch is discarded at inference. X-VLA (zheng2026x) shows that a 0.9B transformer with embodiment-specific soft prompts can match far larger models. Overall, the field has settled on the template and the two structures described above, and the main axis of scaling has moved from parameters, with open-weight VLAs still at 1 to 7B, to data, which now amounts to tens of thousands of hours supplemented by human video, synthetic trajectories and autonomous experience.

6.2.3 Extending Multimodal Inputs

Images and language are the default inputs of a VLA because they are the modalities used for VLM pretraining, but they leave out much of what manipulation depends on, such as events preceding the current frame, how far away objects are, and what happens at the moment of contact. An additional input can enter the sequence of Section 6.2.2 in one of two places. It can be added to the prefix as extra tokens that the backbone attends to together with images and text, or it can be given to the suffix and the action module as a conditioning input that bypasses the backbone. Writing $m_{t}^{\mathrm{multi}}$ and $m_{t}^{\mathrm{multi}\prime}$ for inputs on the two routes, the canonical sequence becomes

 $\displaystyle\underbrace{[\,\mathrm{img}(o_{t}^{1}),\ldots,\mathrm{img}(o_{t}^{N_{\mathrm{view}}}),\ \mathrm{enc}(m_{t}^{\mathrm{multi}}),\ \mathrm{txt}(\ell_{\mathrm{lang}})\,]}_{\text{prefix}}$ 

(6.6)

 $\displaystyle\underbrace{[\,\mathrm{txt}(r_{t}^{\mathrm{reason}})\,]}_{\text{reasoning}}\;\underbrace{[\,\mathrm{emb}(\mathbf{q}_{t}),\ \mathrm{emb}(m_{t}^{\mathrm{multi}\prime}),\ \mathrm{emb}(\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq},\tau_{\mathrm{flow}}})\,]}_{\text{suffix}}.$ 

Multiple camera views, including the wrist camera, are already handled by the vision encoder as described in Section 6.2.2, and proprioceptive state $\mathbf{q}_{t}$ usually takes the second route, so the rest of this section reviews three further extensions, namely temporal history, 3D geometry and contact.

Temporal History and Memory

Most VLAs condition only on the current frame, even though many tasks depend on the past, for example when the arm hides the target, when an object has been placed under a container, or when the robot must keep track of which stages of a task are already done. Concatenating past frames into the prefix, as Octo (octo2024) does, brings sharply diminishing returns beyond one extra frame while adding hundreds of tokens per frame and view, and it also invites causal confusion (de2019causal), in which the policy copies the behavior implied by past observations instead of reacting to the current one. Longer memory therefore comes down to compression, and two recent systems approach it in different ways. MEM (torne2026mem), which underlies $\pi_{0.6}$ (Amin et al., 2026) and $\pi_{0.7}$ (intelligence2026pi), keeps memory inside the sequence at two time scales. Over the short term, a video encoder compresses recent frames, packing six of them into the token budget of a single frame in $\pi_{0.7}$ . Over the long term, a high-level policy rewrites a natural-language summary at every step and places it in the reasoning slot $r_{t}^{\mathrm{reason}}$ , which supports tasks that require up to 15 minutes of memory. RoboTTT (jiang2026robottt) instead moves memory out of the sequence and into the weights. Its test-time training layers update a small fast-weight network with one gradient step per timestep, so history is stored in these weights and inference cost stays constant however long the context becomes. With this design the context reaches 8K timesteps, or about 5 minutes, and pre-training with an 8K-timestep context outperforms pre-training with 1K timesteps, which suggests that context length may be a scaling axis for robot policies just as it is for language models.

3D Information

An RGB image projects the scene onto a plane, so grasp height, clearance and relative depth must be inferred, whereas depth sensors and point clouds supply this geometry directly. The most direct way to use this geometry is to feed it into the model. SpatialVLA (qu2025spatialvla) turns depth from a monocular estimator into 3D positional encodings for the image tokens, while PointVLA (li2026pointvla) converts point clouds into native 3D tokens that only the action module consumes. Explicit geometry improves precision on spatially demanding tasks, but the 3D encoder lacks web-scale pre-training, and commodity depth sensors fail on transparent and reflective objects. Spatial Forcing (li2026spatial) takes a second route and uses geometry only as a training signal. Having found that the visual tokens of an RGB-trained VLA carry little recoverable depth structure, it aligns an intermediate layer of these tokens with the features that the geometry foundation model VGGT (wang2025vggt) extracts from the same images. Since VGGT is needed only during training, inference is unchanged, and training nevertheless becomes faster and more data-efficient, which shows that an input can shape the backbone’s representation without ever entering its sequence.

Force and Tactile Sensing

Contact-rich tasks such as insertion, screwing and handling fragile objects depend on forces that vision cannot observe, and the wrist camera is usually occluded at exactly the moment of contact. Contact information can enter a VLA in three ways. Images from vision-based tactile sensors such as GelSight (yuan2017gelsight) can be fed to the vision encoder as an additional view, albeit across a domain gap. Force-torque readings (cao2021six) can be treated like proprioception and placed in the suffix. And dedicated tactile encoders that cover several sensor types, such as Sparsh (higuera2024sparsh), can produce tokens for the backbone. Tactile-VLA (huang2025tactile) follows the token route, fusing tactile tokens with vision and language inside the VLM and outputting target positions and forces for a hybrid position-force controller, whereas ForceVLA (yu2026forcevla) follows the conditioning route, fusing force-torque tokens with VLM features in a mixture-of-experts module on the action path. TA-VLA (zhang2025ta), a systematic study of torque inputs, comes out in favor of the conditioning route for such signals, finding that torque helps more in the action decoder than in the encoder and that a torque history summarized into a single token works best.

## 6.3 Pre-Training, Post-Training, and Capability Shaping

Figure 6.4: Overview of the embodied VLA training pipeline. Pre-training combines multi-source data under multi-task objectives to produce a VLA base model. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) during supervised post-training behavior-clones demonstrations into an executable initial policy. And reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) during reinforcement learning-based post-training refines the policy from rewards, safety costs, and vision-language evaluator feedback. The stages are discussed in Sections 6.3.1 to 6.3.3

Figure 6.4 summarizes the overall training pipeline for embodied VLA models, which proceeds through three stages. Pre-training uses multi-source data to learn general representations and behavioral priors. Supervised post-training, including SFT, turns these priors into executable policies. Reinforcement learning-based post-training, including RFT, improves the policy through action outcomes. The remainder of this section discusses each stage in turn and then addresses continual learning, which converts deployment experience into lasting capabilities (Figure 6.5).

6.3.1 Pre-Training: Learning General Embodied Representations and Behavioral Priors

Vision-language models can recognize objects, interpret instructions, and reason using commonsense knowledge, but these capabilities do not automatically translate into reliable robotic manipulation. Embodied pretraining must integrate language, visual inputs, robot proprioceptive states, actions, and task outcomes within a common temporal framework, enabling the model to learn relationships among instructions, states, actions, and outcomes. Conditioned on observation histories, previous actions, task instructions, and embodiment characteristics, the model learns how to select actions in the current state. Observations may include not only RGB images but also depth, tactile measurements, force and torque readings, joint states, and equipment telemetry.

Embodiment characteristics include degrees of freedom, end-effector type, control frequency, workspace, and action limits. Explicitly incorporating these conditions helps distinguish shared task structure from embodiment-specific execution mechanisms, providing a basis for transfer across tasks and robot platforms.

Different data sources offer complementary supervision. Internet image-text data provide semantic knowledge about objects, scenes, and tasks. Videos of human activity reveal action sequences, tool use, and state transitions. Robot demonstrations supply action labels associated with specific control interfaces. And simulated interactions provide relatively inexpensive data on contact, forces, collisions, and failures that are difficult to collect at scale. Mixing these sources is intended to combine semantic, temporal, and physical information, rather than merely increase the number of training examples.

This complementarity also offers a way to address the scarcity of labeled robot actions. Video prediction, inverse dynamics, and latent action models can extract task-relevant behavioral representations from human videos, which an embodiment adaptation module can subsequently decode into executable actions. Studies such as UniVLA (bu2025univla) show that task-centered latent action representations can exploit video data spanning different embodiments and viewpoints. Nevertheless, their physical executability still requires calibration through robot interaction. Acquiring behavioral knowledge from human video therefore also requires aligning that knowledge with robot control interfaces, sensor feedback, and physical outcomes.

To support this alignment, embodied pretraining commonly combines action prediction, language understanding, state recognition, task progress estimation, and outcome prediction. These objectives correspond to different forms of supervision available in embodied data. Consider a bottle-opening task as an example. Action supervision specifies the robot actions needed to approach, grasp, and rotate the cap, and is typically obtained from teleoperated or scripted demonstrations recorded in the robot’s own action space. State supervision describes the relevant object and contact conditions, such as the poses of the bottle and cap and whether the end effector is in contact with the cap. In simulation these labels come from ground-truth physics, while on real robots they are estimated by the perception stack or annotated offline. Progress supervision identifies the current stage of the task, such as approach, grasp, rotation, release, or completion. This supervision can be supplied by scripted stage detectors, human annotators, or a vision-language evaluator of the kind used in reinforcement learning-based post-training. Outcome supervision indicates whether the bottle has ultimately been opened, which can be determined from a terminal physical observation or task-specific success criterion. Language supervision associates the visual and behavioral sequence with the task instruction, such as “open the bottle”, and is available whenever trajectories are paired with instructions or narrations. These five objectives train distinct, complementary capabilities.

Table 6.2: Correspondence between heterogeneous data sources, the supervision they provide, the objectives of Eq. (6.7) they support, and the model components primarily updated.
