These objectives can be summarized by a weighted multi-task loss of the form

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pre}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{a}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{action}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{state}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{p}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{progress}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{o}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{outcome}}+\lambda_{\ell_{\mathrm{lang}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{language}},$ 

(6.7)

where the coefficients balance action learning, state understanding, progress estimation, outcome prediction, and language supervision. This schematic loss combines objectives whose labels may be available on different samples. Each loss is evaluated only where its supervision is available, with missing labels handled by masking the corresponding objective.

Table 6.2 summarizes how this masking scheme applies to each data source, which objectives in Eq. (6.7) it can support, and which model components the resulting gradients primarily update. Because available supervision varies by data source, the same foundation model is trained by applying different subsets of the objectives to different data sources. The resulting training process aligns semantic, temporal, state, and action representations without requiring a homogeneous label space across the entire dataset.

How such multi-task, multi-embodiment data are curated, balanced, and mixture-weighted is a data engineering question treated in Chapter 4. This section examines how the composition of the mixture enters optimization. On the training side, a curriculum may progress from short-horizon skills with limited contact to multistage tasks, perturbed states, and failure recovery, and it should specify success and failure boundaries so that the model learns when to continue execution, acquire new observations, or terminate safely. As action learning progresses, retaining existing multimodal knowledge becomes an additional concern. When an action expert is connected to a pretrained vision-language backbone, gradient updates from action learning may interfere with established semantic representations. Staged unfreezing, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, gradient isolation, and knowledge distillation can help preserve language understanding and visual knowledge while new action capabilities are acquired. The heterogeneous joint training used in $\pi_{0.5}$ and the Knowledge Insulation approach illustrate this principle. Training across diverse data sources expands task and environmental coverage while limiting interference with existing multimodal knowledge.

Pretraining should consequently be evaluated using more than training loss or offline action prediction error. Evaluation should also examine closed-loop performance on unseen objects, novel combinations of instructions, and mildly perturbed conditions. These tests assess whether shared representations support perception, decision-making, and action under the new conditions. Pretraining supplies an initialization for the task- and embodiment-specific adaptation discussed next. Where the prior does not yet support the target task or embodiment, supervised post-training is one route to consistent execution. Outcome-based adaptation provides another, as developed below. Some pipelines also introduce an explicit alignment stage between broad pretraining and task adaptation. Section 6.6.2 examines these choices for dexterous hands through EgoScale on Sharpa Wave.

6.3.2 Supervised Post-Training: From General Priors to Executable Policies

Supervised post-training uses expert demonstrations, teleoperation trajectories, task procedures, and high-quality simulated data to adapt general behavioral priors to specific tasks, embodiments, and environments. Behavioral cloning increases the likelihood of expert actions conditioned on observations, task instructions, and embodiment characteristics, bringing the policy closer to the behavioral distribution represented in the demonstrations. Its effectiveness depends first on whether demonstrations cover the complete task. Training examples should include task initiation, critical contacts, transitions between stages, completion verification, and safe termination, rather than being restricted to locally standardized actions extracted from successful trajectories. For multistep tasks, stage labels, subgoals, and outcome criteria should also be recorded to support learning of temporal relationships among actions.

Adaptation to a new task or embodiment may then use full-parameter fine-tuning, updates to selected modules, or parameter-efficient methods such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA). Full-parameter fine-tuning offers greater scope for parameter adjustment but requires more data and computation. Parameter-efficient methods facilitate rapid iteration, although their effectiveness may be limited by discrepancies between the new task and existing representations. For a VLA initialized from a pretrained vision-language model, parameter-efficient adaptation has a further benefit. The backbone can be kept frozen so that the semantic priors built during pre-training are preserved, while a small number of action-side parameters are learned. Gradient isolation during pre-training addresses the same interference concern. Results reported for OpenVLA and Octo (kim2024openvla; octo2024) indicate that large-scale multitask pretraining can substantially reduce the data required for downstream adaptation. Performance after adaptation nevertheless depends on appropriate treatment of sensors, action spaces, and embodiment characteristics.

Even with high-quality demonstrations, behavioral cloning faces a discrepancy between training and deployment state distributions. Training typically uses states visited by an expert, whereas deployment states are determined by the model’s own actions. A small localization error can cause subsequent observations to depart from the demonstration distribution, allowing errors to compound over time. Interactive dataset aggregation addresses this problem by executing the current policy, requesting expert actions or corrections at the off-distribution states it encounters, and adding these examples to the training set. DAgger exemplifies this approach to distribution shift in sequential decision-making. For a fine-tuned VLA, the expert is typically a teleoperator who shares the policy’s action interface, so corrective labels can be appended to the training set without retargeting, and interactive aggregation becomes a natural extension of demonstration collection rather than a separate pipeline. Demonstration collection thus extends beyond recording ideal execution to include difficult states and recovery behaviors encountered by the model itself.

Human intervention data should be differentiated according to their training function. Valid actions preceding a takeover can serve as positive demonstrations. Human corrections can provide supervised labels for off-distribution states. And failure outcomes can support the training of success classifiers or value models. Erroneous actions, however, should not automatically become imitation targets. This treatment preserves both the conditions under which errors arise and the corresponding recovery strategies, enabling supervised post-training to learn normal execution as well as recovery to feasible states. Nevertheless, supervised post-training primarily learns conditional relationships between states and actions in demonstration data. It does not directly optimize completion time, energy consumption, precision, or long-term success rate. It is well suited to establishing a stable initial policy, particularly when operating procedures are clearly defined and expert demonstrations are of high quality, but reductions in training loss cannot substitute for closed-loop validation on the physical system.

Validation should therefore cover instruction following, action executability, critical state transitions, outcome assessment, and termination under abnormal conditions. For tasks such as liquid transfer and precision assembly, success criteria should also incorporate mass, flow rate, applied forces, leakage, and instrument readings, explicitly distinguishing the execution of action commands from the achievement of task objectives. When a model can reliably follow procedures but remains limited in efficiency, contact precision, or recovery from complex disturbances, feedback from action outcomes is needed to support policy improvement beyond imitation.

6.3.3 Reinforcement Learning-Based Post-Training: Improving Policies Through Action Outcomes

Behavioral cloning can reproduce demonstrator behavior, but its objective does not directly address efficiency gains subject to success-rate requirements, action adjustment under changing contact conditions, recovery from states outside the demonstration distribution, or improvements in action sequences discovered through autonomous interaction. Reinforcement learning evaluates the long-term consequences of actions through environmental feedback, enabling continued policy improvement toward task objectives. For Physical AI, it is particularly relevant to precise contact interactions, long-horizon tasks, disturbance recovery, and efficiency optimization. Reinforcement learning is not, however, necessary for every task. When procedures are stable, demonstrations provide sufficient coverage, and performance already meets requirements, supervised training and deterministic control may be more appropriate. The decision to introduce reinforcement learning-based post-training should depend on the limitations of the existing policy and whether environmental feedback provides an effective signal for addressing them.

Compared with virtual environments, reinforcement learning on physical robots involves slow interactions, costly resets, equipment wear, delayed rewards, and safety risks. States are often partially observable, contact and friction exhibit discontinuities, and outcomes may also depend on material batches, temperature, and tool condition. Large-scale random exploration in the physical world is therefore generally impractical. Under these constraints, policy optimization typically seeks to maximize expected cumulative return while accounting for task rewards, safety costs, and energy consumption, with discounting controlling the relative weight of returns over different time horizons. For physical robot tasks, this objective can be written as

 $J(\pi_{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{\mathrm{ep}}\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T}\gamma^{t}\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{g}}r_{t}^{\mathrm{goal}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{p}}r_{t}^{\mathrm{progress}}-\lambda_{\mathrm{safe}}c_{t}^{\mathrm{safety}}-\lambda_{\mathrm{e}}c_{t}^{\mathrm{energy}}\right)\right],$ 

(6.8)

where the terms represent task achievement, progress, safety cost, and energy consumption, respectively. Task rewards, progress, safety constraints, and resource consumption should be recorded separately to determine whether apparent gains reflect improved task performance or exploitation of a particular metric. Safety penalties can help a policy learn risk boundaries, but they cannot replace independent limit enforcement, collision detection, emergency stops, or human takeover mechanisms. Reward design must likewise guide learning while remaining verifiable against physical outcomes. Terminal success signals are simple and reliable but too sparse for many long-horizon tasks. Intermediate rewards can capture distance to the goal, contact quality, trajectory error, completion time, and stage progress, yet may be exploited in ways that diverge from the actual objective. Reward design should therefore prioritize observable, independently verifiable physical quantities, such as changes in mass, position error, peak force, leakage status, and instrument readings, and validate them against independently assessed final outcomes.

Alongside rewards, value functions estimate how current states and actions contribute to future task outcomes, helping the policy identify behaviors with long-term benefits. Vision-language evaluators can infer progress, completion, and stagnation from successive observations, providing denser feedback for physical robots. Such evaluators may nevertheless misclassify outcomes, and policies may exploit evaluation biases through reward hacking. Calibration against physical outcomes is therefore necessary. VLAC (zhai2025vlac) illustrates an approach that uses vision-language models for progress estimation and asynchronous reinforcement learning on real robots. These methods broaden the sources of feedback while reinforcing the need to cross-check intermediate evaluations against final outcomes.

For a fine-tuned VLA, a practical pipeline begins offline. The demonstrations, successful and failed trajectories, and human corrections already accumulated during supervised post-training form the dataset from which values are estimated and a policy is derived, reducing the risks of physical exploration. A subsequent online stage can collect a limited amount of autonomous execution data, focusing on states associated with model uncertainty, repeated failures, or high informational value. Training should constrain the policy from deviating excessively from behaviors supported by the data, thereby limiting overly optimistic value estimates for actions absent from the dataset. Human intervention can also be adjusted as the policy improves. Takeovers can prevent hazardous exploration early in training, corrective actions can address difficult states at intermediate stages, and later interventions can be confined to infrequent anomalies. HIL-SERL (luo2025hilserl) combines demonstrations, reward classifiers, and progressively reduced human intervention to improve the sample efficiency of reinforcement learning on physical robots, illustrating the complementary roles of demonstrations, autonomous interaction, and human correction.

For large VLA models, conventional online policy-gradient methods such as PPO (schulman2017ppo) often entail substantial sample requirements and challenges in training stability. An alternative is to collect experience in batches and update the policy between collection rounds. The RECAP method used in $\pi^{*}_{0.6}$ (Amin et al., 2026) integrates autonomous execution outcomes, human corrections, and existing demonstrations within iterative offline reinforcement learning. It estimates advantages using a value function and then derives an improved policy through advantage conditioning. This approach illustrates how reinforcement learning on physical robots can alternate between batch data collection, offline policy updates, and validation on the robot, without modifying model parameters after every action. The same workflow supports independent validation between updates to determine whether policy improvements persist during physical execution.

To further reduce physical interaction costs, world models can compare the short-term consequences of candidate actions before execution, helping to screen out behaviors likely to cause collisions, slippage, leakage, or task failure. They can also generate supplementary experience in simulation or latent space. However, world models are subject to modeling errors, which a policy may exploit to obtain inflated estimates of return. They are therefore useful for candidate evaluation, risk prediction, and data augmentation, but cannot replace physical outcome measurements, low-level controllers, or independent safety mechanisms. Regardless of the training approach, evaluation should report success rate, completion time, precision, failure recovery rate, the number of physical interactions, human intervention rate, and the number of safety incidents. Improvements beyond demonstration performance can be established only when gains persist on independent test tasks and under physical disturbances. Retaining and extending those gains during long-term deployment additionally requires continual learning.

6.3.4 Continual Learning: Turning Deployment Experience into Lasting Capabilities

Figure 6.5: The continual learning loop for embodied agents in long-term deployment. Deployment interactions are logged as experience records (success, failure, takeover, recovery), and each iteration updates the policy version $v_{k}$ to $v_{k+1}$ through gap identification, targeted collection, offline update, validation, and gated deployment. The process is detailed in Section 6.3.4

Long-term deployment exposes embodied agents to situations that cannot be fully anticipated during pretraining or post-training. The resulting need for continued adaptation can be understood in light of Sutton’s Big World Hypothesis. As JavedSutton2024 articulate, many decision-making environments are far larger and more complex than an agent’s perceptual, representational, and computational resources can accommodate. An agent must therefore act on an incomplete understanding of its environment, learning and revising the knowledge most relevant to its current decisions rather than relying on an exhaustive representation of all possible states and optimal actions. For embodied systems, this perspective provides a rationale for continual learning. Capabilities acquired before deployment provide an initial basis for action, but must be evaluated and refined as interaction reveals unfamiliar states, changing task demands, and limitations of the current policy. Such refinement must also preserve previously acquired skills that remain relevant. Supporting this process requires experience records that retain the temporal, spatial, and embodiment context of each interaction, including the model version, task instruction, sensor state, commanded action, observed outcome, and any anomaly or human intervention. Distinguishing successful execution, failure, warnings, takeovers, and recovery within these records allows deployment experience to inform subsequent supervised training, value estimation, and policy improvement.

As experience accumulates, the central challenge in continual learning shifts from increasing data volume to identifying the learning value of individual experiences. Samples can be selected according to failure frequency, model confidence, state novelty, intervention points, and environmental changes, while balancing task value, information gain, collection cost, and risk. Recurrent grasp slippage, for example, calls for additional data on contact states and recovery actions. Occasional instrument anomalies require complete telemetry and procedural context, rather than a final failure label alone. Active sampling should also help identify capability boundaries, allowing the system to distinguish tasks already mastered under current conditions from changes addressable through context updates and changes requiring parameter updates or retraining. This distinction links newly collected data to specific capability gaps and prevents local adaptation from being conflated with improvements in general competence.

Clarifying the form of adaptation is also essential to managing the relationship between new and existing capabilities. Immediate adaptation through context or memory, and runtime calibration through updates to state estimates or embodiment parameters, do not necessarily modify the foundation model. Long-term learning that changes model parameters, by contrast, requires model version control and regression testing. As new tasks arrive and parameters are updated, catastrophic forgetting, interference across tasks, and policy drift may occur. Continual learning therefore needs to optimize new-task adaptation while retaining previously acquired capabilities (kirkpatrick2017ewc; dohare2024plasticity), using an objective of the form

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CL}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{new}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{retain}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{retain}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}},$ 

(6.9)

where $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{new}}$ measures adaptation to new tasks, $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{retain}}$ preserves previous capabilities, and $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}$ limits undesirable parameter changes. Replay of representative experiences can preserve coverage of previous task distributions. Knowledge distillation can constrain the new model’s behavior on earlier tasks. Parameter regularization can limit changes to parameters important for retained knowledge. And modular architectures can isolate new skills within specific components. Methods such as elastic weight consolidation (kirkpatrick2017ewc) mitigate forgetting by restricting changes to important parameters, although their effectiveness in embodied tasks must still be validated through physical interaction. Continual learning should therefore be evaluated in terms of both gains on new tasks and retention of existing skills.

As illustrated in Figure 6.5, continual learning should follow a controlled iterative process to make capability gains verifiable. The process should identify capability gaps, collect targeted experience, update the model offline, jointly validate performance on new and existing tasks together with compliance with safety constraints, and deploy only after predefined performance and safety requirements are met. Previous model versions should remain available for rollback. For high-risk tasks, validation should begin in simulation, hardware-in-the-loop settings, or restricted workspaces before the scope of physical operation is gradually expanded. Each update should establish whether performance on new tasks has improved, whether previous capabilities have been retained, how much data and human effort adaptation required, and whether failure recovery has become more reliable. Deployment experience can be regarded as a source of established system capabilities only when these results are reproduced across independent tasks, different batches of objects, and sustained operation. It can then provide a reliable basis for subsequent task adaptation and policy optimization.

As summarized in Figure 6.4, capability development in foundation models for robot manipulation thus proceeds through a feedback loop of prior acquisition, task adaptation, outcome-based optimization, and experience accumulation, rather than a direct transition from large-scale pretraining to autonomous operation. Pretraining supports shared semantic and behavioral structure. Supervised post-training enables execution of procedures on specific embodiments. Reinforcement learning-based post-training uses physical outcomes to improve precision, efficiency, and recovery. And continual learning supports the long-term retention of these gains and their transfer to new tasks and environments. Each stage has a distinct training emphasis, while demonstrations, interaction feedback, and deployment experience connect them. Together, they support the progression from demonstration-driven behavioral learning toward continual policy optimization grounded in physical feedback.

## 6.4 Multi-Embodiment Modeling and Model Adaptation

The action interfaces in Section 6.2 specify how a model generates behavior, while the pre-training and post-training procedures in Section 6.3 establish reusable behavioral priors. Realizing these priors on a different physical system requires compatible observation and action interfaces, together with adaptation to its morphology and interaction dynamics. Here, an embodiment denotes the robot platform together with its end-effectors, sensing and actuation systems, and control interfaces. Replacing a parallel gripper with a dexterous hand therefore changes the embodiment even if the manipulator remains unchanged. The substitution alters the available contact modes, action dimensionality, sensing geometry, and feasible manipulation strategies. Multi-embodiment modeling seeks to transfer task-relevant knowledge across these configurations while preserving the physical distinctions that determine executable behavior. Cross-robot training in Open X-Embodiment provides empirical evidence that heterogeneous interaction data can support such transfer, although its reported evaluations do not establish generalization to arbitrary unseen robots (openx2024).

Following the partially observable formulation in Chapter 2 and the distinction between physical state and internal representation in Chapter 5, let $e\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{emb}}$ index an embodiment and write

 $\mathcal{M}_{e}=(\mathcal{S}_{e},\mathcal{A}_{e},P_{e}^{\mathrm{tr}},R_{\ell_{\mathrm{lang}},e},\mathcal{O}_{e},O_{e},\gamma),$ 

(6.10)

where $\mathcal{S}_{e}$ includes the physical state of the robot and its environment. $\mathcal{A}_{e}$ is the action space at the declared control interface. $P_{e}^{\mathrm{tr}}$ is the transition kernel. $R_{\ell_{\mathrm{lang}},e}$ specifies the reward for instruction $\ell_{\mathrm{lang}}$ . $\mathcal{O}_{e}$ is the measurement space. $O_{e}$ is the observation likelihood, and $\gamma$ is the discount factor. The measurements comprise exteroceptive observations $o_{t}$ and proprioceptive measurements $\mathbf{q}_{t}$ , retaining their separate notation from Section 6.1. The kernel $P_{e}^{\mathrm{tr}}$ corresponds to the embodiment-conditioned transition kernel $T$ in Chapter 5, with elapsed time included when required. The measurement pair $(o_{t},\mathbf{q}_{t})$ belongs to $\mathcal{O}_{e}$ , whereas $O_{e}(o_{t+1},\mathbf{q}_{t+1}\mid s_{t+1},\mathbf{a}_{t})$ denotes its conditional observation likelihood. Actuator memory and other dynamic variables must be included in the physical state when needed for the Markov assumption. The subscript on $\mathcal{S}_{e}$ allows robot configurations with different state dimensions. A shared task representation does not require identical physical state spaces.

Using the history $h_{t}=(o_{0:t},\mathbf{q}_{0:t},\mathbf{a}_{0:t-1})$ and action chunk $\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}=[\mathbf{a}_{t}^{\top};\ldots;\mathbf{a}_{t+H-1}^{\top}]$ defined in Eq. (6.1), the policy interface remains

 $\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}\sim\pi_{\Theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t},\ell_{\mathrm{lang}},e),$ 

(6.11)

where $\Theta$ denotes the complete set of policy parameters, while $\theta$ and $\psi$ below denote representation and action-generation parameters, respectively. The horizon $H$ counts action steps. Its physical duration also depends on the command intervals. A current-observation policy is a restricted instance of this history-conditioned formulation. The modeling objective is to share information about task goals, object relations, and behavioral organization while retaining the embodiment information required for action feasibility and contact regulation.

6.4.1 Embodiment-Aware Data Representation and Alignment

Pooling trajectories across robots requires compatibility of physical meaning, not merely compatibility of tensor shapes. Let $\mathcal{D}_{e}$ denote the collection of trajectories associated with embodiment $e$ . Each trajectory retains its instruction, ordered observations and actions, outcome annotations, and acquisition metadata. Let $m_{t}^{\mathrm{meta}}$ denote acquisition metadata. Metadata should identify the robot and end-effector configuration, sensor calibration, coordinate frames, units, control mode, timestamps, command duration, latency, and the data-collection policy or operator. These fields determine how a recorded command relates to an observed physical consequence.

Semantic, Geometric, and Dynamic Alignment

Semantic alignment concerns task goals, object roles, and stages of behavior. Two robots can share the goal of opening a container while requiring different grasps and motion sequences. Geometric alignment concerns reference frames, pose conventions, kinematics, and correspondences between observation and action representations. A command expressed in a camera frame, tool frame, or joint space requires an explicit interpretation before it can be transferred. Dynamic alignment concerns the embodiment-dependent transition kernel $P_{e}^{\mathrm{tr}}$ , including actuator response, payload, friction, compliance, and execution delay. Geometric correspondence alone does not establish equivalent contact behavior.

These distinctions also delimit what data standardization achieves. The RT-X experiments use a canonical camera view and a coarsely aligned end-effector action interface, with dataset-specific action normalization. The original control conventions are retained, and action coordinate frames are not fully aligned across datasets (openx2024). Thus, numerical normalization facilitates joint training without making identical action vectors physically interchangeable. UMI illustrates a complementary interface-level approach in which relative trajectories and inference-time latency matching support transfer of demonstrations collected with handheld grippers to compatible robot systems (chi2024umi_ch6). Neither approach removes the need to verify reachability, tracking, and contact behavior on the receiving embodiment.

Heterogeneous Sensing and Action Interfaces

Observation interfaces may differ in camera count, viewpoint, and calibration. They may also differ in whether proprioceptive, force, or tactile measurements are available. Modality-specific tokenizers, sensor identity encodings, and validity masks can expose these differences to a shared model. Octo supports adding or removing observation tokenizers and adapting to new sensory inputs. HPT uses embodiment-specific input stems to map heterogeneous visual and proprioceptive inputs into a common token interface (octo2024; wang2024hpt). Missing measurements should remain distinguishable from valid zero-valued measurements. For high-rate contact signals, timestamps and observation windows must also preserve the temporal relationship between commands and measured interaction.

Action interfaces require comparable care. A Cartesian displacement, joint target, velocity command, and force target define different interventions even when their numerical dimensions coincide. Padding and normalization can accommodate dimensional heterogeneity, but do not resolve differences in units, control mode, or effective duration. The original $\pi_{0}$ implementation pads state and action vectors to a common dimensionality and masks unused image slots (black2024pi0). Such implementation choices should be specified for the particular model rather than treated as universal conventions of cross-embodiment learning. Likewise, resampling a trajectory does not establish dynamic equivalence between robots operating at different control rates.

Complementary Supervision Sources

Human video provides evidence about task structure, object transformations, and behavioral stages, but usually lacks robot-executable action labels. Robot demonstrations and teleoperation provide action-grounded supervision under a specified interface. Simulation supports controlled variation of morphology and dynamics, whereas autonomous rollouts expose the state distribution induced by the executing policy. These sources therefore supervise different aspects of transfer, as discussed in Section 6.3.1 and Chapter 4. HPT combines data from robot teleoperation, deployed robots, simulation, and human video through heterogeneous input and output interfaces (wang2024hpt). For human video without robot action labels, it uses estimated poses and two-dimensional positions as surrogate supervision rather than treating visual motion as a robot command. Failures, interventions, corrections, and recovery segments should remain identifiable because they represent different supervision signals and operating conditions.

Embodiment-aware representation consequently establishes the conditions under which data can be combined or transformed. The desired internal representation $z_{t}$ should suppress irrelevant variation while preserving information about physical differences that affect the next decision. It is a learned summary of available evidence, following Chapter 5, rather than a physical state or a calibrated belief distribution by definition.

Figure 6.6: Shared modeling, embodiment-specific adaptation, and adaptation evaluation for manipulation. (a) Observation interfaces, shared task representations, and executable outputs illustrate complementary token, prompt, adapter, action-head, and latent-decoder mechanisms. (b) Changes in camera mounting pose (with camera count unchanged), end-effector degrees of freedom (DoF), and interaction dynamics motivate corresponding adaptation targets. (c) Independent closed-loop trials assess target success and budget-matched transfer gain, retention on previously supported embodiments, adaptation data efficiency, and physical execution. For compactness, panel (a) depicts current-observation inputs and deterministic execution mappings. Eq. (6.12) gives the general history-conditioned policy formulation

6.4.2 Shared Representations, Execution Interfaces, and Adaptation

The decomposition introduced in Eq. (6.2) can be specialized to heterogeneous observation and action spaces. Let $\eta_{e}$ describe the relevant morphology, sensing, actuation, and control properties of embodiment $e$ . A modular policy may be written as

 $\displaystyle\bar{h}_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=E_{\rho_{e}}(h_{t}),$ 

(6.12)

 $\displaystyle z_{t}$ 
 $\displaystyle=f_{\theta}(\bar{h}_{t},\ell_{\mathrm{lang}},\eta_{e}),$ 

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}$ 
 $\displaystyle\sim\pi_{\psi_{e}}(\cdot\mid z_{t},\ell_{\mathrm{lang}},\eta_{e}),$ 

where $E_{\rho_{e}}$ is an observation-interface encoder, $f_{\theta}$ is a shared representation model, and $\pi_{\psi_{e}}$ generates action chunks in $\mathcal{A}_{e}^{H}$ . This notation retains $\theta$ for representation parameters and $\psi$ for policy parameters, as in Section 6.1. The subscripts identify the functional interfaces that may depend on embodiment. They do not require a separate network for every robot. Architectures may share some or all of $\rho_{e}$ and $\psi_{e}$ and condition their computation on $\eta_{e}$ . A deterministic decoder $\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}=g_{\psi_{e}}(z_{t},\mathbf{q}_{t})$ , as depicted in Figure 6.6, is a special case. $\mathbf{q}_{t}$ is already contained in $h_{t}$ but may also enter the decoder directly.

The descriptor $\eta_{e}$ may comprise measured calibration quantities, a learned embedding, a structured prompt, or an estimate inferred from interaction history. Explicit identity conditioning and inferred physical parameters serve different purposes. An identity token can index a known configuration, whereas adaptation to unobserved payload or compliance requires evidence about the changed dynamics. Shared features need not be strictly embodiment-invariant. For example, a representation of a feasible grasp should depend on hand geometry even when the object and task are unchanged.

Embodiment Representations and Adaptation Mechanisms

The descriptor and interface modules in Eq. (6.12) can be implemented through tokens, prompts, adapters, dedicated action heads, or latent action decoders. These mechanisms differ in where embodiment information enters the model and which components are adapted. They are complementary rather than mutually exclusive. A soft prompt can itself consist of tokens, and a dedicated action head can incorporate a latent decoder.

Embodiment information can be introduced as learned identity embeddings or structured tokens encoding morphology and control properties. Structured tokens expose joint attributes and kinematic relationships to the shared transformer, providing a representation of physical configuration beyond a categorical robot label. Suzuki et al. combine joint-wise kinematic action tokens with topology-aware attention and joint-attribute conditioning (suzuki2026morphology_ch6). Their kinematic tokens organize action trajectories, while topology and joint descriptors introduce morphological information. The latter instantiate embodiment context associated with $\eta_{e}$ . The action tokens themselves should be distinguished from an identity descriptor. An identity embedding indexes a known configuration, whereas generalization to an unseen configuration requires a representation of its relevant physical properties.

An embodiment-specific prompt supplies contextual information that modulates shared computation. A structured textual prompt may describe available sensors or the action interface, while a soft prompt represents such context through trainable continuous embeddings. X-VLA introduces separate learnable soft prompts for heterogeneous data sources, together with domain-specific projections for action-related inputs and outputs (zheng2026x). This illustrates how embodiment-dependent context can be incorporated without duplicating the shared backbone. Prompt conditioning should be distinguished from the task instruction $\ell_{\mathrm{lang}}$ . The former describes the execution configuration, while the latter specifies the desired behavior.

Parameter-efficient adapters introduce a restricted set of trainable parameters within a pretrained model, allowing the shared computation to be adjusted for a target configuration. LoRA parameterizes weight updates through low-rank factors, and OpenVLA evaluates this approach for data-efficient robot-policy fine-tuning (hu2022lora_ch6; kim2024openvla). In Eq. (6.13), the adapter parameters can constitute $\Theta_{\mathrm{upd}}$ while the remaining pretrained weights are fixed. The resulting update changes the model’s internal computation. It does not by itself define a compatible observation or action interface.

An embodiment-specific head maps shared features to the dimensionality, units, and control semantics required by the target robot, implementing $\pi_{\psi_{e}}$ or its deterministic counterpart $g_{\psi_{e}}$ . HPT explicitly combines a shared transformer trunk with embodiment-specific input stems and policy heads, reinitializing the head for transfer to a new embodiment (wang2024hpt). Octo similarly permits new observation tokenizers and action readouts when sensory inputs or action spaces change (octo2024). Interface modularity does not prescribe a head-only update. Input modules, readouts, and shared features can be adapted jointly rather than restricting learning to the action head.

A shared latent action space permits policy learning over a common behavioral representation while an embodiment-specific decoder reconstructs executable actions. Unlike the context representation $z_{t}$ , which summarizes evidence for decision-making, the latent action represents the behavior proposed by the policy. Latent Action Diffusion learns aligned end-effector action representations using contrastive encoders, trains a diffusion policy in that latent space, and selects the corresponding embodiment-specific decoder during execution (bauer2025latent_ch6). The action-generation interface is thereby factorized into shared latent prediction and embodiment-dependent reconstruction. Its transfer capacity depends on the learned alignment and the target decoder’s ability to realize feasible actions.

These mechanisms instantiate different parts of the shared-execution decomposition. Tokens and prompts principally supply embodiment context, adapters modify selected internal computations, and action heads or latent decoders determine how shared information becomes an executable output. The appropriate combination depends on whether the mismatch concerns sensing, morphology, action semantics, or interaction dynamics.

Adaptation Targets and Learning Regimes

For a target configuration $e^{\star}$ , adaptation should address the source of mismatch. A change in camera mounting position or orientation, even with the same number of cameras, primarily affects observation encoding and calibration. A change in end-effector degrees of freedom, such as replacing a parallel gripper with a dexterous hand, affects action dimensionality, kinematic retargeting, feasible contact configurations, and action decoding. Changed payload, friction, or actuator response affects dynamics estimation and feedback-dependent execution. Several components may require joint adaptation, but the update scope should follow the identified mismatch rather than being determined solely by a generic fine-tuning recipe.

Zero-shot transfer uses the pretrained policy and a declared target interface without target-specific learning data. Any calibration or robot description available at inference should be reported separately. Few-shot adaptation uses a stated, limited target-data budget. Offline and online adaptation describe when the adaptation evidence is collected and used, and are independent of the number of demonstrations. Moreover, adaptation through context, state estimation, or calibration need not change model weights, whereas fine-tuning does. RoboCat explicitly studies adaptation to new tasks and embodiments using target demonstrations (bousmalis2023robocat).

Target Performance and Capability Retention

The complete parameter set $\Theta$ includes the representation parameters, relevant input and action-interface parameters, and any trainable embodiment descriptors. Let $\Theta_{0}$ denote their values before target adaptation, including the initialization of newly introduced interface modules, and let $\Theta_{\mathrm{upd}}$ denote the selected trainable subset. Following Eq. (6.9), parameter adaptation can be formulated as

 $\displaystyle\Theta_{\mathrm{upd}}^{\star}$ 
 $\displaystyle\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\Theta_{\mathrm{upd}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{adapt}}(\Theta),$ 

(6.13)

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{adapt}}(\Theta)$ 
 $\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{new}}(\Theta;\mathcal{D}_{e^{\star}})+\lambda_{\mathrm{retain}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{retain}}(\Theta;\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ret}})+\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}(\Theta,\Theta_{0}).$ 

All parameters outside $\Theta_{\mathrm{upd}}$ remain fixed. The target loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{new}}$ uses the action-generation objective appropriate to Section 6.2, such as token likelihood, regression, diffusion, or flow matching. The retention dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ret}}$ represents previously supported embodiments, and its loss can use replay supervision or behavioral distillation. The nonnegative coefficients control the relative weighting of these objectives. Consistent with Section 6.3, $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}$ constrains undesirable parameter changes. Data and computational budgets are reported separately rather than identified with this regularizer. Elastic weight consolidation exemplifies parameter-based protection of previously acquired knowledge (kirkpatrick2017ewc), but such a regularizer does not guarantee retained closed-loop manipulation performance.

Negative transfer can result from incompatible action semantics, an imbalanced training mixture, or shared features that omit information essential to one embodiment. Embodiment-aware sampling, modular interfaces, replay, and targeted regression evaluation can reduce these sources of interference. Physical feasibility and interaction limits must additionally be enforced and validated at the relevant execution interface. Minimizing Eq. (6.13) alone does not establish them.

6.4.3 Adaptation Validation and Deployment Handoff

Claims of successful embodiment adaptation require evaluation on independently collected target-embodiment trials. Offline action agreement does not measure the state distribution visited by the executing policy or its response to contact disturbances. Evaluation should distinguish supported embodiments from held-out embodiments and separately control changes in task, object, scene, operator, and acquisition period. Splits should be made at the trajectory or collection-session level, with paired or retargeted versions of one demonstration grouped together, to prevent correlated samples from inflating generalization estimates.

Target Performance and Transfer Gain

Let $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{emb}}^{\mathrm{tgt}}\subseteq\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{emb}}$ be a finite, nonempty set of target embodiments, and let $\mathcal{K}_{e}^{\mathrm{eval}}$ be the finite, nonempty evaluation task set for embodiment $e$ . Write $\mathrm{SR}_{N_{\mathrm{demo}}}(e,k)\in[0,1]$ for the success rate on task $k$ after adaptation with $N_{\mathrm{demo}}$ target demonstrations. Here, $N_{\mathrm{demo}}$ is the adaptation-data budget, distinct from the number of evaluation trials. Task completion criteria, initial-state distributions, and aggregation weights must be fixed before comparison. Report absolute target success separately from improvement over a baseline. A budget-matched transfer-gain measure is

 $\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathrm{fwd}}(N_{\mathrm{demo}})$ 
 $\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{emb}}^{\mathrm{tgt}}}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{e}^{\mathrm{eval}}}w_{e,k}\bigl[\mathrm{SR}^{\mathrm{adapt}}_{N_{\mathrm{demo}}}(e,k)-\mathrm{SR}^{\mathrm{base}}_{N_{\mathrm{demo}}}(e,k)\bigr],$ 

(6.14)

 $\displaystyle w_{e,k}\geq 0,\qquad\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{emb}}^{\mathrm{tgt}}}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{e}^{\mathrm{eval}}}w_{e,k}=1.$ 

For example, the baseline may use the same architecture trained without cross-embodiment pre-training, under the same target-data and target-training budget. This comparison matches the adaptation budget. Pre-training data and computation must be reported separately. A positive difference then supports the benefit of the initialization under that protocol, rather than being inferred from target success alone. Zero-shot comparisons require a separately specified reference policy. This measure is inspired by transfer evaluation in continual learning (lopezpaz2017gem_ch6), but is defined here for embodiment adaptation and is not identical to the original sequential-task forward-transfer metric. Cross-robot specialist comparisons in Open X-Embodiment likewise motivate stating the reference system explicitly (openx2024).

Retention on Previously Supported Embodiments

Let $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ret}}$ be a finite, nonempty set of previously supported embodiments on which retention is assessed, excluding the adaptation target when appropriate. Use the same tasks, initial-state distributions, evaluation criteria, and task-aggregation weights before and after adaptation, and define

 $\Delta_{\mathrm{ret}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ret}}|}\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ret}}}\bigl[\mathrm{SR}_{\mathrm{after}}(e)-\mathrm{SR}_{\mathrm{before}}(e)\bigr].$ 

(6.15)

Negative values indicate average degradation under the stated protocol. Retention testing should also report individual embodiment and task results, because an average gain can conceal a substantial loss on one configuration. Any acceptance tolerance should be chosen before adaptation and interpreted with trial counts and uncertainty. This operational measure is related to backward transfer (lopezpaz2017gem_ch6). It evaluates retained behavior rather than directly measuring the training loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{retain}}$ .

Adaptation Data Efficiency

For a target embodiment $e^{\star}$ , a prespecified success threshold $s_{\min}\in[0,1]$ , and a set of tested demonstration budgets $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{demo}}\subseteq\mathbb{N}_{0}$ , define

 $N_{\mathrm{demo}}^{\star}(s_{\min})=\min\bigl\{N_{\mathrm{demo}}\in\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{demo}}:\mathrm{SR}_{N_{\mathrm{demo}}}(e^{\star})\geq s_{\min}\bigr\},\qquad\min\varnothing:=+\infty,$ 

(6.16)

where $\mathrm{SR}_{N_{\mathrm{demo}}}(e^{\star})$ denotes a prespecified weighted average of $\mathrm{SR}_{N_{\mathrm{demo}}}(e^{\star},k)$ over the fixed target task set, with nonnegative weights summing to one. The condition $N_{\mathrm{demo}}=0$ represents zero-shot evaluation when included. This is an empirical summary over tested budgets, not a guarantee of monotonic improvement with additional demonstrations. Report the full adaptation curve, uncertainty across trials and training runs, demonstration duration, and the amount of any additional calibration or interaction data. RoboCat’s evaluation across demonstration budgets illustrates why data requirements should accompany final success rates (bousmalis2023robocat). Adaptation time, computational resources, and the number of updated parameters provide complementary cost measures. These evaluation quantities assess distinct aspects of adaptation. They are not in one-to-one correspondence with the three optimization terms in Eq. (6.13).

Physical Validation and Deployment Interface

Target trials should include the failure modes that motivated adaptation, such as grasp loss after an end-effector change, tracking error after a control-interface change, or unstable contact under altered compliance. Alongside task success, relevant measurements include executable-command rate, trajectory deviation, contact stability, recovery success, and intervention frequency. Proposed model outputs and applied controller commands should be recorded separately, so that success obtained through controller corrections can be distinguished from intrinsic policy performance.

The deployment handoff comprises more than a neural checkpoint. It should specify the embodiment and controller configuration, observation and action contracts, normalization statistics, calibration and timing information, descriptor and adapter versions, validated operating conditions, and behavior when required inputs or model outputs are unavailable. Unsupported conditions should remain identifiable, and updates must preserve compatibility among these components. Multi-embodiment modeling thus connects reusable task representations with verified, embodiment-specific physical behavior.

## 6.5 Model Deployment and Efficiency Optimization

A trained policy becomes a useful embodied capability only when its decisions arrive in time to influence the physical process. Deployment therefore concerns more than fitting a checkpoint into accelerator memory. It connects sensor acquisition, preprocessing, model execution, action interpretation, and feedback control into an operating system with finite computation and variable delay. A policy with higher offline accuracy can perform worse on a robot if it acts on older observations, pauses between action chunks, or loses contact information during preprocessing. The objective is to improve task performance under a specified resource and timing budget.

6.5.1 Deployment Architectures and the Execution Pipeline

Where the Model Runs

Onboard deployment keeps sensing and inference close to the robot and avoids dependence on a network for every policy update. Its limits are accelerator capacity, memory bandwidth, power, and heat dissipation. A nearby workstation or local server can support a larger model and several robots, but introduces transmission and scheduling delays. Cloud deployment provides elastic computation and centralized model management, while adding a wider-area communication path whose delay and availability may be difficult to bound. These are engineering trade-offs rather than a hierarchy in which a more remote or larger computer is necessarily better.

The computation can also be split. A remote process may interpret instructions or generate task context, while an onboard policy produces actions and a local controller regulates motion. The partition should follow decision time scales and communication dependencies. A task goal can remain useful for seconds, while contact feedback may lose value within a small fraction of that interval. Sending every force sample through a remote language model can consequently increase bandwidth and delay without improving the decision that requires the sample. Conversely, splitting a transformer across machines can create repeated inter-device dependencies and be slower than moving the whole policy to one machine.

Table 6.3 compares the deployment choices. The appropriate configuration depends on the task’s tolerance for delayed decisions, the expected concurrency, and the behavior available when an inference request is late. For a manipulation system, task reasoning and learning can often be remote even when action validation, control, and timeout handling must remain local.

Table 6.3: Deployment placement and its principal performance constraints

Placement

Useful property

Main constraint

Typical allocation

Robot onboard

Short communication path, local autonomy

Memory, power, cooling

Compact policy and local feedback

Local server

Larger shared accelerator capacity

Network and queueing variability

VLA inference with local execution

Cloud

Centralized resources and fleet-level services

Wide-area delay and outages

Task reasoning, training, and non-urgent analysis

Split deployment

Different compute budgets for different time scales

Context consistency and interface design

Slow reasoning with fast local action updates

The Online Data Contract

Every inference request needs a reference time, an instruction, an embodiment identifier, the observations it requires, and a clear record of what is missing or delayed. The preprocessing pipeline must reproduce the training convention for image crops, color channels, camera ordering, state normalization, action scaling, and coordinate frames. A model trained on relative tool-frame displacement cannot be deployed by interpreting its output as an absolute base-frame pose. Likewise, reversing the sign of a gripper command or applying normalization statistics from another embodiment can invalidate an otherwise correct prediction.

To align modalities sampled at different times, retain each modality’s acquisition time and validity mask and construct the input history according to the model’s convention. Interpolation can work well for smoothly varying joint positions, but averaging across a contact onset may erase the very event the policy needs. Training augmentations such as random cropping should also be distinguished from the deterministic preprocessing used for evaluation. These details link deployment directly to the data representation of Section 6.4.

For a sequential execution path, a useful latency decomposition is

 $L_{\mathrm{e2e}}=L_{\mathrm{acq}}+L_{\mathrm{pre}}+L_{\mathrm{net}}+L_{\mathrm{queue}}+L_{\mathrm{model}}+L_{\mathrm{decode}}+L_{\mathrm{dispatch}},$ 

(6.17)

where the terms describe acquisition, preprocessing, communication, queueing, model execution, action conversion, and dispatch to the control interface. Overlapped implementations should instead measure the critical path without double counting concurrent work. The interval ends once a command is available to the controller. When measuring response to a disturbance, the physical actuator response adds further delay. Even with fast accelerator kernels, waiting for camera frames, host-device copies, and server queues can account for substantial delay.

The deployed controller should retain both the requested and the applied command. Saturation, rate limiting, inverse kinematics, or a lower-level safety filter can alter an action after model inference. Subsequent history and learned dynamics should reflect what actually took effect. Recording only the unmodified output makes later failures appear to be modeling errors even when their cause lies in the execution interface.

6.5.2 Model Compression and Inference Acceleration

Optimization begins with profiling the actual execution path. A large VLM backbone may be bottlenecked by weight movement and visual-token processing. An autoregressive policy may be slowed by repeated sequential decoding. A generative action expert may spend most of its time on repeated denoising evaluations. For a small policy, preprocessing, device transfers, and Python-level dispatch can become the dominant cost. The benefit of the same optimization therefore varies across architectures and hardware.

Compression of Parameters and Activations

Quantization stores selected weights or activations at reduced numerical precision. It can lower memory use and data movement, but speed gains require supported kernels and favorable tensor shapes. OpenVLA studies quantized deployment as part of its efficiency analysis (kim2024openvla). Calibration for a robot policy should include the states where precision matters, such as small displacements near contact, rare sensor values, and transitions between action modes. Keeping sensitive output projections or normalization operations at higher precision may be preferable to applying the same precision everywhere.

Structured pruning removes channels, heads, layers, or entire processing branches. Unstructured sparsity does not necessarily accelerate dense hardware kernels, and removing a rarely used feature can damage a rare but important recovery behavior. Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student to reproduce useful teacher behavior or representations (hinton2015distilling_ch6). The student can be trained on actions, subgoals, intermediate features, or generated trajectories. For closed-loop control, training should cover perturbed states and the teacher’s corrections, and recovery should be tested after the student’s own errors.

A lightweight action expert provides another form of computation allocation. The expensive backbone constructs semantic context, while a smaller module performs repeated action-generation steps. This division is exemplified by $\pi_{0}$ and studied through knowledge insulation (black2024pi0; driess2025insulation_ch6). Parameter-efficient methods like LoRA mainly cut the cost of adapting a model. They do not, however, make the original backbone any cheaper to run. An adapter merged into supported weights can avoid extra adapter operations, but the main model still runs.

Reducing Work Per Decision

For autoregressive policies, action tokenization determines the number of sequential backbone evaluations. FAST compresses temporal action structure and thereby changes this trade-off (pertsch2025fast_ch6). Parallel prediction can remove token-by-token dependencies, but must be supported by the training objective and attention structure. OpenVLA-OFT combines parallel decoding, action chunking, and continuous regression (kim2025oft_ch6). Its result should not be described as merely running the original autoregressive policy faster.

For diffusion and flow-based policies, fewer sampling steps reduce the number of action-expert evaluations. An excessively coarse solver can change action quality, especially at sharp transitions or for narrow contact tolerances. Few-step distillation, combined with suitable training objectives, can improve this trade-off. Reducing the number of inference steps requires a new closed-loop evaluation. The number of steps generated, how many are actually executed, and how often new observations arrive should all be tuned together.

Visual token reduction can lower the cost of processing several camera views. Cropping, token pooling, selective view use, and compact history encoders are possible choices, but the retained information must match the task. A small contact region can occupy few pixels while determining success. Compression that works for reaching may therefore fail during insertion or when distinguishing two similar tools.

Execution-Level Optimization and Cache Validity

Operator fusion, compilation, fixed-shape execution, preallocated buffers, and reduced host-device synchronization can remove overhead without intentionally changing the policy function. IO-aware attention implementations such as FlashAttention reduce attention memory traffic (dao2022flash_ch6). Their end-to-end benefit still depends on whether attention dominates the deployment workload. Warm-up and compilation cost should be separated from steady-state inference, while occasional recompilation and shape changes should remain visible in tail-latency measurements.

Caching is useful only when the dependency being cached is unchanged. Within a flow or diffusion solve, the observation-language prefix can be reused if it cannot attend to changing action tokens. Across different robot observations, cached visual features generally become stale. Even an unchanged instruction does not imply that every text hidden state can be reused if the backbone mixes text and images bidirectionally. A deployment should distinguish reusable tokenization or independent encodings from context-dependent transformer states. This distinction prevents apparent speed from silently reducing responsiveness.

Efficiency should be reported at a consistent boundary. If the policy generates $H$ actions in $L_{\mathrm{model}}$ seconds, its nominal action-generation throughput is

 $R_{\mathrm{gen}}=\frac{H}{L_{\mathrm{model}}}.$ 

(6.18)

This quantity describes generated commands. It does not count independent decisions made from fresh measurements. Comparisons must hold the action duration, prediction horizon, execution horizon, input views, sampling settings, and hardware conditions sufficiently explicit to interpret the number.

6.5.3 Asynchronous Inference and Real-Time Closed-Loop Control

Four Distinct Frequencies

The sensor frequency determines how often measurements become available. The policy frequency determines how often a new observation-conditioned prediction is produced. The command frequency determines how often targets are delivered to the lower-level controller. The servo frequency determines how often that controller updates actuator inputs. These frequencies can differ by orders of magnitude. Interpolating a predicted trajectory or streaming a long action chunk raises the command frequency without raising the policy’s feedback frequency.

Let $\Delta t$ be the interval between action targets, $H$ the predicted chunk length, and $N_{\mathrm{exec}}\leq H$ the number of actions selected for execution before replacing the remaining plan. The prediction horizon is $H\Delta t$ , whereas the nominal replanning interval is $N_{\mathrm{exec}}\Delta t$ . Action chunking captures temporal correlations and amortizes inference. Receding-horizon execution retains only a prefix and uses new evidence to reconsider the rest. Longer $N_{\mathrm{exec}}$ reduces inference demand but delays responses to unexpected changes. The appropriate value depends on the physical event, not only on available compute.

Observation age gives a more direct measure of responsiveness. If a command applied at physical time $t_{\mathrm{apply}}$ is based on a reference observation acquired at $t_{\mathrm{obs}}$ , define

 $\Delta_{\mathrm{age}}=t_{\mathrm{apply}}-t_{\mathrm{obs}}.$ 

(6.19)

For multimodal policies, ages may also be reported separately by modality. A small model runtime does not guarantee small observation age when old frames are queued or a long action prefix is committed. Dropping obsolete requests can improve feedback freshness even when it reduces the total number of processed frames.

Overlapping Prediction and Execution

In synchronous execution, a robot may finish a chunk and wait for the next inference. Naively removing this pause creates a different problem. The next chunk was generated from a state that no longer coincides with the state at which it will begin. The remaining trajectory must account for commands executed during inference. Real-time chunking addresses this issue for flow and diffusion policies by conditioning the new chunk on a committed prefix while regenerating the uncommitted future (black2025rtc_ch6).

If a request requires $L_{\mathrm{req}}$ seconds from input availability to usable output, the approximate number of command intervals that elapse during the request is

 $d_{\mathrm{delay}}=\left\lceil\frac{L_{\mathrm{req}}}{\Delta t}\right\rceil.$ 

(6.20)

The overlap procedure should preserve the commands that are already committed during those $d_{\mathrm{delay}}$ intervals and use current timing information to select the replacement suffix. For example, at a command rate of $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$ , a $100\,\mathrm{ms}$ request spans five action intervals. A 50-action chunk has a one-second prediction horizon, but neither that horizon nor the command rate implies 50 fresh policy decisions per second. This is an illustrative timing calculation, not a benchmark result.

A simple buffer feasibility condition is

 $N_{\mathrm{buf}}\Delta t\geq L_{\mathrm{req}}^{(p_{\mathrm{quant}})}+L_{\mathrm{margin}},$ 

(6.21)

where $N_{\mathrm{buf}}$ is the number of validated buffered commands, $L_{\mathrm{req}}^{(p_{\mathrm{quant}})}$ is a selected latency percentile, and $L_{\mathrm{margin}}$ accounts for dispatch uncertainty. This condition cuts down on buffer underruns under the measured latency distribution. It does not guarantee anything in the worst case. A deeper buffer also commits the robot further into an old plan. Responsiveness requires replacing the uncommitted portion when new evidence arrives and defining task-appropriate behavior when the buffer is exhausted.

Chunk transitions require semantic as well as numerical consistency. Averaging two trajectories may smooth a position jump while mixing incompatible modes, such as opening and closing a gripper or maintaining and releasing contact. Continuity should be checked for the commanded quantity and its physical role, including pose, velocity, force targets, and discrete events. A late result associated with an earlier instruction or aborted task should be rejected rather than appended to the current action stream.

Slow Context and Fast Correction

A multi-rate system can update task context or predictive features less frequently than local action decisions through the following decomposition

 $c_{k}^{\mathrm{ctx}}=F_{\theta}^{\mathrm{ctx}}(h_{t_{k}},\ell_{\mathrm{lang}},e),\qquad\mathbf{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{seq}}=G_{\psi}(c_{k(t)}^{\mathrm{ctx}},o_{t}^{\mathrm{recent}},\mathbf{q}_{t},e),$ 

(6.22)

where $k(t)$ selects the latest valid context. The fast module uses recent evidence, including contact history when available, while the slow module revises task interpretation or predicted futures. For this separation to work, the action module must be trained to operate in context of varying age and must receive enough current information to correct behavior. Merely caching an old full-policy output does not create such a capability.

Replanning can combine periodic updates with event triggers. Target motion, grasp loss, unexpected force, a completed subtask, or a change in instruction may invalidate the current context. Thresholds and hysteresis can prevent excessive switching around noisy events. The event path itself needs a delay bound. Also, a task-level replan should not interrupt a local stabilization response that is physically necessary. The control principles for this fast feedback layer are developed further in Chapter 7.

6.5.4 Deployment Evaluation and Operational Maintenance

Deployment evaluation should compare complete operating configurations. Alongside model weights, record numerical precision, input resolution and views, action horizon, execution horizon, sampling steps, device, concurrent workload, and communication conditions. Otherwise, a higher throughput may reflect a larger chunk or a less responsive execution schedule rather than an improvement in the same task interface.

The evaluation should connect computation to behavior. Table 6.4 links deployment measurements to their interpretations and test conditions. Relevant computational quantities include end-to-end latency, latency percentiles and variability, observation age, missed deadlines, peak memory, and power. Relevant physical quantities include task success, completion time, trajectory and contact accuracy, recovery after disturbances, and human intervention. Energy per completed task is often more informative than accelerator power alone. A faster inference configuration may consume more instantaneous power but finish the task sooner, while a slower configuration may increase robot holding time.

Table 6.4: Deployment measurements and the questions they answer

Measurement

Interpretation

Useful test condition

Median and tail latency

Typical response and occasional late decisions

Concurrent requests, warm-up, sustained load

Observation age, deadline misses

Freshness of feedback used in execution

Moving targets, delayed frames, network jitter

Memory, power, task energy

Resource feasibility and operating cost

Long runs at the intended thermal limit

Success and completion time

Whether speed changes useful performance

Matched tasks and initial-state distributions

Contact error and recovery

Precision and response beyond nominal motion

Insertion, slippage, unexpected contact

Interventions and fault recovery

Dependence on operator support

Timeouts, sensor loss, server interruption

A staged evaluation can first compare numerical outputs on recorded observations. Next, test timing under replay or hardware-in-the-loop execution, and finally measure closed-loop behavior. Recorded-data agreement is a diagnostic rather than a substitute for robot trials. Dynamic-target tasks expose delayed feedback, contact tasks expose precision loss, and long-horizon tasks expose accumulation of small errors. Comparisons should use matched task conditions and report trial counts and uncertainty. A speedup measured on one accelerator does not establish a hardware-independent property.

Operational logs should connect each input snapshot to its model version, preprocessing version, inference timestamps, proposed action, applied command, and observed outcome. This makes it possible to distinguish recognition errors from stale observations, action conversion errors, or controller overrides. Model weights, tokenizer or action decoder, normalization statistics, embodiment adapters, and runtime configuration form one deployment version. Rolling back weights while retaining incompatible normalization or action decoding is not a complete rollback.

Timeout behavior must be appropriate to the task. Holding position may be reasonable in free space but undesirable during a forceful contact. Stopping a pouring motion can require a controlled change in orientation. Such responses should be implemented and validated at the execution layer, with a clear path to human takeover where needed. After compression, compiler changes, or hardware migration, a fixed regression suite should test both nominal skills and the disturbances that previously caused failures.

Deployment is where this chapter’s modeling loop closes. Training creates behavioral priors. Adaptation makes them an embodiment-specific interpretation. The execution system then decides when those priors can actually affect the world. Efficiency is established when reduced computation or communication produces timely, accurate behavior under the intended operating conditions. The resulting execution traces then supply the evidence needed for the next round of capability improvement.

## 6.6 Dexterous Manipulation Foundation Models

Most of the models discussed in this chapter act through a parallel gripper, whose action is a wrist pose and a single opening width. A multi-fingered hand breaks three assumptions behind that design. The action space grows to 20 or more finger joints, and whether an object stays under control depends on how those joints move together. Many decisive events, such as a finger beginning to slide or load shifting onto the palm, happen at contacts the cameras cannot see. Robot data are scarcer still. Teleoperating 20 joints is much harder than teleoperating one, and every hand defines its own action space. Human hands, meanwhile, manipulate objects constantly and on camera, which makes human data the obvious place to look for scale.

The subsections examine how to represent finger actions (Section 6.6.1) and how to learn from human hands, with EgoScale as the worked example of the stages in Section 6.3 (Section 6.6.2). They then examine how much of a policy can be shared across hands, extending Section 6.4 (Section 6.6.3), where touch helps (Section 6.6.4), and what current results establish (Section 6.6.5). The hands themselves are described in Section 9.6, and the low-level hand controllers that sit beneath these models in Sections 7.4.4 and 7.4.5.

6.6.1 Action Representations for Multi-Fingered Hands

A dexterous policy has to fix the meaning of its action vector before data collection begins. Current systems use one of three options. Joint targets for a specific hand are directly executable but bind the model to that mechanism. Fingertip or keypoint targets are closer to what human data measure, but need a solver to turn them into joint commands. Functional coordinates give each entry a meaning shared across hands, such as index flexion or thumb opposition, and keep a separate map from those entries to each hand’s joints. Most systems also command the wrist separately, as a relative change in hand pose. The choice decides which data can supervise the model and how much of it can be shared between hands.

Human data enter through retargeting, the geometric alignment of Section 6.4.1, which for hands can be written as

 $\min_{\mathbf{q},\mathbf{T}}\ \sum_{i}w_{i}\|\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathrm{robot}}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{T})-\widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{i}^{\mathrm{human}}\|^{2}+\lambda\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{prev}}\|^{2},\quad\mathbf{q}_{\min}\leq\mathbf{q}\leq\mathbf{q}_{\max},$ 

(6.23)

where $\mathbf{q}$ is the robot hand configuration, $\mathbf{T}$ aligns the wrist frames, $\mathbf{p}_{i}$ is a fingertip position, and $w_{i}$ weights its importance. The second term penalizes abrupt changes. The objective is illustrative, not the loss of a particular study, and practical versions add collision and contact constraints. As Figure 9.15 shows, a MANO pose vector and a robot joint vector do not correspond one to one. Retargeted human motion is useful supervision only insofar as the mapped action keeps the relevant interaction. More data widen coverage but do not remove a systematic geometric mismatch.

6.6.2 Learning from Human Hands: Pretraining, Alignment, and Post-Training

EgoScale is the clearest evaluated example of the training stages of Section 6.3 applied to a dexterous hand. It is evaluated on a Galaxea R1Pro with two 22-DoF Sharpa Wave hands and three RGB cameras (zheng2026egoscale). The hands are described in Section 9.6.3. Figure 6.7 lays out the stages.

Figure 6.7: The learning chain on Sharpa Wave. The upper path follows
EgoScale’s training stages, with human and robot observations connected

 (zheng2026egoscale; nvidia2026egoscaleproject). The lower panels

Pretraining: Learning Reusable Wrist-Finger Coordination

EgoScale represents human-video motion as relative wrist displacement plus retargeted hand actions (nvidia2026egoscaleproject). Predicting articulated actions pushes the model to encode how the wrist and fingers move together. Carrying a bottle without losing the grasp is a different coordination pattern from twisting its cap. Patterns like these recur across tasks and can be learned before any target-robot data are collected. The representation also commits early to an execution interface. Relative wrist motion transfers easily, but the finger component has to be realizable in the target hand’s joint space, so the retargeting of Eq. (6.23) is already present during pretraining.

Alignment: Connecting Human Observations to Robot Actions

EgoScale’s aligned mid-training uses about 50 hours of human and 4 hours of robot play data. The human capture matches the robot’s camera viewpoints and intrinsics, with Vive wrist tracking and MANUS hand capture synchronized to video (zheng2026egoscale). The question at this stage is which differences in appearance and motion come from the embodiment and which signal a different task state. A human finger and a robot link may occupy different parts of the image while doing the same job of supporting a cup, and similar silhouettes may hide different reachable contact surfaces. In the terms of Section 6.4.1, matched viewpoints and retargeting reduce observation and geometric mismatch, while robot play exposes dynamic mismatch under load. The capture hardware and its calibration are described in Section 9.6.4.

Post-Training: Specializing the Prior to a Physical Task

Task-specific robot data then tie the prior to the actual arm, hand, objects, and cameras. For a handle grasp, the prior may already organize approach, closure, and transport, but only the target setup determines how far the fingers must close to engage the handle and which wrist path leaves room for the next step. In EgoScale’s scaling experiment, direct post-training without aligned mid-training raises the average task-completion score from 0.30 to 0.71 as human pretraining grows from 1,000 to 20,000 hours (zheng2026egoscale). This experiment varies the amount of human data, unlike the comparison with and without pretraining summarized in Section 2.3. A separate one-shot protocol uses 1 robot demonstration plus 100 aligned human demonstrations per object, after the earlier stages (nvidia2026egoscaleproject). The two experiments answer different questions concerning whether more prior experience helps, and how little robot data is then needed to select a behavior the model already supports. Section 4.5 discusses what such scaling variables can and cannot establish.

Two other studies on Sharpa hands use human data in narrower roles. CAIP aligns images with hand-action proxies to pretrain a visual encoder and evaluates policies without tactile input (sharma2026caip). Do as I Do reconstructs and retargets human hand-object motion into robot trajectories on a dual-UR3e Sharpa system (paliwal2026doasido). Each improves one ingredient, the representation or the execution data. EgoScale shows how the ingredients fit into one training sequence.

6.6.3 Sharing Actions Across Hands

UniDex asks which finger-level action roles can be shared when joint structures differ. Its dataset spans eight hand types and is built by retargeting human demonstrations, with interactive correction and visual alignment. Its Function-Actuator-Aligned Space (FAAS) assigns joints with the same function to common coordinates, the functional-coordinate option of Section 6.6.1, and keeps a map to each hand. A policy conditioned on point clouds, language, and proprioception predicts action chunks (unidex2026project).
