A spray bottle shows what such a mapping has to preserve. The thumb must reach the trigger while the other fingers resist its reaction force. Moving the wrist for better trigger access can weaken the support or misaim the nozzle. And once the trigger moves, the fingers must let it return without dropping the bottle. Minimizing each joint error separately preserves none of these relations.

The Wuji experiments in UniDex use the 20-DoF hand on a Franka arm with RGB-D sensing, on tasks that include a spray bottle, scissors, and a computer mouse, with 50 robot demonstrations per task for adaptation (zhang2026unidex). The robot demonstrations correct systematic differences in grasp placement, response, and observation that human data cannot reveal. Table 6.5 reports both outcome measures. Pretraining improves intermediate progress and final success, but because the aggregate pools Wuji and Inspire tasks, it does not isolate the contribution of the Wuji hardware.

Without further training, an Inspire-trained policy transferred to Wuji reaches 40% average task progress over 10 trials (zhang2026unidex). A shared flexion coordinate lets the parameters be shared, but the resulting fingertip motion still depends on link lengths, couplings, and joint ranges, so task structure transfers while contact execution is only partly preserved. SimToolReal (Section 7.4.4) takes the opposite approach. It places the shared interface at the object and leaves finger coordination to the controller.

6.6.4 Where Tactile Input Helps a Dexterous Policy

Section 6.2.3 describes three ways contact information can enter a VLA. For dexterous hands the narrower question is at which decision a tactile signal changes the outcome. Two XHAND studies give opposite answers.

DexUMI collects demonstrations with an exoskeleton fitted to the target hand and replaces the human hand in the images with the robot hand (Section 9.6.4). Its policy predicts wrist and finger actions from visual and tactile input (xu2025dexumi). In an XHAND kitchen task of turning a knob, moving a pan, and adding salt, touch matters in the salt step because the fingers are hidden from view, and closing the hand to a plausible posture does not show that they reached the salt.66
 6

 DexUMI Team, DexUMI: Using Human Hand as the Universal Manipulation Interface for Dexterous Manipulation, project page and demonstrations, 2025. With relative actions and visual adaptation fixed, accumulated success through the salt stage is 75% with tactile input and 15% without, over 20 episodes per task (xu2025dexumi).

In the shared-autonomy system of cui2025sharedautonomy, DexGrasp-VLA controls the 12-DoF hand from vision and touch during data collection, and the resulting trajectories, supplemented by corrective demonstrations, train an arm-hand VLA with separate arm and hand feature branches. The full system reaches 88.7% pick-and-place success across 50 objects with 3 trials each. In an ablation, adding tactile features directly to the arm-hand policy lowers success from 95% to 82%, although the same features help the hand-only controller (cui2025sharedautonomy).

The difference lies in the decision the signal feeds. Touch helps where the next action depends on a contact that vision cannot resolve, and hurts where it becomes one more input to a policy that primarily selects where to reach and place. A third option keeps touch out of the foundation model and uses it in a faster refinement loop beneath it, as T-Rex does (Section 7.4.5).

6.6.5 Evaluating Dexterous Foundation Models

The studies above report different endpoints (task-completion score, stage-wise progress, final success, and accumulated success through a sequence) on different hands, arms, cameras, objects, and trial counts, and some pool results over several hands. They cannot be ranked against each other. Each supports a narrower claim. EgoScale shows that a larger human prior improves post-trained performance under a fixed protocol. UniDex, that a functional action space allows pretraining across hands and some zero-shot transfer. DexUMI and DexGrasp-VLA, that tactile input pays off only at decisions it can change.

Three questions remain open. Does human pretraining keep scaling once tasks require sustained force, not just reaching the right configuration? Can a shared action space carry contact strategies across hands, or only task structure? And how should a model with slow visual updates hand authority to faster contact-driven control, the interface studied in Chapter 7? Answering them requires the closed-loop protocols of Chapter 11, applied to whole tasks from grasping through recovery on declared hardware.

## 7 Foundation Models for Whole-Body Motor Control

Humanoid and other whole-body robots are an important class of physical embodiments. With improvements in hardware, more recent work focuses on controlling the entire body as a coordinated system. This chapter discusses how to extend current foundation-model algorithms to whole-body motor control. The whole-body control connects task-level decisions to coordinated physical action: it uses control interfaces to regulate motion and contact within the robot’s dynamic limits, while adjusting in real time to external forces, terrain changes, and contact transitions. Each of them is discussed in detail as follows.

## 7.1 Scope, Taxonomy, and Control Interfaces

Task-level objectives specify what a robot should accomplish, but generally leave open how its joints and contacts should be coordinated under the body’s dynamics and actuation limits. Motor control addresses these execution requirements through feedback from the body and its environment, as Figure 7.1 illustrates. This section defines the role of whole-body motor control in this process, traces the control principles underlying it, and identifies the interfaces needed to reuse motor capabilities across tasks. In humanoid tasks that combine locomotion and manipulation, body support must be coordinated with arm motion and hand-object contacts.

Figure 7.1: The whole-body motor controller in the robot stack. A task-level planning layer issues goals to a goal-conditioned sensorimotor closed loop, which reads proprioceptive and exteroceptive measurements and issues control commands through the actuator interface. Contacts couple the body to the environment, and measured execution returns to constrain planning. Section markers indicate where Sections 7.1 to 7.5 develop this loop

7.1.1 Functional Scope and Foundation Models

In this chapter, a whole-body motor controller is a goal-conditioned sensorimotor model that coordinates robot motion and physical interaction through closed-loop control. It uses available observations of the body, contacts, and task-relevant environment to select and revise actions at high frequency as forces and contact conditions change. Building on this feedback capability, a foundation model for whole-body motor control acquires reusable motor capabilities through broad pretraining and exposes them to multiple downstream objectives or control modes (zeng2025behavior; zeng2026scaling).

This role complements task-level planning. Task-level models interpret instructions, select objectives, and organize activities. Motion or behavior generators express those objectives as body velocities, end-effector poses, contact requirements, or reference trajectories. The motor controller executes these targets using the available state information. A specified hand position, for instance, may admit different arm configurations, trunk postures, and support arrangements. Selecting a realization requires accounting for its effects on the rest of the body (khatib1987).

A motor objective remains subject to execution feedback after it is issued. Small disturbances may be corrected locally. Persistent tracking errors, unexpected contacts, or sustained actuator saturation from torque demands beyond hardware limits may require the upstream planner to revise the target or its timing. Information must therefore flow in both directions. Goals guide execution, while measured execution constrains subsequent planning. A planner must account for estimates of the state reached during execution, including deviations from the preceding reference.

Realizing this feedback loop also requires observation processing, state estimation, target interpretation, actuator interfaces, and mechanisms for enforcing execution limits. Some components may be learned jointly. Others remain explicit. A pretrained tracking policy can provide the core motor capability while relying on external estimation and low-level servos. Such architectures combine explicit control components with learned motor capabilities, drawing on complementary developments in model-based control and reinforcement learning.

7.1.2 From Control Principles to Reusable Motor Capabilities

For articulated robots, the main difficulty is that control objectives are coupled through mechanics. Operational-space control expresses motion and force objectives in task coordinates and relates them to joint actuation, making end-effector behavior an explicit object of control (khatib1987). Impedance control further regulates the dynamic relationship between motion and interaction force, rather than requiring exact position tracking in all circumstances (Hogan1985). Classical work on robot hands similarly analyzes grasping through fingertip geometry, force transmission, and frictional interaction (mason1985hands). Together, these methods establish that an appropriate motor interface can specify a physical interaction rather than a complete sequence of joint configurations. In legged robots, the same mechanical coupling must be coordinated across repeated contact transitions. raibert1984hopping decompose hopping into regulation of forward velocity, body attitude, and hopping height.

To account for future motion and support requirements, MPC makes the consequences of candidate actions explicit over a finite horizon. At each update, it optimizes a control sequence from the current state estimate, applies the initial input, and repeats the optimization after receiving new feedback. State and input constraints can be included directly, although feasibility and stability depend on the model, formulation, and assumptions (mayne2000constrained). In 2003, zero-moment-point preview control provides a related predictive formulation for biped walking, using future support references to shape the current motion through optimal linear feedback (kajita2003preview). By 2018, the MIT Cheetah 3 controller uses convex MPC to optimize ground-reaction forces over a finite horizon, while a gait state machine and swing controller supply contact timing and swing-leg motion (dicarlo2018).

In the late 2010s, deep reinforcement learning (RL) expands the use of simulated interaction to acquire feedback policies. DeepMimic combines reference-motion imitation with task rewards to learn coordinated skills for physics-based characters (peng2018deepmimic). hwangbo2019 train policies for ANYmal using a simulator that combines rigid-body dynamics with an actuator model learned from robot data, then deploy those policies on the physical robot. lee2020 extend locomotion to challenging terrain by training a privileged teacher and distilling its behavior into a student that uses proprioceptive history. History-conditioned adaptation further uses recent observations and actions to infer information about unobserved dynamics, including changes in load or ground interaction. Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) makes this inference a dedicated learned module that conditions a locomotion policy (kumar2021). The estimation methods supporting such adjustment are developed in Section 7.2.

A parallel line develops motor knowledge that downstream tasks can reuse. Neural probabilistic motor primitives (NPMP) compress expert skills into a shared latent representation (merel2018npmp). An adversarial motion prior (AMP) learns a distributional motion prior that shapes policy optimization (peng2021amp). Adversarial Skill Embeddings (ASE) learns a skill-conditioned policy whose latent space can serve as the action space of a downstream controller (peng2022ase). A distributional prior shapes policy learning, while a skill-conditioned policy generates executable actions. Their shared contribution is to separate the acquisition of coordinated movement from the specification of a particular downstream task.

Modern systems develop both hybrid execution architectures and more reusable command interfaces. Deep Tracking Control combines an online trajectory-optimizing planner with a learned tracking policy that executes its references under model mismatch and disturbances (jenelten2024). This combination retains explicit predictive structure while learning the feedback needed during execution. More recent humanoid controllers extend reuse to the control interface. HOVER distills motion-tracking capability into a policy supporting multiple command modes (he2025hover). A behavior foundation model (BFM) uses motion imitation and masked online distillation to pretrain a shared behavioral repertoire, while ScaleBFM studies direct goal-conditioned RL pretraining with varied motion data and model capacity (zeng2025behavior; zeng2026scaling). These humanoid approaches allow downstream applications to invoke learned movement through different target specifications, as developed in Section 7.4.

These approaches reflect two complementary design choices concerning the execution mechanism and how motor knowledge is acquired and reused. Table 7.1 shows representative combinations.

Table 7.1: Selected control approaches compared by execution mechanism and the acquisition and reuse of motor knowledge

7.1.3 Architecture and Interfaces

Figure 7.2: Closed-loop architecture and interfaces of a whole-body motor controller. Goal processing supplies $g_{t}$ , observation processing supplies $h_{t}$ and $\hat{s}_{t}$ , and the control model outputs $\mathbf{a}_{t}$ , which the actuator interface realizes as joint torques $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{t}$ through actuator dynamics and low-level loops. Measurements close the loop. Operation at multiple update rates requires explicit temporal alignment

A motor-control architecture connects state representation, goal interpretation, and action generation, as Figure 7.2 illustrates. In a humanoid, moving the arms changes whole-body dynamics, while stepping changes the support configuration and the position from which the hands act. A requested behavior therefore has to be realized through coordinated body motion and corrected as the resulting motion and contacts evolve.

Figure’s Helix 02 provides a concrete example through its publicly described System 2-System 1-System 0 hierarchy.77
 7

 Figure, Introducing Helix 02: Full-Body Autonomy, January 27, 2026. System 2 interprets scenes and language, sequences behaviors, and supplies latent goals to System 1. Conditioned on these latents, System 1 combines head-camera and palm-camera images, fingertip tactile sensing, and full-body proprioception to generate full-body joint targets at 200 Hz. System 0 is a learned whole-body controller that tracks these targets, using full-body joint state and base motion to produce joint-level actuator commands at 1 kHz. This division connects semantic goals to visuomotor targets and then to feedback execution that handles balance, contact, and whole-body coordination. The additional sensing also serves specific feedback needs. Palm cameras provide in-hand visual feedback when an object is occluded from the head camera, and fingertip tactile sensors detect contact forces.

Throughout this chapter, $s_{t}$ denotes the physical state at control step $t$ , including the robot and any environment variables needed to describe its evolution. The observation $o_{t}$ contains information available during execution. An explicit state estimate is denoted by $\hat{s}_{t}$ . Neither is assumed to equal the full state. A finite observation-action history is

 $h_{t}=(o_{t-L+1},\mathbf{a}_{t-L+1},\ldots,o_{t-1},\mathbf{a}_{t-1},o_{t}),\qquad\mathbf{a}_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t},g_{t}),$ 

(7.1)

where $L\geq 1$ is the history length, $\theta$ denotes policy parameters, and $g_{t}$ is the command representation. The policy $\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t},g_{t})$ is a conditional action distribution, and $\sim$ denotes sampling from it. For $L=1$ , $h_{t}=o_{t}$ . A recurrent state or learned history encoding can summarize longer histories.

Privileged observations provide training-time access to variables that can be read directly in simulation but are difficult to obtain reliably from the robot’s sensors. HUGWBC uses base linear velocity, ground friction, and foot contact forces as such variables (xue2025hugwbc). In its asymmetric actor-critic training, the critic combines these quantities with proprioception and commands to predict returns. Its value estimates then enter the advantage estimates used to update the actor with PPO (schulman2017ppo; hugwbcCode2026). This allows the simulator’s richer information to contribute to policy optimization through the critic. The actor’s execution inputs include recent proprioceptive history, commands, and estimates of selected hidden quantities obtained from that history (xue2025hugwbc; hugwbcCode2026).

Command granularity determines how much of the movement the controller must choose. A desired body velocity leaves freedom in foothold placement and posture, as in the locomotion commands of Section 7.3. A full reference motion constrains the coordinated body trajectory more closely, while targets for only selected body links leave the remaining movement free to accommodate support and interaction constraints. Desired reference quantities are denoted by $s_{t}^{\rm ref}$ , with the hat reserved for estimates. The policy receives their command representation $g_{t}$ , which can encode a velocity request, a reference horizon, or selected body targets. For partial targets, a mask identifies the specified components and distinguishes an unspecified target from a specified value of zero, as in the masked-target representation of Section 7.4.

Executing these goals requires translating the policy’s action $\mathbf{a}_{t}$ into physical joint actuation. When $\mathbf{a}_{t}$ contains joint-position targets, a low-level servo converts position error and joint feedback into torque commands. Actuator dynamics then determine the actual joint torque $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{t}$ , including the effects of saturation and delay (hwangbo2019). Policies may instead output joint-velocity targets, direct torque commands, or a residual added to an existing controller, changing what the downstream control interface must realize. For a stochastic training policy, $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\theta}(h_{t},g_{t})$ denotes its action mean, which can also be used for deterministic execution.

Consider a hand target fixed in the world while the humanoid turns or takes a step. The target stays fixed, but its pose relative to the body changes, so a body-frame encoding must be updated using the current body pose. An object-relative target instead follows the object’s motion. Timing matters for the same physical reason. A reference computed for one support configuration may need revision after touchdown or lift-off. When perception, goal generation, and actuation update at different rates, a controller can receive observations or references describing an earlier body or contact state. Feedback correction between target updates must therefore relate these inputs to the current motion. A measurement timestamp indicates the time of the observed state, and a reference’s validity interval indicates when it is intended to apply. Delayed information can increase tracking error, motivating the latency analysis in Section 7.5.

For a humanoid traversing uneven ground through a low passage, successful motion requires both placing the feet and keeping the torso clear of overhead obstacles. Proprioceptive history reflects body motion and the response to contact, supporting correction of ongoing execution. Exteroceptive observations supply the geometry ahead of the robot so that motion can be adapted before contact. Visual servoing uses the discrepancy between current and desired visual features to correct robot motion (chaumette2006visual). For perceptive locomotion, Miki et al. combine proprioception with terrain-height observations from a robot-centric elevation map, allowing the controller to adapt its motion before contact while retaining feedback from body motion (miki2022). A ground-height map, however, does not preserve all geometry relevant to a humanoid’s whole body. Gallant instead uses LiDAR-derived voxel grids together with proprioception to represent lateral obstacles and overhead constraints as well as ground-level terrain (ben2025gallant). These examples illustrate control-oriented perception, in which the system retains the information needed to select a physical action and correct it as the body interacts with its surroundings.

7.1.4 Generality, Dexterity, and Evaluation

Generality concerns reuse under changes in objectives and physical conditions. Reproducing many training motions establishes behavioral coverage. A more demanding test is whether the controller can combine familiar capabilities to meet new task requirements. Goal flexibility allows an existing capability to be invoked through different target representations, while task transfer asks whether it remains useful in a new activity. A controller may track new references yet need substantial retraining for new interaction dynamics. Reuse therefore involves both executing new goal combinations and adapting coordinated behavior to changes in load, terrain, or contact.

These demands become tightly coupled when locomotion and manipulation share the same body. Maintaining an object pose during locomotion imposes constraints that are absent from either unconstrained walking or stationary manipulation (fu2022). For a humanoid carrying an object with both hands, body acceleration changes the forces required to support the object, while arm configuration affects both reach and whole-body balance. Dexterous execution additionally requires finger configurations that maintain the grasp. An end-effector pose specifies a hand’s position and orientation but leaves its internal contact configuration unresolved. In bimanual manipulation, the two hands interact through the shared object. Their contact forces jointly determine object motion, but different force distributions can produce the same resultant wrench while imposing different grasping loads. Coordinated execution must therefore account for support, object motion, and contact maintenance together, especially during load transfer or changes in the grasp (bicchi1994forces). The learned hand-control and force-adaptive balance examples in Sections 7.4.4 and 7.4.5 provide concrete examples of contact execution and load-dependent body support.

Extending this reuse to another embodiment introduces changes in the body itself. Robots differ in topology, geometry, actuation, and sensing, so a shared controller must represent these differences or accommodate them through embodiment-specific components. Morphology-conditioned transformers provide one approach to sharing control representations across bodies (gupta2022metamorph). Task-space and contact-based goals can reduce dependence on a particular joint layout, but the mapping from those goals to actions remains constrained by each robot’s capabilities. Transfer to a physical platform additionally depends on its actuator and sensor characteristics, beyond the morphological variation represented in simulation.

The carrying example makes these forms of generality directly testable. Changing walking speed and object-pose targets tests the composition of movement requirements. Varying the carried load tests adaptation. Using a robot with a different morphology tests embodiment transfer. Tracking error, object slip, and loss of balance assess target execution, grasp maintenance, and body support, respectively. For goals or conditions that require further learning, the benefit of pretraining can be measured by the data and optimization needed to reach a given task performance, compared with learning from scratch (merel2018npmp; zeng2025behavior).

## 7.2 Body Dynamics and State Estimation

Figure 7.3: Floating-base dynamics, contacts, and actuation of a legged robot. Joint torques act through the selection matrix on the joint rows only, so contact forces are central to movement. Contacts contribute forces subject to sticking, unilateral, and friction-cone constraints, and the delivered torque follows the commanded torque through a first-order lag with saturation

The motor-execution layer is a high-frequency control loop around a physical system. Figure 7.3 depicts floating-base dynamics, contact constraints, and the actuation interface. It receives task commands from the planning layer, reads proprioceptive measurements (joint encoders and an inertial measurement unit, IMU) together with exteroceptive ones such as depth cameras and LiDAR, and issues control commands realized through the actuator interface. Three questions organize this loop, asking how the body moves, where it is now and what it touches, and what the model is getting wrong. This section develops the three answers in turn. Throughout, $s_{t}$ denotes the actual state, $\hat{s}_{t}$ its estimate, and $s_{t}^{\rm ref}$ a commanded reference.

7.2.1 Motion-Control Foundations: Floating-Base Dynamics, Contacts, and Actuators

A legged robot is a floating-base system. Six base degrees of freedom carry no actuators, and only the joints are driven. Throughout this section, $\mathcal{W}$ denotes the inertial world frame and $\mathcal{B}$ the base frame, and a left superscript marks the frame in which a quantity is expressed. The world vertical is opposite the gravity direction, and ${}^{\mathcal{W}}\mathbf{R}_{\mathcal{B}}$ maps base-frame vectors to world coordinates. With $n$ actuated joints, the configuration combines the base pose with the joint angles, and the generalized velocity stacks the base spatial velocity (linear and angular), expressed in $\mathcal{B}$ , with the joint rates, giving

 $\begin{gathered}\mathbf{q}=\left({}^{\mathcal{W}}\mathbf{p}_{\mathcal{B}},{}^{\mathcal{W}}\mathbf{R}_{\mathcal{B}},\mathbf{q}_{j}\right)\in\mathrm{SE}(3)\times\mathbb{R}^{n},\\
\boldsymbol{\nu}_{\mathcal{B}}=\begin{bmatrix}{}^{\mathcal{B}}\mathbf{v}_{\mathcal{B}}\\
{}^{\mathcal{B}}\boldsymbol{\omega}_{\mathcal{B}}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{6},\qquad\mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\nu}_{\mathcal{B}}\\
\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{j}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{6+n}.\end{gathered}$ 

(7.2)

The base twist $\boldsymbol{\nu}_{\mathcal{B}}$ contains the linear velocity of the base origin and its angular velocity, both expressed in $\mathcal{B}$ . Using this velocity convention consistently is essential. Configuration derivatives are not simply $\dot{\mathbf{q}}=\mathbf{v}$ . In particular, ${}^{\mathcal{W}}\dot{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathcal{B}}={}^{\mathcal{W}}\mathbf{R}_{\mathcal{B}}{}^{\mathcal{B}}\mathbf{v}_{\mathcal{B}}$ , and rotation evolves through the base angular velocity. The equations of motion are

 $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\dot{\mathbf{v}}+\mathbf{b}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{S}\boldsymbol{\tau}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{contact}}}\mathbf{J}_{i}(\mathbf{q})^{\top}\mathbf{f}_{i}+\mathbf{J}_{\rm ext}(\mathbf{q})^{\top}\mathbf{w}_{\rm ext},$ 

(7.3)

where $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\in\mathbb{R}^{(6+n)\times(6+n)}$ is the symmetric positive definite mass matrix. The bias term $\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{v})\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{q})$ collects Coriolis, centripetal, and gravity forces. The vector $\boldsymbol{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ contains the joint torques. The selection matrix

 $\mathbf{S}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{0}_{6\times n}\\
\mathbf{I}_{n}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(6+n)\times n}$ 

(7.4)

places torques on the joint rows only. $\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{contact}}$ is the set of active point contacts, with world-frame forces $\mathbf{f}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ . $\mathbf{J}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times(6+n)}$ maps the generalized velocity to the world-frame velocity of contact point $i$ . A contact patch can be represented by multiple such points. The six-dimensional external wrench $\mathbf{w}_{\rm ext}$ and its spatial Jacobian use matching world-aligned coordinates and the same moment reference point. Additional external interactions contribute analogous terms. Written blockwise, the dynamics are

 $\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{M}_{\mathcal{B}\mathcal{B}}&\mathbf{M}_{\mathcal{B}j}\\
\mathbf{M}_{j\mathcal{B}}&\mathbf{M}_{jj}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\dot{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{\mathcal{B}}\\
\ddot{\mathbf{q}}_{j}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{b}_{\mathcal{B}}\\
\mathbf{b}_{j}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{0}_{6}\\
\boldsymbol{\tau}\end{bmatrix}+\mathbf{J}_{\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{contact}}}^{\top}\mathbf{f}_{\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{contact}}}+\mathbf{J}_{\rm ext}^{\top}\mathbf{w}_{\rm ext},$ 

(7.5)

where $\mathbf{J}_{\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{contact}}}$ stacks the Jacobians of the active contacts and $\mathbf{f}_{\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{contact}}}$ their forces. The equations expose the central structural fact of legged robotics. The first six rows contain no joint torque, so no actuator acts directly on the base. Joint torque moves the base through inertial coupling (an airborne robot can pitch its trunk by swinging its legs) and through contact with the environment. Internal joint forces cancel in the center-of-mass (CoM) balance, so changing limb or trunk posture cannot create horizontal CoM acceleration when the net external horizontal force is zero. Foot friction, hand contacts, and other external interactions supply such forces. This underactuation makes contact forces central to movement (wensing2024).

Contacts enter the equations both as forces and as constraints on admissible motion. A foot in sticking contact with stationary ground satisfies $\mathbf{J}_{i}(\mathbf{q})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ . Each contact is unilateral. The ground pushes but does not pull, and friction bounds the tangential force. In world coordinates, let $\mathbf{n}_{i}$ be the unit surface normal and $\mu_{i}$ the friction coefficient, and split $\mathbf{f}_{i}$ into a normal part $f_{i,\mathrm{n}}=\mathbf{f}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{n}_{i}$ and a tangential part $\mathbf{f}_{i,\mathrm{t}}=\mathbf{f}_{i}-f_{i,\mathrm{n}}\mathbf{n}_{i}$ . Unilateral contact and Coulomb friction require

 $f_{i,\mathrm{n}}\geq 0,\qquad\|\mathbf{f}_{i,\mathrm{t}}\|_{2}\leq\mu_{i}f_{i,\mathrm{n}}.$ 

(7.6)

The pinned foot turns the stance leg into a reconfigurable strut that couples the base to the ground, and the same coupling is what lets the base state be inferred from joint encoders and an IMU, as the next subsection shows. Contact forces must also be compatible with the available joint torques. Contacts are ultimately hybrid. A contact is open, sticking, or sliding, and impact is discontinuous. Time-stepping complementarity formulations capture this without pre-specifying a mode sequence (stewart1996; posa2014), while deployed controllers often fix a contact sequence from a gait or footstep plan and optimize the force distribution within each mode (dicarlo2018).

Two further properties of the dynamics recur throughout control and identification. The Coriolis matrix can be chosen with an energy property that underlies passivity-based control arguments, and the dynamics are linear in the inertial parameters, with ten parameters per rigid link. This linearity forms the basis of classical identification (khalil2002; featherstone2008). Standard recursive algorithms evaluate inverse dynamics and unconstrained forward dynamics in time linear in the number of joints. Forming a dense mass matrix, resolving contacts, and solving control optimizations have additional costs (featherstone2008). Any gap between the simulated body and the real one is a model error the deployed controller must absorb.

So far the joint torque is a free input. On hardware it is not. The actuator sits between the commanded torque and the torque that reaches the joint. Three common designs illustrate different trade-offs. Hydraulic actuation provides high force density, as on HyQ (semini2011). Series elastic actuation introduces compliance that protects the drivetrain and makes torque measurable from spring deflection at the cost of bandwidth (pratt1995). And quasi-direct drive uses high-torque motors behind a low-ratio gearbox, as on the MIT Cheetah and Mini Cheetah (seok2015; katz2019). A simplified torque-interface model uses a first-order lag with saturation,

 $\dot{\boldsymbol{\tau}}=\frac{1}{T_{\tau}}\left[\operatorname{sat}_{\boldsymbol{\tau}^{\max}}\left(\boldsymbol{\tau}^{\rm cmd}\right)-\boldsymbol{\tau}\right],\qquad T_{\tau}>0,$ 

(7.7)

where saturation clips each commanded torque to its admissible interval, and the time constant $T_{\tau}$ is measured in seconds. Initialized within those intervals, this model preserves the torque bounds. Position-target actions additionally require a model of the intervening servo. Some actuator physics is difficult to capture with a hand-written model. Hwangbo et al. train an actuator network on physical-robot data, mapping a history of joint position errors and velocities to delivered torque, and policies trained with this model transfer to hardware (hwangbo2019).

7.2.2 Explicit State Estimation: Attitude, Velocity, Contact, and Local Terrain

Figure 7.4: Explicit and implicit state estimation on a legged robot. Explicit estimation fuses inertial and kinematic measurements, joint encoders, and an estimated contact set into a body state estimate through a propagate-correct loop. Implicit estimation maps recent observation-action history to a task-relevant latent. Deployed systems combine the two routes

In an explicit state-estimation architecture, the controller acts on physical quantities reconstructed from sensor measurements. Figure 7.4 contrasts explicit estimation with implicit estimation from observation history. On a legged robot the fused body state includes the base pose and velocity and the joint states, while the estimation pipeline additionally determines the contact set and, on perceptive platforms, maps the local terrain. Joint encoders observe joint configuration, with velocity obtained through sensor processing. An IMU provides angular velocity and specific force. Neither directly measures base position or translational velocity. The estimator must account for sensor orientation, lever arms, timestamps, and coordinate transforms.

A torso-mounted IMU, taken to sit at the base origin, provides two high-rate signals. The gyroscope measures angular velocity up to a slowly drifting bias. Integrating it gives short-term attitude that accumulates drift. The accelerometer measures specific force, physical acceleration minus gravity expressed in the sensor frame. At rest it reads not zero but a vector opposite gravity. Aligning the predicted gravity direction with the measured one corrects roll and pitch when other accelerations are modeled or sufficiently small, while yaw requires an external reference such as vision or a magnetometer. Complementary fusion trusts gyro integration at high frequency and the gravity reference at low frequency, implemented on the HRP-4 humanoid as an extended Kalman filter (EKF) (caron-estimation). The EKF loop propagates the state and its covariance with the model and then corrects both with each measurement. On the rotation manifold, the error-state Kalman filter (ESKF) propagates a nominal orientation and estimates a small rotation-vector error (sola2017). The contact-aided invariant extended Kalman filter (InEKF) has log-linear, estimate-independent error dynamics under its idealized deterministic model and improves convergence and consistency in the reported Cassie comparisons. IMU-bias augmentation weakens some theoretical guarantees, and covariance accuracy still depends on the model and noise assumptions (hartley2020).

The contact set is itself an estimate. Simple detectors threshold contact-force estimates obtained from joint-torque measurements using the leg Jacobian and a dynamics model. Classification is particularly sensitive during touchdown and lift-off transients. Probabilistic estimators maintain a per-foot contact probability from proprioceptive signals, with explicit impact detection, on HyQ (camurri2017), and filter-based estimators fold contact uncertainty into the measurement update (bloesch2012). A false stance introduces an incorrect constraint, while a false swing discards a useful update. With the contact set decided, a foot in firm stance on stationary ground provides a velocity constraint. Its world-frame velocity is zero, so the base velocity follows from the gyroscope, the encoders, and the leg Jacobian. This inference is the legged analog of wheel odometry. Bloesch et al. carry the foothold positions and IMU biases in the filter state and fuse these measurements with IMU propagation in one EKF (bloesch2012). Leg odometry is only as good as its premise. Slipping feet and misclassified swings bias the estimate. During flight phases, the estimator propagates inertially without contact corrections, and uncertainty grows according to sensor quality and the assumed dynamics.

Figure 7.5: Local terrain estimation for perceptive locomotion. Depth measurements are fused, under an uncertain estimated pose, into a local elevation map in which each cell retains a height estimate and a variance. The map is anchored to the estimated state and updated below the control rate, so it must be aligned to the current estimate before use

Even perfect fusion leaves global translation and rotation about gravity unobservable when only inertial and relative kinematic measurements are available (bloesch2012; hartley2020). Anchor schemes reduce accumulated drift by assuming that a selected stance-foot point occupies its planned world location and combining this with orientation and encoder-based forward kinematics. In Caron’s reported HRP-4 stepping-in-place example, the maximum lateral base-position error relative to VICON is $0.8\,\mathrm{cm}$ . The anchor assumption can fail with sliding, misplaced footholds, or foot flexibility (caron-estimation).

In addition to the body state, locomotion over unstructured ground needs a local terrain model, commonly an elevation map that fuses depth measurements under an uncertain robot pose and retains a height estimate and variance for each cell, as illustrated in Figure 7.5 (fankhauser2018). Because the map is anchored to the estimated state, pose drift affects the geometry supplied to control. The perceptive internal model (PIM), for example, uses an elevation map produced from point clouds and odometry and sampled around the robot in a gravity-aligned frame (long2025perceptive). Miki et al. show on ANYmal that a policy trained over corrupted maps can learn to discount unreliable perception (miki2022). Maps are computed in an estimated pose and updated at lower rates than the control loop, so they must be aligned to the current estimate before use. Occlusion and outdated geometry further motivate control that tolerates imperfect perception.

7.2.3 Implicit Estimation from Observation History

Explicit estimators rely on nominal dynamics, measurement models, and uncertainty assumptions. Real deployments introduce effects outside these models. Scree is slipperier than the simulated friction coefficient assumes, a carried payload changes the inertial parameters, actuators wear, and encoders are miscalibrated. Classical identification estimates such parameters offline from designed excitation, while a deployed robot can also infer its current response from recent observation-action history $h_{t}$ . In implicit estimation, a learned encoder recovers a compact, task-relevant representation $\mathbf{z}_{t}$ without naming every hidden physical parameter. The history must be temporally aligned and sufficiently informative. Actuator saturation, for example, can make the requested action differ from the input actually experienced by the body.

Training-time randomization varies the physics (masses, friction, and actuation) so that deployment conditions appear as further variations (tobin2017domain; peng2018). Randomization alone does not require a dedicated estimate of the current dynamics, although a history-conditioned policy may learn adaptation. A complementary line trains with a targeted adversary in which a learnable disturber selects destabilizing pushes, with an H-infinity-style constraint relating control cost to disturbance intensity (long2025hinf). Privileged teacher-student distillation explicitly trains a student to reproduce a privileged teacher’s behavior from proprioceptive history (lee2020). The history thereby supplies information about hidden conditions that the teacher observes directly.

RMA makes the estimator a dedicated module (kumar2021). A base policy acts on the current observation and a latent vector, and an adaptation module produces the latent from 50 recent observation-action steps, corresponding to $0.5$  s in the reported implementation. During training the latent is supervised to match a privileged encoder. At deployment the module updates it with no gradient computation. The latent encodes how behavior should change without requiring accurate recovery of friction or payload parameters. The hybrid internal model (HIM) combines an explicitly estimated velocity with an implicit response representation trained against successor observations (long2024hybrid). Its humanoid extension, the PIM, adds terrain sampled from the robot-centered elevation map described above (long2025perceptive). Learned estimation can therefore expose physical state, latent response information, or both. The pattern spans platforms. A history-conditioned humanoid transformer combines sequence-model pretraining with reinforcement learning (radosavovic2024). Deep whole-body control unifies manipulation and locomotion on a quadruped with an arm through regularized online adaptation (fu2022). And Deep Tracking Control (DTC) pairs a trajectory-optimizing planner with a learned tracking controller (jenelten2024).

Generalized momentum, the product of the mass matrix and velocity, provides a dynamics residual through a momentum observer (deluca2003). This residual can indicate unmodeled interaction, but also contains torque or model mismatch, so it cannot uniquely separate a push from a payload change. It complements learned response representations with a physics-derived diagnostic.

Several limits shape the division of labor. Distinct physical conditions can produce indistinguishable histories, and conditions outside the training distribution can invalidate a learned latent. A conventional latent vector carries no calibrated confidence measure. An EKF covariance also remains conditional on its model and noise assumptions. History can recover local motion and dynamic response, but inertial and relative kinematic inputs cannot supply a missing absolute position or yaw reference. Implicit representations cover model-resistant effects such as friction variation, actuator response, and soft-ground compliance, while explicit tools provide named physical estimates and external references. Deployed systems combine the two (miki2022; jenelten2024). A learned policy can consume the latent directly, while a model-based controller uses physical estimates, parameter corrections, or a momentum residual.

Table 7.2 summarizes sensor inputs, estimated quantities, controller uses, and characteristic failure modes. The control interface specifies the components supplying $\hat{s}_{t}$ , $h_{t}$ , and $\mathbf{z}_{t}$ , together with their frames and timestamps. Persistent estimation or tracking errors may require a slower command, a different contact plan, or upstream replanning, connecting local estimation to the task-level feedback in Section 7.1.
