## 7.3 Command-Conditioned Motor Control

A motion controller converts an abstract request such as “walk forward at a given speed” into a time sequence of coordinated joint actions. For a humanoid, this conversion is difficult because the request is multi-dimensional, the body is underactuated during foot contact, and the same joint motion simultaneously affects translation, turning, balance, foot clearance, and upper-body posture. A useful controller must therefore expose commands at a semantic level while learning (or solving) the coordination needed at the joint level. A velocity command leaves joint configurations and foot placement largely unspecified, while posture and phase commands specify body configuration and support timing. Reference-conditioned tracking, developed in Section 7.4, supplies more detailed time-varying motion targets.

7.3.1 Command Interfaces and Controller Families

Framework and Modules

A model-based controller separates prediction over a future horizon from instantaneous enforcement of whole-body dynamics. A reference generator converts velocity, posture, and gait commands into trajectories and a contact schedule. Nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) plans the motion and support wrenches. And a faster whole-body controller (WBC) realizes them through joint commands. State estimation combines IMU and encoder measurements with contact kinematics, while a robot-model module supplies the dynamics and Jacobians. Figure 7.6 adapts this organization to a humanoid robot.

NMPC: Anticipating Bipedal Support

Use the configuration $\mathbf{q}$ and generalized velocity $\mathbf{v}$ of Section 7.2.1, with $n$ actuated joints. A centroidal formulation (LocManMPC2021RAL) uses the state $\mathbf{x}=(\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{G}},\mathbf{q})$ and input $\mathbf{u}=(\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{L}},\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{R}},\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{j})$ , where $\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{G}}=(\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{G}},\mathbf{k}_{\mathrm{G}})$ contains linear and angular momentum about the center of mass, and $\mathbf{w}_{i}=(\mathbf{f}_{i},\boldsymbol{\mu}_{i})$ is a six-dimensional foot wrench. Here $\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{G}}$ is linear momentum in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$ , $\mathbf{k}_{\mathrm{G}}$ is angular momentum in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{2}/\mathrm{s}$ , and $m_{\mathrm{robot}}$ in the centroidal equations is robot mass in $\mathrm{kg}$ . Here momentum is unnormalized and each foot-wrench moment is taken about its foot-frame origin. With all terms expressed in world coordinates,

 $\dot{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathrm{G}}=m_{\mathrm{robot}}\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{acc}}+\sum_{i\in\{\mathrm{L},\mathrm{R}\}}\mathbf{f}_{i},\qquad\dot{\mathbf{k}}_{\mathrm{G}}=\sum_{i\in\{\mathrm{L},\mathrm{R}\}}\bigl[(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{c}_{\mathrm{G}})\times\mathbf{f}_{i}+\boldsymbol{\mu}_{i}\bigr],$ 

(7.8)

where $\mathbf{c}_{\mathrm{G}}$ is the CoM position and $\mathbf{r}_{i}$ the foot origin. External loads are omitted here. The centroidal momentum matrix $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{G}}(\mathbf{q})$ relates momentum to velocity by $\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{G}}=\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{G}}\mathbf{v}$ . Together with joint rates and configuration kinematics, this determines the state flow $\dot{\mathbf{x}}=F_{\sigma_{\mathrm{contact}}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{u})$ for a prescribed contact schedule $\sigma_{\mathrm{contact}}$ .

Figure 7.6: Model-based humanoid motion control, illustrated with Unitree G1. Command paths connect reference generation, NMPC, WBC, and joint control. Feedback paths supply estimated state, robot-model quantities, and local joint measurements

At each update, NMPC minimizes

 $\displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{u}(\cdot)}$ 
 $\displaystyle\Phi_{\mathrm{term}}(\mathbf{x}(t+T))+\int_{t}^{t+T}\ell(\mathbf{x}(\tau),\mathbf{u}(\tau),\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau,$ 

(7.9)

 $\displaystyle\ell={}$ 
 $\displaystyle\|\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{G},\mathrm{xy}}-\mathbf{v}^{\rm cmd}_{\mathrm{xy}}\|_{\mathbf{Q}_{v}}^{2}+\|\omega_{\mathrm{B},\mathrm{z}}-\omega_{\mathrm{z}}^{\rm cmd}\|_{Q_{\omega}}^{2}+\|\mathbf{e}_{\rm torso}\|_{\mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{R}}}^{2}$ 

 $\displaystyle+\|c_{\mathrm{G},\mathrm{z}}-c_{\mathrm{G},\mathrm{z}}^{\rm ref}\|_{Q_{c}}^{2}+\|\mathbf{q}_{\rm upper}-\mathbf{q}_{\rm upper}^{\rm ref}\|_{\mathbf{Q}_{a}}^{2}+\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u}^{\rm ref}\|_{\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{u}}}^{2},$ 

subject to the estimated initial state, centroidal dynamics, joint limits, and mode-dependent contact constraints. Here $\|\mathbf{e}\|_{\mathbf{Q}}^{2}=\mathbf{e}^{\top}\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{e}$ , $\Phi_{\mathrm{term}}$ is a terminal tracking cost, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{G}}=\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{G}}/m_{\mathrm{robot}}$ , and $\mathbf{e}_{\rm torso}$ is a torso-orientation error. The nonnegative scalars $Q_{\omega}$ and $Q_{c}$ weight the angular-velocity and CoM-height errors, respectively. Their weighted squares are $\|e\|_{Q_{\omega}}^{2}=Q_{\omega}e^{2}$ and $\|e\|_{Q_{c}}^{2}=Q_{c}e^{2}$ for a scalar error $e$ . Velocity commands are transformed into the same frames as the predicted velocities before comparison. The upper-body target specifies waist and arm posture. Desired support wrenches and joint rates define $\mathbf{u}^{\rm ref}$ . The humanoid objective therefore couples commanded travel to upright posture, CoM height, and upper-body motion.

A stance sole remains stationary. A swing foot carries zero wrench and follows a clearance trajectory. Each supporting foot must satisfy unilateral contact, friction, center-of-pressure bounds inside its sole, and admissible yaw moment. These surface-wrench constraints are essential when transferring load between one and two supporting feet. A prescribed schedule fixes contact order and timing. Optimizing those discrete choices requires an additional planner. Multiple shooting and sequential quadratic programming provide one implementation route. Only the current portion of the optimized trajectory is passed to WBC before replanning.

WBC: Realizing the Plan on the Full Body

Between contact switches, WBC solves at the current estimated configuration for $\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{WBC}}=(\dot{\mathbf{v}},\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{L}},\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{R}},\boldsymbol{\tau})$ . A representative task objective is

 $\min_{\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{WBC}}}\quad\sum_{k\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{WBC}}}\|\mathbf{J}_{k}\dot{\mathbf{v}}+\dot{\mathbf{J}}_{k}\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{a}_{k}^{\rm des}\|_{\mathbf{W}_{k}}^{2}+\|\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{w}^{\star}_{\rm NMPC}\|_{\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{f}}}^{2}+\|\boldsymbol{\tau}\|_{\mathbf{W}_{\tau}}^{2},$ 

(7.10)

where $\mathbf{W}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{task},k}\times d_{\mathrm{task},k}}$ , $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{f}}\in\mathbb{R}^{12\times 12}$ , and $\mathbf{W}_{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ are symmetric positive-semidefinite weight matrices, with $\|\mathbf{e}\|_{\mathbf{W}}^{2}=\mathbf{e}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{e}$ . The positive integer $d_{\mathrm{task},k}$ is the dimension of task $k$ ’s acceleration residual. The vector $\mathbf{w}=(\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{L}},\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{R}})\in\mathbb{R}^{12}$ stacks the two six-dimensional foot wrenches, and $\boldsymbol{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ contains the torques of the $n$ actuated joints. The optimization is subject to the hard constraints

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{M}\dot{\mathbf{v}}+\mathbf{b}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\mathbf{S}\boldsymbol{\tau}+\sum_{i}\mathbf{J}_{w,i}^{\top}\mathbf{w}_{i},$ 

(7.11)

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{J}_{w,i}\dot{\mathbf{v}}+\dot{\mathbf{J}}_{w,i}\mathbf{v}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\mathbf{0}$ 

 $\displaystyle(i\text{ in stance}),$ 

 $\displaystyle\mathbf{w}_{i}$ 
 $\displaystyle\in\mathcal{W}_{i}^{\mathrm{wrench}}(\sigma_{\mathrm{contact}}),\qquad\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\min}\leq\boldsymbol{\tau}\leq\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\max}.$ 

The six-row Jacobian $\mathbf{J}_{w,i}$ maps generalized velocity to foot twist, extending the point-contact model of Section 7.2.1. $\mathcal{W}_{i}^{\mathrm{wrench}}$ is the admissible wrench set, reduced to $\{\mathbf{0}\}$ in swing. The torque bounds in Eq. (7.11) apply componentwise. Tasks $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{WBC}}$ track CoM motion, torso orientation, swing-foot pose, and waist/arm posture, with feedback embedded in $\mathbf{a}_{k}^{\rm des}$ . Linearized friction bounds give a quadratic program. Weighted tasks express trade-offs. Strict priorities instead require hierarchical quadratic programs (QPs) that preserve higher-priority optima (2016RasHermiteSplines). Joint position and velocity limits can be enforced through bounds on predicted motion over the control step.

The resulting torque is combined with local joint feedback,

 $\boldsymbol{\tau}^{\mathrm{cmd}}=\boldsymbol{\tau}^{\mathrm{ff}}+\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{p}}(\mathbf{q}_{j}^{\mathrm{d}}-\mathbf{q}_{j})+\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{d}}(\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{j}^{\mathrm{d}}-\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{j}).$ 

(7.12)

Desired joint motion is obtained from the whole-body tracking solution, with the feedforward and feedback terms sharing the actuator torque budget. Predictive planning anticipates support changes. WBC enforces instantaneous feasibility. Their performance remains dependent on state estimates, contact assumptions, and timely optimization. A learned controller moves much of this coordination into training, while retaining a comparable command interface.

7.3.2 A Unified Command Space

The HUGWBC controller provides a compact example (xue2025hugwbc). Its policy receives task commands, behavior commands, proprioceptive history, and an intervention indicator, and emits the whole-body action at 50 Hz. Its design brings command following, disturbance rejection, and motion quality into a common training framework. In the released implementation, the task command contains desired base-frame longitudinal and lateral linear velocity and the base-frame angular-velocity $z$ component, which need not equal the Euler yaw-angle derivative,

 $\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\rm cmd}=[v_{\mathrm{x},t}^{\rm cmd},v_{\mathrm{y},t}^{\rm cmd},\omega_{\mathrm{z},t}^{\rm cmd}]^{\top}.$ 

(7.13)

This representation allows the policy to select footholds and body motion while being judged by the achieved velocity. The command is augmented with behavior variables including gait frequency $f_{t}^{\mathrm{gait}}$ , maximum foot clearance $\ell_{t}^{\mathrm{clear}}$ , body-height command $z_{t}^{\rm cmd}$ , body pitch $\beta_{t}^{\mathrm{pitch}}$ , waist yaw $\chi_{t}$ , phase offset $\psi_{t}^{\mathrm{phase}}$ , leg phases $\phi_{i,t}$ , and stance duty factor $d_{t}^{\mathrm{stance}}$ , forming

 $\mathbf{c}_{t}^{\rm beh}=[f_{t}^{\mathrm{gait}},\ell_{t}^{\mathrm{clear}},z_{t}^{\rm cmd},\beta_{t}^{\mathrm{pitch}},\chi_{t},\psi_{t}^{\mathrm{phase}},\phi_{1,t},\phi_{2,t},d_{t}^{\mathrm{stance}}]^{\top}.$ 

(7.14)

The clearance command is measured relative to a contact-height reference, and the duty factor specifies the fraction of a periodic cycle allocated to stance. The phase variables provide a low-dimensional clock shared by the legs and the reward terms. They are internal clocks advanced from frequency and phase offset, rather than independent operator inputs. The periodic mapping below uses $0<d_{t}^{\mathrm{stance}}<1$ . Standing instead fixes the phases. For a control interval $\Delta t$ ,

 $\phi_{1,t+1}=(\phi_{1,t}+f_{t}^{\mathrm{gait}}\Delta t)\bmod 1,\qquad\phi_{2,t+1}=(\phi_{1,t+1}+\psi_{t}^{\mathrm{phase}})\bmod 1.$ 

(7.15)

A walking gait uses half-cycle phase separation, whereas a jumping gait synchronizes both legs. In the paper’s nominal definitions, standing fixes both phases at $0.25$ , and hopping fixes the airborne leg at $0.75$ while the other leg cycles. HUGWBC uses one policy for standing, walking, and jumping, and a separate policy for hopping. Both the reported settings and the public default configuration fix $d_{t}^{\mathrm{stance}}=0.5$ .

The raw phase is normalized so that stance and swing occupy equal phase intervals according to

 $\bar{\phi}_{i,t}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\phi_{i,t}}{2d_{t}^{\mathrm{stance}}},&0\leq\phi_{i,t}<d_{t}^{\mathrm{stance}},\\[3.0pt]
\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\phi_{i,t}-d_{t}^{\mathrm{stance}}}{2(1-d_{t}^{\mathrm{stance}})},&d_{t}^{\mathrm{stance}}\leq\phi_{i,t}<1.\end{cases}.$ 

(7.16)

Thus stance maps to $[0,\frac{1}{2})$ and swing to $[\frac{1}{2},1)$ . The actor receives an encoded command $\mathbf{c}_{t}=[\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\rm cmd};\tilde{\mathbf{c}}_{t}^{\rm beh}]$ , where $\tilde{\mathbf{c}}_{t}^{\rm beh}$ replaces the two phase entries by $\sin(2\pi\bar{\phi}_{i,t})$ . The complete command separates what the robot should accomplish from how the motion should look, while leaving the policy free to discover the joint-level realization.

7.3.3 From Commands to Coordinated Actions

The policy observes a history of joint positions and velocities, base angular velocity and gravity direction, and its previous action, using $h_{t}$ defined in Eq. (7.1). Write $g_{t}=(\mathbf{c}_{t},I_{t}^{\mathrm{ext}})$ for the command input, where $I_{t}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ indicates whether an external upper-body controller is active. The deployed action mean is

 $\mathbf{a}_{t}=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\theta}(h_{t},g_{t}).$ 

(7.17)

During training, exploration uses a stochastic policy around this mean. A history encoder and state estimator supply estimated translational velocity, body height, and foot clearance. The privileged critic additionally sees linear velocity, body-height error, foot clearance, contact forces, friction, terrain samples, and collision indicators during training. The history allows the policy to infer quantities that are not directly measured or are delayed, a practical form of implicit state estimation.

The action is interpreted as a joint target (or a residual around a nominal posture) and passed through the robot’s low-level actuator loop. Consequently, a velocity command is not converted to a fixed stride table. The policy coordinates stance-leg actuation, swing-leg trajectories, trunk inclination, and arm motion to reduce the velocity error. Contact forces are controlled indirectly through body motion and joint actuation.

To describe a smooth contact target, let $\Phi$ be the standard normal cumulative distribution function and $\sigma_{\phi}>0$ a dimensionless smoothing width. For normalized phase $z\in[0,1)$ , define

 $\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{contact}}(z)={}$ 
 $\displaystyle\Phi(z/\sigma_{\phi})[1-\Phi((z-\tfrac{1}{2})/\sigma_{\phi})]$ 

(7.18)

 $\displaystyle+\Phi((z-1)/\sigma_{\phi})[1-\Phi((z-\tfrac{3}{2})/\sigma_{\phi})],\qquad C_{i,t}^{\mathrm{contact}}=C_{\mathrm{contact}}(\bar{\phi}_{i,t}).$ 

 $C_{i,t}^{\mathrm{contact}}$ is high in the intended stance interval and low in swing, with smooth transitions near phase boundaries. This command-derived expected contact weight is distinct from the sensor-based contact estimates of Section 7.2. The smooth weighting gives the contact objective a finite transition interval between stance and swing.

7.3.4 Contact Penalties and Swing Targets

Command following alone can admit motions that track velocity on average while making unnecessary contacts or moving the support foot. HUGWBC adds a periodic contact-swing objective. The public implementation uses nonnegative saturating functions (hugwbcCode2026) given by

 $g_{f}(x)=1-\exp(-x^{2}/s_{\mathrm{F}}),\qquad g_{v}(x)=1-\exp(-x^{2}/s_{\mathrm{V}}),\qquad s_{\mathrm{F}},s_{\mathrm{V}}>0.$ 

(7.19)

The denominators have units compatible with squared force and squared speed. With positive effective weights $w_{\mathrm{F}},w_{\mathrm{V}}$ that absorb control-interval scaling by $\Delta t$ , the combined penalty can be written as

 $r_{t}^{\rm contact}=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{2}\left[w_{\mathrm{F}}(1-C_{i,t}^{\mathrm{contact}})g_{f}(\|\mathbf{f}_{i,t}^{\rm foot}\|_{2})+w_{\mathrm{V}}C_{i,t}^{\mathrm{contact}}g_{v}(\|\mathbf{v}_{i,t}^{\rm foot}\|_{2})\right],$ 

(7.20)

where $\mathbf{f}_{i,t}^{\rm foot}$ is the three-dimensional contact force and $\mathbf{v}_{i,t}^{\rm foot}$ the three-dimensional world-frame foot velocity. This follows the released implementation. The paper expresses its velocity term using horizontal components. The code defaults are $s_{\mathrm{F}}=50$ , $s_{\mathrm{V}}=5$ , and reward weights $2$ and $4$ , respectively, before control-interval scaling. During stance the penalty encourages a planted support foot. During swing it discourages premature contact. The phase-dependent weight smooths the transition between these soft objectives.

In the paper, the vertical swing target is generated with a piecewise quintic polynomial whose coefficients satisfy position, velocity, and acceleration boundary conditions. A convenient mathematical expression uses

 $q_{\mathrm{interp}}(u_{\mathrm{interp}})=10u_{\mathrm{interp}}^{3}-15u_{\mathrm{interp}}^{4}+6u_{\mathrm{interp}}^{5},\qquad 0\leq u_{\mathrm{interp}}\leq 1,$ 

(7.21)

which satisfies $q_{\mathrm{interp}}(0)=0$ , $q_{\mathrm{interp}}(1)=1$ , and zero first and second derivatives at both endpoints. For equal starting and ending contact heights, the relative clearance is

 $\ell_{i,t}^{\rm target}=\ell_{t}^{\mathrm{clear}}\begin{cases}0,&0\leq\bar{\phi}_{i,t}\leq\frac{1}{2},\\
q_{\mathrm{interp}}(4\bar{\phi}_{i,t}-2),&\frac{1}{2}<\bar{\phi}_{i,t}\leq\frac{3}{4},\\
q_{\mathrm{interp}}(4-4\bar{\phi}_{i,t}),&\frac{3}{4}<\bar{\phi}_{i,t}<1.\end{cases}.$ 

(7.22)

The target is zero in stance, reaches the commanded height $\ell_{t}^{\mathrm{clear}}$ in mid-swing, and returns to the contact reference before touchdown. With fixed clearance and duty commands and constant phase rate during a cycle, height, velocity, and acceleration match at lift-off, the apex, and touchdown. For different endpoint heights, each half is written as $p_{0}+(p_{1}-p_{0})q_{\mathrm{interp}}(u_{\mathrm{interp}})$ using its time-ordered endpoints and a local coordinate $u_{\mathrm{interp}}$ increasing from zero to one.

The paper’s folded variable $u_{\rm fold}=\frac{1}{4}-|\bar{\phi}_{i,t}-\frac{3}{4}|$ gives the equivalent swing expression $\ell_{t}^{\mathrm{clear}}\sum_{k=0}^{5}a_{k}^{\mathrm{swing}}u_{\rm fold}^{k}=\ell_{t}^{\mathrm{clear}}q_{\mathrm{interp}}(4u_{\rm fold})$ , with $(a_{0}^{\mathrm{swing}},\ldots,a_{5}^{\mathrm{swing}})=(0,0,0,640,-3840,6144)$ . This form makes the boundary conditions explicit. A swing penalty is

 $r_{t}^{\rm swing}=-w_{\ell}\sum_{i=1}^{2}(1-C_{i,t}^{\mathrm{contact}})(\ell_{i,t}^{\rm target}-\ell_{i,t}^{\rm foot})^{2},\qquad w_{\ell}>0,$ 

(7.23)

where $\ell_{i,t}^{\rm foot}$ is actual clearance in the same convention. The polynomial supplies a smooth vertical reference, while the policy learns the coordinated foothold and body motion. The released implementation includes both linear and polynomial clearance rewards, with the default configuration enabling the linear term and assigning zero weight to the polynomial term (hugwbcCode2026).

7.3.5 Environment Rewards and Mirror Regularization

The environment reward contains task tracking, behavior tracking, and regularization terms, combined as

 $r_{t}=r_{t}^{\rm task}+r_{t}^{\rm behavior}+r_{t}^{\rm reg}.$ 

(7.24)

Task terms track the three velocity components with dense exponential errors. Behavior terms track height, pitch, and waist yaw, and include the contact and swing terms above. Regularization penalizes torque, joint-speed limit violations, joint acceleration, and action increments. Collision-based termination discourages failed execution. In particular, an action-rate term $-\|\mathbf{a}_{t}-\mathbf{a}_{t-1}\|^{2}$ discourages frame-to-frame jitter. These rewards define the rollout return and advantages used by PPO.

Mirror consistency is a separate training loss. Let $\mathcal{F}_{h}$ mirror body observations and past actions at each history step, $\mathcal{F}_{g}$ mirror the associated commands, and $\mathcal{F}_{a}$ mirror actions across the robot’s sagittal plane. The intervention indicator is unchanged. For rollout minibatches $\mathcal{D}_{\rm roll}$ , the released implementation uses

 $\mathcal{L}_{\rm sym}=\lambda_{\rm sym}\mathbb{E}_{(h_{t},g_{t})\sim\mathcal{D}_{\rm roll}}\left[\frac{1}{n_{a}}\left\|\operatorname{sg}[\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\theta}(h_{t},g_{t})]-\mathcal{F}_{a}\!\left(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{h}(h_{t}),\mathcal{F}_{g}(g_{t}))\right)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right],$ 

(7.25)

where $n_{a}$ is the action dimension and $\operatorname{sg}$ denotes stop-gradient. The default $\lambda_{\rm sym}=0.5$ . Symmetry is applied to observations, past actions, and commands as well as the action output, so it remains useful when the same policy is asked to produce left-right variants of an otherwise identical behavior (symmetry2018tog).

The optimizer minimizes the PPO actor and value losses minus the entropy bonus, plus $\mathcal{L}_{\rm sym}$ and the state-estimation loss when jointly trained. The mirror loss does not enter each-step reward, discounted return, or advantage. An independent foot-position symmetry reward used for non-walking gaits can enter the environment return. It is distinct from policy mirror consistency (hugwbcCode2026).

7.3.6 Couplings Between Commands

The learned controller exposes several useful couplings. At approximately steady forward speed, the pair $(v_{\mathrm{x}},f^{\mathrm{gait}})$ controls displacement per cycle. At fixed speed, raising frequency shortens each cycle’s displacement. At fixed frequency, raising speed requires greater displacement. The pair $(f^{\mathrm{gait}},\ell^{\mathrm{clear}})$ trades clearance against swing speed and work. Lateral velocity and turning interact with foot placement, phase offset, and waist orientation. Body height $z^{\rm cmd}$ changes leg configuration and effective workspace, while pitch $\beta^{\mathrm{pitch}}$ changes body geometry and the relation between base-frame and world-frame velocity. Finally, phase offset $\psi^{\mathrm{phase}}$ and duty factor $d^{\mathrm{stance}}$ specify the intended contact rhythm. A unified policy can learn these trade-offs from the return, while coordinated actuation and contact still limit the command combinations it can realize.

The reward weights also interact with these commands. For example, a high-frequency, high-clearance target increases the acceleration required by the swing trajectory, so an action-rate penalty suitable for walking may over-damp hopping. Curriculum sampling gradually expands command ranges and intervention magnitude. Massive parallel simulation makes such coverage practical (rudin2022learning). Periodic reward composition and multiplicity of behavior provide related examples of diverse gait learning through explicit command spaces (2021BipedalPeriodicReward; margolis2022walktheseways).

A useful diagnostic is therefore a command-interaction map rather than a list of single-command errors. Evaluate tracking error and smoothness on a grid of $(v_{\mathrm{x}},v_{\mathrm{y}},\omega_{\mathrm{z}},f^{\mathrm{gait}},\ell^{\mathrm{clear}},z^{\rm cmd},\beta^{\mathrm{pitch}},\chi)$ , then inspect where one command degrades another. Such tests assess behavior between command combinations as well as at isolated settings. They also expose saturation. If increasing $f^{\mathrm{gait}}$ no longer changes measured cadence, actuator or contact limits may be responsible, but further tests are needed to distinguish these limits from inadequate command conditioning.

7.3.7 Disturbance Rejection and External Control

Robustness is trained as part of motion generation. Upper-body intervention replaces the policy’s arm actions with sampled joint targets or bounded noise, while the lower-body command remains active. The intervention indicator tells the policy which control mode is present, and the intervention is interpolated over a finite interval rather than switched instantaneously. Regularization rewards for the intervened joints are masked, while velocity tracking, contact objectives, collision-based termination, and lower-body regularization remain active. A curriculum gradually increases the contribution of external actions once baseline velocity tracking is reliable. This trains trunk and leg compensation for arm motion while preserving the commanded gait, supporting loco-manipulation.

The resulting architecture closes the feedback loop at each control step. A semantic command is encoded as velocity, posture, and phase variables. Temporal proprioception supports state estimation. A command-conditioned policy maps the combined input to joint targets. And contact and motion-quality objectives shape the solution. Low-level torque limits and deployment checks complement this learned control. For deployment, the most important tests jointly assess command tracking under phase changes, recovery after external impulses, action-rate and contact behavior, and retention of lower-body stability during upper-body intervention. Maintaining this coordination on hardware also depends on the delays and actuator limitations examined in Section 7.5.

## 7.4 Motor Pretraining and Dexterous Whole-Body Control

Command-conditioned control exposes a specified behavior domain. Motor pretraining seeks capabilities that can be reused across downstream objectives. Three approaches serve different roles. Reference tracking learns to execute supplied motions. Learned priors and skill representations support downstream policy learning. And multi-mode pretraining or distillation exposes a shared repertoire through varied commands (peng2018deepmimic; peng2021amp; peng2022ase; he2025hover; zeng2025behavior). These approaches can be combined. This section first develops tracking as a common learning objective, then examines behavior foundation models, and finally shows that the same dynamics, estimation, tracking objectives, and command interfaces carry over to the multi-fingered hand, where the held object rather than the robot’s base is the unactuated body.

7.4.1 Motion Tracking

Motion tracking formulates humanoid whole-body control as the reproduction of a reference motion under the robot’s dynamics. Reference trajectories provide a time-varying description of the desired behavior, capturing the coordinated movement of the body across different skills. DeepMimic (peng2018deepmimic) establishes a reinforcement-learning formulation of this approach in physics-based character animation. Recent humanoid systems, including BeyondMimic (liao2026beyondmimic) and SONIC (luo2026sonic), build on this principle to acquire physically executable skills and broad behavior repertoires. The reference specifies how the robot should move, while reinforcement learning discovers the feedback control needed to reproduce that movement under physical dynamics.

Formally, consider a reference motion sequence

 $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{motion}}=(s_{0}^{\rm ref},s_{1}^{\rm ref},\ldots,s_{T}^{\rm ref}),$ 

(7.26)

where $s_{t}^{\rm ref}$ specifies the target kinematic quantities at timestep $t$ , such as joint configurations, body poses, and velocities. At each timestep, the policy selects an action conditioned on the available history and reference command, and the system evolves according to

 $\mathbf{a}_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t},g_{t}),\qquad s_{t+1}\sim P(\cdot\mid s_{t},\mathbf{a}_{t}),$ 

(7.27)

where $\pi_{\theta}$ is the policy parameterized by $\theta$ , $\mathbf{a}_{t}$ is the action, $h_{t}$ is the observation-action history defined in Eq. (7.1), $g_{t}$ is the reference-derived command, and $P$ denotes the transition dynamics. The full physical state $s_{t}$ may include privileged information accessible in simulation but unavailable to the deployed policy.

The discrepancy between the executed and reference motions provides a dense learning signal. A generic tracking reward takes the form

 $r_{t}^{\mathrm{track}}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{track}}}w_{k}\exp\!\left[-\frac{d_{k}(s_{t+1},s_{t+1}^{\rm ref})}{{\sigma_{k}^{\mathrm{track}}}^{2}}\right],\qquad w_{k}\geq 0,$ 

(7.28)

where $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{track}}$ indexes the tracked quantities, $d_{k}$ measures the corresponding squared discrepancy, $w_{k}$ determines its relative contribution, and $\sigma_{k}^{\mathrm{track}}>0$ controls the sensitivity to tracking errors. Additional costs can regularize physical execution through a reward of the form

 $r_{t}=r_{t}^{\mathrm{track}}-\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}c_{j}(s_{t},\mathbf{a}_{t-1},\mathbf{a}_{t},s_{t+1}),\qquad\lambda_{j}\geq 0,$ 

(7.29)

where $c_{j}$ denotes a nonnegative regularization cost and $\lambda_{j}$ its weight. The preceding action is included to allow action-rate penalties. Such costs can penalize undesirable behavior, including abrupt action changes or joint-limit violations. Motion tracking therefore provides a shared behavioral objective while retaining regularization appropriate for physical execution.

The policy is trained to maximize the expected discounted return according to the objective

 $\max_{\theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{motion}}\sim\mathcal{D},\,\zeta_{\mathrm{traj}}\sim p_{\theta}(\zeta_{\mathrm{traj}}\mid\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{motion}})}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^{t}r_{t}\right],$ 

(7.30)

where $\gamma\in[0,1)$ is the discount factor, $\mathcal{D}$ is the reference-motion distribution, and $\zeta_{\mathrm{traj}}$ is an executed state-action trajectory. The trajectory distribution $p_{\theta}$ is induced by the policy, transition dynamics, and initialization distribution. For a single-clip policy, $\mathcal{D}$ concentrates on one reference motion. For a controller trained on a motion corpus, it samples across multiple clips. In both settings, reference motions specify the desired outcomes, while interaction with the environment supplies the experience used for policy optimization. PPO (schulman2017ppo) is commonly used to optimize this objective, as exemplified by SONIC (luo2026sonic).

Several practical strategies support effective learning. Reference state initialization starts episodes from sampled reference configurations and velocities, exposing the policy to later phases of a motion before it can reliably reach them from the beginning. Early termination ends episodes when predefined failure conditions are met, such as excessive tracking errors, avoiding prolonged rollouts in unsuccessful states. Adaptive sampling further directs training effort toward challenging motions or segments. For example, BeyondMimic (liao2026beyondmimic) prioritizes temporal regions with high estimated failure rates while retaining a uniform sampling component to preserve coverage. Together, these strategies determine where rollouts begin, when they end, and how experience is distributed across the reference corpus.

7.4.2 Behavior Foundation Model

Motion tracking provides a shared learning objective, but a general-purpose controller must also accommodate the diverse commands used in downstream applications. A complete reference sequence may be suitable for motion replay, whereas interactive control may specify targets for only a few body links. This motivates behavior foundation models, humanoid controllers pretrained on large-scale motion data to acquire a broad repertoire of reusable whole-body behaviors and execute them in response to diverse behavioral specifications (zeng2025behavior; zeng2026scaling). By combining broad behavioral coverage with a versatile control interface, BFMs enable learned motor capabilities to be shared across multiple control modes and downstream tasks.

In this formulation, a behavior is defined as a trajectory of body states and actions, where $s_{t}^{\mathrm{p}}$ denotes the proprioceptive body variables selected from $s_{t}$ . The trajectory is written as

 $\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{seq}}\triangleq(s_{0}^{\mathrm{p}},\mathbf{a}_{0},s_{1}^{\mathrm{p}},\mathbf{a}_{1},\ldots,s_{T-1}^{\mathrm{p}},\mathbf{a}_{T-1},s_{T}^{\mathrm{p}}).$ 

(7.31)

Goal specifications are treated as external conditions that guide or constrain the execution of a behavior. A single behavior may satisfy different specifications, while a given specification may admit multiple physically valid behaviors. For example, specifying a hand target leaves considerable freedom in the robot’s stance and the movement of its other arm. Separating goals from the definition of $\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{seq}}$ therefore distinguishes the executed behavior from the conditions used to specify it.

From this perspective, BFM pretraining requires both a shared objective for acquiring diverse behaviors and a versatile interface for specifying their execution. Motion tracking provides the former through coordinated demonstrations and dense tracking rewards. The control interface provides the latter by allowing downstream applications to specify only the aspects of movement relevant to their objectives. Motion tracking thus serves as a proxy task for learning reusable motor capabilities, which can subsequently be invoked through commands that need not describe a complete whole-body trajectory.

One practical realization of this interface uses masked Cartesian body targets. Let $\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\mathrm{target}}$ contain target poses and tracking errors expressed in the robot’s current root frame, and let $\mathbf{m}_{t}$ be a binary mask selecting the commanded body links. The command and policy are then

 $g_{t}=(\mathbf{m}_{t}\odot\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\mathrm{target}},\mathbf{m}_{t}),\qquad\mathbf{a}_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t},g_{t}),$ 

(7.32)

where $h_{t}$ retains the history definition in Section 7.1.3, and the mask is applied to the features associated with each link. An entry $m_{t}^{\ell}=1$ indicates that link $\ell$ is specified. An all-one mask requests full-body tracking, while a sparse mask specifies selected links and allows the controller to coordinate the remaining body movements. Including the mask explicitly distinguishes an unspecified target from a valid target whose encoded value is zero. Sampling different masks during pretraining enables a single controller to learn from multiple forms of behavioral specification. For globally specified targets, root-relative encoding uses the robot pose relative to the target.

Figure 7.7: Visualization of the Humanoid Transformer architecture applied in ScaleBFM (zeng2026scaling)

The original BFM implementation trains a motion-imitation policy and transfers its behavior through masked online distillation. It also evaluates learning new behaviors through a residual decoder with the BFM frozen (zeng2025behavior). ScaleBFM studies direct goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning pretraining, examining the joint effects of training data and model capacity (zeng2026scaling). Its findings highlight the complementary roles of reference-motion diversity and on-policy experience. Diverse references expand the range of behaviors available for learning, while rollouts supply the interaction experience needed to acquire them. Effective scaling therefore calls for coordinating these two resources with an architecture capable of translating diverse behavioral specifications into coordinated actions.

As its model backbone, ScaleBFM introduces the Humanoid Transformer, which combines temporal context with goal-conditioned control, as illustrated in Figure 7.7. Proprioceptive states and past actions are encoded as interleaved tokens and processed through self-attention to capture the recent execution history. A learnable query token aggregates this information for action or value prediction. Future goal states, together with their temporal offsets, are encoded into goal tokens and incorporated through cross-attention. This design allows the controller to interpret the requested movement in the context of its ongoing behavior, directly accommodating the history and commands in Eq. (7.32).

ScaleBFM also studies the representations learned through goal conditioning. It applies root mean square normalization (RMSNorm) (zhang2019root) to goal embeddings and analyzes their normalized directions. For the selected motion sequences, neighboring targets yield nearby representations, while behaviors such as forward and backward walking occupy distinguishable regions. Perturbation experiments test how changes in embedding direction affect control performance. These findings provide evidence of local organization and robustness in the learned goal representation.

Together, these components illustrate how the general BFM framework can be instantiated in practice. Motion tracking supplies a shared learning objective, masked targets provide a versatile control interface, and the Humanoid Transformer relates behavioral specifications to the robot’s execution history. ScaleBFM thus offers a concrete example of learning coordinated motor skills and structured goal representations within a single pretrained controller, supporting the reuse of its behavioral repertoire across multiple control modes.

7.4.3 Evaluation Metrics

Evaluating a BFM requires measuring how reliably and accurately it realizes the behavioral specifications supplied through its control interface. Motion tracking provides a direct setting for this assessment because the executed behavior can be compared with a time-aligned reference. Using the tracking metrics reported by ScaleBFM (zeng2026scaling), this chapter considers sequence-level success rate together with mean per-keypoint position and rotation errors in global and local coordinates. These metrics describe complementary aspects of control, including persistent compliance with the command, accuracy in the world frame, and fidelity of the body configuration after horizontal root displacement and heading differences are removed.

Consider a reference motion $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{motion}}$ and the corresponding rollout of $\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t},g_{t})$ . With the initial state indexed by $0$ as above, let $t=1,\ldots,T$ index the frames actually executed and evaluated. For a fixed control mode, the command mask satisfies $\mathbf{m}_{t}=\mathbf{m}$ , and the set of evaluated links is

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{m}}^{\mathrm{links}}=\{\ell\mid m^{\ell}=1\}.$ 

(7.33)

Let $\mathbf{p}_{t,\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and $\mathbf{R}_{t,\ell}\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ denote the world-frame position and orientation of link $\ell$ , extracted from $s_{t}$ , and let $\mathbf{p}_{t,\ell}^{\rm ref}$ and $\mathbf{R}_{t,\ell}^{\rm ref}$ denote their counterparts in $s_{t}^{\rm ref}$ . In SI units, these position quantities are measured in $\mathrm{m}$ . Each rotation matrix maps vectors from the corresponding link frame to the world frame. The reference and executed states refer to the same robot embodiment and the same timestep. Only links in $\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{m}}^{\mathrm{links}}$ contribute to the tracking metrics. Sequences with an all-zero command mask are excluded from the tracking-error means below, and the number excluded is reported. An unspecified link may move differently from the reference while helping the robot satisfy the commanded targets.

Success Rate

For an evaluation set containing $N_{\mathrm{eval}}>0$ reference sequences, let $T_{i}$ denote the full reference length of sequence $i$ in frames, with $T_{i}>0$ and a nonempty selected-link set. Given a positional tolerance $\delta>0$ , the success rate is

 $\operatorname{Succ}(\delta)=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{eval}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{eval}}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq t\leq T_{i}\\
\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{m}}^{\mathrm{links}}\end{subarray}}\left\|\mathbf{p}_{t,\ell}^{(i)}-\mathbf{p}_{t,\ell}^{\mathrm{ref},(i)}\right\|_{2}\leq\delta\right],$ 

(7.34)

where $\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$ is the indicator function. A sequence succeeds only if every selected link remains within the tolerance throughout its execution. A rollout terminated by failure before completing the reference is counted as unsuccessful. ScaleBFM uses $\delta=0.5\,\mathrm{m}$ . The maximum over links and time makes this criterion sensitive to even a single large deviation. Success rate therefore complements average tracking errors, which can conceal brief failures. Since the criterion constrains position alone, orientation accuracy must be assessed separately. The score lies in $[0,1]$ and may be multiplied by $100$ when reported as a percentage.

Global Tracking Errors

For $T>0$ and a nonempty selected-link set, the global mean per-keypoint position error averages the Euclidean distance between corresponding link positions. The error is computed as

 $\mathrm{G\mbox{-}MPKPE}=\frac{1}{T|\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{m}}^{\mathrm{links}}|}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{m}}^{\mathrm{links}}}\left\|\mathbf{p}_{t,\ell}-\mathbf{p}_{t,\ell}^{\rm ref}\right\|_{2}.$ 

(7.35)

This error measures positional agreement in the world frame and is affected by both root motion and body articulation. For example, a controller may reproduce the reference limb configuration while gradually drifting away from the intended path, resulting in a large global position error.

For orientations, define the angular distance between two rotation matrices as

 $d_{\mathrm{R}}(\mathbf{R}_{1},\mathbf{R}_{2})=\arccos\!\left(\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{R}_{1}^{\top}\mathbf{R}_{2})-1}{2},-1,1\right)\right),$ 

(7.36)

where $\operatorname{tr}$ denotes the matrix trace and clipping accommodates numerical roundoff. This distance is the magnitude of the shortest relative rotation, taking values in $[0,\pi]$ . It gives a geometric orientation error without depending on the choice or wrapping of Euler angles. The global mean per-keypoint rotation error is then

 $\mathrm{G\mbox{-}MPKRE}=\frac{1}{T|\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{m}}^{\mathrm{links}}|}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{m}}^{\mathrm{links}}}d_{\mathrm{R}}\!\left(\mathbf{R}_{t,\ell},\mathbf{R}_{t,\ell}^{\rm ref}\right).$ 

(7.37)

Position errors are measured in meters and rotation errors in radians. Both are means of per-link distances, without squaring the errors.

Local Tracking Errors

Local evaluation removes the horizontal root position and heading of each trajectory at each timestep. To make this convention explicit, let

 $\mathbf{c}_{t}^{\mathrm{root}}=\begin{bmatrix}p_{t,\mathrm{x}}^{\rm root}&p_{t,\mathrm{y}}^{\rm root}&0\end{bmatrix}^{\!\top},\qquad\mathbf{H}_{t}=\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{z}}(\psi_{t}^{\mathrm{head}}),$ 

(7.38)

where $\mathbf{p}_{t}^{\rm root}$ is the robot root position, $\psi_{t}^{\mathrm{head}}$ is its heading angle, and $\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{z}}(\psi_{t}^{\mathrm{head}})$ is a rotation about the vertical axis. Define $\mathbf{c}_{t}^{\mathrm{root},\mathrm{ref}}$ and $\mathbf{H}_{t}^{\rm ref}$ analogously from the reference root state. The aligned link poses are

 $\displaystyle\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{t,\ell}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\mathbf{H}_{t}^{\top}(\mathbf{p}_{t,\ell}-\mathbf{c}_{t}^{\mathrm{root}}),$ 
 $\displaystyle\qquad\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{t,\ell}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\mathbf{H}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{R}_{t,\ell},$ 

(7.39)

 $\displaystyle\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{t,\ell}^{\rm ref}$ 
 $\displaystyle=(\mathbf{H}_{t}^{\rm ref})^{\top}(\mathbf{p}_{t,\ell}^{\rm ref}-\mathbf{c}_{t}^{\mathrm{root},\mathrm{ref}}),$ 
 $\displaystyle\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{t,\ell}^{\rm ref}$ 
 $\displaystyle=(\mathbf{H}_{t}^{\rm ref})^{\top}\mathbf{R}_{t,\ell}^{\rm ref}.$ 

The executed and reference poses are thus expressed in their respective heading frames, with each frame origin placed at the root’s horizontal projection onto the ground plane. Because this transformation removes only horizontal translation and yaw, discrepancies in height, roll, and pitch remain measurable. Applying the same position and rotation distances to these aligned quantities yields

 $\displaystyle\mathrm{L\mbox{-}MPKPE}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{T|\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{m}}^{\mathrm{links}}|}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{m}}^{\mathrm{links}}}\left\|\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{t,\ell}-\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{t,\ell}^{\rm ref}\right\|_{2},$ 

(7.40)

 $\displaystyle\mathrm{L\mbox{-}MPKRE}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{T|\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{m}}^{\mathrm{links}}|}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{m}}^{\mathrm{links}}}d_{\mathrm{R}}\!\left(\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{t,\ell},\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{t,\ell}^{\rm ref}\right).$ 

A low local error indicates accurate reconstruction of the commanded body configuration after this alignment. A substantial global position error together with a small local position error can therefore indicate difficulty following the desired root trajectory despite accurate local pose reproduction. Global and local scores should consequently be interpreted together. Their coordinate conventions describe how a rollout is scored and are separate from the coordinate encoding used to provide $g_{t}$ to the policy.

For meaningful comparisons, results should be reported separately for each control mode using matched reference motions, selected links, initialization, and sampling frequency. The formulas above define errors for one sequence. The reported mean is the arithmetic mean of the per-sequence errors, with each included sequence receiving equal weight. The error statistics retain the evaluated frames from failed and truncated rollouts. Because early termination can omit harder parts of a reference, mean errors should be interpreted together with success rate and rollout duration. Applying the same protocol to held-out motions from familiar sources and motions from unseen sources further distinguishes tracking accuracy from cross-source generalization. These measures characterize the realization of behavioral specifications. Downstream scene-interaction tasks additionally require evaluation of their own task outcomes.

7.4.4 Dexterous Hands: Motor Control at the Finger Level

A Cartesian hand target in a body controller specifies where the hand should move, but leaves its finger configuration and object contacts unresolved. Extending motor pretraining to dexterity therefore requires examples of contact transitions, together with an interface that can request useful movement without prescribing every contact.

The Held Object as a Floating Base

A multi-fingered hand needs the same layers of low-level control as the humanoid body, because its control problem has the same structure. Recall from Eq. (7.5) that the first six rows of a legged robot’s dynamics contain no joint torque. The base moves only through inertial coupling and contact. In in-hand manipulation the unactuated body is the held object. With the wrist pose given by the arm, the object twist $\boldsymbol{\nu}_{\mathrm{o}}\in\mathbb{R}^{6}$ and the finger joints $\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{h}}$ evolve as

 $\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{o}}\dot{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{\mathrm{o}}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{o}}=\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{h}},\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{o}})\,\mathbf{f}_{\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{hand}}}+\mathbf{w}_{\rm ext},\qquad\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{h}}(\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{h}})\ddot{\mathbf{q}}_{\mathrm{h}}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{h}}=\boldsymbol{\tau}-\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{h},\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{hand}}}^{\top}\mathbf{f}_{\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{hand}}},$ 

(7.41)

where $\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{hand}}$ is the set of active finger-object contacts, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{o}}$ is the object pose, $\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{o}}$ and $\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{o}}$ its spatial inertia and bias wrench, $\mathbf{f}_{\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{hand}}}$ stacks the forces that the fingers apply at the active contacts, and the grasp matrix $\mathbf{G}$ maps them to the resultant wrench on the object (lynch2017modern). Each contact force must lie in the friction cone of Eq. (7.6). As for the floating base, no actuator acts on the object directly. Joint torque $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ reaches it only through $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{h},\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{hand}}}$ and $\mathbf{G}$ , and only while the corresponding contacts are closed. Contact forces in the null space of $\mathbf{G}$ squeeze the object without moving it. They set the friction margins that keep the grasp stable (bicchi1994forces).

Table 7.3: Correspondence between humanoid whole-body control and dexterous in-hand control. References in the humanoid-body column point to the relevant formulations and sections of this chapter. The dexterous-hand column shows analogous quantities for a multi-fingered hand holding an object

Concept

Table 7.3 extends the correspondence to the rest of the chapter. Two points go beyond the table. First, rolling or sliding fingertips change $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{h},\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{hand}}}$ during a manipulation, much as foot placement changes the stance Jacobian, so the contact mode is part of the state to be estimated. Second, the hand differs in scale and instrumentation. Finger actuators are small, often heavily geared, and work close to their force limits, so the gap between commanded and realized torque in Eq. (7.7) matters more than it does for a leg. Available sensing ranges from motor current to fingertip tactile images (Section 9.6.3). And the hand’s “floating base” has a different mass and shape in every task.

The three routes to reusable motor skills named at the start of this section, namely reference tracking, learned priors, and goal-conditioned interfaces, carry over to the hand with the object in place of the base.

Tracking Human Hand References

TeleDexter makes the desired object motion explicit (li2026teledexter). The operator specifies fingertip positions and object pose in the wrist frame. A recurrent hand policy maps these goals and the observed hand-object state to residual joint-position commands, while independent inverse kinematics tracks the operator’s wrist with a fixed-base Franka FR3 arm. Training uses consecutive hand-object subgoals, with sparse goal-reaching rewards supplemented by dense tracking rewards. The hand can discover contact strategies between subgoals rather than reproduce every reference frame. Deployment runs at 30 Hz. Reaching and initial grasping use kinematic retargeting before the operator switches to the learned in-hand controller. Its training signal follows Eq. (7.28), but the reference covers the object and fingertips instead of every joint, much like the sparse masked targets of Eq. (7.32).

On a SharpaWave hand, TeleDexter achieves 75.2% mean success over seven reorientation and tool-use tasks, with 15 trials per task. Reusing the human reference data after retargeting and training a separate LeapHand controller yields 60% and 73.3% success on two reorientation tasks. This is reuse of data and a training procedure across hand morphologies. The current controller remains object-specific. A new object requires reference collection and policy training.

A Learned Motion Prior for Fingers

DexterityGen gives a concrete pretraining implementation (yin2025dexteritygen). Simulation reinforcement learning generates transitions between nearby sampled grasps, supplemented by free-finger and precision-manipulation behaviors. Varying object geometry, wrist motion, and physical parameters broadens the resulting dataset. A diffusion model then learns a distribution of future finger-keypoint motion conditioned on proprioceptive history and a mode indicator. An inverse dynamics model maps sampled motion to joint-position targets. At deployment, an external motion command guides diffusion sampling toward the requested finger movement while the learned prior favors motions represented in the training data. Thus, the command enters through sampling guidance. It is not simply copied to the joints. As in a behavior foundation model, a prior learned from broad simulated experience supplies coordinated motion, and a sparse command selects among behaviors it already supports.

The experiments demonstrate reuse on an Allegro hand attached to a separately controlled Franka Panda arm, with human teleoperation supplying motion commands. Test objects are absent from the pretraining dataset. Assisted teleoperation improves object retention and completes reorientation and regrasping tasks, but complete screwdriver and syringe tasks succeed in only 3/20 and 4/20 trials, respectively. These results support a reusable hand-motion prior while identifying the difficulty of composing skills into long tasks. The low-level controller uses proprioception rather than visual or tactile input. Control errors provide only an indirect contact cue.

Object-Goal Control Learned in Simulation

SimToolReal asks whether simulated experience can produce a controller that follows object goals taken from a human demonstration. It uses a 22-DoF Sharpa hand on a KUKA iiwa arm and trains a recurrent goal-reaching policy on procedurally generated tool-like objects. At deployment, a human RGB-D demonstration supplies a sequence of object poses. The policy observes proprioception, the current object pose, a grasp-region bounding box, and the current goal, and commands arm and hand joint targets (kedia2026simtoolreal). A demonstration can thus specify how a brush should be oriented without saying which finger releases first, and the controller is free to rotate the brush in the hand when moving the whole arm would hit the table. This is the object-centered goal representation of Section 8.3.1. The study evaluates 120 real rollouts over 24 trajectories, 12 tool instances, and six categories. Its Task Progress metric counts the fraction of demonstrated poses reached within a distance threshold and does not measure each tool’s effect (kedia2026simtoolreal). Reaching the intended hammer trajectory is not the same as driving a nail to depth. In the terms of Table 7.3, SimToolReal tracks a reference for the unactuated body itself and leaves the contact schedule to the policy, as a velocity command leaves footstep placement to a locomotion controller.

Adapting a Prior to Tight Contact

Play2Perfect, also on a Sharpa hand and KUKA arm, pretrains object manipulation in free space and then fine-tunes in CAD-derived assembly environments with sparse goal rewards. In 10 real trials at 0.5 mm insertion clearance, the fine-tuned policy succeeds 6 times and the play-only policy never (lum2026play2perfect). The deployment is zero-shot sim-to-real, but the policy for the assembly task itself was trained in simulation. Free-space reorientation can reach the right pose through many contact arrangements. Insertion cannot, since a small angular error produces an edge contact that jams the part, and the grasp must still allow corrective motion.

This is the hand counterpart of adapting a pretrained body controller to a new behavior, as the residual decoder of the original BFM does. The prior makes the approach reachable, and task-specific training concentrates on the final contact.

The interfaces exposed by the four controllers to the layer above are fingertip and object goals (TeleDexter), guided finger-keypoint motion (DexterityGen), object-pose sequences (SimToolReal), and a task reward in simulation (Play2Perfect). Any of them could be where a manipulation foundation model (Section 6.6) hands a goal to a hand controller, as a semantic planner hands targets to a humanoid controller (Section 7.1.3). None yet combines broad object coverage with contact sensing, the subject of the next subsection.

7.4.5 Contact Feedback and Force-Adaptive Body-Hand Coordination

Contact execution requires feedback that distinguishes mechanically different states. Similar finger positions can occur during pressing, sliding, or a failed regrasp. TeleDexter excludes contact-force and tactile observations. Its failure analysis links tracking stalls to the inability to distinguish pressing against an object from sliding past it. Tool impacts also perturb grasps beyond its free-space hand-object training distribution. Motion targets specify intended interaction, while contact feedback helps determine whether it is being realized.

One response is to give the controller a state that keeps evidence the current image has lost. WM-Craftnet combines wrist depth, binary tactile contact, proprioception, and previous actions in a recurrent World Synesthesia Model, whose state conditions a PPO policy that outputs relative targets for the 22 joints of a Sharpa Wave hand. Simulation supplies clean-depth reconstruction targets during training. At deployment the state is updated from noisy sensor data (yin2026wmcraftnet). The model gives the policy context and does not generate imagined rollouts, so it is a history-based state estimator in the sense of Section 5.1.2, serving as the hand counterpart of the RMA-style estimators of Section 7.2.3, with the object and its contacts as the hidden state. On an unseen double-notched block, WM-Craftnet meets the rotation criterion (more than half a revolution within 20 seconds) in 8 of 10 real trials, while a policy using WSM-denoised depth succeeds in none (yin2026wmcraftnet). This favors recurrent interaction context over image denoising alone, although matched comparisons of history, capacity, and objectives would be needed to pin down the source of the gain.

Touch can also correct execution between visual updates. T-Rex, evaluated on a fixed-base dual-arm system with two Sharpa Wave hands, refines actions asynchronously from recent fingertip deformation and force history, reusing the visual-language context instead of recomputing it for every refinement (niu2026trex). A separate 300 Hz thread tracks the updated targets. Recent contact evidence can therefore change finger motion while the action chunk remains valid at the task level, the multirate interface of Section 7.1.3. In a six-task ablation, the average score is 65 for the full system, 42 without touch, and 60 without asynchronous refinement, under the paper’s task-specific scoring (niu2026trex). Both the tactile signal and the way it is integrated contribute. The split between slow refinement and a fast servo is the hand version of the latency budget of Section 7.5. The tactile rates that make it necessary are given in Section 9.6.3.

Body-hand coordination introduces a further mechanical constraint. When a held object accelerates with the body, its required net contact force changes. Arm configuration can also change the moment transmitted to the base. With both hands on one object, their forces jointly determine its resultant wrench. Force components that cancel at the object can still change internal grasp loading and friction margins (bicchi1994forces). Coordinating a feasible object trajectory therefore also requires maintaining contacts and body support.

FAME provides direct evidence for force-adaptive standing (pudasaini2026fame). An encoder jointly maps 15 torso-and-arm joint positions and the two three-dimensional hand forces to an eight-dimensional latent, which conditions a lower-body policy. Training combines an upper-body pose curriculum with sampled hand loads. Deployment estimates each hand force from measured joint torques $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{t}$ , rigid-body inverse dynamics, and the hand Jacobian, without wrist force/torque sensors. The policy outputs 12 leg-joint position offsets at 50 Hz. Upper-body motion remains externally specified. This force estimate describes the load transmitted through an arm.

In simulation, FAME is evaluated on 100 upper-body configurations sampled from the training pose distribution, with 25 load draws per configuration. Success requires remaining upright, preserving the stance, and limiting force-induced hand displacement. At a 150 mm tolerance, success is 38.9%, compared with 16.6% when the same force information is supplied without jointly encoding force and upper-body configuration. On a Unitree H1-2, FAME maintains stance in all three asymmetric single-arm and all three symmetric bimanual loading trials. The pose-only baseline falls in all corresponding trials. These limited hardware tests establish load-dependent leg compensation. Together, the cases identify complementary interfaces. Object-and-finger goals request contact execution, tactile observations refine local actions, and hand-load estimates inform body support. An integrated system would need to be evaluated on simultaneous grasp maintenance, object motion, and balance.

## 7.5 Real-Time Execution, Recovery, and Safety Control

Deploying learned control policies from simulation to real humanoid robots involves challenges that extend beyond the performance of the policy itself. In practice, the system must operate under limited computational resources, perception and communication delays, actuator dynamics, and unexpected external disturbances while maintaining stable, continuous, and safe control. This is particularly challenging for humanoid robots due to their high-dimensional, strongly coupled, and partially underactuated dynamics, where local errors can propagate into whole-body deviations or even loss of balance. Therefore, real-world deployment requires jointly addressing real-time inference, motion smoothing, sim-to-real adaptation, anomaly monitoring, disturbance rejection, and recovery, ultimately forming a closed-loop safety framework from normal execution to failure handling and task recovery. Standing up from a fallen, seated, or leaning posture brings several of these requirements together. The robot must reorganize its contacts, control the resulting motion, and settle into stable support. HoST, introduced in Learning Humanoid Standing-up Control across Diverse Postures, provides a concrete example of learning this recovery capability (huang2025host).

7.5.1 Real-Time Execution and the Sim-to-Real Gap

Deploying learned control policies on physical humanoid robots requires bridging a substantial gap between simulation and the real world. This gap arises from multiple mismatches between the simulated and physical systems across dynamics, actuation, sensing, computation, and environmental interaction. An implementation with explicit state estimation can be summarized as

 $o_{t}\longrightarrow\hat{s}_{t}\longrightarrow\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\hat{s}_{t},g_{t})\longrightarrow\mathbf{a}_{t}\longrightarrow\text{actuator and physical system}\longrightarrow o_{t+1},$ 

(7.42)

where $o_{t}$ denotes the observation at time $t$ , $\hat{s}_{t}$ is the estimated robot state, $\pi_{\theta}$ is the learned policy, $g_{t}$ is the command, and $\mathbf{a}_{t}$ is the resulting action. The schematic suppresses the estimator’s memory and any additional policy history. A history-conditioned policy can instead use $h_{t}$ directly or combine it with explicit estimates. In practice, the discrepancy between the simulated and real execution of this loop can progressively degrade motion tracking, stability, and task performance. The major sources of the sim-to-real gap are discussed below.

Dynamics and Physical Parameter Mismatch

The physical dynamics of a humanoid robot are difficult to reproduce exactly in simulation. Differences in mass distribution, center of mass, inertia, joint friction, damping, actuator strength, gear transmission, and joint limits can cause the simulated robot to respond differently from its physical counterpart under the same control command. Contact-related parameters, such as ground friction, restitution, and collision geometry, further introduce discrepancies during locomotion, jumping, and other highly dynamic motions. Although system identification and domain randomization can reduce these differences, the real robot inevitably exhibits unmodeled dynamics and parameter variations that are difficult to capture completely during training.

Actuation and Low-Level Control Mismatch

The action produced by a learned policy is not directly realized as an idealized control input on a physical robot. Instead, it is typically converted through a low-level controller, actuator dynamics, communication interfaces, and hardware-specific constraints. Differences between simulated and real actuator response, including torque tracking errors, motor bandwidth, saturation, dead zones, and control frequency, can therefore introduce discrepancies between the commanded and realized motion. These errors become particularly significant for fast motions, where accurate timing and high-frequency torque responses are essential.

Perception and State-Estimation Errors

In simulation, the policy can often access accurate robot states, object positions, or environment information, whereas real systems must estimate these quantities from noisy and delayed sensor measurements. Camera noise, depth errors, occlusions, motion blur, imperfect calibration, and tracking failures can lead to discrepancies between the true physical state and the state provided to the policy. Such errors can alter both the magnitude and timing of the resulting control actions, especially for tasks involving fast-moving objects or rapidly changing contacts.

Control Latency and Asynchronous Execution

Real-time execution also introduces computational and communication delays across perception, state estimation, policy inference, communication, and actuation. For a sequential processing path, the total latency can be approximated as

 $d_{\rm total}=d_{\rm perception}+d_{\rm estimation}+d_{\rm policy}+d_{\rm communication}+d_{\rm actuation},$ 

(7.43)

where each $d$ is a time duration. In asynchronous or overlapping pipelines, the observation timestamp and actual execution time determine information age. The sum alone is insufficient. Given a control period $\Delta t$ , a large $d_{\rm total}$ means that the action is effectively computed from an outdated state, introducing a phase lag into the control loop. This effect is particularly detrimental to fast dynamic motions and balance control, where even a small temporal mismatch can result in noticeable tracking errors. In addition, asynchronous execution between perception, policy inference, and low-level control can introduce variable delays, making the effective control dynamics different from those assumed during simulation.

HoST illustrates how policy updates and joint feedback operate at different rates. On the 23-DoF Unitree G1, a three-layer MLP uses a short proprioceptive history, including body roll and pitch, angular velocity, and joint states, together with the previous action and action scale. The policy updates joint-position targets at 50 Hz, while the physical robot’s proportional-derivative (PD) servos run at 500 Hz (huang2025host). Joint feedback thus continues between policy updates. The simulation uses a 200 Hz PD loop, illustrating why transfer depends on the response of the complete policy-servo system as well as the policy update rate.

Contact and Environmental Mismatch

Physical interaction with the environment is another important source of discrepancy. Contact locations, collision geometry, ground compliance, friction conditions, and external disturbances are often simplified in simulation but can vary substantially in the real world. For humanoid robots, small differences in foot-ground contact or object interaction can change the resulting contact forces and consequently alter the entire-body motion. Such discrepancies are particularly challenging for behaviors involving impacts, rapid changes of support, or interaction with non-rigid or unstructured environments.

Reference-Tracking Error

For systems that generate reference motions and subsequently track them with a learned controller, the sim-to-real gap can be further amplified by tracking errors. Even if a kinematic trajectory generated by a planner is physically plausible, the real robot may not reproduce it exactly due to actuator limitations, modeling errors, latency, and state-estimation noise. The resulting deviation between the reference trajectory and the executed motion can accumulate over time, causing the robot to gradually drift away from the intended state. This issue is especially important in hierarchical architectures, where the output of one module becomes the input or conditioning signal of another.

Error Accumulation in Hierarchical and Autoregressive Systems

The effect becomes more pronounced when motion generation and control are coupled through multiple sequential modules. Consider a hierarchical system consisting of a high-level motion planner and a low-level tracking controller. If the planner generates a reference trajectory $\mathbf{q}_{t:t+H}^{\rm ref}$ spanning the current step and $H$ future control steps and the tracker executes it with tracking error, the actual state can deviate from the planned trajectory. When subsequent planning decisions use execution feedback, this deviation can propagate to future references. Errors in previously generated references can also propagate through the history used by an autoregressive planner.

This problem is particularly evident in autoregressive kinematic planners. Instead of generating an entire trajectory independently, an autoregressive planner predicts future motion conditioned on previously generated reference states and a planning condition $c_{t}^{\rm plan}$ according to

 $\mathbf{q}_{t+1}^{\rm ref}=F_{\rm plan}(\mathbf{q}_{0:t}^{\rm ref},c_{t}^{\rm plan}),$ 

(7.44)

where $F_{\rm plan}$ is the motion generator. Consequently, an error in an earlier prediction can become part of the input to subsequent predictions, resulting in accumulated prediction error over a long horizon. In a hierarchical planner-tracker architecture, tracking errors introduce another source of deviation between the planned and physically executed states. When execution feedback enters $c_{t}^{\rm plan}$ or another planning input, these state deviations can change future references. This coupling is particularly important for long-horizon and highly dynamic behaviors, where small local discrepancies can progressively amplify over time. Deep Tracking Control combines an optimization-based planner with a learned tracker (jenelten2024). AdaPT conditions a tennis planner on robot and ball information and adapts the reference execution speed (huang2026towards). These examples illustrate how planner-tracker interfaces connect motion generation with physical execution. Figure 7.8 summarizes sources of sim-to-real mismatch and their propagation through a planner-tracker system.

Figure 7.8: Sources of sim-to-real mismatch and their propagation through a planner-tracker system. The latency sum depicts a sequential processing path. The dashed state-to-planning connection applies when execution feedback conditions the planner

7.5.2 Motion Smoothing and Continuous Execution

In addition to inference speed, the temporal continuity of policy outputs is critical for stable real-world execution. Directly executing the actions produced by a learned policy at each timestep may result in high-frequency oscillations, particularly under observation noise, out-of-distribution states, or discrepancies between simulated and real dynamics. Such oscillations can introduce unnecessary joint acceleration, actuator load, and mechanical wear.

Locally Lipschitz Continuous Constraint (L2C2) regularization encourages local smoothness of policy and value functions during training (kobayashi2022l2c2). It penalizes changes under nearby input perturbations, helping reduce sensitivity to small observation changes. For highly dynamic behaviors, the resulting action continuity must be considered together with the responsiveness needed to preserve task-relevant motion components.

HoST applies L2C2 to the actor and each critic, constructing nearby inputs from differences between successive observed states. This training objective encourages smoother actor and value outputs. In hardware experiments with 5 trials in each of 4 settings (ground, platform, wall, and slope), HoST succeeds in 20/20 trials, compared with 11/20 after removing L2C2 (huang2025host). These results connect local function smoothness to the reliability of physical execution under the tested conditions.

Motion amplitude introduces a complementary trade-off. Large actions aid exploration but can produce violent transitions. HoST bounds the policy output and constructs each joint target relative to the current joint position according to

 $\mathbf{q}_{j,t}^{\mathrm{d}}=\mathbf{q}_{j,t}+\alpha_{\rm act}\mathbf{a}_{t},\qquad\mathbf{a}_{t}\in[-1,1]^{n},$ 

(7.45)

where $\mathbf{q}_{j,t}$ and $\mathbf{q}_{j,t}^{\mathrm{d}}$ are the measured and desired positions of the $n$ actuated joints, and $\alpha_{\rm act}$ scales the target increment in radians. Meeting an episode-end head-height criterion advances an action-scale curriculum that reduces $\alpha_{\rm act}$ from 1 toward 0.25 (huang2025host). This bounds the requested displacement at each update and indirectly moderates motion through the PD response. Gradual tightening retains early exploration while encouraging less abrupt execution as the skill develops.

For tracking a reference motion with specified timing, smoothing must also preserve the required movement speed. The objective is to suppress high-frequency noise while preserving the temporal structure and key dynamic characteristics of the original motion. Excessive smoothing may, for example, reduce the speed of a tennis swing or alter the timing of a dynamic motion. Therefore, motion smoothing should be designed jointly with motion phase, robot dynamic capabilities, and task constraints. The planner-tracker decomposition in AdaPT converts generated motions into executable commands through a dedicated tracking controller.

7.5.3 Sim-to-Real Adaptation

The deployment mismatches described above motivate training and adaptation across variations in dynamics, sensing, and latency.

A widely used approach is domain randomization, where physical and environmental parameters are randomized during training by sampling from a distribution

 $\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\rm sim}\sim p(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\rm sim}),$ 

(7.46)

where $\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\rm sim}$ may include robot mass, friction coefficients, joint damping, actuator strength, observation noise, control latency, and external disturbances. By exposing the policy to a distribution of possible environments, the learned controller can become less sensitive to modeling errors.

Another approach is to calibrate the simulation using real-robot data through system identification, thereby reducing the discrepancy between simulated and physical dynamics. In practice, these approaches can be combined. Real-robot data are first used to estimate the dominant physical parameters, while domain randomization is then applied to cover the remaining uncertainty.

HoST combines coverage of initial support conditions with randomization of physical parameters. Ground, platform, wall, and slope settings expose training to different starting postures and contacts. Within these settings, randomization includes base center-of-mass offsets of up to $\pm 3$  cm and control delays from 0 to 100 ms, alongside friction, actuator strength, and PD gains (huang2025host). Hardware deployment also adjusts hip and knee PD stiffness to compensate for differences in torque response. The example shows how broad simulation coverage and servo-gain adjustment contribute jointly to transfer.

For humanoid motion control, an important observation is that a motion that is kinematically feasible in simulation is not necessarily dynamically executable on the real robot. Consequently, the training pipeline should account not only for task-level objectives but also for the actual controller, state estimation process, and execution constraints used during deployment. For systems that generate high-level motion references, the generated motion must ultimately be converted into executable behavior by a tracking controller that accounts for these constraints.

7.5.4 Balance Protection and Fall Recovery

For humanoid robots, a particularly important aspect of safety control is the possibility of losing balance and falling. A complete safety framework should therefore not assume that the robot never falls, but should also provide mechanisms for controlled falling, post-fall recovery, and subsequent task resumption.

Balance protection can be organized into several stages according to the severity of the instability. The first stage is rapid disturbance rejection, such as adjusting foot placement, torso orientation, and motion speed. If the robot can no longer recover its standing state and a validated protective controller is available, the system can enter a controlled fall mode and modify the body configuration to reduce impact. After falling, a dedicated, trained and validated get-up controller can bring the robot back to a stable standing configuration.

Learning such a controller requires objectives that guide the robot through changing support configurations. HoST learns standing-up motion without reference trajectories, using height-dependent reward activation to organize righting, rising, and stable standing (huang2025host). Its four reward groups (task, style, regularization, and post-task) describe progress, motion quality, and the stability of the achieved posture. Each group has a separate critic. Its generalized advantage estimates are normalized within the training batch, then combined in a weighted sum to update a shared actor with PPO. This separates return estimation for signals with different scales and temporal structure while learning a policy that coordinates their requirements.

Exploration is especially difficult before the robot discovers how to raise its body into a supported posture. HoST therefore applies an upward force to the base during training when the trunk is nearly vertical. As the episode-end head-height criterion is met, the assistance decreases from 200 N in 20 N steps until it reaches zero. Together with the action-scale curriculum, this lets training first discover the recovery motion and then refine its execution with reduced assistance and smaller target increments. Post-task rewards favor low base linear and angular velocities and the maintenance of body height and posture. Consistently, simulation success requires the base to reach the target height and remain above it for the rest of the episode (huang2025host). Recovery thus includes stabilizing the terminal posture.

Executing a learned recovery skill also depends on the available space around the body. HoST reports collisions with the surroundings in some seated-start trials using proprioception alone (huang2025host). Such cases motivate environmental checks when selecting and initiating a recovery motion. Incorporating the skill into an autonomous system further requires fall detection, controller handover, and task resumption. The HoST study leaves this integration for future work.

Task recovery should go beyond simply returning the robot to a standing posture. The system should also restore the task context. For example, if the robot loses balance during a long-horizon motion imitation task, the recovery module should determine the current task phase and decide whether to restart the current motion, resume from an intermediate state, or replan a new executable trajectory. Integrating these decisions with balance protection makes recovery part of the task-level control process.

Future humanoid control systems should account for dynamic feasibility while integrating motion generation, real-time control, failure detection, risk mitigation, recovery, and task resumption. These functions need validation within the intended operating conditions.

## 8 Physical Agents

For a long time, research on the interaction between AI and the physical world has focused primarily on short-term actions and isolated skills, such as executing a single grasp or traversing a short stretch of terrain. Yet a true embodied agent must be able to operate continuously in real environments over extended periods of time. Achieving this requires more than low-level perception, motor skills, and future prediction.
