Instead, it demands a capable cognitive core that can perform long-horizon planning and adapt as conditions change.

This chapter discusses how to build such an integrated system, which is a physical agent, that can interact with the physical world continuously in a closed loop. To this end, the chapter first defines the scope of physical agents and clarifies how they differ from purely digital agents and conventional robots. It then discusses how physical agents scale to adapt to entity-level, composite, and system-level constraints. Building on this foundation, it explains how physical goals become assessable task specifications, how available skills are organized into feasible behavior, and how execution feedback supports verification and recovery. Finally, it examines collaboration among heterogeneous agents and the emergence of distributed capabilities.

## 8.1 Definition of Physical Agent

As artificial intelligence extends from digital information spaces into the physical world, the notion of an intelligent agent acquires additional requirements. A digital agent may pursue goals, maintain memory, reason over observations, and invoke software tools, while its actions primarily alter informational states. A physical agent must additionally operate through an embodied system whose actions are constrained by geometry, dynamics, contact, sensing limitations, actuation uncertainty, time, energy, and safety (RussellNorvig2020; PfeiferBongard2006; SicilianoKhatib2016). Its decisions can change not only the state of the task, but also its own physical configuration, the surrounding environment, and the observations and actions that become available afterward.

A physical agent should therefore not be understood simply as a robot equipped with an artificial intelligence model. The relevant distinction lies in how the system organizes perception and action around an objective under physical constraints. In this chapter, the term refers to systems that are physically situated, possess some degree of autonomy in selecting their behavior, and continuously use the consequences of physical interaction to guide subsequent decisions. This perspective provides a common basis for discussing agents implemented as mobile robots, manipulators, legged systems, aerial vehicles, autonomous machines, or more distributed physical systems (brooks1991intelligence; Liu2025EmbodiedAI).

8.1.1 Concept and Boundary of Physical Agent

A Working Definition

In this chapter, a physical agent is defined as a goal-directed, relatively autonomous unit that perceives physical conditions, selects and executes feasible actions through its embodiment, and uses feedback from their physical effects to adjust subsequent behavior. Its embodiment determines what it can sense and how it can act, while environmental conditions, resource limits, and assigned authority constrain admissible behavior. Feedback connects intended outcomes to observed changes in the agent and its surroundings, enabling it to continue execution, correct its actions, or revise its plan.

This definition treats physical agency as a relationship among objective, embodiment, environment, action, and feedback. The agent is situated because its behavior takes place in an environment governed by spatial and physical relationships rather than solely by symbolic or computational rules. It is goal-directed because its behavior is organized around a desired outcome rather than a fully prescribed sequence of actions. It is autonomous or semi-autonomous because at least part of the mapping from a task objective to concrete actions is determined during operation rather than completely specified in advance.

Figure 8.1: Closed-loop interaction between a physical agent and the physical world. Perception and task-relevant representations inform decision-making, which may include optional prediction and scenario simulation. Decisions are realized through embodied physical actions, and these actions change the physical state of the agent and/or environment. The resulting state gives rise to new observations that inform subsequent decisions. Here $x_{t}$ is the joint physical state at step $t$ , $x_{t+1}$ its next state, and $o_{t+1}$ the resulting observation

Physical embodiment is essential to this definition. The embodiment includes the system’s mechanical structure together with its sensors, actuators, onboard computation, and the interfaces through which it exchanges information and physical influence with the environment. It determines what the agent can observe, which actions are feasible, and what physical consequences those actions may produce. The embodiment is therefore not merely a carrier on which an intelligent algorithm is deployed. It constitutes part of the agent’s sensing and action capabilities and thereby defines part of its operational boundary (PfeiferBongard2006; SicilianoKhatib2016).

The definition also requires closed-loop interaction (brooks1991intelligence; Åström and Murray, 2008). An action produces a physical consequence, that consequence gives rise to new observations, and those observations may alter subsequent behavior. This interaction is illustrated in Figure 8.1.

Perception and action are coupled in this loop. Actions change the world from which future observations are obtained, and new observations change which actions are subsequently selected.

Physical Agents and Digital Agents

A physical agent and a digital agent share several fundamental properties. Both may be goal-directed, maintain internal state, use memory, reason over uncertain information, invoke tools, and revise their behavior according to feedback. The distinction therefore does not lie in whether the system performs reasoning or planning.

The more consequential difference concerns the domain in which actions take effect. A digital agent primarily changes informational states, for example by generating text, editing files, querying a database, executing code, or invoking a software service. These actions may indirectly lead to physical consequences when mediated by an external system, but the agent’s immediate action space is digital.

A physical agent acts through a physical embodiment. Its actions may change its position, orientation, velocity, configuration, contact state, or energy state, as well as the location, configuration, or physical condition of external objects. Such actions are subject to feasibility constraints and may produce delayed, uncertain, or irreversible consequences. A manipulator cannot instantaneously move its end effector to an arbitrary pose. An aerial vehicle cannot change velocity without satisfying its dynamics. A mobile robot cannot traverse an occupied region merely because a planner identifies it as geometrically desirable.

The distinction can therefore be expressed in terms of the state directly affected by action. Digital agents act primarily on informational states, whereas a physical agent directly participates in the evolution of physical states. This difference introduces requirements that are less prominent in purely digital settings, including dynamic feasibility, physical safety, execution uncertainty, limited sensing, resource constraints, and the need to verify the actual outcome of an action rather than only whether a command was issued.

Physical Agents and Robots

The terms robot and physical agent also overlap without being synonymous. A robot primarily identifies a class of embodied machines capable of sensing, computation, and actuation. The concept of a physical agent places greater emphasis on how such capabilities are organized around an objective and how much of the resulting behavior is selected during interaction with the environment.

Consider an industrial manipulator that repeatedly follows a predetermined welding trajectory. The system is clearly a robot, and it may employ sophisticated feedback control to achieve high precision. Nevertheless, if the task, sequence, and responses to relevant situations are almost entirely specified in advance, its behavior exhibits relatively little agent-level autonomy. By contrast, a manipulation system that is given a desired outcome, selects an appropriate grasp and motion strategy from the observed scene, detects unsuccessful execution, and chooses an alternative course of action has stronger agentic properties even if the underlying physical platform is similar.

The distinction is therefore one of emphasis rather than a strict separation of system categories. A robot characterizes the physical means through which sensing and action are realized, whereas a physical agent characterizes a mode of operation in which perception, decision-making, physical action, and feedback are organized in pursuit of a goal. Many modern robotic systems satisfy both descriptions, while some robots remain primarily automated machines with narrowly prescribed behavior.

8.1.2 Functional Organization and Interaction Loop

Building on the four elements in Chapter 1 (Section 1.3), this section distinguishes five functional roles by discussing world representation and physical prediction separately. These roles comprise physical state perception and estimation; physical representation and world models; physical prediction and simulation; physical decision-making, planning, control, and execution; and closed-loop feedback and multiscale adaptation. A physical agent realizes this same loop within an identifiable operational boundary. The following account applies those elements to agent-level behavior, without prescribing separate software modules. Their functions may be explicitly implemented, learned jointly, or distributed across computational and physical subsystems (SicilianoKhatib2016; Liu2025EmbodiedAI).

Embodiment, objectives, and operating constraints provide the conditions under which all five functional roles function. The embodiment includes mechanical structure, sensors, actuators, computation, and environment interfaces. It determines which observations and physical actions are available. A wheeled platform, manipulator, and aerial robot may therefore use different strategies for the same objective. Goals specify desired outcomes, while kinematic and dynamic limits, collision avoidance, energy, time, permissions, and safety requirements delimit acceptable behavior. These conditions guide the entire loop. Memory supports continuity across its elements, and safety mechanisms constrain and monitor their operation.

Physical State Perception and Estimation

A physical agent generally lacks direct access to the complete state of the world. Cameras, depth sensors, LiDAR, tactile and force sensors, inertial units, encoders, and other instruments provide incomplete measurements affected by noise, occlusion, calibration errors, and latency (SicilianoKhatib2016). Perception and estimation construct task-relevant descriptions of the body’s state and surroundings, including pose, motion, object configurations, contact, free space, or process quantities such as temperature. The required information and its accuracy depend on the decisions and control actions that follow.

Physical Representation and World Models

Representations organize estimated information into spatial, semantic, relational, or physical descriptions that support action. Memory retains earlier observations, explored regions, attempted actions, and outcomes, enabling the physical agent to reason beyond its current view. A world model may encode object relationships, affordances, and transition regularities. Such information can be explicit, implicit in a learned policy, or distributed across components. A comprehensive internal simulator is therefore unnecessary. The relevant requirement is a representation adequate for the task and operating conditions.

Physical Prediction and Simulation

Prediction uses available representations to anticipate how candidate actions, disturbances, or other participants may change physical conditions. Scenario simulation can compare alternative sequences before committing to execution, using analytical dynamics, learned models, or other approximations. Its usefulness depends on the prediction horizon, uncertainty, and computational cost. This element need not be a separate predictive module. A reactive controller or learned policy may incorporate local expectations implicitly, while explicit prediction supports longer horizons and more complex dependencies. Forecasts remain conditional on their assumptions and must be checked against interaction outcomes.

Physical Decision-Making, Planning, Control, and Execution

This element connects estimated conditions and the objective to feasible physical intervention (RussellNorvig2020; Kober2013). A complex objective can be decomposed into intermediate goals and realized through reusable skills, such as approaching, grasping, transporting, or inspecting. Planning coordinates these skills and their dependencies. Control converts the selected behavior into trajectories, velocities, forces, torques, or actuator commands compatible with the embodiment. An instruction to grasp a container may thus require approach motion, alignment, contact establishment, closure, and force regulation. Modular architectures may expose these stages individually, while learned policies may combine them. In either case, action selection remains conditioned on the task, current information, and admissible operating conditions.

Closed-Loop Feedback and Multiscale Adaptation

Execution changes the physical state and produces new evidence. Feedback compares intended and observed outcomes and informs corrections at different scales (Åström and Murray, 2008). A controller can regulate contact force, a skill can adjust its motion, and a task planner can replace an unsuccessful operation. Over repeated operation, calibration and retained experience can support adaptation to equipment drift or changing conditions. Adaptation may update estimates, representations, predictions, or behavior without necessarily changing learned parameters online. Safety mechanisms operate throughout the loop by restricting candidate actions, monitoring execution, and triggering recovery, fallback, or intervention when limits are approached. Feedback therefore connects local regulation, task-level revision, and longer-term adaptation, sustaining the closed-loop organization described in Chapter 1 and its application loop (Section 1.5.1).

A Formal View of Physical Interaction

The interaction of a physical agent with its environment can be represented as a partially observable closed-loop decision process (Kaelbling1998). Let $t$ be a nonnegative integer indexing interaction steps, $B_{\mathrm{emb}}$ describe the embodiment and its sensing and actuation capabilities, and $\mathcal{X}$ be the space of joint physical states of the body and environment. Then

 $x_{t}\in\mathcal{X}$ 

(8.1)

denotes the physical state at step $t$ . The physical agent receives an observation $o_{t}$ in an observation space $\mathcal{O}$ according to

 $o_{t}\sim p(o_{t}\mid x_{t},B_{\mathrm{emb}}),$ 

(8.2)

where $p(o_{t}\mid x_{t},B_{\mathrm{emb}})$ is the conditional observation distribution and $\sim$ denotes sampling from that distribution. It accounts for the sensing capabilities of the embodiment and measurement uncertainty.

Let $m_{t}^{\mathrm{mem}}$ denote retained information from earlier interactions, $g$ the task objective, $c_{t}^{\mathrm{constr}}$ the currently relevant constraints, and $o_{\leq t}=(o_{0},\ldots,o_{t})$ the observation history through step $t$ . The policy $\pi$ is a conditional action distribution that selects an action $a_{t}$ from the embodiment’s action space $\mathcal{A}_{B_{\mathrm{emb}}}$ , subject to $c_{t}^{\mathrm{constr}}$ :

 $a_{t}\sim\pi\left(a_{t}\mid o_{\leq t},m_{t}^{\mathrm{mem}},g,c_{t}^{\mathrm{constr}},B_{\mathrm{emb}}\right).$ 

(8.3)

The physical state then evolves according to

 $x_{t+1}\sim p(x_{t+1}\mid x_{t},a_{t},B_{\mathrm{emb}}),$ 

(8.4)

where $p(x_{t+1}\mid x_{t},a_{t},B_{\mathrm{emb}})$ is the conditional state-transition distribution, including environmental uncertainty and the effects of embodied actuation. The notation $p$ denotes the appropriate conditional distribution in each equation. Deterministic sensing, policies, or dynamics are special cases of these distributions.

Eqs. (8.2) to (8.4) specify the observation, action-selection, and physical-transition relationships, rather than a particular control or learning architecture. Estimation, representation, and any explicit prediction support the policy. Feedback supplies subsequent observations and updates. The resulting interaction is

 $x_{t}\rightarrow o_{t}\rightarrow a_{t}\rightarrow x_{t+1}\rightarrow o_{t+1},$ 

(8.5)

where arrows indicate the causal and informational progression of one cycle. Actions affect both the physical state and the evidence available for later decisions, coupling sensing and acting throughout the loop.

8.1.3 Autonomy and the Transition from Automation to Agency

Autonomy as a Continuum

The distinction between a physical agent and a conventional automated system is not binary. Physical systems exhibit different degrees of autonomy, and many useful machines occupy intermediate positions between fixed automation and general goal-directed agency (Parasuraman2000).

In fixed automation, task structure and action sequences are largely specified before deployment. A production system may repeatedly execute the same sequence with high precision, while conventional feedback control compensates for deviations in variables such as position, velocity, force, or temperature. Such feedback is essential to reliable physical operation, but local error correction alone does not imply that the system selects its behavior at the task level.

As sensing, computation, and adaptive control become more capable, physical systems can respond to a wider range of environmental variations. A mobile robot may choose a different route when an aisle is blocked, and a manipulator may adjust its motion when an object is displaced. In such cases, some aspects of behavior are determined online, although the range of possible tasks and responses may remain strongly bounded by predefined representations and skills.

A more agentic system shifts the specification from actions toward outcomes. Rather than being provided with a complete trajectory or procedure, it may receive a target state or higher-level objective and determine an appropriate sequence of actions from the current situation. The progression can be represented schematically as

 $\text{Fixed Automation}\rightarrow\text{Feedback Control}\rightarrow\text{Adaptive Robotics}\rightarrow\text{Goal-Directed Agency}.$ 

(8.6)

This sequence should be interpreted as an organizing continuum rather than a strict taxonomy. Real systems may combine characteristics from several stages and may exhibit different levels of autonomy in different parts of the same task.

Goal-Conditioned Action Selection

A central feature of agency is that the same objective can lead to different actions depending on the current physical situation. If a direct route becomes obstructed, a mobile agent may select an alternative path. If an intended grasp is infeasible, a manipulation system may choose another grasp configuration or reposition itself before trying again. The objective remains unchanged while the means of achieving it are revised.

This distinguishes goal-conditioned action selection from a fixed input-output response. The agent’s action depends jointly on the current state, the desired outcome, the available capabilities, and the constraints under which it operates.

Adaptation Under Uncertainty

Physical environments are only partially observable and are rarely perfectly predictable. Objects may move, materials may behave differently from expected models, sensing may degrade, and the effect of an action may differ from its nominal prediction. A physical agent must therefore operate despite uncertainty about both the current state and the consequences of its own actions (Kober2013; Brunke2022).

Adaptation in this context does not necessarily imply online learning of model parameters. It more generally refers to the ability to revise behavior as new evidence becomes available. The agent may update a state estimate, change a planned path, select another skill, reduce speed, request additional observations, or transfer control to a human operator. These mechanisms differ in implementation but serve the same role by preventing execution from being tied irreversibly to assumptions made before interaction.

Outcome-Driven Correction and Recovery

An important consequence of closed-loop autonomy is that issuing an action is not equivalent to completing it. Physical execution must be assessed in terms of outcomes. A command to close a door is not successful merely because the corresponding motor command was sent. The agent must establish, to the extent required by the task, that the resulting physical state satisfies the intended condition.

When execution does not produce the intended outcome, an agent may need to distinguish among transient error, action failure, environmental change, or an infeasible objective. Recovery can then involve repeating the action, selecting an alternative action, revising the plan, modifying the objective within permitted limits, or requesting external intervention. The ability to make such distinctions becomes increasingly important as tasks extend over longer horizons and involve larger numbers of dependent actions.

Autonomy Does Not Imply Unrestricted Operation

Autonomy should not be equated with the absence of human control. In practical physical systems, autonomous behavior is typically bounded by authority, safety, and operational constraints. A robot may plan its own route while requiring authorization for a safety-critical manipulation, or it may execute a task independently while requesting human assistance when uncertainty exceeds an acceptable threshold.

For this reason, a physical agent is more appropriately described as an autonomous or semi-autonomous system than as a necessarily fully autonomous machine. Its autonomy concerns the degree to which action selection and adaptation are delegated to the system within a specified operating envelope.

Autonomy should also not be treated as synonymous with intelligence. A narrowly specialized machine may operate with little human intervention while possessing limited ability to generalize beyond a predefined task. Conversely, a system with sophisticated perception, reasoning, or learning capabilities may intentionally operate under substantial human supervision. The development of Physical AI should therefore be considered along multiple dimensions, including autonomy, task diversity, environmental openness, uncertainty, temporal horizon, and the complexity of adaptive behavior.

From this perspective, the transition from automation to physical agency is characterized less by the addition of any single algorithm than by a change in how behavior is organized. The system moves from executing actions specified in advance toward selecting and revising actions in response to goals, physical constraints, and interaction outcomes. This concept provides the foundation for the subsequent discussion of goal representation, perception, world modeling, planning, learning, control, and other capabilities required for a physical agent.

## 8.2 Physical Forms of Physical Agent

A physical agent can take different forms, distinguished by how its body provides access to the world. A manipulator changes an object’s pose through contact, a mobile robot changes position and viewpoint, and a laboratory installation transforms and measures samples. These differences arise from both bodily morphology and the arrangement of sensing, actuation, computation, and resources. Accordingly, physical form denotes the organization through which an agent acts, including systems whose action interfaces are distributed across several devices. Situated robotics and embodied intelligence provide the conceptual foundations for relating behavior to the coupling of controller, body, and environment (brooks1991intelligence; pfeifer2007self).

Under the working definition adopted in this chapter, a physical agent is a relatively autonomous, goal-directed unit that perceives physical conditions, selects feasible actions, changes those conditions, and adapts through feedback. A robot is one possible realization of its body. Agency is a property of the complete operational loop, including the executive and its authority over physical interfaces. Software that recommends an action remains a digital agent at that boundary. Attributing physical agency to a software-equipment installation requires including the equipment that executes the action and the measurements used to evaluate it.

Figure 8.2: Physical forms distinguished by the boundary of attribution, the organization of action, and the scope of the task. Dashed outlines delimit the selected agent. Solid dark arrows denote physical action or flow, green arrows commands, and dashed blue arrows information. The three views can be nested. Original analytical synthesis informed by pfeifer2007self; yim2007; monostori2016

Figure 8.2 introduces three complementary views. An entity-level view treats a coherent acting body as one unit. A composite view resolves functionally separable action subsystems that fulfill a joint mission. A system-level view encompasses distributed resources coordinated across an operational domain. This is the chapter’s analytical framework, rather than a standardized taxonomy or an autonomy ranking. For example, a mobile manipulator can be one entity in a transport study, a base-arm composite in a manipulation study, and a resource within an autonomous laboratory. The chosen view should follow the capability being explained.

Three criteria make that choice explicit, namely command authority, observable outcomes, and the allocation of responsibility to people or other systems. They distinguish an operational boundary from a building perimeter or a network membership list. Task objects usually remain part of the environment, even while grasped. Materials and mechanisms can themselves support adaptive behavior, as emphasized in physical intelligence research (sitti2021physical). The working definition here additionally requires a goal-directed action loop. With this boundary established, physical forms can be examined through the interfaces and constraints that make particular actions possible.

8.2.1 Entity-Level and Composite Forms of Physical Agent

Entity-Level Forms and Their Action Interfaces

An entity-level physical agent has a coherent body and an identifiable action interface. Mobility, contact geometry, compliance, workspace, payload, and sensing arrangement describe how that body interacts with its surroundings. Figure 8.3 pairs representative morphologies with the physical variables through which they act.

Figure 8.3: Morphology, action interface, and limiting conditions for six representative forms. Shaded reach and sensing regions are qualitative. Arrows indicate motion or interaction directions. The compliant gripper contrasts nominal straight fingers with deformed contact. These original schematics describe physical affordances, not the autonomy of a particular product

Fixed Manipulators

An arm controls end-effector pose and interaction forces within a bounded workspace. Operational-space control formalizes the relationship between joint actuation and end-effector motion or force (khatib1987). Geometric reach is only one requirement. Tool shape, friction, collision clearance, and admissible contact loads also determine whether an operation is feasible. Pairing two arms adds complementary contact roles, such as stabilizing and inserting. ALOHA demonstrates learned fine manipulation using such a bimanual arrangement and human demonstrations (zhao2023). At the installation scale the pair can be treated as one manipulation unit. A composite view makes its coordination requirements explicit.

Ground-Mobile Robots

Wheeled bodies provide efficient transport where supporting surfaces are traversable. Legged bodies can select footholds across uneven terrain, with balance and contact transitions forming part of the action problem. miki2022 integrate terrain information with proprioception for quadrupedal locomotion under unreliable perception. Terrain estimates support action through the footholds and dynamics available to the body. Humanoids extend this family with human-like proportions and manipulation interfaces. Resemblance to people is not a criterion for physical agency.

Aerial Robots

Flight provides three-dimensional access and changes the sensor’s viewpoint without continuous ground support. This capability couples navigation to lift, attitude stabilization, obstacle clearance, and energy availability. loquercio2021 demonstrate high-speed autonomous flight using onboard sensing and computation. Inspection and delivery build on aerial access but additionally depend on task-specific sensors, payload interfaces, and operating conditions.

Process Equipment and Compliant Bodies

Stationary equipment can change geometry, temperature, pressure, or composition through tools and process inputs. Cyber-physical manufacturing architectures connect such equipment to state assessment and adaptive responses (lee2015). Soft structures, meanwhile, support conformal interaction by distributing deformation over a body (rus2015). Passive dynamic walking offers a complementary demonstration of mechanics contributing to organized motion (mcgeer1990).

Composite Forms: Coordinated Action Across Modules

A composite physical agent combines functionally separable action subsystems under one mission and outcome criterion. Typical combinations join locomotion with manipulation, ground transport with flight, or sample handling with experimental processing. The analytical emphasis lies on the interfaces between these capabilities. Mechanical attachment is one coupling mechanism. Shared timing, resources, and responsibility can also bind modules that separate in space.

Figure 8.4: Two forms of inter-module dependence. (a) Base configuration $\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{B}}$ and arm configuration $\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{A}}$ jointly determine tool pose. $\mathrm{W}$ , $\mathrm{B}$ , and $\mathrm{E}$ denote world, base, and end-effector frames. (b) Separate routes require compatible recovery times and sufficient flight energy. Symbols within the schematic are defined in the accompanying text. The reach boundary and waiting timeline are qualitative. Original schematics informed by mobile manipulation (fu2025) and truck-drone routing (murray2015)

The schematic in Figure 8.4 uses $x_{\mathrm{B}}$ and $z_{\mathrm{B}}$ for base-frame axes. For frame labels $\mathrm{F}$ and $\mathrm{H}$ , the homogeneous transform ${}^{\mathrm{F}}\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{H}}$ maps coordinates from $\mathrm{H}$ to $\mathrm{F}$ , so ${}^{\mathrm{W}}\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{E}}={}^{\mathrm{W}}\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{B}}(\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{B}}){}^{\mathrm{B}}\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{E}}(\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{A}})$ composes the base and arm transformations. In the routing example, $\mathrm{L}$ , $\mathrm{D}$ , and $\mathrm{R}$ label launch, delivery, and recovery sites. The arrival times $t_{\mathrm{C}},t_{\mathrm{D}}$ and nonnegative waiting times $w_{\mathrm{C}},w_{\mathrm{D}}$ belong to the carrier and drone, respectively. $t_{\mathrm{recovery}}$ is their common recovery time. The terms $E_{\mathrm{sortie}}$ , $E_{\mathrm{reserve}}$ , and $E_{\mathrm{available}}$ denote required sortie energy, required reserve, and available drone energy.

Mobile Manipulation

Base motion extends access beyond a fixed arm’s workspace while changing its reference frame, sensing viewpoint, and collision envelope. The pose relation in Figure 8.4(a) expresses this geometric dependence. Contact forces and stability introduce additional dynamic constraints. Mobile ALOHA combines a mobile base, two arms, and whole-body demonstration collection to learn coordinated tasks, including cabinet operation and use of a kitchen faucet (fu2025). Locomotion establishes access to a work location, while manipulation determines where the base can operate. The cited study evaluates learned execution after demonstration collection, so its teleoperation apparatus and its autonomous policy serve distinct roles.

Vehicle-Drone Systems

A carrier can move a drone between launch sites while the drone serves locations through complementary aerial routes. The flying sidekick traveling salesman problem models the resulting route, endurance, and rendezvous dependencies (murray2015). Figure 8.4(b) makes one consequence visible. Arrival at the recovery site must be synchronized, potentially through waiting. This is an optimization formulation, with human driving of the truck retained in the original problem setting. A composite interpretation becomes useful when one mission executive is responsible for both delivery and recovery. Separate vehicles with independently assigned goals invite a multi-agent interpretation.

Multi-Device Experimental Platforms

Dispensing, processing, transfer, and measurement modules can form a composite when they execute a bounded protocol. burger2020 connect laboratory stations through a dexterous mobile robot in a photocatalyst search. Transporting one vial can be attributed to the robot, whereas conducting the experimental search also requires the stations and experiment-selection software. The example shows how changing the attributed outcome changes the necessary physical boundary.

Composite form can itself be variable. Modular self-reconfigurable robots alter the connectivity and arrangement of their modules (yim2007). Self-modeling robots can revise their behavior after bodily damage (bongard2006selfmodeling). Capability consequently depends on current connectivity, calibration, module condition, and coordinated skills. This dependence becomes still more prominent when the acting resources form a persistent, distributed installation.

8.2.2 System-Level Physical Agents

A Distributed Body with an Operational Boundary

A system-level physical agent acts through distributed sensors, robots, process equipment, computing nodes, and control networks. Its operational unity comes from an objective and the coordinated use of resources across a domain. Physical distribution and controller organization are separate design choices. A distributed body may use centralized, distributed, or hybrid coordination. Holonic manufacturing provides an early account of autonomous units participating in a larger production organization (vanbrussel1998). Cyber-physical production connects computational coordination with physical processes (monostori2016).

Two related graphs clarify the organization of such a body:

 $\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{phys}}=(V_{\mathrm{phys}},E_{\mathrm{phys}}),\qquad\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{info}}=(V_{\mathrm{phys}}\cup V_{\mathrm{comp}},E_{\mathrm{info}}),$ 

(8.7)

where $\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{phys}}$ and $\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{info}}$ are the physical-dependency and information-exchange graphs. The resource vertex sets $V_{\mathrm{phys}}$ and $V_{\mathrm{comp}}$ contain sensing/acting and logical computation resources, respectively. Computation may be hosted on the same devices. The edge set $E_{\mathrm{phys}}$ encodes mechanical, material-transfer, or process dependencies. The edge set $E_{\mathrm{info}}$ encodes sensing, coordination, or command exchange. The union $V_{\mathrm{phys}}\cup V_{\mathrm{comp}}$ comprises both resource types. Figure 8.5 illustrates the organization of a system-level physical agent. This descriptive model distinguishes the existence of a communication path from the existence of an executable physical operation. For example, rerouting a part requires a compatible transport path as well as a revised assignment.

Figure 8.5: Physical and informational organization of a system-level physical agent. Coordination functions operate through shared interfaces, while individual resources retain local feedback and interlocks. Commands, observations, and material flows are distinguished explicitly. The layers describe functional responsibilities and do not prescribe a centralized network architecture. Original synthesis based on holonic and cyber-physical manufacturing (vanbrussel1998; lee2015; monostori2016)

Attribution of agency at this scale requires an actionable system objective, authority over the necessary equipment, and measured outcomes that change subsequent interventions. A production objective, for example, becomes operational through coordinated transformation, transport, and quality evaluation. Sensor aggregation alone supplies only part of that loop. Similarly, a fixed command sequence can automate execution while leaving adaptation to an operator. The relevant distinction concerns who selects and revises physical actions when conditions change.

The operational boundary also spans different timescales. Fast contact and motion loops coexist with slower production and experiment cycles. Local stabilization and protective responses must remain effective within the coordination architecture. Human supervisors can set objectives, replenish resources, and authorize exceptional operations, provided these responsibilities are stated. A system-level physical agent can therefore contain local agents and depend on specified human support. What justifies the higher-level description is the additional feedback loop that coordinates resources to achieve an installation-wide outcome. Smart factories, intelligent mines, and autonomous laboratories are representative realizations of a system-level physical agent.

Protocols and Standards for a Physical Agent

For a system-level physical agent, interoperability determines whether independently developed resources can participate in a common course of action. Robots, instruments, and process equipment need shared ways to describe their capabilities, accept delegated work, and report what occurred. Protocols specify these exchanges, while standards establish common information models and requirements against which implementations can be checked. Together, they make the relationships between reasoning, coordination, and physical execution explicit enough to support integration across manufacturers and applications.

A useful organization separates objective formation and revision, task coordination, and local execution. Protocols connect these responsibilities by carrying capability descriptions, task requests, and execution feedback. This separation allows planning methods and equipment implementations to evolve while preserving agreed interfaces. The Model Context Protocol (MCP), for example, specifies how AI applications discover and invoke tools with structured input and output descriptions (mcp2025). Applying such interfaces to physical resources requires their descriptions and results to carry the operational meaning needed by the task, including which objects are affected, which conditions permit execution, and what observations establish completion. Anthropic’s Model Hardware Standard (MHS), introduced as a research preview in collaboration with HHMI Janelia Research Campus in 2026, addresses the discovery and operation of programmable physical devices.88
 8

 Anthropic, Previewing the Model Hardware Standard, research preview, August 27, 2026. MHS combines standardized drivers with descriptions of device characteristics and operating limits, and supports access through MCP, command-line interfaces, and code. It thus provides a concrete example of connecting general agent interfaces to laboratory and manufacturing equipment.

The central abstraction is the capability that a resource makes available to the wider system. This may be a measurement, a material-processing operation, a robotic skill, or an established procedure involving several devices. A common description helps an agent determine what can be requested and what information it can expect in return. The Web of Things Thing Description provides one foundation for describing interactions with heterogeneous devices (w3c2023wot). At the system level, this suggests a way to organize access around useful functions while retaining the specialized knowledge and control methods within each resource. The same planning system could then work with different combinations of equipment through compatible descriptions.

An autonomous laboratory illustrates how this organization connects reasoning with diverse physical capabilities. In an illustrative materials study, a scientific agent might propose candidate compositions and the properties to be measured. A laboratory coordination system would relate this plan to available preparation, processing, and characterization capabilities. Dedicated instruments would perform established procedures, while robots could contribute manipulation or transport where needed. The protocol would connect these contributions to the same experimental objective and return their results in an interpretable form. The OPC UA Laboratory and Analytical Device Standard supports this kind of integration through common models for device functions, program execution, and results (opc2023lads). Here OPC UA denotes OPC Unified Architecture.

The significance of this connection extends to what the agent can learn from an intervention. In the laboratory example, measurements become useful feedback when they remain associated with the candidate material, preparation history, and conditions under which they were obtained. The agent can then compare outcomes, revise an explanation, or select a subsequent experiment. Similar relationships arise when a production system uses inspection results to adjust processing conditions, or an environmental monitoring system directs further measurements toward an uncertain region. Across these settings, a protocol should preserve the context that makes returned observations relevant to the objective. This connects access to physical resources with the continuing development of the agent’s understanding.

Shared descriptions also create opportunities for reuse across tasks and facilities. A preparation-and-measurement procedure could be offered as a composite capability for later studies, while its constituent functions remain available for other combinations. Another facility could contribute a complementary measurement or a compatible processing operation. Industrial asset representations such as the Asset Administration Shell provide standardized structures for accessing asset information and services (iec2023aas). Research linking these representations with capability models and OPC UA communication explores how such descriptions can support reconfigurable systems (justmann2024mapping). Reuse still depends on whether the available methods, materials, and operating conditions fit the new task.

From this perspective, protocols and standards provide shared infrastructure through which physical capabilities can accumulate and be used by different agents. A common core can organize capability discovery, task interaction, and contextualized feedback, while domain-specific descriptions express the knowledge needed in manufacturing, laboratories, or other settings. As models, instruments, and procedures improve, compatible interfaces could allow those advances to benefit multiple workflows. The broader opportunity is to connect independently developed intelligence and physical resources into systems that can pursue objectives, evaluate their interventions, and draw on a growing range of capabilities. Autonomous laboratories offer a concrete setting in which to examine these relationships.

8.2.3 Correspondence Between Form, Capability, and Application

Reaching an object, exerting a controlled force, and checking the result require different physical provisions. A long reach does not establish that an operation can be performed at every reachable position. A large payload does not establish precise control of contact. Connecting form to application therefore requires examining how the body produces the actions a task needs, and under what conditions it can produce them reliably.

Geometry and Motion

Link lengths, joint arrangements, and movement limits determine which positions and orientations a mechanism can reach. Its current posture also matters. Joint motion can produce end-effector motion more readily in some directions than in others, and this relationship changes as the mechanism moves. This posture dependence is captured by manipulability measures (yoshikawa1985). For capability assessment, the implication is that access to a position and freedom to act there should be examined separately. The relevant description includes the required working posture and motion direction, alongside collision clearance and load conditions. Manipulability supplies one local kinematic measure. The other requirements need their own checks.

Contact and Material Response

Surface geometry, friction, and compliance affect how a body establishes contact and transmits force. Compliance allows a body to deform under contact, sometimes accommodating differences in object shape through its mechanics. A deformable gripping interface, for instance, can conform to an object before stiffening to hold it. Its effectiveness still depends on obtaining suitable contact (brown2010). Changing the object or contact conditions can therefore change the result even when the controller remains the same. Thus, describing a body as compliant or adaptable should be accompanied by the object properties and loads for which that behavior is useful.

Sensing Geometry

The placement and mobility of sensors determine which information the body can acquire. A camera may have adequate resolution while lacking a useful view of the interaction. Moving the sensor or the body can expose an occluded region. Active perception explicitly connects sensing to such purposeful actions (Bajcsy et al., 2018). Physical form consequently affects both the execution of an action and the possibility of obtaining the feedback needed to guide it. Relevant capabilities include reaching an informative viewpoint, maintaining visibility during movement, and accessing the measurements required to verify the result.

Relating Task Requirements to Physical Arrangements

These mechanisms give the form-capability-task-constraint relationship a practical meaning. Form specifies the available physical means, capability describes the actions and performance those means support, task specifies the required effect, and constraints establish the conditions that must hold during execution. A useful comparison starts with requirements such as a working region, permissible contact force, positional tolerance, or completion time, and then examines whether a proposed arrangement can satisfy them together.

Table 8.1 organizes this comparison into five dimensions. It is an analytical synthesis of the mechanisms and performance-assessment approaches discussed here, rather than a standardized classification. The task determines which dimensions and criteria need evaluation.

Table 8.1: Connecting task requirements to physical form and evidence of capability. The dimensions provide a framework for comparison, not a single score of intelligence

Task requirement

Physical properties to examine

Evidence of a suitable match

Spatial access and motion

Dimensions, degrees of freedom, workspace, support and clearance

Required positions and orientations can be reached and the intended motion can be executed

Physical action and load

Tool or process interface, actuation, stiffness, friction and contact geometry

Required loads or process conditions are maintained within the specified tolerances

Observation and verification

Sensor placement, field of view, measurement access and calibration

Task-relevant states and outcomes can be measured with sufficient accuracy

Sustained operation

Energy supply, thermal limits, replenishment and available capacity

Performance can be maintained for the required duration or rate of work

Handover between operations

Physical connections, transfer paths, interface compatibility and shared resources

The output of one operation meets the input conditions of the next

The requirements interact. Extending a mechanism’s reach can alter the actuator effort needed for a motion. Adding mobility changes the relationship between the working tool, its support, and the surrounding space. This interaction motivates the joint design of morphology and control. Research on morphology-control co-design makes this relationship explicit by optimizing mechanical dimensions and actuator placement together with motion trajectories and forces, subject to physical and task constraints (ha2018). This connects design choices to the behavior needed for a specified task. It also explains why improvements in one hardware specification need to be evaluated in the context of the complete operation.

For a composite or system-level physical agent, the same reasoning extends to the physical connections between resources. Cyber-physical production research situates computational coordination within ongoing physical processes (monostori2016). Applying that perspective here, compatible connections between local operations are a prerequisite for system-level capability. A transfer must deliver an object in a state and location that the receiving resource can accept, and shared equipment must be available when required. These conditions must be combined with effective coordination and feedback to achieve the overall task. Communication enables coordination, while physical interfaces and material routes determine which coordinated operations can actually occur. The relevant scale of embodiment follows these dependencies and may take the form of one coherent body, several coupled modules, or a distributed arrangement of resources.

Comparing Forms Through Demonstrated Performance

Capability descriptions should distinguish the physical means available, the performance of the implemented agent, and the consistency of that performance. End-effector benchmarking, for example, measures grasp strength, cycle time, and repeatability separately because they answer different questions about application suitability (falco2020). At the task level, the relevant evidence may include success rate, completion time, error, and required human intervention. Hardware specifications and task results consequently provide complementary evidence when comparing forms.

The conditions of comparison must also be explicit. The YCB benchmarking framework records the task, environment and object states, hardware, prior information, procedure, and execution constraints (calli2015). Following this approach, alternative embodiments should be compared against stated outcome criteria and documented conditions, while allowing each an appropriate means of execution. Repeated trials establish how consistently the implemented system meets those criteria. They also make clear the operating range within which a capability has been demonstrated, rather than assuming that one successful demonstration establishes performance across settings.

The correspondence between form and application is therefore established through a traceable connection. Task requirements identify the necessary physical interactions, bodily organization makes those interactions possible, and evaluation establishes the conditions under which they are achieved. This provides a basis for selecting among entity-level, composite, and system-level forms, and for expressing the physical goals developed in the next section.

## 8.3 Physical Goal Representation and Task Grounding

A physical agent realizes intended changes in the world through actions constrained by its embodiment and environment. A request such as “store the sample safely” must therefore identify an acceptable outcome, admissible interactions, and evidence of completion. This connection applies both to individual robots and to system-level implementations of a physical agent acting through machines, instruments, and control interfaces.

Task realization involves specifying the required outcome, organizing available capabilities to achieve it, and using feedback to assess and revise execution. These functions are examined through the instruction “Place the sealed sample container in cabinet B, keep it upright, and close the cabinet.” The example connects goal semantics and task-relevant state representations to feasible behavior and observed results.

8.3.1 Physical Goal Representation and Semantic Grounding

From an Instruction to a Physical Specification

A goal specifies a desired outcome. A plan describes how available actions may achieve it. The container-storage goal should remain meaningful whether executed by a mobile manipulator or by a fixed manipulator supplied through a conveyor. Separating outcomes from procedures supports alternative plans and transfer across embodiments.

For exposition, a physical task can be summarized as

 $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{task}}=\left(\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{goal}},\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{exec}},\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{pref}},\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{verify}}\right),$ 

(8.8)

where $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{task}}$ is the task specification. Here $\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{goal}}$ specifies acceptable outcomes, $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{exec}}$ constrains execution, $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{pref}}$ expresses preferences among acceptable solutions, and $\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{verify}}$ specifies how outcomes and constraints are assessed. This is an organizing abstraction rather than a prescribed data structure. Reaching the storage region is an outcome. Preserving the seal is a constraint. Minimizing travel time is a preference. Checking placement and closure belongs to verification. Timing and resource requirements may be constraints or preferences, depending on the application.

Let $x_{t}$ denote the joint physical state of the physical agent and environment at decision index $t$ . In this example, $c_{\mathrm{cont}}$ labels the container and $B_{\mathrm{cab}}$ the cabinet. An illustrative Boolean terminal-goal predicate $g$ is

 $\displaystyle g(x_{T})={}$ 
 $\displaystyle\operatorname{Inside}(c_{\mathrm{cont}},B_{\mathrm{cab}})\land\operatorname{Supported}(c_{\mathrm{cont}})\land\operatorname{Released}(c_{\mathrm{cont}})$ 

(8.9)

 $\displaystyle\land\operatorname{Upright}(c_{\mathrm{cont}})\land\operatorname{Closed}(B_{\mathrm{cab}}),$ 

where $T$ is the terminal decision index, $x_{T}$ the corresponding physical state, and $\land$ logical conjunction. Evaluated on $x_{T}$ , the predicates require the container to be inside the intended storage region, physically supported, released by the manipulator, and upright. They also require the cabinet to be closed. Keeping the container upright throughout transport additionally constrains the intervening trajectory. Operational definitions must specify tolerances and evidence appropriate to the task and sensing capabilities. Support and release distinguish completed placement from holding the container at the target.

Complementary Representations and Task Abstractions

Goals may originate from language, images, demonstrations, geometric designs, or numerical process specifications. They may require a terminal state, sustained conditions, or repeated service. Symbolic descriptions express objects, relations, and logical requirements. Geometric representations specify poses, regions, and clearances. Physical variables describe forces, temperatures, or velocities. Temporal specifications distinguish eventual achievement from requirements that must persist throughout execution (kressgazit2009temporal). These descriptions serve different decisions within the same task. A target image communicates arrangement but may omit hidden contact conditions. A learning reward guides optimization but need not fully specify acceptable behavior.

Task-relevant abstractions connect these descriptions to observations. Object properties and relations indicate which conditions currently hold, while action models describe how those conditions may change. Such abstractions can be designed or proposed from language, video, and interaction records, then checked for consistency and against available data. A learned detector may assess whether a cabinet is open, while an action model associates opening with access to its interior. The representation provides an adjustable interface for reasoning, learning, and verification. It need not impose a fixed symbolic vocabulary or a particular architecture. Learning this interface must preserve the task’s specified requirements.

Grounding Entities and Conditions in the Current Scene

Semantic grounding identifies the intended container and cabinet and estimates their task-relevant properties and relations. Recognition alone does not establish that the cabinet is accessible or has sufficient storage space. Even a small observational difference, such as an open versus closed door, changes the conditions from which action must begin. Grounding therefore relates instruction semantics to the current scene and the agent’s capabilities.

Language and vision-language models can supply useful priors. SayCan combines language-based skill relevance with skill value estimates grounded in the robot’s situation (ichter2023saycan). VoxPoser constructs observation-linked spatial value maps to guide motion generation (huang2023voxposer). They illustrate different interfaces between semantic interpretation and physical behavior, each relying on appropriate perception and capability estimates. Figure 8.6 summarizes the grounding process. Action organization is developed in the next subsection.

Figure 8.6: Grounding an instruction in task-relevant objects, state conditions, constraints, and completion evidence. Observations and embodiment capabilities inform interpretation. Unresolved uncertainty may require further observation or clarification

Uncertainty and Evidence Requirements

Physical states are partially observed. The belief state $b_{t}(x)=p(x_{t}=x\mid o_{0:t},u_{0:t-1})$ represents the conditional probability mass or density of a candidate physical state $x$ at decision index $t$ . Here $p$ is the conditional state distribution, $o_{0:t}$ denotes observations from indices $0$ through $t$ , and $u_{0:t-1}$ denotes the executed control inputs over preceding transitions. $u_{t}$ is the control input implementing the selected action $a_{t}$ . This representation distinguishes measured information from inferred conditions and supports information-seeking actions (Kaelbling1998). Implementations may instead use confidence-tagged records, alternative hypotheses, or other uncertainty estimates.

If two containers match the instruction, further evidence may be needed to resolve their identity. An occluded cabinet interior may require inspection before placement. Clarification is appropriate when ambiguity materially changes the intended outcome or acceptable risk. Observation should resolve the uncertainty relevant to the next decision.

Verification requirements must reflect what can be established from evidence. A visually closed door does not establish latching without suitable observations. Conditions should therefore admit an “unknown” assessment when evidence is insufficient. The specification must identify both the required conditions and the evidence that would justify claiming their satisfaction.

8.3.2 Task Decomposition and Action Organization

A Functional Hierarchy from Goals to Control

Task realization connects decisions at different abstractions and timescales. A useful functional hierarchy is

 $\begin{gathered}\text{goal specification}\longrightarrow\text{subgoals and dependencies}\longrightarrow\text{skills}\\
\longrightarrow\text{motion or process references}\longrightarrow\text{control inputs}.\end{gathered}$ 

(8.10)

Upper levels determine desired outcomes and their dependencies. Intermediate levels select skills and parameters. Lower levels generate movement or process evolution. These are functional responsibilities. A learned policy may combine several levels, while a system-level physical agent may refine tasks into instrument commands rather than joint trajectories.

For the storage example, decomposition includes preparing access, acquiring and transporting the container, placing it, and closing the cabinet. The order depends on capability and resource availability. A single-gripper robot may need to open the cabinet before acquiring the container or use an intermediate support surface. An additional manipulator permits other arrangements. Decomposition therefore accounts for resources occupied by each action and conditions needed by subsequent actions.

Task Planning and Dependency Structure

Task planning uses action conditions and predicted effects to identify dependencies and construct plans, as exemplified by the Stanford Research Institute Problem Solver (STRIPS) (fikes1971strips). Hierarchical decomposition organizes recurring procedures into reusable task structures. The planning model should reflect the agent’s available skills and the current environment, so that task steps correspond to capabilities the agent can invoke.

A plan need not impose a total order. Access must precede insertion, and the manipulator must leave the door’s swept region before closure, whereas independent operations may be reordered or run concurrently when resources permit. Logically independent steps may still compete for the same manipulator or instrument. Conditional branches accommodate initially unknown states, such as whether the cabinet is open. The resulting structure separates persistent dependencies from ordering choices that vary with initial conditions and resources.

Coupling Task Planning with Physical Feasibility

Grasp choice, approach configuration, and placement pose affect which task sequences are feasible. A grasp may obstruct passage through the opening, or a placement may leave insufficient room for withdrawal. Task and motion planning (TAMP) addresses these interactions by coupling discrete action and contact choices with continuous configurations, grasps, and trajectories (garrett2021integrated).

The coupling is bidirectional. A task planner proposes actions and required conditions, while geometric and physical reasoning supplies feasible parameters or revises those choices. PDDLStream connects symbolic planning to black-box procedures that generate values satisfying continuous constraints (garrett2020pddlstream). Failure to find suitable parameters can prompt a different grasp, approach, or task sequence. These parameters must support the entire relevant interaction, including approach, contact, transport, and release, rather than merely reaching an isolated pose.

Relevant constraints extend beyond collision avoidance. Container transport requires stability and acceleration limits. Door manipulation involves contact and changing geometry. Manufacturing and laboratory workflows similarly couple operation ordering to machine availability, instrument access, and admissible process or sample states. These conditions must be represented where they affect planning. Geometric feasibility alone cannot capture them all. Figure 8.7 summarizes this organization.

Figure 8.7: Hierarchical action organization with downward task refinement and upward feasibility feedback. Geometric, dynamic, and resource constraints can revise higher-level choices within modular, learned, or hybrid implementations

Skills as Reusable Units of Interaction

Skills such as grasping, opening, docking, and measuring encapsulate temporally extended interactions. In the options framework, a skill comprises an initiation set, an internal policy, and a termination rule (sutton1999options):

 $\sigma_{k}^{\mathrm{opt}}=(\mathcal{I}_{k}^{\mathrm{init}},\pi_{k}^{\mathrm{skill}},\beta_{k}^{\mathrm{term}}),$ 

(8.11)

where $\sigma_{k}^{\mathrm{opt}}$ denotes skill $k$ in the skill library, $\mathcal{I}_{k}^{\mathrm{init}}$ is its set of admissible starting states, $\pi_{k}^{\mathrm{skill}}$ its internal action policy, and $\beta_{k}^{\mathrm{term}}$ its state-dependent termination probability in $[0,1]$ . Practical interfaces may expose parameters, expected effects, operating limits, and completion or failure statuses. Such interfaces support composition independently of whether a skill is programmed or learned.

Composition requires compatible boundary conditions. Grasping must leave the container suitable for transport. Placement must preserve access for withdrawal and closure. Skill quality includes its contribution to subsequent actions. Behavior trees organize conditions, skills, and alternative branches into a modular execution structure (ColledanchiseOgren2018), providing one way to assemble reusable capabilities into longer tasks.

Learning, Adaptation, and Hybrid Organization

Learning can acquire skills from demonstrations or interaction, estimate skill parameters, and support action selection. It can also be used to adapt a planner to a particular task domain and skill library. Learning a planner concerns the selection and organization of actions, whereas learning a skill concerns how an interaction is executed. The two can share experience while retaining distinct objectives. Such adaptation should preserve the relationship between proposed steps, available capabilities, and task constraints.

Generative policies offer expressive representations for skill execution. Diffusion Policy produces observation-conditioned action sequences with receding-horizon updates (chi2023diffusion). OpenVLA connects visual observations and language instructions to learned robotic actions (kim2024openvla). Their use in new settings depends on data coverage and compatibility with the agent’s embodiment and operating conditions. Adaptation may therefore involve updating selected components rather than redesigning the entire hierarchy.

Hybrid organization assigns complementary functions to planning and learned behavior. A planner can select subgoals and skills, while a learned policy handles contact-rich interaction. Code as Policies illustrates another interface by generating programs that compose perception and control functions (liang2023code). The allocation of functions should follow task demands and the evidence available for validating each component.

8.3.3 Closed-Loop Execution and Failure Recovery

Execution as Repeated State-Dependent Commitment

Execution tests a plan’s predictions against a changing world. At each decision point, the physical agent updates its state estimate and task context, then decides whether to continue, obtain information, adjust behavior, or replan. A compact representation is

 $\displaystyle b_{t+1}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\operatorname{Update}(b_{t},u_{t},o_{t+1}),$ 

(8.12)

 $\displaystyle d_{t+1}^{\mathrm{skill}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=\operatorname{Supervise}(b_{t+1},\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{task}},\zeta_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}}),$ 

where $t$ indexes decision steps, $b_{t}$ is the task-relevant belief state, $u_{t}$ is the control applied during step $t$ , and $o_{t+1}$ is the resulting observation. The function $\operatorname{Update}$ revises that belief, while $\operatorname{Supervise}$ selects the next supervisory decision $d_{t+1}^{\mathrm{skill}}$ using the task specification $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{task}}$ and execution context $\zeta_{t}^{\mathrm{exec}}$ . This context records the active skill, verified subgoals, and relevant constraint history. The decision may authorize continuation, information gathering, recovery, replanning, or termination. History matters because terminal observations cannot reveal every earlier constraint violation. If another actor closes the cabinet during transport, the remaining plan must accommodate the changed access condition.

Feedback operates at several timescales. Controllers regulate physical variables, skills assess progress and termination, and task-level supervision revises dependencies. Model predictive control repeatedly solves a finite-horizon problem and executes an initial portion before updating it (mayne2000constrained). Inner Monologue uses success feedback, scene descriptions, and human feedback to inform language-based task planning (huang2023inner). These levels provide complementary corrections. Timely control feedback regulates execution, while task supervision assesses its relevance to the goal.

Monitoring Effects and Diagnosing Discrepancies

Monitoring tests whether prerequisites remain valid, expected changes occur, constraints hold, and goals are achieved. Evidence may include images, joint states, contact measurements, instrument readouts, and elapsed time. Gripper closure does not establish acquisition, a placement pose does not establish support, and a door-close command does not establish closure. The relevant checks concern physical effects.

Diagnosis distinguishes semantic mistakes, state-estimation errors, infeasible plans, skill failures, and external changes. A small alignment error may be corrected locally. Persistent lack of progress may indicate a blocked mechanism or an incorrect condition estimate. Repeated discrepancies also warrant checking the state abstractions and action models used for planning. Execution records can support revisions to initiation conditions or effect predictions, which should be validated before reuse.

Monitoring itself is uncertain. Confirmation over time, complementary sensors, and explicit “unknown” assessments can reduce false alarms and missed detections. Confirmation must nevertheless remain compatible with timely protective action. Figure 8.8 relates these checks to subsequent decisions.

Figure 8.8: Observed effects update state estimates and execution context. Verified progress supports continuation. Discrepancies trigger diagnosis and recovery. Insufficient evidence prompts further observation. Protective monitoring can interrupt the loop independently of task planning

Recovery as Constrained Continuation

Recovery addresses the diagnosed cause while preserving progress that remains valid. Responses range from local correction and renewed observation to another grasp, repositioning, or task-level replanning. Each response starts from the current physical state. A failed placement may leave the container tilted or partially supported, so the conditions for retrying must be reassessed. Previously verified subgoals must also be rechecked when subsequent actions may have disturbed them.

Physical actions can consume resources or cause irreversible changes. Retries should therefore depend on remaining resources, acceptable risk, and evidence that another attempt can address the cause. If no admissible recovery exists, controlled termination or assistance may be required. Changing the destination or relaxing upright transport changes the task specification and requires authorization unless such alternatives were already permitted.

Safety and Bounded Autonomy

Protective mechanisms constrain commands and monitor operating limits independently of unrestricted task-level decisions. Control barrier functions provide one approach to enforcing safety-related state constraints under modeling and feasibility assumptions (Ames et al., 2019). Their guarantees depend on those assumptions, including valid state estimates and available corrective control. Safety requirements therefore need explicit physical conditions and appropriate protection.

Fallback behavior must suit the embodiment and situation. A loaded manipulator may need to maintain support. A moving platform may require controlled deceleration. The scope of autonomy should specify when task execution yields to protective control or an operator, as well as which actions may be initiated.

Execution Evidence and Broader Evaluation

Recorded observations, verified subgoals, constraint violations, and interventions preserve the evidence behind execution decisions. Chapter 11 develops their use in systematic task evaluation, capability comparison, and benchmarking. Here, verification supplies the evidence needed to continue, recover, or terminate the current task.

The connection between task specifications, capability-dependent plans, and execution evidence also underpins the coordination among multiple locally autonomous participants discussed next.

## 8.4 Multi-Agent Collaboration and Distributed Physical AI

Section 8.2.2 describes a system-level physical agent through its operational boundary. Distributed sensors, robots, equipment, and computing resources act toward a system objective, with measured outcomes informing subsequent interventions. This section examines the collaboration among multiple physical agent instances that retain local sensing, decision-making, and action capabilities. The distinction concerns the level at which agency and coordination are analyzed. System-level agency does not require every component to be autonomous, whereas multi-agent collaboration concerns the relationships among locally autonomous participants. A laboratory or production installation may therefore be a system-level physical agent as a whole and a multi-agent organization internally. Centralized task allocation is compatible with local agency. An instrument accessible through an application programming interface (API) that only executes commands can instead remain a supporting resource.

Distributed Physical AI denotes the collective ability of agents to combine observations, complementary capabilities, and coordinated actions across a shared physical environment (parker2007distributed; rizk2019cooperative; wu2025generativeEMAS). Coordination must reconcile local autonomy with collective commitments when decisions are coupled through space, time, resources, and the effects of physical action. Communication supports the exchange of observations and coordination information (zhou2023racer). Shared infrastructure and observed actions also inform coordination. Humans may contribute objectives, expertise, supervision, and intervention. Building on the individual-agent mechanisms in Sections 8.1 and 8.3, the following discussion focuses on the distribution of decision authority, inter-agent coordination, and the capabilities and limitations of the resulting teams.

8.4.1 Organizational Architectures for Distributed Physical AI

Consider a partially collapsed tunnel in which a heterogeneous robot team searches for trapped workers and delivers supplies. An aerial vehicle surveys accessible openings. A quadruped traverses rubble and carries relay equipment. A mobile manipulator transports supplies and removes small obstacles where feasible. Their tasks depend on shared access routes, communication coverage, and complementary capabilities. Organizing the team requires specifying where coordination state, computation, and decision authority reside (yan2013survey). Four representative architectures are centralized, hierarchical, decentralized, and hybrid.

Centralized Organization

A central node aggregates reported state and performs team-level allocation, resource coordination, or joint planning. It may combine automated planning with human supervision. In the tunnel example, it assigns search, relay, and delivery responsibilities using the available map and robot status. Agents retain local execution authority within these assignments. The center’s decisions depend on the coverage and freshness of the information it receives.

Hierarchical Organization

Coordination responsibilities are divided across mission, team, and agent levels. A mission coordinator sets rescue priorities. Team coordinators organize operations within assigned regions. Agents execute their responsibilities locally. Decisions that affect several teams are escalated, while regional details remain within the relevant team. Effective hierarchy requires explicit interfaces between levels and sufficient information to recognize cross-team dependencies.

Decentralized Organization

Agents coordinate without a single team-level decision center, using local observations and information from other agents. After discovering a trapped worker, an explorer can request assistance. Candidates exchange capabilities and costs and agree on responsibility. Coordination may use negotiation, consensus, or distributed optimization. Agents must track the validity of agreements and revise or suspend them when information or connectivity changes.

Hybrid Organization

Different functions or operating conditions use different arrangements. A team may build maps cooperatively while a mission center assigns priorities, or negotiate passage access locally while following centralized scheduling. If communication is interrupted, agents may continue within agreed limits. Such changes require rules for transferring authority and reconciling outstanding commitments when coordination is restored. Figure 8.9 summarizes the four forms.

Figure 8.9: Four organizational architectures for distributed Physical AI, comprising centralized, hierarchical, decentralized, and hybrid

Table 8.2 compares their typical tradeoffs. Actual performance depends on task coupling, network conditions, and the implementation of coordination protocols.
