These architectures describe runtime coordination authority. When coordination policies are learned, centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) describes a separate choice about information available during learning and deployment (Amato, 2024). Training may use global state or centralized value estimates, while deployed policies act on locally available information, potentially including communicated messages. CTDE alone does not determine the team’s runtime allocation or coordination architecture.

8.4.2 Coordination Mechanisms for Distributed Physical AI

Organizational architecture determines where coordination decisions are made. Coordination mechanisms determine how agents align their objectives, information, and actions. The central issue is how decisions made by different agents remain compatible when they depend on shared resources or on one another’s behavior.

Eight interdependent mechanisms organize this discussion, namely establishing shared goals, capability and role modeling, task allocation, collaborative perception, shared state, joint planning, conflict resolution, and execution and reallocation (rizk2019cooperative; wu2025generativeEMAS). They operate concurrently and revise one another as conditions change. Their ordering in the figure is schematic. Figure 8.10 summarizes their relationships.

Figure 8.10: Eight interdependent mechanisms of multi-agent collaboration. The mechanisms may operate concurrently, exchanging information and revising decisions as task conditions and agent capabilities change

Establishing Shared Goals

Agents need a common understanding of overall objectives, priorities, completion criteria, and collaboration protocols (kannan2024smart; obata2024lip). Their assigned subgoals can differ while contributing to the same outcome. In tunnel rescue, searching for trapped people, maintaining communication, and delivering supplies must be coordinated according to agreed priorities. A human decision to prioritize confirmation of vital status over delivery should propagate to affected agents, so that their local objectives remain consistent with the revised mission.

Capability and Role Modeling

Coordination requires descriptions of what each agent can currently contribute. These combine configuration-dependent capabilities, such as locomotion, sensing range, and payload, with changing conditions, including battery energy, communication connectivity, equipment, and health (chen2025emos). Roles express how those capabilities serve the mission. A quadruped carrying relay equipment may maintain communication rather than search, while another takes over exploration. Distinguishing capability from role allows responsibilities to change without assuming that robots of the same category are interchangeable.

Task Allocation

Allocation assigns tasks to agents or temporary groups, accounting for capability matching, dependencies, energy, risk, and completion time (gerkey2004allocation). A delivery task may require both a carrier and a relay, making the assignment a joint choice rather than two independent selections. Centralized optimization, auctions, negotiation, and distributed optimization offer different ways to establish these assignments. Allocation also determines which agents remain available for subsequent demands. Minimizing the immediate travel distance can therefore conflict with preserving scarce capabilities for later tasks.

Collaborative Perception

Collaborative perception combines complementary observations and coordinates sensing effort (xu2024d2slam). An aerial vehicle can survey the tunnel structure, while ground robots inspect occluded regions and assess traversability. Agents can divide observation responsibilities according to uncertainty and information value, reducing unnecessary duplication. Time synchronization, coordinate transformations, and target association support observation fusion across viewpoints (hu2022where2comm). Fusion should preserve relevant uncertainty and identify conflicting observations.

Shared State

Shared state maintains information needed for joint decisions, including maps, targets, agent locations, resource occupancy, and task progress. Unlike collaborative perception, which concerns acquiring and combining observations, this mechanism concerns distributing and updating the resulting operational information. State may reside centrally or in local copies. Limited bandwidth favors task-relevant abstractions over continuous transmission of raw sensor data (chang2023hydra). Agents need sufficiently current and consistent information about the resources and dependencies on which their decisions rely. Identical knowledge of the entire environment is unnecessary. The required consistency depends on how tightly the agents’ actions are coupled.

Joint Planning

Joint planning addresses dependencies among agents’ actions in space, time, and resource use. Two robots sharing a narrow passage must coordinate traversal order. A delivery robot may depend on a relay reaching its coverage position first. Plans can be generated centrally or reconciled through iterative negotiation (mandi2024roco). Coordination can concentrate on strongly coupled near-term actions while leaving independent actions locally planned. This limits the need to fix every agent’s full trajectory while retaining explicit commitments where another agent’s progress depends on them.

Conflict Resolution

Conflicts concern spatial occupancy, schedules, power, bandwidth, or incompatible task assignments. They may arise from competing objectives, outdated information, or deviations from agreed plans. Priorities, reservations, negotiation, and replanning can resolve resource contention. Protective intervention may be required for imminent physical conflicts (zhang2025gcbf+; lee2025merry). Resolution must propagate changes to affected commitments so that other agents can revise their dependent actions.

Execution and Reallocation

Execution reports reveal whether assignments and inter-agent commitments remain viable. Agents share progress, exceptions, and remaining resources when these affect collaborators. A blocked route, lost connection, or unavailable executor may require transferring a task or reorganizing a group (liu2025coherent). Reallocation should account for work already completed, current resource reservations, and dependencies on other agents. Updating roles and shared state alongside the assignment prevents a replacement agent from duplicating completed work or continuing under obsolete assumptions.

8.4.3 Open Problems and Trends in Distributed Physical AI

Coordination can extend the coverage, throughput, and range of tasks achievable by a team. These gains depend on how sensing, task dependencies, resources, and failures are managed across its members.

Collective Capabilities

Complementary sensing and coordinated revisits extend spatial coverage and the frequency of environmental updates (francos2023role). Independent subtasks can proceed concurrently, while ordered operations can be pipelined. Under the idealized assumption of equal per-participant execution rates, let $W_{\mathrm{work}}$ denote total workload measured as the time required by one physical agent, $N_{\mathrm{agent}}\geq 1$ the number of participating instances, $L_{\mathrm{crit}}$ the duration of the critical path induced by task dependencies, and $T$ the team’s completion duration. In this bound, $W_{\mathrm{work}}$ , $L_{\mathrm{crit}}$ , and $T$ use the same time unit, and

 $T\geq\max\left(\frac{W_{\mathrm{work}}}{N_{\mathrm{agent}}},L_{\mathrm{crit}}\right).$ 

(8.13)

This lower bound exposes the limits of parallelism (brent1974parallel). Physical contention and coordination overhead can further restrict the benefit of additional agents. Heterogeneous capabilities also expand the feasible task set. Aerial reconnaissance, ground access, manipulation, and infrastructure support can form task chains unavailable to any member alone. Alternative executors and routes can preserve service after failures (bossens2022resilient), but resilience requires substitutes for critical tools, capabilities, and communication links. Realizing these gains raises the following open problems.

Communication, Information Freshness, and Consistency

Communication range changes with robot motion and environmental conditions, while bandwidth, delay, and packet loss constrain information exchange (gielis2022critical). Collaboration requires deciding which observations, task commitments, and resource states to share, and when their expected benefit justifies transmission. Agents must also track whether information remains valid when making coupled decisions. A delayed passage-occupancy update can be more consequential than an incomplete distant map. Maintaining sufficient consistency requires task-specific priorities and rules for conflicting or outdated updates. Because motion changes network topology, communication and physical planning may need to be optimized jointly.

Cross-Embodiment Knowledge and Semantic Interfaces

Different observation spaces, action spaces, and dynamics prevent direct transfer of many policies between embodiments. Cross-embodiment learning provides useful experience (openx2024), but collaboration additionally requires alignment of object identities, task states, capability descriptions, and expected skill outcomes. An aerial vehicle and a mobile manipulator may interpret the same destination while requiring different access conditions and control policies. Shared interfaces should expose these differences so that task assignment and composition remain meaningful. Compatible task semantics must therefore support coordination while preserving embodiment-specific actions and requirements.

Collaborative Safety and Runtime Assurance

Individually acceptable actions can conflict through shared space, resource occupancy, or coupled task dependencies. Updating one learned policy can also change the operating conditions encountered by other agents (garg2024SafeMultiRobot). Assurance must therefore address joint behavior, including the validity of reservations and commitments when communication is delayed or an agent fails. Local protective responses need to respect team interactions. Stopping one robot may obstruct another or interrupt a jointly supported load. Coordination protocols should specify how such responses are communicated and how affected commitments are revised, including the respective authority of agents, coordinators, and human supervisors.

System-Level Evaluation

Embodied multi-agent benchmarks provide a basis for assessing collaborative task performance (chang2025partnr). Evaluation should also measure the benefit and cost of coordination, including team completion time, duplicated work, workload distribution, communication demand, inter-agent conflicts, and recovery after member failures. Tests should vary team size, embodiment combinations, connectivity, and capability availability. Comparisons with suitable single-agent or independently operating baselines help identify gains attributable to coordination. Recovery results should distinguish loss of a replaceable member from loss of a unique capability. These protocols reveal whether performance reflects effective distributed collaboration and whether it persists as the team changes.

The following directions seek to address these limitations.

Shared World Models

Shared world models extend exchanged state records toward predictions of how one agent’s actions affect other agents and the environment (zhang2025combo). For example, moving a relay robot changes the communication conditions under which other agents can proceed. The challenge is to coordinate local models with different spatial resolutions and prediction horizons without requiring a single central model. Their predictions should expose coupled constraints and support comparison of alternative joint actions. Learning these interactions from team experience could improve planning when capability, resource, and communication dependencies cannot be handled independently.

Multi-Agent Foundation Models

Learned coordination components, including collaborative perception (blumenkamp2025covis), suggest a route toward broader models of team behavior. Models trained across tasks and team configurations could acquire priors about capability differences, task dependencies, and other agents’ likely actions. Transfer to new teams would require representations that accommodate variable membership and embodiment-specific capabilities. Such models should provide reusable coordination knowledge for allocation and joint planning, assessed through physical team performance.

Self-Organizing Collaboration in Open Environments

Long-running teams must accommodate agents joining or leaving, newly arising tasks, changing connectivity, and human intervention. Self-organization can form temporary teams, select coordinators, and revise roles according to available capabilities (zhu2024self). Such changes must preserve task ownership and outstanding commitments across organizational transitions. The resulting direction is adaptive coordination that maintains core services while membership and architecture evolve, extending distributed Physical AI beyond fixed teams and predefined operating conditions.

## 9 Hardware and Systems

At last, every Physical AI program ultimately depends on an actual machine to execute proposed actions in the real world. Therefore, this chapter discusses the actual hardware and system through five questions: what physical interactions a body’s morphology can support (Section 9.1), how sensing and actuation close the feedback loop (Section 9.2), where computation can run without missing the time to act (Section 9.3), how software organizes these capabilities (Section 9.4), and how they remain reliable through repeated use and updates (Section 9.5). For the ease of understanding, there are several case studies: a simple component case in Section 9.2, a dexterous-hand case study in Section 9.6 to illustrate how hardware shapes interaction, and a more complex humanoid case that stitches all components together in Section 9.7.

## 9.1 Hardware and Embodiment Taxonomy for Physical AI

A robot opening an unfamiliar drawer must do more than recognize a handle. It must reach it, establish a grip, and discover how the drawer responds to a pull. Resistance may mean that the drawer is heavy, jammed, or still locked. Continuing the same movement could damage the handle. The robot needs evidence that distinguishes these possibilities and a body capable of changing its action. This connection between physical interaction, observation, and correction is central to Physical AI.

9.1.1 From Hardware Components to Embodiment

Cameras, motors, encoders, transmissions, and processors are hardware components. Their arrangement gives a robot its embodiment, comprising its shape and mass distribution, available movements, sensing locations, and ways of making contact. The platform adds power, computation, communication, and the controllers that regulate those movements. Together, these correspond to the broader notion of the embodiment $B_{\mathrm{emb}}$ in Section 8.1. A change anywhere in this system can change what an action means. Replacing a rigid fingertip with a soft pad alters both the grip and the measurements produced during contact.

The drawer example makes these dependencies visible. An external camera may locate the handle but lose sight of it behind the gripper. Joint encoders describe arm movement, while force or tactile measurements can reveal resistance or slip. A small initial pull then serves two purposes by moving the drawer and testing the robot’s prediction about its motion. The outcome can justify continuing, changing direction, or releasing the handle. Such exploratory actions require suitable force limits and feedback. Trial and error is useful only when the body can tolerate the trial and the system can interpret its outcome.

The same mechanics constrain possible corrections. Reach does not guarantee that an arm can sustain a load, and a grip that supports lifting may fail when twisting a cap. Grasp analysis captures this distinction through the forces and torques a set of contacts can resist (ferrari1992grasp). A mobile robot may reach the handle yet lack room to reposition or sufficient support to resist the pull. Planning must therefore consider how to remain controllable after the first movement, as well as whether that movement is possible.

Useful feedback must also arrive before the opportunity to correct is lost. A detailed image delivered after an object has slipped provides evidence for later learning but cannot rescue that grasp. Sensor placement and task-state observability (Section 9.2.3) must be considered together with control delay and actuator response (Section 9.2.2). Better inference can extract more from available signals. Sustained performance still depends on obtaining the right evidence and acting within the body’s limits.

Table 9.1: Common embodiments and the feedback their tasks require.

Table 9.1 compares embodiments through the interactions they support. A liquid handler is an example of a fixed instrument. An arm on a wheeled base is a mobile manipulator. A biped with arms belongs to the legged and humanoid category. These categories describe different physical advantages, rather than successive levels of intelligence. Suitability depends on the task and on what each body can measure while performing it.

Autonomous laboratories illustrate why capability often comes from a combination of bodies. Instruments provide controlled processes and measurements, while arms or mobile robots transfer samples and operate equipment (burger2020; szymanski2023alab; dai2024). The resulting system must track whether each transfer and operation actually succeeded. These interfaces connect embodiment to the system-level agents in Section 8.2.

9.1.2 Embodied Model-Hardware Co-Design and Multi-Embodiment Adaptation

Model-hardware co-design starts from a coupled choice. The body determines which states can be observed and which actions can be realized, while the model and controller determine how much of that capability is used. A camera added to expose a contact changes the policy’s inputs and training data. A softer fingertip changes contact dynamics and may reduce the precision the policy must achieve. A larger model can improve inference yet lose that advantage if its delay exceeds the time available to correct a slip. These choices must therefore be evaluated as a system, against the same physical task and operating limits.

A model influences the world through a control interface. It may request a tool movement, joint positions, or forces. Local controllers translate those targets into actuator behavior. An embodiment adapter handles the robot’s command conventions, coordinate frames, and limits. Figure 9.1 shows three arrangements of these responsibilities. All require a return path from the physical outcome to the next decision.

Figure 9.1: Models reach the world through different control arrangements.
A modular hierarchy exposes intermediate estimates and plans. An
end-to-end policy learns a more direct observation-to-action mapping. An agent calls skills and checks their outcomes. Local feedback supports
timely motion and contact regulation in each arrangement

A modular pipeline estimates an object’s pose, plans a motion, and tracks it with a controller. Its intermediate quantities make some failures easier to locate. The object may have been misidentified, the path may have been infeasible, or contact may have differed from the prediction. An end-to-end vision-language-action policy learns a more direct mapping from images and instructions to actions, as in OpenVLA (kim2024openvla). It can exploit visual cues without requiring an explicit object pose at every step, but its output still has the units and physical consequences defined by the controller. Without incorporating new observations, neither arrangement can revise its task-level response to an unexpected event.

An agentic hierarchy adds task-level decisions, such as selecting a tool or deciding to retry. Systems that compose skills from language illustrate this separation (ichter2023saycan; liang2023code). During drawer opening, a fast controller may limit contact force while the higher-level system decides whether resistance calls for another strategy. A completion message from a skill is useful only insofar as it is supported by evidence about the drawer. Execution checking in Section 9.4 and reliability assessment in Section 9.5 develop this requirement further.

Transfer to another robot changes the relationship between observation and action. Knowledge that a drawer translates along a guide may remain useful. Camera appearance, reachable poses, finger contacts, motor limits, and the forces generated by a command may all change. Expressing a desired movement relative to the tool can reduce dependence on a laboratory’s coordinates, but does not make the new robot mechanically equivalent. The receiving body must still support the intended motion and contact.

Training across robots can reveal useful shared regularities. The Open X-Embodiment study demonstrates benefits from combining data across robots (openx2024). Octo supports adaptation to new observation and action spaces through fine-tuning (octo2024), while HPT combines a shared model with embodiment-specific input and output modules (wang2024hpt). These approaches organize what can be shared and what must be adapted. Their physical value must be established on the receiving robot, including its contact behavior and recovery from errors (Section 6.4). Success on familiar images alone does not establish that the transferred commands produce the intended forces.

Hardware design can make this adaptation easier. ALOHA’s matched leader and follower arms give demonstrations a direct relationship to robot joint movements (zhao2023). UMI coordinates a handheld gripper, camera geometry, and action representation to support transfer from portable demonstrations (chi2024umi_ch6) (Section 9.2.1). A compliant fingertip can also tolerate small placement errors, while tactile sensing reveals how the contact develops. Joint optimization can extend to the mechanism itself. caoChen2021HardwarePolicy optimize mechanical and control parameters together and build an underactuated hand from the resulting design. Such optimization still depends on whether the modeled contacts and actuator response describe the physical machine.

For the drawer task, a useful co-design cycle begins by identifying the failed correction. If the handle disappears behind the fingers, changing the viewpoint or adding touch may resolve missing evidence. If resistance is measured but force cannot be reduced promptly, transmission, compliance, and controller bandwidth become the relevant design variables. If the state is observed and the action is feasible but the policy chooses poorly, additional training may be the appropriate change. Each candidate requires data collected or transformed for its own observation and action interface, followed by evaluation on held-out physical trials. Comparing an unchanged policy across bodies measures transfer. Allowing each body the same adaptation budget tests the quality of the co-designed system. Reporting both prevents a favorable match to one policy from being mistaken for a universal hardware advantage. The final comparison is cost per valid output, including collection, computation, interventions, and maintenance, as developed below and in Section 9.5.

9.1.3 Task-Oriented Embodiment Selection, Validation, and Evaluation

Figure 9.2: Embodiment selection develops through increasingly realistic
evidence. Task analysis and specifications identify candidates. Operation-level tests, complete workflows, and continued use reveal
whether the proposed body and controller meet the requirements

Selecting a robot begins with a complete task, including the measurements that establish success. Reach and payload can exclude an unsuitable arm, but do not establish whether it can thread a cap without damaging a vial. Figure 9.2 moves from requirements to tests of individual operations, complete workflows, and continued use. Failures can motivate a change in the policy, sensing, mechanics, or protocol.

Candidates should meet the same requirements for workspace, load, precision, contact force, time, and recovery. Among feasible options, the cost per valid output introduced in Section 1.5 gives a useful comparison. Divide the fully allocated average cost of an attempt by the measured fraction that produces a valid result. The cost includes failed attempts, human interventions, and recovery. Early estimates remain provisional until tested under the intended workload.

A laboratory preparing metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), porous materials built from metal-containing units and organic linkers (furukawa2013mof), provides a concrete example. A synthesis workflow may involve opening vials, transferring solids and liquids, heating, separation, and loading instruments (tom2024sdl). Successful motion is insufficient. The sample must retain its identity, composition, and integrity. A balance may verify a transfer that the arm’s camera and encoders cannot establish by themselves.

Consider opening a sealed vial, dispensing a specified quantity, and seating the vial in an instrument. Table 9.2 compares four possible configurations through the questions these operations raise. Their exact arms, grippers, sensors, and controller settings must be specified before testing. Additional fingers or lower transmission ratios change the possibilities for interaction. Their practical benefit depends on how well that interaction is observed and controlled.

Table 9.2: Questions for evaluating four candidate configurations in a
MOF workflow. These are mechanisms to test, not measured rankings.
The first three configurations use parallel grippers

Tests should use the same protocol, object batches, starting-condition distribution, and definition of success. Repeated trials distinguish a reliable advantage from a fortunate grasp (Section 9.5.1). Recording observations, commands, and measured outcomes helps explain failures by distinguishing whether the robot lacked information, chose an unsuitable action, or could not physically realize it. The diagnosis then guides a concrete change and another test.

The preferred solution may combine specialized machines, provided their transfers and coordination remain reliable. Continued operation must then test calibration drift, worn contact surfaces, thermal limits, and recovery after interruptions. This closes the design loop. Experience changes the model and, where necessary, the body that supplies its evidence and carries out its decisions.

## 9.2 Sensors, Actuators, and Intelligent Materials

To lift a glass vial, a robot must first find it, then recognize contact, and finally hold it firmly without breaking it. A camera helps with the approach. Joint encoders report how the fingers and arm have moved. Touch and force measurements reveal what happens when the fingers meet the glass. Electric motors supply the motion, but their response depends on the transmission, the controller, and the load. Physical AI emerges through this interaction. The robot acts, measures the consequences, and adjusts its behavior. A model can infer an object’s properties from experience only when the hardware exposes useful evidence and can carry out the resulting decisions.

The relevant hardware therefore extends from visible cameras and grippers to the electronics inside a joint, including encoders, current sensors, power transistors, and local control processors. These components determine both what a learning system can observe and how its actions affect the world. Figure 9.3 connects the measurements collected during learning to the feedback used during execution. Section 3.2 discusses sensor physics and fusion more generally. Here the emphasis is on their consequences for robot learning and physical interaction.

Figure 9.3: Measurements connect learning to physical action. Calibrated,
synchronized observations become training trajectories. During execution,
the policy supplies targets, while local controllers use fresh body and
contact measurements to drive the actuators. The commanded movement and
the movement actually achieved need not be identical

9.2.1 Acquiring Physical Experience for Learning

Before a robot can learn from a recorded movement, its sensors must agree on where and when that movement occurred. Camera calibration relates image coordinates to the robot. Joint positions and a kinematic model locate the tool. For a wrist camera, hand-eye calibration identifies the fixed relationship between camera and gripper (zhang2000flexible; tsai1989handeye; park1994handeye). Timing is equally important. A 20 ms mismatch for a tool moving at 0.5 m/s corresponds to 1 cm of displacement. Hardware triggering, synchronized clocks, and measured delays help align images, joint states, and forces. A receipt timestamp is not necessarily the acquisition time. These details can determine whether a demonstration teaches the robot to react to contact or, mistakenly, to a state that occurred afterward.

A useful trajectory records observations, measured body state, and the commands sent to the controller together. It also preserves their units, coordinate frames, calibration, and control mode. A command to advance the tool by a centimeter means something different from a command to exert a force. Even identical position targets can produce different contact behavior under different controller gains. Changes to the camera, gripper, or controller consequently change the learning problem, not just the equipment inventory. If actions are normalized numbers or relative tool motions, deployment must preserve the same scaling and coordinate conventions when converting them into controller targets.

Different collection methods preserve different parts of this physical experience. Robot teleoperation, as in ALOHA and DROID (zhao2023; khazatsky2024droid), records demonstrations through a robot’s own body and controller. Handheld devices such as UMI make collection more portable by combining a gripper with a camera and motion estimation (chi2024umi_ch6). Their trajectories can describe real contact, but the human holding the device does not have the robot’s inertia, reach, or torque limits. Human video supplies broader examples of activities and object use, while motion-tracking gloves and exoskeletons add hand or arm kinematics (grauman2022ego4d; wang2024dexcap; fang2024airexo).

Surface electromyography (sEMG) adds a different kind of observation. Electrodes on the skin record the electrical activity associated with muscle recruitment (farina2014emg). This is the modality denoted EMG (electromyography) in Figure 9.4. It can reveal motor intent when movement is slight or visually occluded, making it a useful complement to video during demonstration collection (ctrllabs2025emg). Its interpretation nevertheless depends on the person, posture, and electrode placement. Neither visible motion nor muscle electrical activity directly specifies the contact forces a robot must reproduce. Recordings should therefore synchronize EMG with kinematics and video, preserve the electrode configuration and calibration, and include force or tactile measurements when contact-force supervision is required. These sources complement robot recordings rather than serving as mechanically interchangeable substitutes.

The data pyramid in Figure 9.4, motivated by GR00T N1 (bjorck2025gr00t), places abundant human video below synthetic and robot-free demonstrations, with robot execution at the top. Its distinction is the kind of evidence available, as well as its volume. Simulation can supply complete robot actions while approximating friction and contact. Human recordings contain real interactions without the robot’s execution dynamics. A weighted training objective retains these differences through

 $\min_{\theta}\sum_{j}w_{j}\,\mathbb{E}_{\zeta_{\mathrm{sample}}\sim\mathcal{D}_{j}}[\mathcal{L}_{j}(\theta;\zeta_{\mathrm{sample}})],\qquad w_{j}\geq 0,\quad\sum_{j}w_{j}=1.$ 

(9.1)

Figure 9.4: Sources of experience for Physical AI. Human video
offers broad coverage. Simulation and handheld devices address different
parts of the gap between observation and execution. Robot recordings
capture the target body’s behavior. The levels describe complementary
evidence, not a universal ranking of dataset quality. EMG denotes
electromyography. It records muscle activity rather than robot contact
forces

Here each source $\mathcal{D}_{j}$ supports its own learning objective $\mathcal{L}_{j}$ . Robot actions can supervise action prediction, whereas human video can support visual prediction or activity understanding. Reweighting cannot turn an unmeasured quantity into direct supervision (Section 4.1).

9.2.2 Closing the Loop from Measurements to Motion

When a finger touches a hard surface, force may rise before a large model has processed another image. The robot must therefore respond at several timescales. A learned policy can choose a grasp, a movement, or a desired compliance. A local controller follows that target. The motor drive regulates electrical current. Fast joint feedback remains useful even when the policy is learned end to end. Playing a predicted sequence of actions rapidly is also different from reacting rapidly to new evidence.

The electronics make this distinction concrete. A drive switches power transistors to apply voltages to the motor windings. Current-sensing circuits and analog-to-digital converters report the resulting currents. An encoder or other rotor-position sensor tells the controller how the rotor is oriented. The drive adjusts these voltages to produce the desired torque. Filtering suppresses noise but introduces delay, and electrical switching can contaminate small sensor signals. Consequently, sensing, computation, and power delivery must be designed together (ti2025humanoidcurrent; kollmorgen2020servo).

The total delay includes sensing, communication, inference, and actuation. In a linearized feedback loop, a delay $\Delta$ adds a phase lag $\omega\Delta$ at angular frequency $\omega$ . The controller increasingly acts on an outdated state. This explains why contact regulation usually stays close to the hardware, while slower reasoning can run elsewhere (Section 9.3). Each interface must specify reference frames, units, timestamps, control modes, and limits. The return path should report the measured motion and available forces or currents, together with faults and temperature. Without this feedback, a learning system can confuse a saturated actuator or a delayed measurement with an incorrect plan.

9.2.3 Task-State Observability: Cameras, Encoders, and Contact Sensing

The camera is often the most recognizable sensor on a physically intelligent robot. An RGB camera measures light and provides the appearance cues used to recognize objects, interpret a scene, and connect language to action. Depth cameras add geometric information. Stereo systems compare two viewpoints. Structured-light systems observe a projected pattern. Time-of-flight systems estimate distance from the travel time or phase of returned light. These approaches have different sensitivities to distance, illumination, and surface appearance. An integrated RGB-D sensor makes color and depth available together, as illustrated by the RealSense architecture (keselman2017intel). However, transparent glass, shiny metal, and low-texture surfaces can leave missing or misleading depth. ClearGrasp addresses one such problem by inferring geometry for transparent objects (sajjan2020cleargrasp). Inferred geometry still requires validation when an action can damage the object.

Placement determines what the camera can contribute. A head or external camera sees the overall workspace but may lose the contact behind the hand. A wrist camera follows the approach and reveals small features, although its view moves with the arm and may become obstructed at the final instant. Exposure, motion blur, field of view, and timing can matter more than the advertised pixel count. For a vision-language-action model, moving the camera also changes the relationship between an image and a successful action. Calibration aligns geometry. Training must still account for the change in appearance.

While cameras look outward, encoders measure the body’s own movement. A rotary encoder converts shaft rotation into an electrical position reading. Optical encoders read a patterned disk. Magnetic encoders sense the orientation of a magnet. Inductive designs use electromagnetic coupling. Incremental encoders count changes and generally need a reference after startup, whereas absolute encoders identify position within their specified measurement range. More digital counts do not by themselves guarantee more accurate position. Mounting error, alignment, mechanical deformation, and calibration also matter (heidenhain2023dualencoders). Velocities are often estimated from successive position measurements, which introduces a trade-off between noise and delay.

A motor encoder and a joint-output encoder observe different shafts. With an ideal rigid gearbox, motor angle divided by the reduction ratio gives joint angle. Real transmissions have friction, lost motion, and elastic deformation. An output encoder can reveal movement errors that the motor encoder misses, particularly during reversals and under load. Joint measurements and the robot’s geometry then estimate the tool’s pose, but do not directly reveal whether an object is slipping between the fingers. On a walking or mobile robot, an IMU adds angular velocity and specific force from gyroscopes and accelerometers. Combined with joint and contact measurements, it helps estimate body motion. Integration alone accumulates error, and gravity must be accounted for when interpreting acceleration. Figure 9.5 presents examples of cameras, encoders, and current-sensing shunts.

Figure 9.5: Different measurements support different parts of an action.
A camera observes the scene, an encoder reads shaft angle, and a shunt
converts electrical current into a small voltage. The opened encoder
shows its coded disk. These examples illustrate principles rather than

CC BY-SA 3.0

Touch becomes especially valuable once the hand hides the contact. In a vision-based tactile sensor, a small camera looks inward at a soft surface rather than outward at the scene. Pressing an object against that surface changes its shape and, in some designs, moves printed markers. GelSight uses controlled illumination to recover fine contact geometry. DIGIT packages a related optical approach into a compact fingertip (yuan2017gelsight; lambeta2020digit). Figure 9.6 shows why optics and material design are inseparable here. The camera observes the deformation of a purpose-built skin. Images can support estimates of local shape, shear deformation, and incipient slip. They are not direct force maps. Recovering force requires calibration or a learned model of the skin and its loading.

Figure 9.6: Optical touch converts contact into an image of a deformable
surface. The reflective coating and illumination allow surface shape to
be recovered independently of the contacted object’s optical appearance.
Reproduced from Figure 2 of yuan2017gelsight, under
CC BY 4.0.
The illustration describes the sensing principle, not the packaging of
every modern fingertip

This information changes what a policy can learn. A gripper can tighten when the contact patch starts to slip, or adjust the direction of insertion when an edge presses unevenly. A compliant skin may also wear, creep, or change with temperature, shifting the relationship between image and force. Other tactile technologies measure changes in resistance, capacitance, or magnetic field. ReSkin, for example, uses a deformable magnetic skin (bhirangi2021reskin). The choice is therefore between useful measurements, spatial coverage, durability, and processing demands, rather than between a sensor that “has touch” and one that does not.

Force sensing complements this local picture. A six-axis wrist force-torque sensor measures three force components and three moments transmitted through the wrist. Strain gauges detect tiny deformations of an elastic structure. Calibrated combinations of their signals recover the load. The reading includes the tool’s weight and inertial loading, which must be compensated when estimating contact force (ATI Industrial Automation, n.d.). A joint torque sensor measures twisting load about one joint axis, often on the output side of the transmission. Its location matters. A sensor upstream of a lossy gearbox does not measure the same load as one downstream. Multiple joint measurements can support estimates of external contact, but these depend on the robot’s dynamics and contact assumptions. Specialized joint force-torque sensing has even supported touch localization over a robot’s body (iskandar2024intrinsictouch). An ordinary single-axis torque sensor does not automatically provide that capability.

Current sensors offer another source of evidence already needed by the drive. A small shunt resistor produces a voltage proportional to current. Magnetic current sensors infer it from the surrounding magnetic field. For a suitable motor model, torque-producing current estimates motor torque. It does not directly measure force at the fingertips. Friction, acceleration, gravity, and transmission losses contribute to the same signal. Current remains valuable for control, overload detection, and learning about loading, provided these ambiguities are recognized (ti2025humanoidcurrent; wensing2017proprioceptive).

The purpose of combining sensors is to resolve uncertainty that matters for an action. In the Jenga experiments of fazeli2019seefeelact, vision locates blocks and force measurements during interaction help infer how they can move. The contact supplied information unavailable from an image alone. A similar principle applies when opening a drawer or seating a connector. The robot must distinguish free motion from resistance, then decide whether to continue, change direction, or retreat. This is task-state observability in practical terms. The most useful sensor is the one that reveals the distinction in time to change the action, at a precision appropriate to the task.

9.2.4 Electric Motors and the Mechanics of Actuation

An actuator converts supplied energy into mechanical work. Electric motors are a practical default for many robot arms, grippers, mobile bases, and legged platforms because electrical power is readily distributed, motor drives are mature, and feedback can regulate motion and torque. These advantages depend on scale and duty. Hydraulic, pneumatic, and material-based actuators remain useful where their force capacity or mechanical behavior better fits the task.

Inside an electromagnetic motor, current in windings interacts with a magnetic field to turn a rotor. The stationary part is the stator. Sustained rotation requires the winding currents to change as the rotor turns, a process called commutation. In a brushed direct-current (DC) motor, physical brushes and a segmented commutator perform this switching. Such motors are straightforward to drive and remain useful in compact or inexpensive mechanisms, but the brushes wear and create electrical noise. A coreless brushed motor removes the iron core from the rotating winding, reducing rotor inertia and cogging. It still needs careful thermal design. “Coreless” describes construction, rather than a separate feedback control method (faulhaberDCtechnical).

Brushless permanent-magnet motors place commutation in the electronics. The rotor carries magnets and the stator carries windings. The drive energizes the phases according to rotor position. Eliminating brushes removes a wear mechanism and enables efficient, controllable drives, at the cost of more complex electronics. The labels brushless direct-current (BLDC) motor and permanent-magnet synchronous motor (PMSM) describe closely related motor families. In a common convention, BLDC designs are associated with trapezoidal back-electromotive force and block commutation, whereas PMSMs are associated with sinusoidal waveforms. Products and control methods overlap, so the label alone is insufficient to predict torque quality. Field-oriented control regulates current components relative to the rotor field, allowing smooth torque control over a useful operating range (ti2020bldcpmsm; ti2025humanoidcurrent).

Packaging creates further options within these families. An inrunner places the rotor inside the stator. An outrunner rotates an outer shell, often providing a larger torque-producing radius. A frameless motor supplies the rotor and stator for integration into the robot’s own bearings and housing. A hollow center can accommodate cables, while different winding and rotor designs trade speed, torque, inertia, cooling, and space. These are engineering choices rather than a universal ranking. An easily accelerated rotor can benefit a responsive finger, whereas a large joint must also carry sustained load and reject heat. Figure 9.7 illustrates motor construction and feedback integration.

Figure 9.7: Motor construction and feedback integration. (a) A lightweight
winding removed from a coreless DC motor. (b) Stationary windings of a
brushless motor with its rotor removed. (c) A stepper motor, whose motion
follows commanded magnetic alignments. (d) A hobby servo showing the
motor, reduction gears, and output-position sensor. The servo is an
integrated feedback system, not a separate electromagnetic motor family.
Photos: (a) Avsararas,
(b) DnaX,
and (d) Jstapko,
CC BY-SA 3.0;
(c) Dolly1010,
CC BY 3.0

A stepper motor also uses electronically switched windings, but is designed to advance through discrete angular equilibria. Counting commanded steps can provide simple positioning in lightly loaded fixtures, dispensers, and laboratory mechanisms. The count is a command history, however, not proof of actual position. An overloaded open-loop stepper can lose steps. Microstepping makes the commanded motion smoother without guaranteeing correspondingly finer absolute accuracy. Closed-loop steppers add feedback, and the best choice depends on speed, load, efficiency, and required disturbance response (orientalmotorStepperBasics). For Physical AI, this distinction affects the data as well as the motion. A dataset should not silently treat requested steps as measured joint states.

The word servo describes feedback-controlled operation, not a unique electromagnetic motor type. A servo system combines a motor, a drive, a position or velocity sensor, and a controller. It may also contain a gearbox (kollmorgen2020servo). A small hobby servo and an industrial brushless servo share this principle while differing greatly in precision, torque control, response, and access to measurements. For a learning system, the interface matters. Position-only commands offer different possibilities from current or torque commands, and a nominally identical target can behave differently under another drive’s limits and gains.

The transmission then converts motor motion into joint motion. Planetary, strain-wave, and cycloidal gearboxes are transmission mechanisms, not types of motor. They allow a relatively fast motor to turn a slower joint with greater torque. Direct drive couples the motor to the load without reduction. Quasi-direct drive combines a high-torque motor with a modest reduction. Neither approach is free of trade-offs. Removing reduction requires the motor itself to supply more torque, often increasing its size or thermal burden. Under an idealized constant-efficiency approximation,

 $\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\simeq\eta_{\mathrm{gear}}N_{\mathrm{gear}}k_{\mathrm{t}}i_{\mathrm{q}},\qquad\omega_{\mathrm{j}}=\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{m}}}{N_{\mathrm{gear}}},\qquad I_{\mathrm{refl}}=N_{\mathrm{gear}}^{2}I_{\mathrm{m}},$ 

(9.2)

where $N_{\mathrm{gear}}$ is motor speed divided by joint speed, $\eta_{\mathrm{gear}}$ is transmission efficiency, and $k_{\mathrm{t}}i_{\mathrm{q}}$ is electromagnetic torque in an appropriate torque-current convention. For a simple brushed motor, armature current replaces $i_{\mathrm{q}}$ . The last relation shows why a large reduction can make the rotor’s inertia strongly felt at the joint. Actual output also depends on acceleration, friction, elasticity, and direction of power flow, so this equation is not an external-force measurement.

These effects become apparent when a foot lands or a hand meets an unexpected obstacle. A transmission that can be driven readily from the joint side is called backdrivable. Low reduction and low friction can improve this response and make motor current more informative about joint loading, as explored in the MIT Cheetah’s proprioceptive actuators (wensing2017proprioceptive). High-reduction joints can instead use output torque sensing and feedback to yield under external load, as in the DLR lightweight robot (Albu-Schäffer et al., 2007). A series elastic actuator places a spring in the force path. Its calibrated deflection estimates transmitted torque and cushions disturbances, while introducing additional dynamics that the controller must handle (pratt1995).

Peak torque is only part of the operating envelope. Winding heat grows approximately with current squared times resistance, so a joint may produce a large torque briefly but be unable to sustain it. At higher speed, the motor’s back-electromotive force and the supply voltage limit the current the drive can establish. A policy that repeatedly asks for unavailable torque experiences delayed or incomplete movement. Temperature-dependent limits can make an identical command behave differently later in a task. Training and evaluation should therefore include the relevant torque-speed limits, thermal duty, friction, and control delay, rather than treating an actuator as an unlimited source of prescribed motion (maxon2024continuous; gealy2019quasidirect). In the ANYmal experiments of hwangbo2019, a learned actuator model helps bridge this gap by representing the real response between commands and torque. The result shows why actuator and controller dynamics must be accounted for when transferring behavior from simulation to the physical robot.

For contact, the controller must also decide how strongly to resist position error. Impedance control makes a robot respond like a chosen spring and damper (Hogan1985). A softer response can absorb a small alignment error. A stiffer response may be needed to support a load. In a simple, slowly varying contact model,

 $F_{\mathrm{contact}}\approx k_{\mathrm{eff}}e_{\mathrm{contact}},\qquad k_{\mathrm{eff}}=\left(\frac{1}{k_{\mathrm{r}}}+\frac{1}{k_{\mathrm{e}}}\right)^{-1},$ 

(9.3)

where $e_{\mathrm{contact}}$ is the position error along the contact direction, and the robot and environment stiffnesses, $k_{\mathrm{r}}$ and $k_{\mathrm{e}}$ , act in series. An effective stiffness of $10^{5}$  N/m turns a 1 mm error into about 100 N. Lower stiffness reduces this quasi-static force, although collision severity also depends on mass and speed. Learning can select compliance together with motion (martinmartin2019vices; hou2025acp). Fast feedback must still realize that choice within the actuator’s limits. A position-controlled robot can instead use force feedback to adjust its position target, an approach called admittance control. This is how a learned intention to “insert gently” acquires a measurable physical meaning.

9.2.5 Fluid Power, Compliance, and Functional Materials

Electric motors do not cover every useful form of actuation. Hydraulic systems use pressurized liquid to move pistons or hydraulic motors. Large force can be generated in a compact actuator, making fluid power attractive for demanding loads, but the complete machine also needs pumps, valves, seals, and fluid routing. Valve dynamics, leakage, friction, and fluid temperature affect the response a controller must learn or model. Electrically powered pumps and local hydraulic circuits can combine electrical distribution with hydraulic force generation. “Hydraulic” does not necessarily mean a remote central pump.

Pneumatic systems use compressed gas. Air can inflate a soft finger that wraps around an object with relatively simple mechanics, but its compressibility, flow restrictions, and material hysteresis complicate precise positioning. Pressure is useful feedback, yet does not uniquely determine the fingertip force when shape and contact change. Both fluid technologies therefore need sensing appropriate to their dynamics, rather than relying on pressure commands alone (rus2015; laschi2016soft).

Figure 9.8: Functional materials become useful to physical intelligence
through measured interaction. (a) In a conceptual HASEL cross-section, electrostatic attraction redistributes liquid and deforms the pouch.
(b) Self-sensing contributes to feedback, while task measurements
establish whether the interaction achieved its purpose
 (Acome et al., 2018; ly2021hasel). Shapes are illustrative, and the
diagram does not imply that capacitance alone measures contact force

Functional materials offer an emerging route to combining actuation, sensing, and compliance within the body. They remain under active investigation alongside the motor-driven platforms discussed above. Thermal and electrochemical artificial muscles offer distinctive combinations of strain, force, and response time (mirvakili2018muscles), but their value for physical intelligence depends on the interaction they enable. Hydraulically amplified self-healing electrostatic (HASEL) actuators, for example, use electrostatic forces to redistribute a liquid dielectric inside flexible pouches, producing motion. Changes in capacitance also reveal deformation (Acome et al., 2018). By integrating driving electronics, capacitive self-sensing, and computation, ly2021hasel demonstrate feedback control of a Peano-HASEL-powered arm. The actuator therefore supplies both mechanical work and a measurement that can guide the next action.

Figure 9.8 connects this component behavior to task feedback. A compliant finger may accommodate an object’s shape mechanically, while its deformation provides evidence for adjusting the grasp. Yet compliance alone does not reveal whether the object is secure, slipping, or being compressed excessively. That distinction requires calibrated sensing and a controller whose response remains useful under changing loads. High-voltage electronics, nonlinear mechanics, material drift, and fatigue must be considered together with control bandwidth and replacement needs. Progress should therefore be measured through repeatable task performance, including sensing, power delivery, and maintenance, as well as the properties of an isolated material sample.

Even without an unusual actuator, the body’s structure can simplify control. A compliant insertion fixture can guide a misaligned peg, and an underactuated hand can conform to an object using fewer motors than moving joints (whitney1982rcc; dollar2010sdm). This is a practical form of sharing the work between mechanics and computation. The same softness that accommodates contact can make shape harder to estimate. Electronic skins and learned sensing models help address that problem (shih2020electronicskins). For physical intelligence, the useful question is which part of an interaction the body can handle reliably, and which changing circumstances still require observation, inference, and a new action.

The following cases examine a hand and a humanoid as complete sensing and actuation systems (Figure 9.9). Section 9.6 then compares three dexterous hands at the level of actuation, tactile sensing, and demonstration hardware.

Figure 9.9: Product hardware and the feedback needed for Physical AI.
(a) RobotEra XHAND 1 links visual and optional tactile observations to
commanded finger motion and renewed contact measurements.
(b) Gallant on Unitree G1 links 3D terrain perception to learned joint
