9.2.6 Case Study: RobotEra XHAND 1

RobotEra’s XHAND 1 illustrates the measurement-motion loop at the level of one component. Its host sends joint targets, controller gains, and torque limits. The hand returns joint positions, motor-current information, temperature, and error status, together with contact measurements when the optional fingertip sensors are fitted (robotera2026xhandmanual; robotera2024xhandprotocol). Section 9.6.3 compares the mechanism, loading capacity, and communication timing with other hands. The question here is how these signals support correction during a grasp.

Vision can locate an object before contact, while joint feedback records how the fingers move toward it. Once a finger meets the object, target position alone no longer describes the interaction. Controller gains, effort limits, and transmission mechanics determine the load. Tactile measurements, when available, can reveal changes in contact that require a revised finger target. Motor current supplies useful actuator telemetry but does not locate that contact. The host must align these observations with the commands that produce them and respond while the grasp is still recoverable.

The same boundary applies to transferred demonstrations. ManipTrans uses Realman arms and Inspire hands, fitting 12 simulated hand coordinates to six hardware coordinates before smoothing and replay (li2025maniptrans). Applying such motion to XHAND requires a new mapping through its joint axes, ranges, and contact surfaces. Matching a pose vector is only one step. The deployed hand must sustain the intended contact under load. Section 9.6.4 examines how demonstration hardware and collection interfaces address this correspondence.

9.2.7 Case Study: Unitree G1 and Perceptive Locomotion

Gallant illustrates how a humanoid’s useful workspace depends on the sensing and control system built around its body (ben2025gallant). The task is to move a 29-degree-of-freedom Unitree G1 through stairs, gaps, narrow passages and overhead obstacles. Two torso-mounted LiDARs provide complementary views of the surrounding geometry. A head-mounted Livox Mid360 supports localization. A voxel representation preserves the vertical structure that a ground-height map discards, allowing the controller to account for both footholds and body clearance.

The software connects point-cloud processing, proprioception and learned control on an onboard NVIDIA Orin NX. A convolutional encoder extracts spatial features, which are combined with the robot state to generate joint commands. Sensor placement and the representation used during training must therefore remain consistent at deployment. Changing the visible space changes the information available for each action. In the initial deployment, LiDAR traffic and robot-state messages share a software pipeline and incur substantial communication delay. Restricting transmitted point clouds and using shared memory reduce this overhead (ben2025gallant). These changes concern the age of the feedback reaching the controller, rather than the size of the policy alone.

The real-robot evaluation uses 15 trials per terrain and compares the full system with perception and training ablations (ben2025gallant). This provides evidence for the integrated locomotion loop within the tested environments. On approach to a low ceiling, observed clearance and current body configuration must jointly determine posture. A correct map delivered too late cannot support that correction. The useful capability belongs to the complete perception-action loop.

## 9.3 Device-Edge-Cloud Collaboration and Real-Time Communication

9.3.1 Distributed Architecture

The purpose of Physical AI is to enable intelligent agents, under finite computational resources, to interact continuously with the physical environment through perception, decision-making, and action and to accomplish a given physical objective in real time, effectively and safely. Resources in computation, energy, storage, communication, and control cycles must be allocated across perception, state estimation, prediction, planning, policy generation, and execution control at different nodes. These functions have different temporal scales, resource requirements, and spatial distances. This creates a central challenge for Physical AI. High-level computation tends to be low-frequency, computationally intensive, and spatially remote, whereas physical perception and interaction must be high-frequency, computationally limited, physically proximate, and temporally continuous.

Figure 9.10: The challenge of physical AI and device-edge-cloud collaborative
Architecture

The device-edge-cloud distributed architecture provides a way to balance these requirements (Figure 9.10). It decomposes a unified perception-decision-action loop according to distinct timescales, spatial scopes, and responsibility boundaries (lee2026middleware), organized around validity deadlines, distributed networks, and responsibility horizons. The device connects directly to the body, sensors, and actuators. It handles the fastest state perception, servo control, contact responses, and safety constraints so that the minimum safety-critical loop does not depend on the network. The edge operates at the physical site with greater computational resources. It performs multimodal fusion, local world modeling, policy inference, trajectory generation, action-chunk generation, and coordination of multiple bodies, transforming site-level state into executable commitments that remain valid. The cloud operates over longer timescales across tasks, devices, and sites. It supports goal decomposition, experimental design, long-term memory, experience accumulation, model updates, and cross-site orchestration. Computation can migrate according to task requirements, but physical responsibility cannot migrate arbitrarily. The closer a responsibility is to a physical consequence, the more it must be assumed by a trusted node close to the body.

Accordingly, device-edge-cloud collaboration is better understood in terms of migratable responsibility boundaries rather than as a fixed three-layer computational hierarchy. When real-time communication is healthy, prediction, planning, and policy generation can migrate toward the edge or cloud in exchange for stronger model capabilities. When real-time communication becomes abnormal, responsibility must contract toward the physical object and switch to validated degraded modes.

Furthermore, device-edge-cloud collaboration exchanges node state and commitments with physical semantics. At least three categories of state should be distinguished. Physical state includes pose, joint state, force, contact, limits, environmental conditions, and execution mode. It must carry sampling time, coordinate frame, units, and effective range. Action state includes action chunks, task phase, resource occupancy, execution progress, and version information. It must distinguish among “generated,” “sent,” “received,” “acknowledged,” and “physically acted upon.” Evidence state includes credit, measurement identity, experimental conditions, execution confirmation, anomalies, and recovery records. It determines whether a result is sufficiently grounded to be treated as a fact by subsequent reasoning. Confusing these categories produces characteristic failures in Physical AI closed loops, including treating a plan as a fact, transmission as execution, or an old observation as the current state.

The following sections address four questions within this Physical AI framework. What information must the device maintain, and what must it guarantee? How does the edge transform site-level state into valid action? How does the cloud provide low-frequency, high-level intelligence? How can real-time communication ensure that information transferred across these responsibility boundaries remains physically valid?

9.3.2 Device-Side Computing

The device is the computational and control node closest to the point of physical action in the Physical AI loop. It typically includes sensor interfaces, actuator interfaces, body-state estimation, safety control, local policies, and an adaptation layer for real-time communication with higher-level systems (ortega-kral_rio_2026). Device-side computing must ensure that the physical system does not enter an unacceptable state simply because it is waiting for remote information, even under the worst real-time communication conditions. Hosting the largest model is secondary to this requirement.

The device must first establish a time-aligned multimodal state. Cameras, encoders, force sensors, tactile sensors, and motor feedback do not inherently share the same sampling instant. A visual-frame timestamp may correspond to exposure or acquisition time. Joint state may originate from a controller cycle. Force signals may contain additional delay introduced by filtering, transmission, and mechanical response. Device state should therefore be represented by states carrying timestamps, source identities, safety attributes, spatial coordinate frames, units, and quality indicators, rather than simply by a collection of “current values.” Only then can the system determine whether different trusted observations describe the same contact event and, when a sensor is missing, represent the state as “unknown” rather than incorrectly reusing the previous frame.

The device must also maintain a local execution state machine. The state machine should at least distinguish standby, preparation, execution, constrained execution, pause, fault, and recovery, while specifying which actuator actions are permitted in each state. Its purpose is to make device-native safety enforcement independent of interpretation by a high-level model. A policy model may recommend “continue grasping,” but if a joint is approaching its limit, force exceeds a threshold, or the real-time communication lease has expired, the device-side state machine must be able to reject the action. Policy output and execution permission are distinct. The policy proposes an action, whereas the safety layer determines whether it is currently allowed.

For real-time control, the device typically uses a fixed-period or event-triggered local closed loop. The real-time communication layer provides references, targets, parameters, or action chunks. It should not require every servo cycle to wait for a remote system to generate the next joint command. This prevents network jitter from entering the innermost control loop and turns network failure into an explicit operating state rather than an accident handled only after it occurs. Based on the remaining validity of an action chunk, local state, and safety rules, the controller can continue execution, execute in a degraded mode, perform a controlled stop, or stop immediately, thereby implementing device-native safety.

Device computation is also constrained by physical considerations. Larger models imply higher memory consumption, power draw, thermal load, and computational latency, and may also alter the weight distribution, power capacity, and onboard compute budget of a mobile system. Model size therefore cannot be discussed independently of the control cycle. For tasks requiring rapid contact feedback, a more complex but slower model may be unsuitable for direct participation in the execution loop. It can instead support slower action generation, candidate selection, or anomaly interpretation, while the fast loop remains the responsibility of lightweight models, controllers, and safety logic.

9.3.3 Edge-Side Computing

Edge-side computing provides site-level computation and coordination. It is closer to the physical process than the cloud while offering substantially more computational and coordination capability than the device. Edge nodes are well suited to policy inference, local world models, trajectory generation, resource coordination, and multimodal fusion (community2026xpolicylab). These computations, however, have physical control value only when their outputs still correspond to the current state of the site.

In this architecture, an action chunk serves as a time-bounded execution commitment with explicit semantics. An action chunk should include, at minimum, the target device or body identity, reference time, validity interval, sequence number, control units, execution mode, and necessary constraints. The device can then determine whether the action still belongs to the current task, whether it has expired, and whether it has been superseded by a newer version. The key metric for an edge closed loop is not average inference time, but the end-to-end interval between the observation reference time and the instant at which the action begins to take effect. This interval must be shorter than the validity deadline permitted by the physical action, rather than merely satisfying a requirement that model inference itself be fast enough. Loss of an action chunk must not be interpreted by default as “continue executing the previous chunk,” because doing so hides communication failure inside the control state. A more appropriate execution rule uses a lease. When the lease expires without a new valid commitment, the device enters a predefined safe state.

The edge should also keep the world model decoupled from the controller. A world model may predict “what might happen if this grasp continues,” but that prediction does not thereby acquire direct control authority. Its output can condition action generation, candidate-action selection, or risk estimation, while final execution must still pass through the device-control interface and safety state machine. This allows independent checks before execution and lets the world model be upgraded independently.

In site-level distributed collaboration, the edge is better suited to maintaining resource semantics than to replicating all internal device data. For example, when multiple robots compete for the same tool, the edge needs information about tool occupancy, reservation expiry, task priority, and current execution phase. It does not need to continuously aggregate high-frequency joint data from every robot. Resource state can be encoded using leases, version numbers, or monotonic sequence numbers, making “who owns the resource” a state that can be checked rather than a conclusion inferred from whichever message arrives last.

9.3.4 Cloud-Side Agents

Cloud-based agents operate on the longest time scale and are suited to processing information across experiments, devices, and sites. They can maintain long-term memory, compare historical results, generate scientific hypotheses, plan resources, and select subsequent tasks, but should not directly assume millisecond-scale contact control. Communication between the cloud and the physical site therefore primarily concerns task state and evidence state, rather than the next joint command.

The cloud must distinguish plan, request, confirmation, and fact. A plan describes what is intended to happen. A request specifies what the site is asked to execute. A confirmation indicates that the site has accepted the request. A fact originates from an identified, timestamped physical measurement. These four concepts cannot substitute for one another. For example, when the cloud generates a task to “close the valve,” this does not mean that the valve has closed. Even if the actuator reports “completed,” sensor evidence may still be required to confirm the final physical state. Only states supported by site-level measurements should enter the evidence set used for subsequent experimental reasoning.

Accordingly, communication between cloud and site is better implemented through event-driven state synchronization than through continuous replication of all raw signals. High-frequency data can be aggregated, compressed, or selectively uploaded on site. The cloud receives task-relevant measurements, summaries, anomalies, and evidence. For experiments that must be reproducible, uploaded records must also carry identities for samples, devices, experimental conditions, and software versions. Otherwise, historical results become difficult to interpret reliably.

When the cloud becomes unavailable, an action that has already started should not be extended indefinitely while waiting for a cloud response. The site should complete, pause, or stop according to device- and edge-level state. After recovery, the cloud should first re-read site-level facts and only then select the next action. In particular, “the last transmission succeeded” must never be interpreted as “the experiment has completed.”

9.3.5 Real-Time Communication

The central metric for real-time communication in Physical AI is the physical validity of information when it arrives relative to the physical process, rather than throughput alone. Average latency, average bandwidth, and average packet-loss rate are therefore insufficient to characterize a physical closed loop. At minimum, one must also consider latency bounds, jitter, queueing time, observation age, action validity, reordering, duplication, and the duration of disconnection (sajid2026embodied).

A simple serial end-to-end real-time constraint (diao2025task) can be written as

 $T_{\mathrm{e2e}}=T_{\mathrm{sensor}}+T_{\mathrm{encoder}}+T_{\mathrm{uplink}}+T_{\mathrm{compute}}+T_{\mathrm{downlink}}+T_{\mathrm{decoder}}+T_{\mathrm{actuator}}.$ 

(9.4)

The terms correspond, in order, to the stages of one remote closed loop, namely on-device sensing, observation encoding, uplink transport, computation at the edge or in the cloud, downlink transport, command decoding, and the onset of actuation. For one observation and its resulting action, the stage intervals cover sensing start to actuation onset without gaps or overlaps, including any queueing time. Their sum is $T_{\mathrm{e2e}}$ , with stage boundaries specified and timestamps mapped to a common clock domain. $T_{\mathrm{deadline}}$ is not an arbitrary parameter chosen by the real-time communication system, but a deadline determined by the physical process, and $T_{\mathrm{e2e}}$ must be strictly less than it. Contact, balance, and high-speed motion may require deadlines close to the control cycle, whereas experimental steps and resource scheduling may tolerate delays of seconds, minutes, or even longer. A distributed physical AI can therefore contain multiple real-time classes simultaneously. A single “real-time/non-real-time” label cannot adequately describe all of its communication.

In device-edge-cloud collaboration, asynchronous execution and queueing affect which observation an action uses. The age of information (AoI) (yates2021aoi) complements end-to-end latency by measuring information freshness. At an evaluation time, standard AoI is the interval since generation of the freshest state update available at the receiver. The observation age of an action measures the interval from generation of the observation actually used for that action to the action’s execution. Both age calculations use timestamps mapped to a common clock domain. For the same update stream and receiver, the two ages coincide at action execution if the action uses the freshest available update. The action’s observation age is greater if it uses an older update. These quantities should not be conflated with the simple serial latency estimate above. A backlog of action chunks can make nominal network latency appear normal while delaying execution and increasing the age of the observation used by the current action, potentially beyond its validity period. For real-time action generation, skipping queued observations that are no longer useful to the current control computation can prevent queue buildup. Older observations may still be retained for state estimation, sensor fusion, or historical analysis. For example, a model requiring only 5 ms for inference can still produce an unusable action if its input waits 100 ms in a queue. Conversely, a slower model may be entirely acceptable for second-scale task planning.

The action side requires complementary execution rules. An action prefix that has already begun execution generally cannot be arbitrarily rolled back, whereas an unexecuted suffix can be regenerated according to new observations. This distinction avoids excessive action oscillation while allowing new information to modify future behavior. When an action chunk expires, the system should stop extending the commitment rather than repeatedly copying the last action.

Real-time communication must also handle semantic loss. Undetected message loss can leave the receiver with an incorrect view of task or safety state. Losing a frame used only for visualization may be harmless, whereas silently losing an event indicating that a device has entered a safe state could cause the cloud to schedule the next experiment incorrectly. Communication protocols must therefore distinguish discardable information from information that requires acknowledgment, and provide the latter with confirmation, sequence numbers, timeouts, and idempotent semantics (zhang2024middleware; kluner2025automotive; chovet2024middleware; liang2023zenoh).

In multi-body collaboration, real-time communication should likewise not force all bodies to share a single high-frequency state. When two robots compete for the same tool, the edge must make tool-occupancy and release events visible before a conflict occurs. If occupancy information arrives late, its effect is equivalent to having no information. Force feedback within a body should remain in a local closed loop, because elevating it to an inter-body network only increases real-time communication latency and the risk of failure.

A real-time communication system with explicit responsibility boundaries should provide at least four capabilities, including timestamping, state versioning, validity control, and explicit fault representation. Timestamping identifies when a state was observed, versioning identifies the plan or policy that produced it, and validity control determines whether it remains usable. Explicit fault representation identifies who is responsible for entering the safe state when the information is no longer usable. Together, these capabilities establish state and responsibility semantics for maintaining the Physical AI closed loop in addition to transporting messages.

9.3.6 Self-Driving Laboratories

A self-driving laboratory (SDL) provides a validation setting for device-edge-cloud collaboration (gao2025unilabos). A typical dry/wet experimental SDL simultaneously contains millisecond-scale device control, second-scale experimental operations, and minute-to-hour-scale scientific decision-making. Instruments and robots must execute rapidly. The site must continuously maintain the state of samples, devices, and the environment, while higher-level scientific-discovery agents typically operate in a relatively predefined experimental world, running a “hypothesis, execution, measurement, and next selection” loop. The objectives, workflow, instruments, and basic interpretive framework for measurements are specified before an experimental campaign begins, and the system primarily optimizes parameters and actions within those predefined boundaries.

An open-governance architecture for SDLs emphasizes a transition from closed-loop optimization in a predefined world to open-world scientific discovery. This motivates designing the InternLab platform (li2026internlab) to advance Physical AI from a single-laboratory closed loop to a governable capability network across laboratories and institutions.

InternLab’s device-edge-cloud distributed architecture organizes physical capabilities into a governed network without centralizing all laboratories into a single cloud. Scientific agents can use it to discover and compose experimental capabilities dynamically from nodes across the devices, sites, and cloud systems of multiple laboratories and institutions. Its three mutually coupled layers are Physical Intelligence & Distributed Network (the capability layer), Lab OS Runtime (the execution and orchestration runtime connecting the capability and governance layers), and Native Governance (the governance foundation).

The Capabilities Network Layer transforms “equipment owned by a laboratory” into “capabilities callable by a network.” Robotic manipulation, scientific instruments, analytical models, and experimental skills are no longer merely private components within a site. They can be described as capabilities with explicit applicability conditions. The Capability Graph describes which nodes can provide which capabilities under which conditions. Scheduling & Routing selects qualified nodes according to sample state, temporal constraints, instrument availability, and governance conditions. The Composition Engine combines multiple capabilities serially or in parallel into an experimental route.

The Lab OS Runtime Layer transforms continuously changing scientific intent into executable physical actions and brings the resulting outcomes back into the scientific loop. Its core can be abstracted into four runtime functions, namely Task Routing, Live State, Authorization Checks, and Trace Return. Task Routing delivers tasks or action chunks to bodies, instruments, or sites with the required capabilities, rather than requiring every servo cycle to wait for a remote command. Live State maintains site state with timestamps, coordinate frames, and validity intervals, enabling higher-level decisions to determine whether observations remain fresh. Authorization Checks verify the necessary governance prerequisites before an action enters the physical system. Trace Return brings execution results, anomalies, and recovery information back into the next round of scientific reasoning.

The Native Governance Layer is the foundation that enables InternLab to move from a conventional automation network to an open experimental network. InternLab explicitly contains at least five inseparable conditions, including Permission, Safety, Calibration, Provenance, and Credit. Permission specifies who may invoke a capability, for what purpose, over which sample scope, and within which risk boundary. Safety is not a local property of a single action, but an end-to-end property spanning hardware, environmental monitoring, action validation, and fail-safe recovery. Calibration determines whether an instrument or sensor is currently in a measurement state that can be trusted. Provenance records sample identity, protocol version, data source, and operational chain so that cross-site evidence can be audited and reproduced. Credit preserves attribution for contributions across institutions. Most importantly, the design goal is not merely “post hoc auditing,” but governance-native execution. Governance conditions are part of the interface when a capability is defined and invoked, and they propagate together with the execution context. When any prerequisite fails, the capability should be rejected, degraded, re-authorized, or escalated to human handling.

The two InternLab pilot deployments (li2026internlab) demonstrate that the device-edge-cloud collaboration and responsibility model extends to an open spatial scale. The local safety loop at the device, site-level state and resource coordination at the edge, and long-horizon scientific reasoning in the cloud therefore do not disappear when collaboration becomes cross-site. They become embedded within a network of capability discovery, task routing, governance checks, and evidence return. The evolution from SDL to the InternLab design extends Physical AI from a single, predefined, closed experimental loop to an open-world loop that spans bodies, sites, and institutions and supports re-planning, re-composition, and governance-native execution. This makes device-edge-cloud collaboration and real-time communication operational infrastructure for open-world, distributed Physical AI.

## 9.4 Software Stacks and Development Infrastructure

A robot carrying a vial cannot wait for a language model to finish reasoning before responding to a slipping grasp. Nor does a completed arm trajectory establish that the vial reached the correct rack. These two observations define the software problem. Physical regulation must continue at the rate required by the body, while task execution must remain accountable to measured outcomes. Software connects these timescales through interfaces that specify what a component may command, what evidence it consumes, and what happens when that evidence or the component itself becomes unavailable.

Section 9.3 establishes where computation can run across the device, edge, and cloud. This section examines the software boundaries that make that distribution workable. The architecture comprises nested feedback loops, hardware and data interfaces, a runtime for controllers and learned policies, and a task execution framework. This chapter uses Embodied Intelligence Harness as its organizing term for the last of these. It brings together established mechanisms for skill composition, state management, execution monitoring, and recovery. The term denotes their integration for this chapter rather than a new middleware standard.

9.4.1 Layered Software Architecture and Physical Interaction Loops

Robotics software separates perception, estimation, planning, and control because these functions have different computational and physical requirements. Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) provides a widely used framework for composing such components through explicit interfaces (macenski2022robot). Learning changes what can be implemented inside a component, and foundation models expand how tasks can be specified and decomposed. Neither change removes the need to assign ownership of state, control authority, and failure responses. A hierarchy is useful only if its feedback paths and failure boundaries are equally explicit.

Figure 9.11 distinguishes three loops. The task loop interprets instructions, selects skills, checks their applicability, and evaluates their effects. It can revise a plan when a rack is occupied or an object’s identity is uncertain. The local control loop regulates motion or contact using measurements available on the device. Its execution period follows the plant dynamics and the controller design. The protection path detects conditions requiring intervention and can inhibit or limit actuation within its specified response time. It may use drive electronics, a separate controller, or other independently provisioned hardware. These functions can exchange evidence without sharing a single execution path.

Figure 9.11: Nested feedback loops with distinct control authority. Task proposals pass through the Harness and a skill interface before reaching local execution. Sensor feedback closes the control loop directly on the device. A separate protection path can inhibit actuation. Dashed paths carry perception evidence and executor status to the Harness. Protection-event reporting to the supervisor is omitted for clarity. Intervention uses the local path

The task loop admits a request such as “transfer vial A to slot B” while the local controller processes encoder samples and motor updates. At admission, the executor assigns a skill instance a lease, which grants authority to issue task commands until a deadline on the executor’s monotonic clock. Each command or action chunk also has an expiry determined by its intended execution interval and the validity of its observations. The executor applies task commands only while both the lease and the command remain valid. A new policy output cannot renew the lease. An admitted segment must fit within this joint interval. The executor begins its preconfigured fallback no later than expiry, allowing for detection and switching delay. That fallback has separate local authority and a specified completion or holding limit.

Crash, stall, and network partition exercise this boundary differently. A crashed Harness stops renewing its lease. A stalled task monitor must also stop renewal, even if a separate heartbeat thread is alive. Renewal follows a completed monitoring cycle with valid evidence. A partition can leave both sides running with divergent state. The executor therefore checks skill identity, supervisor epoch, sequence, and freshness before accepting a renewal. One implementation uses an executor-issued challenge with a local response deadline. Delayed responses cannot start a fresh lease merely by arriving. Expired or superseded authority requires re-admission. The lease duration must accommodate the admitted renewal delay while leaving time for the tested fallback. Until expiry, locally available regulation and protection continue within the existing authority.

The correct fallback depends on the physical state. A moving base may brake. A loaded gripper may need to maintain a limited holding force. A gravity-loaded joint may require controlled braking rather than abrupt removal of torque. Holding has thermal and energy limits and needs an escalation or unloading procedure. If sensing or the controller fails, an independent protection channel handles the faults assigned to it. Merely placing two processes on the same computer does not establish independence from kernel failure, power loss, or resource exhaustion. A task-level cancellation request is not an emergency-stop mechanism. Industrial implementations specify and validate the safety-related control and drive functions under applicable standards, including ISO 13849-1 and IEC 61800-5-2 (iso138492023software94; iec61800). The required functions follow the machine’s risk assessment.

Runtime assurance provides a related logical architecture. An advanced controller operates while a monitor retains authority to transfer control to a verified fallback under stated assumptions (desai2019soter). Its guarantees depend on the plant model, measurements, recovery region, and timely execution of the monitor and fallback. Implementing that logic in a separate fault domain is an additional engineering decision. The local sensing, compute, power, and actuation paths must survive the faults for which continued operation is claimed. This separation preserves the autonomous device loop emphasized in Section 9.3 while slower layers improve task selection and recovery.

9.4.2 Hardware Abstraction, Sensor Data, and Robotics Middleware

A hardware interface should hide transport details while exposing the physical properties on which correct action depends. The ros2_control framework, for example, separates controllers from hardware components through state and command interfaces, with a controller manager coordinating the read-update-write cycle (roscontrol2026architecture). An interface named “position” is still incomplete without joint units, coordinate conventions, limits, supported modes, calibration state, and the conditions for switching modes. A simulated actuator and a physical drive can satisfy the same software signature while differing in delay, saturation, compliance, and failure behavior. Closed-loop substitution consequently requires testing the dynamics as well as the API.

Sensor interfaces need similar precision. An observation should carry its acquisition time, clock domain, frame, calibration identity, and validity information alongside the measurement. Covariance or another uncertainty representation is needed when the estimator relies on it. Receipt time alone conceals camera exposure, transport, and queueing delays. Combining a recent force sample with an old image can create a plausible state that never existed. The estimator must either align the measurements to a common time, propagate them using an explicit motion model, or mark the combination as unsuitable for the intended decision. Missing and invalid measurements must remain distinguishable from a measured zero.

Sensor validity can be expressed on the executor’s clock. Let $\hat{t}_{\mathrm{s}}$ be the mapped acquisition time, with a clock-mapping error bounded by $\epsilon_{\mathrm{sync}}$ . The estimated age of this particular observation at use time $t$ , rather than standard AoI for the latest available update, is

 $\Delta_{\mathrm{age}}(t)=t-\hat{t}_{\mathrm{s}},\qquad\Delta_{\mathrm{age}}(t)+\epsilon_{\mathrm{sync}}\leq\Delta_{\mathrm{age}}^{\max},$ 

(9.5)

where $\Delta_{\mathrm{age}}^{\max}$ is a configured age limit for the particular observation and use. It can differ for a cached object label and a force estimate. The test applies at admission and at each intended actuation time, so age continues to grow across an action chunk. For commands that depend on this observation, it limits expiry to $\hat{t}_{\mathrm{s}}+\Delta_{\mathrm{age}}^{\max}-\epsilon_{\mathrm{sync}}$ . Additional constraints may shorten the interval. If the clock mapping or its error bound is unavailable, the receiver needs another validated freshness mechanism or must reject the observation for that use. ROS 2 distinguishes ROS time, which can follow simulation, from steady time (foote2018clock94). Physical watchdogs and leases use the latter. Simulation tests must state how their virtual timing maps to that mechanism.

Middleware carries these interfaces but does not supply their physical meaning. ROS 2 offers topics for streams, services for request-response interactions, and actions for longer operations with feedback and cancellation (macenski2022robot; ros22026actions). The Data Distribution Service (DDS) specifies data-centric publish-subscribe communication and quality-of-service (QoS) policies, including reliability, history, deadline, and liveliness (omg2015dds94). Zenoh combines publish-subscribe with query-based data access, and rmw_zenoh integrates it beneath ROS 2’s middleware interface (zenoh2026overview; rmwzenoh2026design). These technologies occupy different layers. ROS 2 defines the action protocol above the underlying DDS or Zenoh transport.

QoS choices should follow the consequences of delay and loss. A high-rate state stream may benefit from a shallow queue that favors recent samples. A configuration transaction may require acknowledged delivery. Retransmission can improve delivery while increasing age, and a growing queue can turn a responsive estimator into a consumer of historical data. DDS deadline and liveliness events make some communication failures observable. They do not stop a motor or prove that a task is progressing. Backend support also differs. The Jazzy implementation of rmw_zenoh does not implement deadline or lifespan policies. A design that depends on those policies must verify the selected release and enforce the necessary command-expiry behavior locally (rmwzenoh2026design).

The resulting boundary is practical. Middleware transports typed information. The application establishes freshness, ownership, and permissible use. A command should identify its producing skill and sequence, its coordinate and control modes, and its validity interval. The receiver rejects incompatible or expired commands before they enter the actuator path. Configuration changes are versioned and checked before activation. These conventions allow a developer to distinguish a transport failure from a stale observation, a conflicting controller, or an invalid request, each of which calls for a different response.

9.4.3 Real-Time Runtimes and Learned Policy Integration

A controller needs its next input before a deadline, whereas a learned policy may have variable inference time. Running both in one callback chain makes physical timing depend on model execution, memory allocation, and accelerator contention. ROS 2’s real-time guidance identifies page faults, dynamic allocation, and indefinitely blocking synchronization as hazards in a time-critical path (ros22026realtime). Deployment therefore separates the bounded control cycle from inference, logging, visualization, and network-facing task services. Separation may require dedicated threads, priorities, memory discipline, processor allocation, or a separate controller. The necessary arrangement depends on the faults and interference the system must tolerate.

For a periodic local update, a useful timing budget is

 $C_{\max}+B_{\max}+J_{\max}<T_{\mathrm{deadline}}\leq T_{c},$ 

(9.6)

where $C_{\max}$ bounds computation and input/output (I/O) on the selected path, $B_{\max}$ bounds blocking and scheduling interference, $J_{\max}$ bounds release jitter, $T_{\mathrm{deadline}}$ is the deadline, and $T_{c}$ is the control period. This is an accounting condition for that path, not a complete schedulability or stability proof. The bounds require evidence for the actual workload and hardware. A finite benchmark’s largest observed latency is not automatically a worst-case bound. A complete assessment also includes sensing delay, communication, actuator response, and the controller’s tolerance to missed updates.

Learned policies fit this structure through explicit adapters. OpenVLA illustrates a vision-language-action model that maps observations and instructions to robot actions (kim2024openvla). ACT predicts sequences of actions for fine-grained manipulation (zhao2023). Their outputs may be joint targets, end-effector increments, or other embodiment-specific commands. The adapter must preserve the model’s normalization, reference frames, action period, and control mode, and establish compatibility with the receiving controller. Position, velocity, and force checks constrain admission. Collision avoidance and contact stability additionally depend on the controller and its operating envelope.

Figure 9.12 shows an asynchronous arrangement. An inference worker consumes a timestamped observation and produces a candidate action sequence with a sequence identity and validity horizon. A local executor continues its fixed-rate cycle from an already admitted buffer while the candidate is computed. Before a buffer switch, the receiver checks observation age at the scheduled use times, command order, frame, operating mode, lease, and relevant limits. It rejects late results whose assumptions are no longer valid. The gate also applies a controller-specific continuity rule before the buffer is switched atomically. Otherwise the handover can introduce a discontinuity in velocity, force, or target pose. To avoid fallback, a replacement must finish inference, transport, and admission before the current buffer expires. When inference runs at the edge, the freshness budget includes both outward observation transport and returning commands. A small learned controller with a demonstrated execution bound can instead run inside the periodic path and is subject to Eq. (9.6).

Figure 9.12: Asynchronous inference coupled to local execution. Variable-duration policy computation produces candidate action chunks, while the local loop consumes a validated buffer at its own period. Admission and a controlled buffer switch connect the two. Expired results are discarded. Loss of valid command authority activates a local fallback. The control ticks are schematic. The gate checks continuity as well as validity before the atomic buffer switch

Action chunks reduce the frequency at which a model must be invoked, but they also commit the robot to predictions made from an earlier observation. A longer chunk can absorb inference delay while delaying the response to a changed scene. Real-time chunking addresses this interface by generating a new chunk asynchronously while accounting for actions committed during inference (black2025rtc_ch6). It coordinates policy execution under delay through a continuation consistent with the committed prefix. Deployment still requires measurement and validation of the complete runtime. Contact-sensitive control and protection still require timely local measurements, even when the high-level action sequence remains valid.

The runtime should make buffer expiry, inference overrun, and observation dropout first-class events. Repeating the last action indefinitely can be especially dangerous when the action is a velocity or torque. At the earlier of lease and command expiry, the executor begins the plant-specific fallback described above, records the transition, and prevents a delayed response from restoring authority. Resumption requires fresh state and an explicit re-admission. Thus learning can change the motion strategy without making the availability of a large model a prerequisite for every control update.

9.4.4 The Embodied Intelligence Harness and Skill Contracts

Table 9.3: An illustrative transfer_vial skill contract. Symbols denote configured bounds, not universal thresholds. The local executor enforces command validity and fallback independently of the task supervisor

Contract field

Concrete interface and obligation

Input

request_id, vial identity, source and destination fixture IDs, pose and frame, calibration version, payload class, and maximum task duration $T_{\mathrm{task}}$ . Duplicate IDs query the recorded execution state rather than starting another transfer.

Preconditions

Identity and source occupancy confirmed, destination empty, pose age satisfying Eq. (9.5), compatible gripper and payload, local controller ready, required interlocks valid. Unknown conditions trigger inspection or rejection.

Resources

Exclusive arm and gripper authority, reservation of the destination slot and shared motion region. Acquisition is bounded. Partial acquisition is released on rejection.

Timing

Task duration $T_{\mathrm{task}}$ starts at local admission. Each phase has its own timeout. Task commands expire at the earlier of the local lease deadline and their observation-limited expiry. Fallback begins no later than that point, independently of Harness cancellation.

Progress

Timestamped phase, controller status, grasp/contact evidence, observation age, and remaining authority. “Goal accepted” and “target pose reached” are intermediate states.

Completion evidence

After release and retreat, destination occupancy and vial identity are observed, the source is empty, and the gripper no longer holds the vial. Return evidence timestamps, confidence or validity flags, and the relevant log references.

Failure and recovery

The executor reports aborted or canceled with the last verified state. A missing result leaves the Harness with an application-level outcome_unknown. Apply the local fallback and re-observe before retrying or releasing resources.

The Harness governs the task loop across these interfaces. It maintains the current goal and evidence, resolves requests against available skills, arbitrates resources, and tracks execution to an observable result. Hierarchical reinforcement learning formalizes temporally extended actions through initiation, policy, and termination components (sutton1999options). Behavior trees provide established mechanisms for composing and monitoring robot behaviors (IovinoEtAl2022). These precedents explain much of the required machinery. Language-conditioned skill selection with affordance scoring, as in SayCan, provides a concrete precedent for connecting model proposals to robot capabilities (ichter2023saycan). In the framework used here, the model proposes skills and arguments. Admission, monitoring, and completion decisions follow explicit contract checks over timestamped evidence.

A skill contract gives the supervisor something more precise than an action name. Table 9.3 develops one example for moving a capped vial between known fixtures. Its parameters and conditions are illustrative design choices, to be set from the actual robot, payload, and procedure. The example separates request acceptance, physical progress, and completion evidence. A ROS 2 action can carry the goal, feedback, result, and cancellation protocol, but resource ownership, physical preconditions, command leases, and evidence requirements remain application responsibilities (ros22026actions).

Admission checks establish that a skill can start. Execution monitoring determines whether its assumptions continue to hold (pettersson2005monitoring94). A fresh target pose may become stale during an approach. Another device may occupy a reserved region. A grasp may be established and then lost. The monitor should therefore associate each predicate with evidence and a validity interval, and distinguish false from unknown. Unknown identity or destination occupancy cannot be converted to success merely because the motion controller reports completion. Learned perception can misidentify a vial or occupancy state. Completion thresholds need calibration, and consequential decisions may require complementary sensing or repeated observation. Conflicting evidence triggers re-observation or a recovery whose own conditions are checked.

Cancellation also has physical semantics. A ROS 2 action server may accept a cancellation request while the underlying mechanism still needs time to decelerate or secure its load. The Harness should wait for the executor’s terminal state and physical evidence before allocating its resources to another skill. If communication fails after a vial has been placed but before the result arrives, a timeout leaves the outcome uncertain. Retrying the transfer immediately could act on an empty fixture or move a second object. Persistent request identities, execution records, and observation of the fixtures allow the supervisor to reconcile state after reconnection. Reliable message delivery alone cannot provide exactly-once physical effects.

Restarting the Harness reconstructs task state from the executor and fresh observations before any new authority is issued. The application-level “outcome unknown” state describes missing physical evidence or a missing result. It is distinct from the unset status represented by ROS 2’s STATUS_UNKNOWN.

9.4.5 Development Infrastructure and Evidence for Deployment

Development infrastructure should test the boundaries just described. A reproducible episode records acquisition and actuation times, frame and calibration versions, model and controller identities, skill requests, authority changes, and the evidence used to declare completion. Tracing the path from a sensor event through callbacks to a command helps distinguish inference delay from scheduling or transport delay. ros2_tracing provides instrumentation for such analysis in ROS 2 (bedard2022tracing94). High-rate recording itself consumes resources, so its effect on the control workload must be measured or isolated.

Recorded-data replay is valuable for comparing estimators and diagnosing failures, but an unchanged sensor log cannot establish the closed-loop outcome of a changed policy. Different actions would have produced different observations. Software-in-the-loop (SIL) testing runs the relevant software against a simulated plant to examine logic, interfaces, and responses to modeled disturbances. Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing runs target firmware on target control electronics against a simulated plant, exposing processor and scheduling effects. Sensor and actuator I/O may still be emulated through a different link, as in PX4’s hardware-in-the-loop (HITL) arrangement (px42026simulation). The test report must identify which physical interfaces were exercised. Gripper friction, camera exposure, and the complete machine’s stopping response require physical trials.

Figure 9.13: Validation stages answer different questions. SIL tests execution logic against a modeled plant. HIL adds target electronics and timing. Bounded physical trials expose sensing, contact, and actuation effects absent from the model. Release decisions apply to a versioned combination of model, firmware, controller, action adapter, calibration, and interfaces. Failure evidence drives component revisions and regression tests

Figure 9.13 organizes these stages around explicit claims. For the vial-transfer skill, SIL can inject a stale pose, a duplicated request, or a lost acknowledgment. HIL can expose queue growth, inference contention, and watchdog delay. Bounded hardware trials can test grip loss and verify a loaded stop. Terminating the Harness, suspending its monitoring loop while a heartbeat remains alive, and partitioning the network are particularly informative. Local regulation and assigned protection must remain available, command authority must expire as specified, and reconnection must reject queued commands and renewals from obsolete epochs. Tests should also challenge sensor loss and the shared resources that could defeat the intended isolation.

The evidence should include the operating conditions, observed latency distribution and misses, age at actuation, time to fallback, recovery outcome, and the physical criterion for success. A release bundles the policy weights, preprocessing and action adapter, controller settings, middleware configuration, firmware, calibration, and skill schema used to obtain that evidence. Changing one of these can invalidate a previously established interface or timing assumption. Regression tests and staged physical trials determine whether the affected claims still hold. Binding evidence to this configuration provides the software basis for the sustained reliability and fleet deployment considered in Section 9.5.

## 9.5 Reliability and Deployment at Scale

A vial-handling robot may complete a demonstration and still fail to produce usable samples over a working day. A cap slips after the fingers warm up, a dispenser delivers less liquid than commanded, or a restart repeats a transfer already completed. Each failure breaks a different connection between an intended action and its physical result. Reliable Physical AI requires that connection to remain observable and correctable. The system must detect a deviation, determine what can still be recovered, and verify the result before proceeding. Experience from these events can improve subsequent behavior, provided the cause is identified and the change is tested. This section follows that loop from one task to a fleet of machines.

9.5.1 From Successful Attempts to Sustained Physical Output

Reliability concerns continuity of correct service. Availability concerns whether a system is ready to work (Avizienis et al., 2004). For a physical task, correct service needs an observable endpoint. A sample is valid only if its identity, quantity, and required process conditions are preserved. Command delivery, completed trajectories, and apparent grasps are intermediate events. Their success matters only through the result they enable. A robot that remains powered throughout a shift but repeatedly requires a person to rescue its samples has poor autonomous productivity.

The measurements should therefore follow the task. Encoders establish arm configuration, touch can reveal loss of contact, and a balance can verify a transfer. Agreement among several signals is useful when they provide independent evidence. Several estimates derived from the same incorrect calibration may agree while the sample is wrong. The task-state observability of Section 9.2.3 thus becomes a reliability requirement. The system must distinguish states that call for different actions while there is still time to intervene. Table 9.4 links this evidence to the scale of correction.

Table 9.4: Reliability depends on matching physical evidence to the scope
of correction. A failure observed at one level may originate at another

Level

Example deviation

Evidence needed

Scope of correction

Component

Gripper response changes after warm-up

Current, temperature, measured motion and load

Reduce duty and inspect the drive or transmission

Skill

Cap slips during opening

Contact change, cap motion, applied torque

Re-establish support and revise the grasp

Workflow

Vial contents disagree with the task record

Sample identity, measured quantity, verified checkpoints

Reconcile progress and recover or reject the sample

Fleet

Failures rise after a policy release

Outcomes by hardware, calibration and software version

Isolate affected configurations and validate restoration

Small errors accumulate over long procedures. Fifty independent steps that each succeed 98% of the time give only about 36% success for the whole sequence ( $0.98^{50}\approx 0.364$ ). Detection and recovery can change this outcome. Let $p_{k}$ be the initial success probability at stage $k$ , $d_{k}^{\mathrm{detect}}$ the probability of detecting an initial failure, and $r_{k}^{\mathrm{rec}}$ the probability that one recovery attempt succeeds given that failure was detected. A simplified model gives

 $P_{\mathrm{task}}=\prod_{k=1}^{N_{\mathrm{stage}}}\bigl[p_{k}+(1-p_{k})d_{k}^{\mathrm{detect}}r_{k}^{\mathrm{rec}}\bigr].$ 

(9.7)

Figure 9.14 shows the effect of this additional path to completion. The product assumes independent stages and successful recovery without hidden damage. Shared calibration errors, accumulated wear, and contamination violate those assumptions. The equation also omits recovery time. A system can eventually succeed yet produce little usable work per hour. Full-workflow tests must therefore measure both outcome and time.

Figure 9.14: Detection and recovery change the probability of completing a
50-stage task. In Eq. (9.7), $p=0.98$ , $d^{\mathrm{detect}}=0.9$ , and
 $r^{\mathrm{rec}}=0.8$ give an effective stage success of 0.9944 and about 76% task
success, compared with 36% for $p=0.98$ and 61% for $p=0.99$ without
recovery. These are illustrative calculations under the stated
assumptions, not measured robot performance

Finite trials also limit what can be claimed. Twenty successes without a failure leave an exact one-sided 95% upper confidence bound of about 14% on failure probability, under independent trials with a fixed protocol (hanley1983zero). Evaluation should state the workload, initial conditions, trial count, allowed assistance, and stopping rules. All attempted tasks, including aborted ones, belong in the record.

9.5.2 Detecting and Diagnosing Failures from Physical Evidence

A monitor must recognize both an abnormal interaction and a missing task result. Rising torque with little movement may indicate a jam. Ordinary joint motion with an unchanged balance reading may indicate an empty transfer. The first can require a rapid local response, while the second requires knowledge of the process. The sensor and actuator interfaces in Section 9.2 provide the measurements. The runtime in Section 9.4 must associate them with the action being attempted and its expected outcome. A successful command acknowledgment closes neither loop.

Detection is easier to interpret when it compares a prediction with a measurement tied to the task. A dynamics observer can compare expected and measured joint loading, subject to its calibration and model assumptions (haddadin2017collision). A task monitor can check whether a cap rotated, a vial moved with the gripper, or mass changed by the required amount. These checks should be conditional on the current phase. Resistance is expected when tightening a cap but may indicate a fault before the threads engage. A fixed threshold applied without that context can either stop useful contact or overlook an abnormal one.

Learned monitors can supplement these checks. Sentinel combines action consistency tests with vision-language assessment of task progress (Agia et al., 2025b). It provides evidence for detecting failures during execution. Detection alone does not establish a correct recovery. Likewise, a plausible explanation from a model remains a hypothesis. A stopped finger may reflect an obstructed object, a current limit, overheating, or loss of communication. Synchronized images, encoder readings, currents, temperatures, and command records help separate these causes. Their timestamps matter because evidence collected after the robot has withdrawn may no longer describe the failed contact.

Detection quality should be measured where it changes the physical outcome. Report missed failures, false stops per scheduled operating hour, and the time from a detectable deviation to the protective response. Delays include sensing, transport, inference, and actuation, as discussed in Section 9.3. An alarm raised after a fragile vial breaks has a different value from one that allows the grasp to be corrected. Evaluate monitors on representative faults as well as normal contact transitions. High accuracy on a dataset dominated by uneventful motion is insufficient.

9.5.3 Recovering Progress and Handling Irreversible Actions

Recovery begins by establishing what is still true. After a slipping cap, the vial may remain supported, the cap may have moved, and the threads may already be partly disengaged. Returning the arm to a previous pose does not restore that state. The system should first preserve support and limit further loading, then acquire enough evidence to choose a feasible continuation. A new view, a gentle probing action, or a quantity check can be more useful than another full attempt. These actions use interaction to reduce uncertainty, which is a central capability of Physical AI.

A recovery should change the conditions responsible for failure. A missed grasp may permit a revised approach. A jam may require controlled withdrawal and realignment. A thermal limit may require reduced duty or cooling. Force, travel, retries, and elapsed time need task-specific bounds. If the cause remains unresolved or those bounds are reached, the robot should stop or request assistance. The physical checks required to resume belong to the recovery procedure itself.

Long tasks need checkpoints defined by verified physical outcomes. After a transfer, the system records sample identity, measured quantity, and completion status outside the policy’s transient state (Section 8.3). On restart, it reconciles that record with the scene before issuing a new command. Otherwise, replaying a command whose acknowledgment was lost can double a dose. An operator may also have moved the container, or a sample may have exceeded its usable holding time. The checkpoint preserves what was verified. Renewed observation establishes what remains valid now.

Some actions admit no useful rollback. Mixing the wrong reagent cannot be undone by restoring a software version. Before an irreversible step, the system should verify its identity and process preconditions and resolve uncertainty while correction is still possible. Action-conditioned world models can simulate candidate interactions. UniSim uses predicted visual outcomes to train planners and control policies (yang2024unisim). These predictions may still omit contamination, weak contact, or damage invisible in an image. They should guide investigation, while the actual process supplies the evidence for committing the action and accepting its result.

9.5.4 Learning from Operation Without Concealing Hardware Drift

The same command can produce a different interaction as pads wear, a camera mount shifts, or actuator temperature rises. Changes also arise from new objects and from states reached after the policy’s own mistakes. These forms of distribution shift demand different remedies. A loose camera mount requires repair and recalibration. Repeated failure on a correctly observed new cap geometry may justify additional demonstrations or a revised control policy. Retraining on every deviation risks teaching the model to compensate for a deteriorating machine.

The operating record should retain the observation, intended action, measured response, hardware and software configuration, intervention, and verified outcome. A successful human rescue is especially informative when it records which state prompted the intervention and what changed. DAgger addresses learning from states visited by the learner through expert feedback (ross2011dagger). Sirius studies learning from robot execution with human monitoring and interventions (liu2023sirius). These approaches support improvement from experience. Intervention frequency and operator time remain part of the deployment result, including the monitoring Sirius requires.

Simulation can test a proposed correction across variations that are costly to reproduce physically. RialTo reconstructs real environments for simulation-based policy improvement (torne2024rialto), while dynamics randomization varies physical parameters to reduce dependence on one nominal model (peng2018). The relevant variation should follow the diagnosed mechanism. Friction is relevant to slip, delay to late correction, and camera placement to an observation mismatch. Randomizing unrelated parameters cannot establish that the observed failure has been addressed.

SIMPLER evaluates agreement between simulated and real policy performance within tested manipulation settings (li2024simpler). Such agreement makes simulation useful for screening candidates, but a favorable ranking does not establish adequate absolute reliability. A revised policy needs fresh physical trials on the failure conditions, earlier successful tasks, and representative operating variation. Development episodes and acceptance trials must be separated. Fast control feedback corrects the current interaction. Learning changes future behavior and therefore requires this additional validation loop.

9.5.5 Deploying Compatible Configurations Across a Fleet

Scaling a policy means preserving its observation-action relationship on multiple physical machines. Differences in camera placement, fingertip wear, controller gains, and firmware can change that relationship even when robots share a model name. Common collection procedures, as used in DROID, help make experience comparable across sites (khazatsky2024droid). Deployment additionally requires evidence that each supported configuration still produces the intended physical outcome under its assigned workload.

Consider a new cap-opening policy for a fleet of vial-handling robots. The release manifest identifies model weights, observation preprocessing, action units and scaling, controller code and gains, drive firmware, and supported hardware revisions. It also binds each robot to its own checked camera, tool, and force-sensor calibration, using a specified calibration procedure and tolerances. Calibration values cannot be copied between machines merely because their parts have the same names. The validated unit is the compatible configuration. Installing new weights with an old action convention can turn a useful learned correction into an unintended movement.

After interface, replay, simulation, and hardware-in-the-loop checks, a small subset runs supervised trials spanning the intended hardware and workload. Robots on the previous release provide a concurrent comparison. Acceptance criteria are fixed beforehand and cover sample quality, completion, contact loads, temperature, interventions, and recovery time. The trials include repeated cycles and warm actuators. Expansion depends on adequate exposure to these conditions, rather than a few successful picks. Results should be separated by configuration. An improved fleet average can conceal a regression on one gripper revision.

Suppose cap slip increases after the update. Further rollout stops and affected robots are removed from the scheduler. Each preserves its load and reaches a validated stopping state where possible. Uncertain samples are held for inspection. Logs retain the complete configuration and the physical evidence around the event. Recovery restores the previously validated compatible configuration where supported, checks calibration, and runs a physical acceptance sequence before returning the robot to service. Firmware that cannot be reversed needs a tested recovery image or maintenance procedure. Software restoration and sample recovery are separate obligations. A spilled sample remains lost after rollback.

Table 9.5 connects these trials to sustained productivity. Faults still unresolved at the reporting cutoff must remain visible, rather than disappearing from recovery-time statistics. Over the same reporting period, the cost per valid output introduced in Section 9.1 is

 $C_{\mathrm{valid}}=\frac{C_{\mathrm{equipment}}+C_{\mathrm{operation}}+C_{\mathrm{assistance}}+C_{\mathrm{maintenance}}+C_{\mathrm{failed\ material}}}{N_{\mathrm{valid}}},\qquad N_{\mathrm{valid}}>0,$ 

(9.8)

where costs are allocated once to that period. With no valid outputs, there is no finite observed unit cost. Better task success can therefore coexist with worse deployment performance if recovery consumes more time or assistance. The release decision should follow the measured physical work, including its interruptions. Those records then identify whether the next improvement belongs in the policy, the sensing and actuation hardware, or the operating procedure.

The cases in Section 9.6 examine this requirement at the contact level. A demonstrated manipulation skill becomes useful within a larger task only when its entry conditions, physical result, and recovery requirements are preserved.

## 9.6 Case Studies in Dexterous Hand Hardware

A hand holding a spray bottle must support the bottle while another finger moves the trigger and the wrist maintains the spray direction. Rotating an object within the palm instead requires changing the contacts that keep it under control. In both cases, what a learned policy can achieve depends on which contacts the hardware can make, sense, and adjust.

Applying Sections 9.1 and 9.2 at the finger level, the following cases examine RobotEra XHAND 1, the first-generation Wuji Hand, and Sharpa Wave W01 through their task requirements, mechanisms, sensing and control interfaces, and demonstrated capabilities. The emphasis is on the hardware conditions under which a result holds. Learning methods are covered in Section 6.6, and low-level hand controllers in Sections 7.4.4 and 7.4.5.

9.6.1 Manipulation Tasks and Contact Requirements

Dexterous tasks place different demands on the hand. Grasp acquisition establishes contact with an object. Transport preserves its relation to the hand. In-hand manipulation changes that relation. Tool operation additionally changes another object or process. Their evaluation boundaries matter. A policy tested with an object already in its palm has not thereby been tested on acquiring it from a table, and reaching a tool pose does not necessarily establish that the tool performed its intended operation.

To move the index finger around a cylinder, the remaining fingers must first sustain the load. Excessive squeezing can prevent rotation, while premature release can lose support. Rolling, sliding, and breaking contact permit different motions. The controller must coordinate the transition between them, as well as the finger positions (lynch2017modern). In tool use, it must also resist the reaction to pressing, cutting, or twisting. A grasp that supports the tool’s weight may be inadequate once the tool meets its target.

Each of these demands is partly a hardware question. Holding a load while another finger moves takes enough independent joints and enough sustained fingertip force. Regulating squeeze instead of position takes a drive that accepts force or impedance commands, or at least torque limits. Catching the onset of sliding takes a contact sensor fast enough to act before the grasp is lost. Resisting a tool’s reaction takes force capacity, and an arm that can carry the hand’s own mass.

9.6.2 Hand Design and the Observation-Action Interface

Figure 9.15: Hand geometry and local rotational coordinates. The surface-smoothed MANO

 (romero2017mano; spider2026xhandassets; wuji2026urdf; sharpa2026urdf).

The hands differ in their independently controlled coordinates (Table 9.6), excluding the arm and wrist (robotera2026xhandmanual; wuji2026v1manual; sharpa2026manual). Thumb opposition, finger spread, joint limits, and available contact surfaces determine what those coordinates can accomplish. More coordinates enlarge both the possible contact arrangements and the coordination problem. They do not alone rank task performance.

Figure 9.15 compares a MANO human-hand mesh with the actual robot geometries and locates their rotational coordinates. MANO represents each of its 15 finger joints by a three-parameter rotation. Its 45-dimensional hand pose is a model parameterization, not a count of independently actuated anatomical motions (romero2017mano). Reconstructed human landmarks and robot joints are different representations. A tracked fingertip need not correspond to one motor, and equal joint-vector dimensions need not imply equal fingertip motion. For a thumb-index pinch, the useful correspondence concerns fingertip separation and opposition relative to the object. Reproducing them may require different combinations of finger flexion, lateral motion, and wrist placement. Moving the wrist can compensate for limited finger reach, but also moves the other contacts.

The retargeting objective in Eq. (6.23) must be constrained by collisions and contact. A small fingertip error does not guarantee that a tool can be held under load.

The observation interface requires the same care. A fingertip contact flag can detect contact without resolving shear load or object pose, while an external camera can locate an object without seeing its supporting contacts. Coverage also matters. A dense fingertip sensor does not observe a load borne by the palm. Rotating without Seeing illustrates the alternative of distributing binary contact sensing over the fingers and palm, supporting learned reorientation on real objects (yin2023touch). Sensors should therefore be compared by the contact decisions they support, not by resolution alone.

Policy targets also differ from actuator response. A finger stopped by an object cannot track every requested position. Its loading depends on gains, transmission, and effort limits. A study therefore has to report both the policy’s targets and the observations it actually used. A tactile sensor listed in a hand’s specification may be absent from a particular policy input. Hardware revisions and additional software development kit (SDK) capabilities should likewise remain separate from the experimental configuration being discussed.
