Mass, Size, and Force Capacity

All three hands approach human hand size, but their masses differ by more than a factor of two (wuji2026v1manual; sharpa2026manual). Hand mass consumes arm payload before an object is lifted and adds to wrist inertia. It must therefore enter the arm’s dynamics model. Maximum fingertip-force ratings do not specify how long a force can be sustained. For a stiff trigger, the relevant test is continuous force within the motor’s thermal limits, evaluated in the geometry of the actual grasp.

Drive and Compliance

The three drives give a policy’s joint target different physical meanings. Wuji’s rotary direct-drive joints operate under position control and are specified as self-locking (wuji2026v1manual). Active yielding to an external load requires the controller to adjust the position target from feedback. Sharpa Wave instead exposes position, admittance, impedance, and zero-force modes, the last being backdrivable for manual guidance (sharpa2026manual). Under impedance control, a blocked finger produces a force that grows with its position error and the stiffness selected, as in the series-compliance relation of Eq. (9.3). Under zero-force mode an operator can move the fingers directly, which is one route to kinesthetic demonstration. XHAND accepts joint targets together with controller gains and torque limits from the host (Section 9.2.6). Joint targets alone therefore underspecify an action. The control mode, gains, and effort limits used during collection must be logged and reproduced at deployment.

Sensing Load at the Joints

Sharpa Wave estimates joint torque from motor current by default and also provides five torque sensors at the thumb carpometacarpal and four metacarpophalangeal joints. Their full-scale ratings are 5 and 3 N m, respectively, with a stated total error of $\pm$ (1% of full scale + 5% of reading) after calibration (sharpa2026manual). XHAND also returns motor-current information. Current-based estimates require calibration for transmission friction and motor temperature. A dedicated torque sensor measures the load through its joint but still does not locate the contact. Section 7.4.5 examines control using such joint-torque force estimates.

Tactile Sensing: Coverage, Rate, and Latency

Each Sharpa Wave fingertip uses an internal camera to image a compliant surface. It reports force, surface deformation, and contact location, with a 30 N force measurement range (sharpa2026manual). For control, their timing is critical. In the standard mode these outputs are computed on board at 30 Hz with a reported nominal latency of about 50 ms. In the high-performance mode raw images stream at up to 180 Hz with a reported nominal latency of about 20 ms and are processed on a host GPU. The joint loop, by comparison, runs at 500 Hz. The reported nominal tactile latencies of 20 to 50 ms correspond to 10 to 25 joint-control periods at 500 Hz. Tactile updates at 30 to 180 Hz arrive approximately 3 to 17 times less frequently than joint-control updates. Systems such as T-Rex therefore refine finger targets asynchronously from tactile history while a separate servo thread tracks them (Section 7.4.5). Sensing latency remains part of the end-to-end budget in Eq. (9.4). XHAND’s optional arrays report fingertip force and temperature (robotera2026xhandmanual). The first-generation Wuji Hand has no tactile sensing. Pressure measured by its companion glove belongs to the operator’s contacts, not the robot’s. In all three cases the palm and the inner finger segments are uninstrumented, so loads that the policy routes there remain unobserved.

Electrical Interfaces, Bandwidth, and Power

The joint interfaces in Table 9.6 impose different update periods (wuji2026v1manual; robotera2024xhandprotocol). Sensor transport can impose a separate constraint. Sharpa Wave’s hand control and 30 Hz tactile outputs fit within 100 Mb/s Ethernet, whereas its 180 Hz raw tactile stream requires gigabit Ethernet (sharpa2026manual). Choosing raw images thus moves computation to the host and raises network load, linking sensing to the device-edge placement decisions of Section 9.3. Power follows the same logic. Sharpa Wave specifies 100 W average and 180 W peak per hand, and 200 W average for a pair. Wuji’s supplied adapter is rated for 420 W 10 ms transients (sharpa2026manual; wuji2026v1manual). On a mobile manipulator, two hands draw from the same battery as the base and arms, and peak currents during simultaneous grasps must be within the supply’s transient capacity.

Durability and Maintenance

The rated hand lifetimes concern unloaded motion, whereas the tactile-skin rating specifies loaded cycles (sharpa2026manual; wuji2026v1manual). These conditions matter in contact-rich learning. Fingertip skins become consumables, and pressure-induced tactile drift calls for recalibration within the maintenance loop of Section 9.5, separate from model updates. Neither stated ingress rating specifies liquid-ingress protection. Covers or gloves needed for spills in kitchen or laboratory tasks also alter friction and tactile response.

The specifications alone already limit what can transfer between hands, whatever the learning method. A policy trained on Sharpa fingertip deformation images cannot run on a hand without tactile sensing. A controller that relies on impedance mode cannot be transferred unchanged to a position-only interface. A refinement loop designed for a 500 Hz joint interface must be retimed for a 12 ms bus update. Section 6.6.3 asks the complementary question of what a shared action representation can transfer.

9.6.4 Demonstration and Data-Collection Hardware

For dexterous hands, data collection must capture wrist motion, articulated finger motion, and contact together. The same tracker and glove can record a person directly manipulating an object or provide commands to a robot. The resulting records describe different bodies and interactions.

Human pretraining data include egocentric video with estimated hand motion and instrumented demonstrations with measured tracking signals. CAIP uses both pose-estimated video and laboratory human recordings with MANUS Metagloves Pro and Vive Ultimate Trackers (sharma2026caip). Instrumented capture reduces dependence on reconstructing occluded fingers, but still requires the hand model and the retargeting of Section 6.6.1. Robot teleoperation additionally records how the deployed arm and hand respond to the mapped commands. This response is the extra evidence needed when a geometrically plausible demonstration does not produce the intended grasp.

A representative teleoperation arrangement pairs a wrist tracker with a data glove. The tracker estimates the hand’s position and orientation in the tracking space. The glove resolves the fingers relative to the hand. MANUS Core supports external tracker poses, including HTC Vive devices, with calibrated offsets between tracker and glove (manus2026tracking). In CAIP’s Sharpa setup, Vive wrist motion drives relative arm targets, while MANUS finger keypoints are retargeted into hand-joint targets (sharma2026caip). The two measurements solve separate parts of the arm-hand coordination problem. Finger tracking alone cannot tell the arm where to place the hand in the workspace.

Wuji’s official teleoperation interface likewise supports Vive tracking with Wuji Glove or MANUS as the hand input (wuji2026teleop). Wuji Glove combines electromagnetic fingertip tracking, a fitted hand model, and pressure sensing on the palmar side (wuji2026glove). MANUS also distinguishes raw sensor measurements from its solved hand skeleton and retargeted output (manus2026datalayers). For supervision, this means that a model-derived joint angle is not an independently measured robot joint angle. Likewise, pressure recorded while the wearer holds an object describes human-side contact. During free-hand teleoperation, the glove does not acquire the remote robot’s contact forces. Those require robot-side sensing. Measuring pressure and rendering force feedback to the operator are separate capabilities.

Calibration has two distinct roles. Tracker-to-hand and tracking-to-robot transforms establish wrist targets, while hand-shape calibration and retargeting establish finger targets. A misplaced wrist tracker shifts every fingertip even when finger articulation is estimated accurately. Recording issued targets alongside measured robot motion helps distinguish this error from failure to reach a target under load.

Exoskeleton interfaces move part of this correspondence into the mechanism. Linkages and encoders relate the operator’s motion to the demonstration hand, and mechanically matched designs can make collected contacts closer to those available during deployment. DexEXO illustrates this approach with a wearable linkage driving a passive hand whose appearance and kinematics match the deployed hand. Aligned wrist-camera images can then be used directly for policy training (zhu2026dexexo). The benefit must be weighed against fit, range of motion, and access around a tool. A bulky finger attachment can prevent a valid demonstration even when the robot itself fits the tool. Passive coupling also differs from an actuated interface that returns robot forces to the wearer. An exoskeleton does not, by itself, imply bidirectional force feedback.

XHAND: Shaping the Collection Interface to the Mechanism

XHAND approaches the correspondence problem from the collection side. A lower-dimensional hand changes which demonstrated finger motions can be reproduced independently, as Figure 9.15 shows. DexUMI investigates this problem on XHAND and Inspire hands. It combines a wearable exoskeleton fitted to the target hand’s kinematics, measured joint motion, matched tactile sensing, and visual replacement of the human hand and device with the robot hand (xu2025dexumi). Mechanical alignment constrains the motion before it becomes training data. Observation alignment makes the same interaction more recognizable after deployment. Neither step alone ensures that the robot can sustain the demonstrated load. The paper also reports tactile drift after high pressure and an inconsistent motor-to-fingertip mapping (xu2025dexumi). Collection and deployment may use nominally identical devices that differ in loading history, so recalibration and loaded tests are part of keeping the demonstration interface valid.

A second XHAND study addresses the difficulty of coordinating the arm and fingers during collection. In the shared-autonomy framework of cui2025sharedautonomy, a person guides a UR3e arm through virtual reality (VR) while DexGrasp-VLA uses vision and touch to control the 12-DoF hand. This division reduces the number of decisions the operator must make simultaneously. The person chooses the approach and places the wrist, and the hand controller handles contact. The benefit depends on that controller. If it closes too early, the demonstration records the error unless the operator corrects it. A useful collection system must therefore expose who controlled each interval, how an intervention changed the action, and whether the resulting grasp served the task. Section 6.6.4 discusses the learning results of both studies, including where tactile input helped.

Figure 9.16: Three routes from demonstration to learning data. A tracker and
glove can record direct human manipulation or drive a robot through
retargeting. A mechanically coupled passive hand supplies another form
of direct demonstration. Solid arrows show motion or control. Dashed
arrows show recording. The exoskeleton row illustrates passive collection,

 (manus2026tracking; wuji2026teleop; zhu2026dexexo)

Figure 9.16 organizes these routes by where the physical interaction occurs. This determines whether the recorded contact belongs to a person, a passive demonstration hand, or the controlled robot. The distinction remains important even when all three routes use similar cameras and motion trackers.

Contact transitions make timestamp alignment consequential. Pairing finger closure with an image acquired after contact changes the state on which the action appears to depend. Records must distinguish pre-contact intent, measured contact, and subsequent correction.

9.6.5 From Demonstrated Skills to Integrated Tasks

Each learning result built on these hands covers one piece of a task. EgoScale learns a target-robot policy from human data (Section 6.6.2), WM-Craftnet rotates a held object, SimToolReal follows object-pose goals, and Play2Perfect adapts to assembly (Sections 7.4.4 and 7.4.5). Sharing a hand does not make them composable. The skill interfaces of Section 8.3.2 require the state produced by one behavior to support the next. An acquired grasp must permit the required finger movement, the object must remain observable, and the transition must preserve its support.

Consider using a tool after picking it up. A grasp that permits lifting may occupy the finger needed to operate the handle. Integration then requires reorientation, a changed grasp, or placement on a support surface before operation can begin. An in-hand rotation result supplies evidence about one of these transitions under its tested initial conditions. It does not establish the complete acquisition-operation sequence. This is where the runtime interfaces of Section 9.4 must connect policy outputs to measured contact and task state. Finishing a motion command is not by itself permission to begin the next skill.

Feedback also has to reach the right level. Recent touch can correct finger targets while the visual goal stays valid, but losing a usable grasp calls for a new task-level decision, and the runtime must route the event accordingly (Section 9.3). With tactile latency spanning ten or more joint-control periods in the reported modes (Section 9.6.3), a faster servo cannot make up for a policy that never receives the evidence of slip.

The reported endpoints (rotation completion, progress along a tool trajectory, insertion success, and accumulated success in a kitchen sequence) do not support a controlled comparison between hands (Section 6.6.5). Complete-task evidence requires grasping, contact transitions, operation, and recovery to succeed together under a declared protocol, with assistance costs reported alongside success.

Across the cases, reusable motor knowledge becomes useful only through a specific sensing and control interface. What transfers may be human coordination, an object-level goal, or a functional finger action. What has to be checked is the contact behavior on the deployed hand. Transfer to another hand, adaptation to assembly, and continued operation through wear are separate achievements. On a humanoid, this interface also depends on the moving body that supports the hand. Section 9.7 extends the analysis to that integrated system.

## 9.7 Case Studies in Humanoid System Integration

Carrying an object across a room connects almost every component considered in this chapter. The hands maintain the grasp, arm motion redistributes the load, stepping changes the support contacts, and the moving cameras must still provide useful observations of the destination. Recent systems built on the Unitree G1 show how these components can be organized for teleoperation, data collection, and autonomous whole-body interaction. They make the co-design problem in Section 9.1 concrete. The task model must express the required movements, and the robot’s mechanics, sensing, and computation must support their execution in closed-loop interaction. The comparison follows a common set of questions concerning what the task demands from the body, how observations and commands cross the interfaces, what was demonstrated, and which operating conditions bound that evidence. G1 provides a common platform for comparing these integration choices.

9.7.1 Embodiment and Whole-Body Coordination

A humanoid’s manipulation workspace depends on how it positions and supports its body. In G1’s 29-DoF configuration, six joints per leg, three at the waist, and seven per arm provide multiple ways to reach and orient an object. Hand joints are counted separately (unitree2026g1docs). Waist and arm motion can extend a reach, but the resulting posture and load must remain compatible with the supporting contacts. The hand’s contact capabilities therefore need to be considered together with the body motions required to use them, extending the hand-design problem in Section 9.6 to the complete robot.

This coupling shapes the division of control between a task model and a motor controller. A task model may specify hand and arm motion while leaving the supporting legs to a local feedback policy. When a foot also manipulates an object, the task interface must convey that contact objective as well. HOMIE and SONIC implement these divisions of control on G1 (ben2025homie; luo2026sonic). Both depend on a motor controller that produces the expected physical response from the assembled robot.

9.7.2 From a Learned Policy to Physical Execution

For a joint-target policy, motion depends on the interaction between its outputs, feedback gains, and actuator mechanics. As the actuation analysis in Section 9.2 explains, matching target angles alone does not match the robot’s response. ASAP addresses this problem on G1 by learning a correction to the simulated action-response relationship from measured robot trajectories, with a focus on the ankle linkage. The correction is used during policy fine-tuning in simulation. The resulting policy executes on the robot without that additional correction model (he2025asap). Physical measurements thus change the dynamics against which the policy is trained, improving transfer without adding that model to the online control loop.

Policy execution also depends on the state estimates and timing of its feedback path. BeyondMimic’s G1 motion-tracking stack combines a 500 Hz state estimator with a 50 Hz policy, whose onboard CPU inference takes less than 1 ms (liao2026beyondmimic). The estimator updates the body-state estimate between policy evaluations, while the policy uses that estimate to update joint targets. Policy frequency, inference latency, and estimation frequency therefore describe different parts of the physical loop. This separation implements the multirate execution discussed in Section 9.4. Timely movement depends on the complete sensing-computation-actuation path, including the stages outside neural-network inference.

9.7.3 Connecting Body Control, Hands, and Task Models

In whole-body manipulation, the division of control determines which aspects of motion a person or task model specifies and which the local controller supplies. HOMIE and SONIC provide two concrete answers (Figure 9.17). Both connect a task-command source to body and hand execution, but they expose different levels of control over the supporting legs.

Figure 9.17: Two G1 integration routes. HOMIE’s teleoperation interface combines arm and hand targets
with velocity, turning, and torso-height commands to a learned
lower-body controller. Its autonomous visual policy predicts arm, hand,
and height targets. In SONIC’s whole-body VLA route, a shared motion

supports body control, and visual observations inform task commands.

 (ben2025homie; luo2026sonic)

HOMIE: A Shared Interface for Demonstration and Autonomous Execution

HOMIE connects an isomorphic arm exoskeleton, motion-sensing gloves, and foot pedals to a G1 equipped with Dex3-1 hands (ben2025homie). The exoskeleton supplies arm-joint targets. The gloves command the hands. The pedals specify forward or backward velocity, turning rate, and torso height. A learned lower-body controller uses robot feedback to walk or squat as the upper-body posture changes. This allocation reduces the operator’s burden. The person directs the reach and grasp while the lower-body policy supplies the compensating motion discussed in Section 7.3. The operator receives no force feedback, however, limiting direct assessment of contact loads through the teleoperation interface.

The same allocation connects data collection to autonomous execution. HOMIE records images, joint states, and task commands during teleoperation, then trains a visual policy to produce arm, hand, and height targets. Its local locomotion policy runs at 50 Hz on the robot’s Jetson Orin. For autonomous manipulation, head- and arm-mounted cameras and joint feedback supply a visual policy on an external RTX 4080 computer through wired Ethernet. This upper-level loop runs at 10 Hz. The task model can therefore replace the operator while retaining the controller that regulates body motion. After collecting 50 demonstrations per task, the system succeeds in 11 of 15 trials of squatting to pick a tomato from a low sofa and 12 of 15 trials of tabletop pick-and-place (ben2025homie).

SONIC: Exposing Coordinated Body Motion to a VLA

Some tasks require the task model to choose a foot contact as deliberately as a grasp. Opening a pedal-operated bin while holding an object, for example, requires placing one foot on the pedal while the other supports the body. SONIC connects a fine-tuned GR00T N1.5 VLA model to a reusable whole-body controller through a learned motion representation (luo2026sonic). In its whole-body mode, the VLA predicts a 64-dimensional motion token and 14 hand-joint targets. The token conditions coordinated body motion. The hand targets command finger configurations. Teleoperated demonstrations populate this same action representation, connecting the motor pretraining discussed in Section 7.4 to task learning.

The G1 motion stack controls 29 body joints and runs onboard a Jetson Orin. Its learned controller updates at 50 Hz, while an independent 500 Hz command publisher streams the latest joint targets to the low-level interface (luo2026sonic). Separating these operations sustains command delivery between policy evaluations. At the task level, the VLA-driven system completes the sequence of picking up a can, walking to a bin, pressing its pedal, and disposing of the can in 6 of 10 trials after training on 1,000 multi-object demonstrations. It also places a drill in a box and carries the box to a shelf with both hands in 7 of 10 trials after 300 demonstrations. These are complete-task results. Grasping, locomotion, and changes in support must succeed within the same execution.

The two interfaces support different task demands. HOMIE assigns the operator or visual policy direct control of the arms and hands and leaves leg coordination to a command-conditioned controller. SONIC’s motion representation also lets the task model request coordinated leg motions, including a foot’s interaction with an object. In both cases, reusing a motor controller becomes useful through an interface that expresses the movements needed to establish and maintain task contacts.

9.7.4 Physical and Perceptual Conditions for Task Execution

A task interface connects learned models to coordinated movement, but the range of executable tasks also depends on the robot’s end effectors, the states it can observe, and the demands of repeated operation. AdaPT’s G1 tennis experiments expose the coupling between the first two. Serving requires both a body capable of the swing and timely observations of the ball (huang2026towards).

For professional-style serving, AdaPT combines a task-specific racket mount with a lightweight parallel gripper that holds and tosses the ball. The heavier Unitree hand, termed Dex-3 in the AdaPT study, is evaluated with simpler amateur motions because the tested configuration cannot maintain balance with that hand during the professional serving motions (huang2026towards). The choice of hand thus changes which whole-body movements are feasible, even though its immediate role is to hold and release the ball. End-effector selection must account for the dynamic task performed by the complete body as well as the local grasp.

Executing the swing also requires observations that arrive early enough to coordinate racket-ball contact. AdaPT’s principal experiments use a 35-camera motion-capture system to track the robot and ball. In a separate field deployment on the Dobot Atom humanoid, stereo vision and HTC VIVE Ultimate Trackers provide ball observations and robot localization, respectively (huang2026towards). The motor skill is therefore evaluated together with a particular source of task-state information. The same dependence appears in locomotion. Gallant’s confined-terrain case in Section 9.2.7 requires three-dimensional geometry over the space occupied by the body. In both settings, sensing must resolve the geometry relevant to making or avoiding contact. Intercepting a moving ball additionally requires predicting where contact occurs.

Sustaining these motions over repeated trials adds thermal and mechanical constraints to those of a single execution. ASAP reports motor overheating and partial damage to two G1 robots during its high-dynamic-motion data collection, limiting the real-world data available for adaptation (he2025asap). This connects the actuator limits in Section 9.2 to the operating-life considerations in Section 9.5. Physical learning depends on how often the assembled robot can repeat the contacts and accelerations needed to collect experience.

9.7.5 From Integrated Demonstrations to Sustained Operation

HOMIE and SONIC demonstrate that a shared command interface can connect data collection, task models, and local body control. Their reported task trials test whether grasping, movement, and changes in support can succeed in one execution. The different tasks, demonstration sets, and trial protocols do not provide a controlled comparison between the two systems. Nor do those trial counts describe how either system performs over a working shift. The measures in Section 9.5 extend the evaluation to valid output, assistance, downtime, and recovery under a declared workload.

Table 9.7 relates the evidence discussed here to those deployment questions. Its final column states further checks for an intended deployment. It does not attribute unreported tests or protective functions to the cited systems. Hardware specifications, measured loop rates, and task success each answer a different part of the system question.
