For a humanoid carrying an object, this distinction becomes concrete when the task computer or its communication link becomes unavailable. A local body controller may still receive proprioceptive feedback, but that alone does not specify whether the last task command remains authorized or how the object is secured. The runtime must define command expiry and the locally executable response for the relevant physical state, as in Section 9.4. Trials then need to establish the response under the faults assigned to that design, including the conditions for resuming the task. These fault-response tests form part of deployment validation. The task trials summarized above do not establish their outcomes.

The hand and humanoid cases bring the chapter’s five questions together. The body determines which contacts and loads are feasible. Sensing makes their consequences observable. Computation must finish while that evidence remains useful. Software assigns authority and connects commands to measured outcomes. Deployment preserves these relationships through repetition, wear, and updates. A change in fingertip material, payload, camera placement, or command timing can alter several of these relationships at once. The unit to validate is therefore the assembled observation-action system under its intended workload. Hardware and software become a dependable physical capability when they repeatedly produce the required result and retain a tested means to detect, contain, and recover from deviations.

## Part III Future Outlook

"The real problem of humanity is the following: we have paleolithic emotions; medieval institutions; and god-like technology."

— Edward O. Wilson

## 10 Physical AGI

Figure 10.1: Overview of physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI). Building on Physical AI, Physical AGI is described by the four capability dimensions of breadth, depth, plasticity, and continuity. It is pursued through four pathways, which are systematic generalization, collaboration between humans and robots, collective Physical AI, and self-evolution. Its ultimate goal is to advance scientific discovery and to enable engineering beyond the reach of human capability

The preceding chapters examine the basic concepts of Physical AI together with perception, data, world models, foundation models for robot manipulation, foundation models for whole-body motor control, agents, and hardware systems. These technologies provide the foundations for systems that perceive, reason, and act in the physical world. The question for this chapter is whether these foundations can support more than a growing repertoire of predefined physical tasks. This monograph focuses on intelligence that can interpret unfamiliar situations, develop new ways of acting, and take part in creating and maintaining the material conditions of human life. It calls the ultimate goal of this line of research physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI). This term denotes an artificial system that integrates broad understanding, learning, and reasoning with reliable action in the physical world and can solve unfamiliar real-world problems across many domains at a level comparable to capable humans.

The qualifier physical gives this goal its specific meaning. An agent must connect its task-relevant knowledge to what its body can actually do, reason about the consequences of intervention, and revise its understanding when the world responds unexpectedly. Recognizing an object or describing a plausible plan is only the beginning. The agent must also find out how the object is supported, what changes once contact is made, and which uncertainties matter for execution. The physical world is thus more than the place where an intelligent system is tested. It supplies evidence, constrains reasoning, and is the medium through which the system achieves its goals.

Physical grounding, a complete technical stack, a larger task repertoire, and greater model scale do not by themselves establish generality. Chollet defines intelligence as skill-acquisition efficiency relative to priors, experience, and generalization difficulty, and thereby separates it from achieved skill (chollet2019measure). High task performance may reflect effective learning, extensive prior training, or both. The relevant contrast is between a fixed repertoire and the ability to meet unfamiliar demands by reusing knowledge and acquiring what is missing. Scale can improve both, and Sutton identifies search and learning as general methods that keep benefiting from increasing computation (sutton2019bitter). For Physical AI, what must be shown is that these gains translate into better understanding, transfer, execution, and adaptation.

Physical AGI must therefore act effectively across tasks, environments, and embodiments, and acquire further competence when existing knowledge falls short, without being redesigned for each task. Section 10.1 makes this requirement precise. It examines what separates such a system from today’s Physical AI and characterizes competence along four dimensions, namely breadth, depth, plasticity, and continuity. As Figure 10.1 shows, the subsections that follow trace four pathways toward Physical AGI, namely systematic generalization, human-robot collaboration, collective Physical AI, and self-evolution, each of which relaxes an assumption of current Physical AI. A concluding subsection considers the proposed purposes of Physical AGI in scientific discovery and in engineering beyond human limits.

## 10.1 Core Capabilities of Physical AGI

Most Physical AI systems today are built and evaluated for a stated set of tasks, settings, and platforms. Within that set they can be highly capable, but their competence is bounded by the scope anticipated by training and engineering, and a new demand typically calls for new data, retraining, or redesign. Physical AGI differs from such systems in generality, the “G” in AGI, rather than in higher performance on the same tasks. A Physical AI system is characterized by the skills it has. Physical AGI is characterized by how far it can carry those skills, and extend them, beyond the conditions covered by its preparation.

This chapter takes generality in this sense to mean the capacity to reuse knowledge and problem-solving processes across diverse tasks, environments, and embodiments, and to acquire or revise competence efficiently when existing knowledge is insufficient. Generality is always relative to a stated scope, performance standard, and resource budget, not to all conceivable tasks.

What makes this definition physical is the relationship between knowledge and intervention. An agent must reason about objects, materials, spatial structure, forces, and its own body well enough to act on them, and it must link an abstract objective, such as repairing an object or assembling a mechanism, to the physical conditions under which that objective can be met. The link runs both ways, since interaction can expose unknown constraints and change how the agent understands the problem. Physical AGI thus acts with available knowledge and also uses action to acquire knowledge for later tasks.

The definition covers both the use of existing competence and the acquisition of new competence, and many unfamiliar conditions call only for the former. A robot may grasp an object with an unseen surface texture using a policy it already has. A narrower container opening may call for a new grasp or a contact-guided insertion, which planning with existing knowledge may still find. New learning becomes necessary only when knowledge and available skills both fall short. The deciding question is whether existing competence still suffices, not whether the situation is unfamiliar.

For the same reason, a large but fixed repertoire is weak evidence of adaptability, and fast learning within a narrow task family is weak evidence of breadth. Generality also does not mean freedom from human help. Demonstrations, feedback, and manual adjustments needed for a new task count toward its adaptation cost. The criterion is whether the system’s own adaptation and learning can meet new demands within its physical, computational, and safety limits, without task-by-task redesign.

To describe both the competence a system has and its capacity to develop further, this chapter uses four dimensions. Breadth and depth describe present capabilities, following the distinction between generality and performance (morris2024levels). Plasticity and continuity describe how competence is acquired and accumulated through experience.

Breadth is the range of physical conditions over which a system acts effectively, including variation in tasks, objects, scenes, tools, dynamics, and embodiments. Counting task names is a poor proxy for this range. Many differently named tasks rely on the same grasp and motion, while a small change in friction can demand quite different control. Breadth should therefore be described by the physical variation over which competence holds. Open X-Embodiment shows that training across robotic platforms can improve performance by transferring experience between them (openx2024), and $\pi_{0.5}$ performs household manipulation in homes absent from its training data (pi2025pi05). Both results demonstrate breadth under their evaluation conditions, but neither addresses arbitrary changes in dynamics or morphology. Sharing parameters across robots makes transfer possible, but whether transfer actually occurs is an empirical question.

Depth is how well the system performs within that range, including its accuracy, compliance, efficiency, reliability, and coordination over long horizons. In physical tasks these qualities are tightly linked. A grasp must support transport, transport must leave the object in a state from which it can be placed, and a small slip can alter the conditions for every later action. Deep competence therefore includes detecting disturbances, maintaining the conditions that later actions depend on, and recovering when those conditions are lost. Hierarchical planning supports long-horizon coordination by decomposing an objective into subgoals and reusing existing policies for familiar low-level actions (sutton1999options; kaelbling2011hierarchical). A system with many fragile skills and one with a few reliable skills are limited in different ways, and describing either requires both dimensions.

Plasticity is the capacity to acquire or revise competence when existing behavior is inadequate. A change in payload or friction may force the agent to revise its model, adjust its control, or learn a different interaction. Plasticity is measured by the experience, time, computation, supervision, and risk that adaptation requires. Two systems may reach the same success rate after very different numbers of physical trials, and their plasticity then differs even though their final performance does not. Plasticity is also distinct from retention. Dohare and colleagues show that standard deep-learning methods can gradually lose the ability to learn in continual-learning settings (dohare2024plasticity). Forgetting concerns what a system can no longer do, whereas loss of plasticity concerns what it can no longer learn.

This chapter treats plasticity as a property of the whole embodied system, not only of its parameter updates. Memory, model-based replanning, and newly generated procedures can all support adaptation (hafner2019planet; wang2024voyager). Replanning with unchanged knowledge may produce an unfamiliar solution without any new competence being acquired, while new knowledge can be stored in memory or executable procedures without changing network weights. This chapter therefore judges plasticity by whether new experience leads to effective behavior, whatever mechanism carries the change.

Learning accumulates only if the results of adaptation outlast the episode and can be recalled when needed. This chapter calls this accumulation of useful competence across encounters continuity. It involves keeping skills that remain valid, revising assumptions that no longer hold, and preserving the ability to keep learning. Elastic Weight Consolidation, for instance, restricts changes to parameters that matter for previously learned tasks (kirkpatrick2017ewc). This can reduce forgetting, but it leaves open when a physical failure calls for learning, which part of the system should change, and when a retained skill should be used. These are system-level decisions, and this chapter measures continuity by the lasting benefit of experience rather than by how long parameters persist.

None of the four dimensions is sufficient alone. Zero-shot success can show breadth without plasticity, and rapid adaptation can occur without continuity. Assessing them jointly is therefore a longitudinal matter. It asks whether experience lastingly extends the conditions under which the system acts effectively, without demanding new learning in every successful encounter.

To make this criterion operational, this chapter introduces the capability boundary, the limit of the conditions under which a system meets a specified performance standard, with computational resources, interaction budgets, human assistance, and safety constraints held fixed. Prior training and accumulated experience should be reported separately from any resources added during evaluation. Success on a task the evaluator has not tried before may reveal competence that was already present, so novelty to the evaluator is not, on its own, evidence of capability expansion.

This chapter distinguishes three outcomes. Direct transfer applies existing competence without acquiring task-specific knowledge, although it may involve substantial search or planning. Episodic adaptation resolves the current difficulty but does not retain the useful change. Persistent capability expansion retains changes that let the system meet the standard under previously unsupported conditions. Claiming it requires evidence of better performance, or of lower interaction, time, or assistance costs, under comparable constraints, together with evidence that valid skills and the ability to keep learning have been preserved. Gains within conditions the system already handled improve performance or efficiency but do not expand the boundary.

Current Physical AI typically assumes that operating conditions resemble those covered by training, that a person specifies the task and the robot merely executes it, that the robot acts alone in a single body, and that people design and run its learning process and fix its physical configuration. Each of these four assumptions confines the capability boundary in a different direction. In the case of collaboration, the boundary in question is that of joint human-robot action rather than of the robot alone. Relaxing each assumption defines a pathway toward Physical AGI, a proposed system independent of all four assumptions. The next four subsections take the pathways in turn, covering systematic generalization (Section 10.2), human-robot collaboration (Section 10.3), collective Physical AI (Section 10.4), and self-evolution (Section 10.5). The four dimensions and the distinction among direct transfer, episodic adaptation, and persistent capability expansion serve as a common yardstick for all four.

## 10.2 Systematic Generalization in Open-World Settings

The first pathway relaxes the assumption that operating conditions resemble those covered by training. Here the distinction between transfer and capability expansion shapes how generalization tests should be read. Many out-of-distribution evaluations vary objects, positions, or task combinations within a predefined family while the basic form of the problem stays the same (koh2021wilds). Success shows transfer within the family but says little about what happens when the sources of change are themselves unknown.

Under open conditions, an agent may first need to work out which factors have changed and whether the knowledge behind its current policy still applies, and only then decide what to learn. A drawer that does not open may be latched, jammed, or poorly grasped, and each explanation calls for a different response. The lack of motion alone does not distinguish these cases, whereas a constrained probe can provide additional evidence. Evaluations of open-world generalization should therefore state the changes introduced, the feedback available, and the adaptation permitted.

The same issue arises when systematic generalization is framed, as it usually is, through combinations of familiar constituents. Lake and Baroni show that meta-learning can support such generalization in controlled sequence-learning tasks (lake2023systematic). Recombination works when the constituent operations keep their meaning and effectiveness. In physical tasks the operations themselves can fail. A change in friction may break a grasp that sits in exactly the right place in the task sequence, and reordering the sequence does not repair it.

This chapter therefore defines system-level systematic generalization as the capacity to identify changes, preserve reusable structure, and find effective solutions when the conditions supporting existing policies no longer hold. It extends the compositional notion to perception, internal models, decision processes, and control without replacing it. A local failure may require changing only part of the system while the rest of its knowledge continues to serve the task. The agent must decide whether and where revision is needed, acquire or repair the missing competence, and test the result.

The structure retained for this purpose need not reproduce every observable detail. World models can predict in an abstract representation space without reconstructing future observations in full (garrido2025intuitive; Assran et al., 2025), and temporal abstractions support prediction over extended actions (sutton1999options). Such a representation must preserve the information needed to evaluate possible outcomes across tasks and changing conditions. Learned largely from observation, it can supply reusable physical knowledge before a new task arrives, so that not all useful structure has to be acquired through reward-driven trial and error (hafner2019planet). Abstraction of this kind is one plausible route to generalization, but it is not part of the definition.

Representations alone do not explain how a system responds when its current solution fails. This chapter distinguishes five functions in that response, namely competence assessment, change characterization, composition and acquisition, interactive validation, and knowledge consolidation. Together they lead from recognizing a difficulty to building, physically testing, and retaining a revised solution. They are roles rather than software modules or a fixed sequence, and they may share representations and recur as new evidence arrives. Not all five are always needed, since existing competence may suffice.

Competence Assessment

The agent judges whether continued execution is likely to remain effective and safe. Unexpected contact forces, mismatches between predicted and observed motion, or uncertain outcomes can warrant further observation, constrained probing, targeted assistance, or a safe stop. Prediction error rises, for instance, when a video shows an event that violates learned physical expectations (garrido2025intuitive). Such a discrepancy is a reason to reassess but offers no safety guarantee, and visual familiarity does not show that a policy remains reliable, because friction can change with no visible sign. An assessment is useful only if it changes behavior early enough, which can happen before the cause of the difficulty is known.

Change Characterization

Detecting a difficulty does not identify its cause. The agent must determine which assumptions need revision and which knowledge remains usable, since holding on to invalid assumptions invites repeated failure and discarding valid knowledge makes adaptation more expensive. The principle of Independent Causal Mechanisms supports selective revision, because under suitable assumptions a change in one mechanism need not require revising the others (scholkopf2021causal). Whether a learned representation has captured the relevant factors is a separate question. The agent may need informative actions to tell competing explanations apart, and it can act on a partial causal account as long as the remaining uncertainty constrains what it does. Learning can then concentrate on the affected parts of the system.

Composition and Acquisition

The agent builds a candidate solution from the knowledge that remains valid and identifies any competence still missing. A world model, drawing on memory and current perception, can predict the outcomes of candidate action sequences and score them against a task objective. Searching over these sequences at inference time can yield an unfamiliar solution without changing the model or learning a new skill (hafner2019planet; Assran et al., 2025). A new objective may still need a learned readout from the representation, as reward prediction does in latent model-based control (hafner2019planet), and such training counts toward the adaptation cost. SayCan combines language-model proposals with value functions that estimate whether learned robotic skills can be executed (ichter2023saycan), so its choices are limited to the skills it already has. When a required interaction is missing or no longer works, the task structure can isolate it as a local learning problem, and the agent can acquire or revise that interaction without relearning the whole task. The new competence then becomes available for other combinations, although any solution built from it still requires physical validation.

Interactive Validation

The agent tests the candidate solution under the physical conditions in which it must work. Limited probes, which must themselves respect force, motion, and safety limits, can reveal resistance, contact constraints, or errors in the state estimate. Predicted trajectories can be checked against task goals and safety constraints before execution (wabersich2021predictive), but only real feedback shows whether the predictions and constraint estimates hold. Inner Monologue uses success detection, scene descriptions, and human feedback to revise robotic plans (huang2023inner). Feedback may also show that the diagnosis itself was wrong and send the agent back to assessment or characterization. A successful recovery resolves the immediate difficulty but remains episodic adaptation unless its benefit is consolidated.

Knowledge Consolidation

The system retains useful experience in a form that can inform later decisions, whether in policies, world models, memory, or executable procedures. Verified constraints and failed strategies are worth retaining alongside successful actions, together with the conditions under which each applies, so that retrieval can judge whether a skill fits the current situation. Consolidation need not take place in model weights. Voyager keeps executable skills in a retrievable library without fine-tuning its underlying language model (wang2024voyager), although its Minecraft setting leaves open how the approach would fare on physical robots. In robotics, RECAP improves $\pi^{*}_{0.6}$ over successive rounds of data collection and training that use autonomous experience and human corrections (Amin et al., 2026). Neither system constitutes a fully autonomous lifelong-learning process, and establishing persistent capability expansion for either would require the longitudinal evidence specified in Section 10.1.

This account extends generalization from unfamiliar samples and task combinations to the whole perception, cognition, decision, and action system. The four capability dimensions specify which improvements to assess, and the five functions describe how experience can produce and preserve them. Because actions can obtain the evidence needed to revise a model or establish a new solution, the functions also connect systematic generalization to physical inquiry. Collaboration with people, the second pathway, supplies another source of such evidence, as well as a setting in which the resulting competence must work.

## 10.3 Human-AI Collaboration and Social Intelligence

The second pathway relaxes the assumption that a person specifies the task and the robot merely executes it. When people and robots share a task, both act on the world, and each changes the conditions under which the other can proceed. One partner’s operation may change access to the workspace, the state of an object, or the support needed for a later action, so a robot can carry out its own step correctly and still leave its partner unable to continue. Joint execution therefore requires coordination between two active participants, and the robot must consider how its actions affect the person as well as the objects and the environment.

Coactive Design distinguishes individual taskwork from the teamwork needed to manage interdependence (johnson2014coactive). Its requirements of observability, predictability, and directability concern access to relevant information, expectations about the other participant’s actions, and the ability to influence the interaction. For a robot, this means making its progress and limitations visible enough for the person to respond as the task unfolds. The participants need the information and physical conditions required to act, not identical internal models or continuous verbal communication.

How an action is performed also matters for coordination. Dragan and colleagues distinguish predictable motion, which matches what an observer expects given a known goal, from legible motion, which helps the observer infer the goal (dragan2013legibility). Their experiments show that motion design affects collaboration even when the movements accomplish the robot’s immediate task (dragan2015motion). A trajectory both changes the physical state and informs the partner’s next action, and a robot should choose how to move with both effects in mind.

At the task level, Chaski selects and schedules robot actions within a shared plan, accounting for the human’s progress and idle time (shah2011chaski). The person need not command each step, yet the person’s own choices still constrain when the robot can act and which operations can follow. Scheduling should therefore aim at joint progress rather than at finishing the robot’s own work as quickly as possible.

In direct physical interaction, the participants’ control behaviors are coupled as well. Li and colleagues combine estimation of the human’s control strategy with a differential-game controller (li2019differential), treating human behavior as part of the coupled dynamics rather than as a fixed trajectory or an external disturbance. Many collaborations involve no direct contact, however, and do not need this form of control.

Coordination can also change with repeated interaction. Nikolaidis and colleagues model uncertainty about how willing a person is to adapt and incorporate it into the robot’s decision-making (nikolaidis2016mutual). In cross-training, participants swap roles to improve coordination within a shared plan (nikolaidis2013crosstraining). Both methods help the partners’ actions fit together during a task, but improvement within one encounter remains episodic unless it is shown to persist or transfer.

Evaluating these interactions therefore requires attention to how the work is coordinated as well as whether it is completed. Hoffman’s notion of collaborative fluency describes how well the participants’ activities mesh and treats it as distinct from task efficiency (hoffman2019fluency). Useful measures include task outcomes, coordination delays, and the effort needed to keep the interaction working. The person’s physical work is part of the joint task and should be reported separately from effort spent compensating for avoidable system shortcomings.

Tests of generality should vary the collaborators as well as tasks and environments, since performing well with a familiar partner does not demonstrate the same ability with a new one. Evaluations should report prior joint training and the additional coordination needed when the pairing changes, separate team competence from the robot’s own competence, and identify gains that come from changes in human behavior. The resulting evidence characterizes the capability boundary of the team and the cost of forming new coordination, which a count of predefined collaborative routines cannot capture.

The longer-term goal proposed here is a physical collaborator that takes part in developing a project instead of merely executing delegated movements. Such a system would help clarify an underspecified goal, explain what it has learned about the environment, propose feasible alternatives, and acquire new methods through joint work. In a repair or construction project, the person and the robot might diagnose a problem together, redesign part of the procedure, and verify the result. Collaboration in this sense concerns participation in shared reasoning and action and does not require a human-like appearance. It also makes the preservation of human initiative, understanding, and authority a design requirement for future Physical AI systems.

Such projects can run for weeks under changing conditions. The system would need to remember why earlier decisions were made, distinguish temporary workarounds from completed repairs, and revise its plans when new evidence undermines an earlier assumption. Shared memory would hold agreements, open questions, and causal context in addition to observations, so that later actions build on earlier decisions instead of treating each encounter as a new task. Such projects rarely involve a single robot, and the same need for shared context arises when competence is distributed across several bodies.

## 10.4 Multi-Agent Systems and Collective Physical AI

The third pathway relaxes the assumption that the robot acts alone in a single body. Once several embodied agents are involved, the organization of physical competence becomes a question about the group. This chapter defines collective Physical AI as Physical AI in which a group achieves physical objectives through coordinated sensing, action, and interaction. Capability is then assessed at the level of the group and depends on how individual skills are organized, what information is exchanged, and how the bodies interact. Control may be centralized or distributed, and coordination may partly emerge from local self-organization. The number of robots and the control architecture do not by themselves indicate generality.

Members need not each possess everything the group can do. Prorok’s mixture-of-robots perspective argues for specialized, interdependent components instead of the same generalist model in every robot (prorok2025extending), which makes the distribution of competence across bodies a design choice. Shared capabilities let one member substitute for another, while specialized capabilities allow contributions tied to a particular embodiment or role (gerkey2004allocation). Bettini and colleagues report benefits from heterogeneous policies and communication in multi-robot reinforcement learning on simulated and physical tasks with heterogeneous requirements (bettini2023heterogeneous), although their results do not show that diversity by itself improves performance. Specialization enables complementary action but also makes the group depend on particular members.

Pooling robot experience to train a policy is a different use of multiple bodies. Shared data can improve a policy that each robot later runs on its own, without any coordinated behavior at deployment. Collective competence instead rests on what members achieve by acting together. Assessing it means measuring how much the observation, manipulation, or control conditions provided by their organization contribute to the outcome.

Such organization depends on coordinating information, since a single robot’s observations may not suffice for the group’s decisions. Tolstaya and colleagues train local controllers by imitating a centralized controller that has global information during training, and at execution time the learned controllers rely on local observations and communicate over graphs that change as the robots move (tolstaya2020decentralized). CoViS-Net pools visual information across robots for relative pose estimation and has been evaluated in real-world multi-robot formation control (blumenkamp2025covis). As robots move, the observations available for later decisions and the coordinated actions that remain feasible change with them (olfatisaber2007consensus). The system must decide what to communicate, when local information is sufficient, and how missing or inconsistent information affects group behavior. Members’ internal representations need to support the task but need not agree in every detail. Evaluations should distinguish the information available during training from that available at deployment.

Sensing networks extend this organization beyond the sensors on individual robots. The term sensing network here denotes connected sensing resources distributed across agents, objects, and environmental infrastructure, building on research on cooperative observation through distributed sensing, local processing, and communication (Akyildiz et al., 2002). A sensing node need not be an autonomous agent. It contributes information about physical conditions that another component needs to understand or act on. The research opportunity for collective Physical AI is to organize such networks around the decisions and interventions they support. In an instrumented workshop, a fixed sensor might detect a change outside a robot’s field of view, a mobile agent might approach to resolve the uncertainty, and a manipulator might then test or repair the affected mechanism, which in turn changes what the network needs to observe next. This requires tracking the origin, timing, and uncertainty of each observation, maintaining local operation when communication or sensing fails, and keeping access to observations of people and shared spaces subject to explicit authorization.

Bodies and environmental structure can also coordinate collective behavior without any explicit exchange of plans. In TERMES, Werfel and colleagues derive locally executable rules whose execution by robots with local sensing produces a specified global construction, with coordination passing through the changes the robots make to their shared environment (werfel2014collective). In particle robotics, Li and colleagues build loosely coupled particles that cannot move individually but move collectively through local oscillations modulated by a global signal (li2019particle). No single component executes a complete locomotion policy, so describing such a system requires an account of its contact relationships and spatial organization as well as its controllers.

Understanding collective behavior thus involves both predicting the outcomes of local interactions and designing interactions that achieve a given objective. Stable behavior under one set of conditions shows only that a particular mechanism works. Generality requires further evidence that the relationship between local behavior and global outcome can be maintained or adjusted when objectives, component capabilities, or physical conditions change. Physical coupling belongs in this analysis as a mechanism whose contribution to task competence needs to be measured.

That relationship also depends on the membership of the group. Stone and colleagues formulate ad hoc teamwork as collaboration without prior coordination, distinguishing cooperation within an established team from cooperation with unfamiliar partners (stone2010adhoc). In a physical group, a member that leaves or is impaired may remove an observation, a manipulation capability, or a source of support on which the task relies, and reassigning task labels cannot restore these conditions. Reconfiguration must find a feasible organization of the remaining capabilities or recognize that none exists.

Scalability, resilience, and generality therefore need separate evidence. Scalability concerns effective operation as group size changes, resilience concerns preserving or restoring function after disruption, and generality requires testing unfamiliar combinations of members, capabilities, and task dependencies. Comparisons should account for hardware, computation, communication, and preparation costs, because adding resources can raise performance without any improvement in how they are organized. Collective generality is ultimately judged by the group’s capability boundary and by the cost of establishing the relationships it requires.

Looking further ahead, collective Physical AI could operate at the scale of a home, a laboratory, or an infrastructure network, with sensing resources tracking local conditions while heterogeneous agents investigate, maintain, and repair different parts of the environment. An observation made by one component could guide an experiment carried out by another, and the resulting knowledge could inform work elsewhere. Its physical reach would depend on the relationships among models, bodies, people, and infrastructure, without every component being generally intelligent or every decision being made centrally. The research challenge is to keep evidence, decisions, and physical consequences consistent as sensing and action pass between components. A related question is how the participating systems might help improve the knowledge, skills, and physical organization on which their collective competence rests.

## 10.5 Autonomous Evolution

The fourth pathway relaxes the assumption that people design and run the learning process and fix the system’s physical configuration. In both individual and collective settings, the question is then how a system can take part in developing its own competence over time. Here, self-evolution of Physical AI denotes the sustained development of physical understanding, prediction, and action through experience that the system increasingly helps to select, acquire, and use. Its objectives, authorization, and resource limits remain explicit. The definition includes learning with a fixed body and with ongoing human support, and it requires neither biological evolution nor unrestricted self-modification. Progress is measured by lasting changes in physical competence.

Tegmark’s Life 3.0 offers a broader frame for this possibility (tegmark2017life). In this conceptual classification, Life 1.0, exemplified by bacteria, has its physical organization and behavioral programs shaped largely by biological evolution. Life 2.0, exemplified by humans, retains an evolved body but acquires much of its behavioral repertoire through learning and culture. Life 3.0 is a prospective technological form of life that can redesign both its software and its hardware. The classification concerns how behavior and physical organization can change, not levels of task performance.

Within a physical system, change can occur in perceptual representations, predictions of action outcomes, knowledge of the body’s capabilities, control policies, or reusable skills, and these components may change at different rates. Bongard, Zykov, and Lipson demonstrate a robot that builds a predictive model of its own body through interactions chosen to discriminate between competing models, and that uses the model to generate locomotion before and after damage (bongard2006selfmodeling). Cully and colleagues instead use a repertoire generated before deployment to guide trial-and-error adaptation after damage (cully2015adapt). Both studies recover a lost function, which differs from acquiring a broader repertoire. Gupta and colleagues evolve morphology jointly with learned control and examine how evolved bodies affect the learnability of new tasks (gupta2021embodied), but only in simulation, so their results do not show that deployed robots can redesign their own hardware.

From the standpoint of Life 3.0, learning a new policy on fixed hardware addresses only the behavioral side. A more ambitious system would use experience to identify a physical limitation, propose a change to its sensing or actuation, and test whether the revised configuration enables new competence. Experience with deformable objects might show, for example, that a system cannot distinguish contact states with its current sensors. Instead of collecting more of the same data, it could propose an additional sensing modality, design an experiment to measure its value, and adapt its control to the new information. The studies above each supply one ingredient of such a process, whether learning, self-modeling, or body-controller co-design. Their integration would be an early technical step toward the co-development of intelligence and its physical substrate, but none of the studies achieves it, let alone artificial Life 3.0. Within authorized limits, such a process might begin with selecting tools or replacing modules and later extend to designing and validating new physical configurations.

A system that helps organize its own learning must also decide which uncertainties, interactions, and skills are worth investigating. Oudeyer, Kaplan, and Hafner use learning progress to direct exploration toward situations in which a robot’s predictive competence can improve (oudeyer2007intrinsic). High prediction error alone is ambiguous, since it may reflect a learnable regularity, noise, or missing information that the available interactions cannot supply. The value of an exploratory action lies in the learning it makes possible, and novelty is only one factor in that judgment. Observation can further reduce how much must be learned through direct intervention. V-JEPA 2 learns first from video by self-supervision and then from robot trajectories with action conditioning, a combination that supports physical planning (Assran et al., 2025). A self-directed learner can likewise use accumulated physical knowledge to select targeted interactions and keep task-specific trial and error to a minimum.

Every physical attempt changes the environment, and automatic resets are not always available. Eysenbach and colleagues learn task and reset policies jointly and use estimates of recoverability to avoid states from which recovery is difficult (eysenbach2018leavenotrace). Resets, recovery, and requests for help belong in the reported cost of learning, and the acquisition of experience must preserve the conditions under which further learning is possible.

Within these limits, current policies can also collect data for their own later training. RoboCat uses a trained multi-task robotic agent to gather experience for subsequent training iterations and evaluates adaptation across tasks and embodiments (bousmalis2023robocat). RECAP combines demonstrations, autonomous rollouts, and expert corrections to improve a vision-language-action policy (Amin et al., 2026). In both systems, tasks, data, or supervision are still supplied externally, so claims of autonomy should be tied to specific stages of the process. As the system takes on a larger role in acquiring and using experience, reliable external criteria for judging improvement need to remain in place.

Whether these learning processes help must be checked against later physical behavior, using the criteria of Section 10.1. Changes in prediction loss, policies, or memory count only if they improve later task outcomes, reduce the experience needed for further adaptation, or make previously unsupported conditions achievable, while valid skills and the ability to keep learning are retained (kirkpatrick2017ewc; dohare2024plasticity). Tests confined to the most recently practiced task cannot determine whether development is cumulative. Persistence, transfer, and autonomy each require separate evidence, since an improvement that persists may be specific to the conditions in which it was learned. Progress need not be monotonic on every task, but gains and regressions should be reported over a stated range and time horizon, together with the costs of data collection, computation, resetting, correction, and physical recovery.

The same assessments decide which updates to accept. Updates selected with success detectors, reward models, or predictive models must be checked against the physical objectives those signals stand in for, including under conditions not used to select them. A verified fallback and the option to intervene or suspend can limit the damage of an unsuccessful update, but any safety claim still rests on the assumptions under which the fallback is valid (wabersich2021predictive). Long-term development should be judged by retained physical competence and by the system’s measured role in organizing its own learning, and continued operation or repeated retraining is not evidence of either.

The horizon extends beyond continual policy improvement. A developing Physical AI system would take a growing part in deciding what to investigate, which capabilities to acquire, and which tools or bodily configurations would enable further progress, and each change to its means of interaction would open new opportunities for understanding. This reciprocal development, more than learning alone, gives the Life 3.0 analogy its concrete content.

## 10.6 Toward the Ultimate Goal of Physical AGI

The preceding subsections examine how Physical AI might extend its capability boundary. This subsection considers what such an extension could enable, with Physical AGI as a long-term research goal. Two prospects illustrate why extending this capability boundary could matter. The first is scientific discovery, where claims about the physical world will ultimately be tested against empirical evidence. The second is engineering at scales, levels of precision, and speeds beyond direct human capability, or in environments inaccessible to people. In both domains, the examples discussed below illustrate progress within problem settings and infrastructures largely defined by people. The prospect envisioned here is a shift toward more open-ended spaces, where systems can formulate new problems, revise their approaches, and test solutions through physical interaction. Progress toward generality would also require transferring these abilities across unfamiliar tasks and environments, supported by coordinated advances across the four pathways discussed above.

Experimental science provides a concrete setting for acquiring knowledge through action. Its cycle of hypothesis, experiment, and revision links reasoning to empirical validation. Parts of this cycle are already automated. The Robot Scientist Adam generated and tested hypotheses in yeast functional genomics (king2009). A mobile robot chemist searched for photocatalysts using instruments built for human researchers (burger2020). Coscientist demonstrated the use of large language models to plan and run chemical experiments (boiko2023coscientist). Kitano frames the long-term aim as an AI Scientist that conducts research at the level of the best human scientists (kitano2021nobel). These experimental demonstrations establish components of autonomous inquiry, while leaving research goals and much of the experimental infrastructure under human specification.

Physical AGI points toward inquiry in which that space is itself open. Such inquiry offers no standard answer to imitate, its feedback may take months, and failure is the normal outcome. This chapter therefore identifies three necessary shifts, from data-driven learning to world interaction, from immediate feedback to long-horizon reasoning, and from imitating correct results to learning from failure. This chapter also regards embodied autonomous exploration as a necessary route to Physical AGI. Attaching a large model to a robot is not enough, because embodied intelligence requires physical feedback that keeps revising the model. Physical Recursive Self-Improvement (Physical RSI) offers a framework for investigating how experience from physical interaction can produce persistent changes to both task capabilities and the procedures that improve them (zhou2026physicalrsi). Its recursive objective is to make subsequent improvement more effective across tasks. In the vision considered here, this could contribute to Physical AGI by enabling systems to refine how they design experiments, acquire skills, and develop new tools. An artificial experimentalist must decide which uncertainty justifies an experiment, design probes that discriminate between explanations, and retain negative results with the conditions that produced them. When existing instruments cannot resolve a question, it may need to build and calibrate a new one, so that the instruments themselves become part of the space of possible designs.

Engineering illustrates how specialized robotics and control can extend human physical reach. A reinforcement-learning controller has demonstrated control over diverse plasma configurations in a tokamak (degrave2022magnetic). Research on untethered microrobots explores the potential for procedures inside the body (nelson2010microrobots). The underwater robot Ocean One has extended an operator’s visual and tactile access through teleoperation in challenging underwater environments (khatib2016oceanone). These examples illustrate specialized control, prospective medical applications, and human-robot collaboration. Extending such capabilities to unfamiliar tasks and operating conditions remains a challenge.

Physical AGI would open this space in two ways. The first is generality in operation, where a Physical AGI system running a fusion device or a planetary outpost would recognize when conditions have moved outside the scope of its controllers’ design and adapt, sometimes faster than a human engineering cycle. The second is open-ended design. When no tool or procedure solves a problem, the system would translate the goal into functional requirements, design and fabricate a candidate, and verify it under the conditions in which it must work. Such work is collective over years of operation, and people unable to act on site still set goals, weigh trade-offs, and authorize interventions. Human intent thus reaches regimes that human bodies cannot.

The two prospects share one arc, from operating within a predefined space to opening it, through new instruments in science and new tools and mechanisms in engineering. They also reinforce each other, since new instruments raise new questions and new understanding enables new engineering. Their value depends on reliable results and on actions that remain safe when they are hard to reverse. This monograph adopts the principle it calls the AI- $45^{\circ}$ Law (yang2024ai45). Over the long term, capability and safety should advance together, with short-term fluctuation permitted but neither persistently outpacing the other. For systems that operate in laboratories, power plants, and natural environments, meeting these requirements is an operational necessity as well as a responsibility of governance. AI may accelerate the expansion of knowledge, but this monograph holds that the compass of scientific exploration should remain human curiosity and human values. Physical AGI, as proposed here, would enlarge what people can investigate and build without displacing their judgment about what is worth pursuing. These capabilities have not yet been demonstrated. Today’s Physical AI systems lay the foundations, and progress toward the goal is measured by the physical results they achieve.

## 11 Evaluation, Safety, and Governance for Physical AI

Physical AI turns decisions into changes in the world, making reliable goal pursuit, bounded consequences, effective human control, and accountability essential to its practical value. This chapter develops an evidence-based framework linking physical-agent evaluation, action and system safety, and lifecycle governance. These concerns are inseparable because competence and risk emerge from interaction among models, software, hardware, embodiment, and the environment. Task completion alone cannot establish safe or autonomous operation. Evaluation and safeguards must therefore address the complete agent under specified operating conditions, with requirements proportionate to its authority and potential physical effects.

Figure 11.1 illustrates this framework around the agent’s perception-decision-action-outcome loop. Physical-world evaluators (Section 11.1) establish evidence for capability assessment, benchmarking, and application readiness (Section 11.2). These findings inform operating limits and action alignment (Section 11.3), while system safety and risk governance (Section 11.4) sustain safeguards through fault containment, monitoring, updates, and maintenance. Law, ethics, standards, and global governance (Section 11.5) provide overarching responsibilities, ethical boundaries, and oversight. Field evidence feeds back into evaluation and governance, supporting reassessment as the agent and its operating conditions change.

Figure 11.1: A prospective framework for evaluating and governing physical agents connects interaction evidence, capability assessment, action alignment, and continuous system safety assurance. Law, ethics, standards, and global coordination provide overarching obligations and oversight. Solid arrows show evidence and constraints, while dashed paths feed operational experience back into evaluation and governance

## 11.1 Physical-World Evaluators

The chapter’s approach begins with evidence about what a physical agent actually does. A physical-world evaluator observes goal-directed, autonomous or semi-autonomous interaction, compares behavior and outcomes with stated requirements, and produces judgments grounded in recorded evidence. Its evaluation unit is the complete agent acting through its embodiment and responding to environmental feedback. The physical significance of model outputs depends on their role in this closed-loop interaction. Intended behavior, issued commands, measured execution, and final physical outcomes may not align.

This section establishes a common framework for the chapter. It first organizes evaluation around reliability, safety, operational controllability, and traceability, linking these concerns to Sections 11.2 to 11.5. It then explains how evidence from the physical agent and its environment can be collected, interpreted, and combined to support assessment, diagnosis, and improvement. A cup-transfer task illustrates the connection between general evaluation objectives and concrete physical evidence.

11.1.1 Evaluation Objectives and the Chapter Framework

The Complete Physical Agent as the Evaluation Unit

Component tests remain useful within physical-agent evaluation. For example, visual recognition benchmarks such as ImageNet measure classification and detection performance (pe_imagenet). These measurements characterize a perceptual capability under specified inputs. They do not establish whether a physical agent can select a feasible grasp, execute it reliably, detect slipping, and recover without damage. RLBench extends evaluation to interactive manipulation tasks with explicit success conditions (pe_rlbench). Nevertheless, completion alone can conceal retries, human assistance, excessive contact force, or delayed damage. Achieving a goal and avoiding unwanted consequences are distinct requirements (Amodei et al., 2016).

The evaluation unit is therefore a complete interaction episode. Perception informs decisions, embodied action changes physical states, and the resulting observations guide subsequent behavior. The sequence perception-decision-action-outcome describes recurring stages within this feedback loop. Evaluation should examine whether the physical agent recognizes discrepancies and appropriately continues, replans, requests assistance, or stops. This perspective applies to modular and end-to-end architectures without prescribing their internal organization.

Claims about autonomy must also match the responsibilities assigned to the physical agent. A trial in which an operator selects every grasp examines a different capability from one in which the agent receives only a goal and selects its own strategy. Evaluation must state which decisions are autonomous, which information is supplied externally, and when assistance is permitted.

Four Objectives Connecting Evaluation, Safety, and Governance

The chapter develops four connected concerns introduced here. Each provides a guiding question and a principal connection to one of the following sections.

• 

Reliability (Capability Evaluation and Benchmarking
(Section 11.2))
Can the physical agent accomplish its goals repeatedly, with a declared
degree of autonomy, under specified operating conditions? This question
motivates assessment of perception, reasoning, manipulation, mobility,
long-horizon execution, and generalization. Section 11.2 develops the
capability tests, benchmarks, and application evaluations needed to
establish what the agent can do and where that competence remains
dependable.

• 

Safety (Physical Safety and Action Alignment
(Section 11.3))
Does the physical agent pursue goals within authorized and physically
acceptable limits? Successful completion may coexist with unsafe
contact, excessive force, object damage, or harmful environmental
changes. Section 11.3 examines how security, environmental safety, and
action alignment constrain the perception-decision-execution loop
so that useful behavior remains consistent with intended and permitted
consequences.

• 

Operational Controllability (System Safety and Risk
Governance (Section 11.4))
Can protective mechanisms and authorized supervision keep the physical
agent within operating limits, intervene in time, and establish an
appropriate fallback state under faults or changing conditions?
Section 11.4 develops this concern through cross-layer failure analysis,
fault containment, runtime protection, and lifecycle risk management.
Here, controllability concerns effective operational intervention,
including automatic protection and human takeover, rather than only
the availability of a stop command.

• 

Traceability (Law, Ethics, Standards, and Global
Governance (Section 11.5))
Can system configurations, decisions, actions, interventions, and
updates be reconstructed and connected to responsible actors?
Section 11.5 relates this evidence to accountability, meaningful human
control, privacy, fairness, standards, and international coordination.
Traceable records support investigation and responsibility reviews. They do not independently determine legal liability or acceptable use.

These connections identify the main emphasis of each section, while the concerns remain interdependent. Reliable capability informs operating limits. Action-safety requirements guide system protection. Traceability connects evidence from all three to oversight and accountability. Human control, for example, requires both effective intervention mechanisms and legitimate authority. Section 11.1 supplies the common evidence framework, which Sections 11.2 to 11.5 develop into capability assessment, safe action, sustained system protection, and accountable deployment.

Conditions and Limits of Evaluation Claims

Every conclusion should identify the tested embodiment, task, degree of autonomy, permitted assistance, and operating conditions, including lighting, payload, and human proximity. The evaluator’s own limitations, such as camera occlusion or missing force measurements, must also be reported. Detecting a hazard does not itself establish that the physical agent can respond safely. Communication, intervention authority, and the physical response must be assessed as well.

11.1.2 Evidence-Based Evaluation of Physical Agents

The four objectives become assessable through a connected process of specifying requirements, collecting evidence across the interaction, applying appropriate assessment methods, and using the results for diagnosis and renewed testing. This process connects component measurements to judgments about the complete physical agent.

Specify the Task and Record the Interaction

In a cup-transfer task, requirements may specify the correct cup, target region, permitted spillage, completion time, and stability period after release. Safety limits, termination rules, and permitted human assistance should be fixed before testing. Records should preserve timestamps for observations, task-relevant state estimates, selected actions, issued commands, measured motion, and interventions. Commands document intended behavior. Physical measurements establish what actually occurred.

Table 11.1 links the interaction stages to evaluation evidence. Records should also capture feedback-driven changes, such as a revised grasp, an additional observation, or a protective stop. External tracking or independently reviewed video can help check the physical agent’s own estimates. Controlled variations should test its response to disturbances. A shifted cup tests state updating and grasp adjustment, a blocked route tests replanning, and slipping tests detection and recovery.

Table 11.1: Evaluation evidence across a physical agent’s interaction episode

Stage

Evaluation question

Evidence and possible output

Perception

Does the physical agent identify and locate the target?

Reference images or tracking, selection accuracy and pose error.

Decision

Are its chosen steps feasible and responsive to feedback?

Task rules and decision logs, satisfied preconditions and appropriate replanning.

Action

Does its embodiment execute commands within constraints?

Joint, force, and tactile records, together with tracking error, slipping, and interventions.

Outcome

Is the required physical state reached and maintained?

Post-action observations, placement, stability, damage, and spillage.

Link Evidence Across Components, Embodiment, and Environment

A common timeline and configuration record should connect the physical agent’s models and decision functions, software, hardware, and integrated embodiment with its environmental conditions. Decision records reveal perception, task-relevant memory, and action selection. Software records reveal message delays and data freshness. Hardware measurements reveal sensing and actuator response. Complete-task observations reveal coordinated motion, grasping, stopping, and supervisory response. Environmental records identify changes in lighting, friction, object properties, and human activity.

These are complementary diagnostic perspectives, not a prescribed architecture. The environment remains the agent’s interaction context, while its embodiment provides the physical means of sensing and action. Dependencies beyond model code are important in machine-learning systems (pe_debt). For physical agents, their effects must also be traced through contact, motion, and feedback. Linking these records helps explain why apparently correct component outputs can still lead to an unsatisfactory physical outcome.

Apply Complementary Assessment Methods

Rules, sensor analysis, multimodal assessment, and optional world-model predictions interpret the shared record for different purposes. Models used by the evaluator are assessment tools and should be distinguished from components of the physical agent being evaluated.

Executable rules test target-region membership, speed or force limits, and prerequisites such as grasp confirmation before lifting. RLBench illustrates task-specific, machine-checkable success conditions (pe_rlbench). Physical trials require corresponding measured inputs. Each rule should specify thresholds, units, temporal scope, and the treatment of missing or uncertain measurements.

Images and depth measurements reveal position and motion, force and tactile signals reveal contact or slipping, and joint measurements reveal execution. Calibration, coordinate frames, timestamp alignment, and data loss must be checked before scoring. Estimates derived from the same sensor should not automatically be treated as independent confirmation.

Instructions and video can support judgments about object selection, action order, and task progress. RoboVQA demonstrates video-based reasoning about success, previous events, and possible future actions (pe_robovqa). Such judgments require explicit rubrics, supporting frames or timestamps, and an “uncertain” option. They should be validated against human-reviewed cases and should not override calibrated measurements that establish a physical constraint violation.

A world model may estimate the consequences of a candidate action as

 $\hat{x}_{t+1}=f_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{t},a_{t};B_{\mathrm{emb}}),$ 

(11.1)

where $\hat{x}_{t}$ estimates the joint state of the physical agent and its environment, $a_{t}$ is a candidate action, and $B_{\mathrm{emb}}$ denotes embodiment. DayDreamer demonstrates world-model-based behavior learning on physical robots (wu2023daydreamer). Related predictions may support risk assessment when their quality is validated for the relevant conditions. Predicted consequences must remain distinct from observed events. Alternative rollouts suggest hypotheses rather than independently establishing causation. World models are optional tools, not a defining requirement of physical agency.

Produce Scores with Explicit Safety and Evidence Status

Scoring rules should be fixed before testing. Binary requirements may receive $0$ or $1$ , while continuous measurements can be normalized to $[0,1]$ , with higher values consistently indicating better performance. If required evidence is sufficient and no predefined critical safety violation is confirmed, an optional aggregate is

 $\displaystyle S_{\mathrm{eval}}$ 
 $\displaystyle=100\sum_{k=1}^{K_{\mathrm{eval}}}w_{k}s_{k}^{\mathrm{eval}},$ 

(11.2)

 $\displaystyle 0\leq s_{k}^{\mathrm{eval}}\leq 1,\qquad w_{k}\geq 0,\qquad\sum_{k=1}^{K_{\mathrm{eval}}}w_{k}=1,$ 

where $s_{k}^{\mathrm{eval}}$ is a criterion score and $w_{k}$ its preselected weight. Weights apply to criteria, not to the methods supplying evidence. Missing required scores must not silently trigger weight redistribution.

A confirmed critical violation gives a failed safety assessment even if the task is completed. Missing or conflicting critical evidence gives a “review required” result unless a violation is already confirmed. In either case, withhold the aggregate while retaining individual measurements. Report completion, safety status, interventions, and evidence quality separately. Across repeated trials, state the trial count and whether completion times include only successful trials. Autonomous and assisted completion must remain distinguishable, as illustrated by RoboVQA’s treatment of cognitive and physical interventions (pe_robovqa). A high score does not establish safety outside the tested scope.

Diagnose Failures and Verify Improvements

Suppose the physical agent identifies the correct cup and selects a feasible route, but the cup slips during transport. Force and tactile records locate the onset of slipping. Video identifies the task stage. Command timestamps and actuator measurements reveal timing and grip response. Environmental observations indicate whether the cup was wet. The evaluation should also examine whether the agent detected the discrepancy, adjusted its grip, placed the cup down, requested help, or continued despite evidence of failure.

Diagnosis links the failed requirement and earliest abnormal event to these records, while separating confirmed events from possible causes. If delay is suspected, a controlled repeat can correct it while keeping the cup, route, and other conditions as consistent as practical. Persistent slipping motivates further checks of grip response and surface conditions. A language model may summarize the evidence, but its explanation requires validation. The evaluator itself should be checked for missed failures, false alarms, disagreement, and incomplete evidence.

After changes to learned components, software, or embodiment, repeat relevant component tests and complete interaction episodes. Simulation can broaden scenario coverage, while physical trials address contact and execution effects it does not reproduce. This connects evaluation to improvement of the complete physical agent and supplies evidence for the capability, safety, system-protection, and governance questions developed in the following sections.

## 11.2 Capability Evaluation and Benchmarking

Building on the evidence framework of Section 11.1, capability evaluation asks what a physical agent can accomplish, how independently it can act, and under which operating conditions its competence holds. Such competence emerges through coordinated perception, reasoning, manipulation, mobility, memory, and adaptation. Benchmarking makes these claims comparable by specifying tasks, embodiments, assistance, and resource budgets. Simulation supports scalable capability diagnosis, while real-robot evaluation provides indispensable evidence of executed behavior and physical consequences. Together, they connect capability profiles to claims about autonomous completion, execution quality, recovery, and deployment readiness.

This section develops a layered capability framework, compares simulation, real-robot, and hybrid benchmarks, and connects their evidence to application evaluation and governance. Figure 11.2 relates benchmark coverage to progressively demanding physical test settings, illustrated by autonomous laboratories, industrial production lines, and agricultural work. The discussion explains how simulation guides diagnosis, why deployment claims require physical trials, and how protocols should account for assistance, uncertainty, and operational variation. These capability boundaries provide the basis for Section 11.3’s treatment of physically safe and appropriately authorized action.

Figure 11.2: A proposed layered framework connects benchmark coverage with real-robot evaluation settings. Each benchmark is shown once at its highest represented layer, indicating partial and overlapping coverage rather than a universal difficulty ranking. Illustrative laboratory, industrial, and agricultural settings show where actions, feedback, and physical consequences must be measured. Claims of sustained deployment require closed-loop evidence from the intended working environments

11.2.1 Layered Capability Evaluation of Physical Agents

A physical agent must convert observations into feasible decisions and coordinated actions, preserve progress over time, and respond to changing conditions. The following capability layers organize these observable responsibilities without prescribing a particular internal architecture. Their integration is the central evaluation problem. An agent must select, combine, and revise its skills as a task unfolds. Generalization and adaptation apply across the layers, while sustained closed-loop autonomy requires evidence that their coordination remains reliable during operation.

The Physical Agent as the Evaluation Unit

The evaluation unit determines what a result can establish. Model-level tests assess a policy under specified observations, actions, and computational resources. System-level tests assess the coupled sensing, decision-making, control, hardware, and protective functions of the physical agent. Application-level tests add sustained workflows and the human effort needed to maintain service. Fixed-platform comparisons help isolate policy differences. Cross-embodiment comparisons assess combined model and hardware capabilities. Reports should identify which responsibilities are autonomous and which depend on external software or operators. Where accessible, both proposed and executed actions should be recorded to reveal interventions by protective controllers. Capabilities outside an embodiment’s scope should be marked as not applicable, with the supported operating conditions stated.

Perception and Active State Understanding

Perception evaluation concerns task-relevant geometry, affordances, and interaction states under partial observability. Recognizing a container, for example, does not establish whether its handle is obstructed or its grasp is stable. Tests should examine whether the agent changes viewpoint or performs a permitted diagnostic action when observations are insufficient. Controlled changes in occlusion, lighting, calibration, and latency can reveal state-estimation accuracy, responses to uncertainty, and the cost of acquiring useful information. Required precision should be determined by the subsequent physical operation.

Reasoning and Physical Consequence Prediction

Reasoning evaluation examines goal interpretation, prerequisite recognition, feasible action sequences, and revision after unexpected outcomes. Embodied Agent Interface distinguishes goal interpretation, subgoal decomposition, action sequencing, and transition modeling (li2024embodied). Agent-level claims require testing these decisions through execution. Paired trials can preserve visual appearance while changing mass, friction, or physical constraints, revealing whether decisions respond to their consequences. Verbal explanations alone provide limited evidence of physical understanding. Behavioral tests establish whether an agent acts appropriately without assuming a particular internal representation.

Manipulation and Adaptive Physical Interaction

Manipulation evaluation spans grasping, placement, assembly, tool use, compliant contact, and deformable-object handling. A capable agent should adjust its interaction strategy as physical properties become observable. Tests can vary mass, friction, stiffness, geometry, tolerance, and pose while measuring placement accuracy, contact forces, damage, and output conformance. Unfamiliar tools and altered contact conditions further test whether strategies transfer beyond practiced object-action combinations.

Mobility and Embodied Coordination

Mobility evaluation covers navigation, obstacle avoidance, transport, balance, and whole-body coordination under changes in payload, floor conditions, and clearance. Successful navigation must deliver a usable configuration for the next operation. Reaching a room while remaining beyond grasping range leaves the workflow incomplete. Tests should therefore assess route choice and final base pose together with subsequent interaction, including revisions when access or stability changes.

Long-Horizon Goal Pursuit and Memory

Long-horizon evaluation examines subgoal formation, progress verification, memory, and transitions between operations. CALVIN evaluates supplied chains of language-conditioned manipulation tasks (mees2022calvin). Autonomous decomposition of a high-level objective imposes additional responsibilities. Tests with interruptions, delayed observations, or revised goals can assess whether the agent preserves valid achievements, updates its task state, and avoids unnecessary repetition. Complete-workflow success and dependence on assistance remain essential measures. Multiplying isolated skill success rates does not generally predict mission reliability, because sensing errors, state changes, and recovery decisions couple successive operations.

Generalization and Learning Through Interaction

Generality must be evaluated under declared shifts in objects, sites, physical properties, task compositions, and embodiments. LIBERO studies transfer and retention during sequential learning (liu2023libero). Frozen-policy transfer, budgeted adaptation, and task-specific training should be reported as distinct evaluation conditions. Learning through interaction additionally requires measuring how efficiently experience improves later decisions and whether prior competence is retained. Data, compute, interaction, and memory budgets make these improvements interpretable. Held-out task compositions test whether familiar capabilities can be reorganized without demonstrations of the complete workflow.

Capability Integration and Diagnostic Tests

Table 11.2 connects capability claims to controlled tests and observable evidence. Isolated trials help locate weaknesses. Integrated missions test coordination under dependencies and uncertainty. A failed retrieval, for example, may originate in perception, planning, navigation, contact control, or their interaction. Diagnosis requires interventions that distinguish these explanations.

Controlled substitutions and matched interventions can support diagnosis, provided any privileged information or external assistance is declared. Systematic variation in visibility, precision, contact complexity, task dependencies, and disturbance magnitude helps establish an operating envelope. The resulting profile should distinguish limitations in individual skills from failures of coordination, rather than infer general physical competence from an aggregate success score.
