Recent simulation suites broaden this coverage. LIBERO-Plus introduces seven perturbation families to expose vulnerabilities hidden by nominal success (fei2026liberoplus). RoboCasa365 expands household mobile-manipulation tasks and supports multiple learning protocols (nasiriany2026robocasa365). The 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge evaluates 100 household workflows using goal-predicate completion and efficiency measures under onboard-observation restrictions (behavior2026challenge). Comparisons should distinguish the full task catalog, the evaluated task panel, and the available training resources, since these quantities describe different aspects of coverage.

RoboLab is a robot- and policy-agnostic simulation platform built on Isaac Lab. Its RoboLab-120 suite comprises 120 tasks organized around visual, relational, and procedural competencies (yang2026robolab). Its analysis extends binary success with graded completion, execution errors, trajectory quality, and sensitivity to environmental variation. The reported evaluation emphasizes policies trained on real-world data without task-specific simulation co-training. These results characterize transfer into a controlled simulated domain. Deployment performance still requires physical validation.

EBench diagnoses generalist manipulation policies through 26 tasks covering mobile pick-and-place, mobile long-horizon execution, and fixed-base dexterous manipulation (gao2026ebench). It decomposes results by scene, atomic skill, temporal horizon, precision, and operating mode, and evaluates controlled shifts in backgrounds, objects, instructions, and their combinations. Success and partial-progress scores reveal capability differences concealed by aggregate performance. The authors do not claim that these simulation scores predict real-robot performance. The suite provides reproducible diagnosis before physical evaluation.

Real-Robot Benchmarks: Direct Physical Evidence

Real-robot benchmarks address physical validity while improving diversity, repetition, and access. RoboArena aggregates distributed double-blind comparisons, using the DROID platform in its reported implementation (Atreya et al., 2025; khazatsky2024droid). AutoEval automates trial scheduling, success detection, and resets (zhou2025autoeval). RoboChallenge provides shared remote robots, while Table30 V2 revises task coverage and held-out evaluation factors (yakefu2025robochallenge; ma2026table30v2). NIST assembly tests and RoboCup@Home relate measurements to industrial and domestic requirements (kimble2020assembly; iocchi2015robocuphome). Their results remain conditional on the selected physical tasks and protocols.

RoboDojo combines simulation and physical evaluation in one infrastructure, with 42 simulated tasks and 18 physical tasks across three real robot embodiments (chen2026robodojo). Its simulation dimensions cover generalization, memory, precision, long-horizon execution, and open-vocabulary instruction following. Success and partial-progress scores expose different failure patterns, while Open tasks exclude task-specific simulation demonstrations. The simulated and physical suites provide complementary coverage rather than one-to-one matched task pairs. A shared interface therefore improves evaluation access and consistency without, by itself, measuring direct sim-to-real transfer.

Why Real-Robot Evaluation Is Indispensable

Simulation permits controlled variation, inexpensive repetition, and targeted diagnosis. Even high-fidelity simulation evaluates a computational representation whose contact parameters, sensing model, actuator response, and timing require physical validation. SIMPLER demonstrates useful simulation-real correspondence within validated settings (li2024simpler). Such correspondence supports screening within that regime rather than unrestricted extrapolation. EBench similarly reserves deployment claims for subsequent physical evaluation (gao2026ebench). The value of simulation lies in exposing hypotheses and weaknesses that can then be examined on the deployed system.

Real-robot evaluation is indispensable because it observes the coupled physical system whose deployment performance is being claimed. A simulated placement may succeed while a physical cup slips because surface properties, grip response, or command timing differ from the model. Physical trials can measure contact forces, object damage, sensing errors, stopping behavior, and recovery effort, including consequences that persist after the last commanded motion. They also reveal the operational costs of resets, interventions, wear, and downtime. This evidence records what the hardware executed and what happened in the world.

Physical evidence remains bounded by the tested conditions and exposure. A laboratory demonstration does not establish unrestricted field autonomy, and incident-free trials do not establish universal safety. A credible evaluation strategy combines simulation screening, standardized physical trials, and external or distributed sites, with uncertainty and coverage reported explicitly. Relative rankings, complete-task success, and partial-progress scores answer different questions and should be interpreted within their respective protocols.

Capability Coverage and Progressively Demanding Physical Settings

Figure 11.2 organizes evaluation from perception and feasible decisions to coordinated manipulation, mobility, long-horizon execution, and sustained autonomy. This ordering is a guide to increasing integration and responsibility, not a universal difficulty scale. A precision assembly task may be harder than a particular long-horizon mission. The physical settings on the right show how each responsibility can be tested through observable actions and consequences.

Each benchmark is displayed once at the highest layer probed by its represented task scope, with RoboDojo identified as a hybrid suite. Placement indicates evidence for dimensions within a layer, not comprehensive coverage or mastery by evaluated agents. Suites shown at higher layers may also test underlying skills, while generalization cuts across the framework. The open gap at the top concerns sustained field autonomy, which episode-level success and robustness tests cannot establish on their own.

Physical settings make these responsibilities observable through controlled changes and integrated work. Cluttered observation tests sensitivity to occlusion, lighting, and calibration. Changed prerequisites test feasibility and replanning. Contact-rich tasks vary fit, friction, payload, and compliance, while shared-space work varies routes, access, and human activity. Interrupted workflows probe memory, resumption, and recovery. Sustained operation across jobs, sites, and days adds evidence about adaptation, wear, service quality, and human effort. The application illustrations show possible working environments rather than results from a particular benchmark.

Simulation can test reasoning, memory, generalization, and long-horizon behavior within its modeled domain. Physical trials establish whether those capabilities remain effective under the coupled sensing, contact, timing, and operational conditions of deployment. Resuming a simulated sequence, for example, does not establish recovery after a fixture moves, a sensor drifts, or an operator changes the job. Sustained autonomy, useful adaptation, and dependable recovery require closed-loop validation on real robots in the working environments covered by the claim. Simplified scenes provide initial measurements. Integrated and longitudinal trials examine whether these measurements support dependable service.

A Real-Robot Evaluation Workflow

The following workflow synthesizes standardized, automated, and distributed evaluation approaches (zhou2025autoeval; Atreya et al., 2025; ma2026table30v2). It is a proposed procedure for this section, rather than the official protocol of every listed benchmark.

1. 

Declare the protocol. Fix goals, quality requirements, operating conditions, model and system versions, training exposure, trial budgets, permitted retries, assistance, and termination rules. Specify whether the claim concerns frozen-policy transfer, adaptation, or a complete product system.

2. 

Calibrate and prepare. Check sensors, coordinate frames, timestamps, control interfaces, end effectors, payloads, and protective functions. Prepare reproducible initial states and record unavoidable variation. Keep calibration and operator preparation distinct from autonomous task execution.

3. 

Execute and record. Run repeated closed-loop trials under the stated protection and supervision. Log observations, proposed and executed actions where accessible, physical outcomes, stops, failures, retries, and all interventions. Preserve unsuccessful episodes and verify the state after each reset.

4. 

Adjudicate and measure. Validate success detectors against independently reviewed physical evidence. Report autonomous completion, execution quality, forces or damage where relevant, intervention burden, recovery, and resource use. Automated scoring and reset errors require their own assessment (zhou2025autoeval).

5. 

Replicate and report. Randomize or counterbalance policy order and repeat across days, task variations, embodiments, or sites as required by the claim. Report uncertainty, exposure, exclusions, and per-condition results. Use discrepancies and field failures to refine scenarios, models, and subsequent physical tests.

Challenges of Authentic Physical Evaluation

Authentic physical evaluation faces variation that a nominal reset cannot eliminate. Object placement, friction, lighting, battery state, temperature, calibration, and wear may change during a campaign. Reset success must therefore be verified, and comparisons should control or record these changes. Distributed evaluation increases environmental coverage, but site and operator differences require stratified reporting (Atreya et al., 2025). Shared hardware and remote access improve comparability without removing dependence on the tested task distribution.

Protective functions and human intervention also affect what trials reveal. A stop may prevent harm while leaving the outcome of the unmodified policy unknown. Reports should distinguish proposed actions, applied safeguards, observed outcomes, autonomous recovery, appropriate handover, and assisted completion. Cost and safety exposure constrain sample size, especially for long-horizon and contact-rich tasks. These constraints motivate targeted scenario selection, validated measurements, transparent trial budgets, and uncertainty estimates. They do not make simulation a substitute for deployment evidence.

Limitations of Current Physical Agent Benchmarks

The first limitation is incomplete assignment of autonomous responsibility. Supplied instruction chains, fixed catalogs, prepared initial states, and external resets may leave goal decomposition, preparation, and sustained recovery outside the test. RoboDojo adds memory and open-task evaluation, while BEHAVIOR extends household workflows, but no listed result alone establishes broad, continuing autonomy. Reports must identify which responsibilities the agent actually performs.

The second limitation is restricted evidence about generalization and physical understanding. High success in familiar settings may depend on narrow scene or instruction distributions. LIBERO-Plus exposes fragility under controlled perturbations (fei2026liberoplus). Visual variation, altered physical properties, novel task compositions, and new embodiments test distinct forms of transfer. Evaluation should separate these factors, examine their interactions, and establish whether observations and instructions influence behavior when they change the required action.

The third limitation is incomplete comparability and consequence measurement. Training exposure, sensor access, retry budgets, evaluators, and hardware can alter scores independently of policy competence. Repetition improves precision within tested conditions but does not automatically broaden coverage. Success and progress measures also leave execution quality, efficiency, safety, recovery burden, and uncertainty only partly characterized. Episodic trials with fresh resets provide limited evidence about accumulated failures, retained memory, and adaptation during prolonged operation.

A Framework for Future Physical Agent Benchmarks

Future benchmarks should link capability claims to a declared coverage matrix spanning goals, physical conditions, embodiments, and consequences. Three complementary test levels are needed: diagnostic skill trials, integrated missions in intended working environments, and longitudinal sequences of changing tasks. High-level goals, partial observations, interruptions, and recoverable failures should be introduced under specified initial conditions, assistance rules, and acceptance criteria. Coverage can then be assessed against the intended application domain.

Stable anchor tasks support comparisons over time, while sequestered missions and controlled interventions test generalization and adaptation. Holdouts should cover the sites, object families, physical properties, and task compositions relevant to the claim. Frozen-policy, budgeted-adaptation, and continual-learning tracks need distinct rules for exposure and memory retention. Matched interventions can probe consequence-sensitive decisions and active information acquisition. Adaptive challenge selection requires reproducible rules and comparable resource budgets.

Evidence should connect simulation, genuinely matched physical trials, and independent sites, identifying where correspondence holds and where rankings change. Hybrid suites with different simulated and physical tasks provide complementary coverage rather than matched transfer measurements. Consequential weaknesses found in simulation should guide physical tests, which should be repeated after changes to sensing, contact, timing, or protection. Reports should combine autonomous task completion with efficiency, quality, robustness, safety, recovery, and adaptation cost. Success detectors and resets need independent validation, and partial progress remains diagnostic when mandatory conditions fail. Eq. (11.5) specifies the protocol fields needed to document these comparisons.

Maintained benchmarks also require declared roles, exposure records, controlled feedback, adjudication procedures, uncertainty estimates, and reviewable trial evidence. Changes to tasks, hardware, or scoring should be versioned and connected through anchor comparisons. Operational failures should inform revision. These proposed requirements extend a benchmark from a static score to a maintained account of what an agent can do, how efficiently it adapts, and where its reliability has been established.

11.2.3 Application Evaluation and Governance for Physical Agents

Application evaluation turns capability evidence into a decision about a defined product role. Evaluation governance makes that evidence traceable and comparable across scenarios, embodiments, and tasks. The connection depends on explicit responsibilities, measurable physical outcomes, and clearly bounded deployment claims.

Application Evaluation in Product Scenarios

Product evaluation begins with the intended workflow, users, operating environment, and accepted output. It specifies autonomous responsibilities, permitted human involvement, quality tolerances, resource budgets, and conditions for stopping or handing over control. Acceptance concerns the integrated model-software-hardware-embodiment-environment system. A successful motion matters only if it delivers the required physical result under those conditions. Simulation can guide stress-case selection and development, while acceptance requires trials on the physical configuration and operating conditions covered by the claim.

Success, quality, efficiency, and reliability should be assessed together. For $N_{\mathrm{eval}}>0$ protocol-valid trials, including unsuccessful executions, let $Y_{i}^{\mathrm{aut}}=1$ when the agent meets all goal and quality requirements within budget, without assistance in its assigned autonomous responsibilities, and let $Y_{i}^{\mathrm{aut}}=0$ otherwise. The observed autonomous completion rate is

 $\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{aut}}=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{eval}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{eval}}}Y_{i}^{\mathrm{aut}}.$ 

(11.3)

First-attempt success, completion after autonomous retries, and assisted completion should be reported separately. Appropriate handover should be scored according to the product workflow. Complementary measures include accepted outputs per scheduled operating hour, energy and human effort per accepted output, availability, and execution quality. Resource accounting must include failed attempts, resets, and recovery, with external evaluation overhead identified separately. Mandatory quality and safety conditions remain acceptance requirements rather than tradeable additions to a success score.

Product trials should vary objects, illumination, access, payload, and equipment availability according to the intended operating distribution. Immediate robustness should be distinguished from improvement after permitted adaptation. For $N_{\mathrm{rec}}>0$ prescribed recoverable-failure trials, let $Y_{j}^{\mathrm{rec}}=1$ when the agent detects the failure and restores acceptable progress within budget, and let $Y_{j}^{\mathrm{rec}}=0$ otherwise. The observed recovery rate is

 $\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{rec}}=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{rec}}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{\mathrm{rec}}}Y_{j}^{\mathrm{rec}}.$ 

(11.4)

Undetected failures remain in the denominator. Required safe termination should be assessed separately from recovery. Recovery time, additional effort, naturally occurring failure frequency, and intervention-free operating time help establish whether repeated task completion can support dependable service.

Industrial evaluation emphasizes assembly quality, cycle time, and tolerance variation. NIST task boards provide reproducible test artifacts (kimble2020assembly). Household evaluation combines navigation, manipulation, and interaction under unfamiliar layouts and changing requests, drawing on RoboCup@Home (iocchi2015robocuphome). Autonomous laboratories additionally require procedure ordering, sample identity, precision, contamination control, and traceability. Agricultural work adds changing crop geometry, access, and handling requirements. Across these domains, integrated trials should test whether the agent diagnoses disruptions, preserves valid progress, revises its workflow, and seeks appropriate assistance while meeting product requirements.

Unified Evaluation Governance Across Diverse Settings

A common evidence framework can support scenario-specific evaluation modules. Shared definitions establish task terminology, metric meanings, protocol fields, assistance rules, and evidence requirements. Each module specifies its goals, difficulty, operating distribution, and acceptance thresholds. NIST’s test-method program illustrates the separation of repeatable capability measurements from mission-specific performance requirements.99
 9

 NIST, Performance of Emergency Response Robots, program overview. This principle supports comparability while preserving the physical requirements of different applications.

A task protocol can be represented as

 $\mathcal{B}_{k}^{\mathrm{bench}}=(\mathcal{G}_{k},\rho_{k}^{\mathrm{init}},\mathcal{I}_{k}^{\mathrm{io}},\mathcal{H}_{k},\mathcal{C}_{k}^{\mathrm{ctrl}},\mathcal{U}_{k}^{\mathrm{budget}},\mathcal{M}_{k}^{\mathrm{meas}},\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\mathrm{log}}),$ 

(11.5)

where $k$ indexes a specified task-scenario-embodiment condition. The components are, respectively, goals and quality requirements $\mathcal{G}_{k}$ , the initial-state distribution $\rho_{k}^{\mathrm{init}}$ , observation-action interfaces $\mathcal{I}_{k}^{\mathrm{io}}$ , hardware and calibration $\mathcal{H}_{k}$ , controllers and protective functions $\mathcal{C}_{k}^{\mathrm{ctrl}}$ , resource budgets $\mathcal{U}_{k}^{\mathrm{budget}}$ , measurements $\mathcal{M}_{k}^{\mathrm{meas}}$ , and evidence records $\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\mathrm{log}}$ . Common identifiers should connect scenarios, embodiments, tasks, and protocol versions. Sensors, end effectors, payloads, communication delays, training exposure, and adaptation allowances must be recorded so that the evaluated agent and its external support are identifiable.

Cross-embodiment comparisons should begin with shared functional outcomes. A fixed arm, mobile manipulator, and humanoid can be compared on an assembly operation when workspace access, quality requirements, and difficulty are matched. Embodiment-adapted fixtures require validation that these conditions remain comparable. Absolute physical measurements should accompany any baseline-normalized indicators. Capability profiles should declare coverage and non-applicable tests. Product assessment must still count a workflow failure when an unavailable capability is required by the claimed role.

Results should be stratified by goal type, difficulty, physical conditions, and embodiment before matched groups are compared. Per-group performance, uncertainty, and coverage should precede aggregation. Equal-task averages characterize breadth, whereas deployment-weighted averages characterize a specified use distribution. Both require a common task panel and declared weights. Denominators, exclusions, and adaptation budgets should be published, with consequential low-frequency conditions retained. Cross-platform policy transfer and independently optimized product systems also require distinct comparison tracks.

Governance assigns stewards to maintain protocols, operators to prepare trials, evaluators to adjudicate outcomes, and reviewers to examine disputes. Combined roles and conflicts should be disclosed. Automated judgments and resets need validation against independently checked trials. Randomization or counterbalancing, declared stopping rules, and treatment of clustering across sites and days make comparisons interpretable. Incident reports should state severity and exposure. For $N_{\mathrm{eval}}>0$ independent Bernoulli trials with a common incident probability, zero observed incidents yields the one-sided 95% upper bound

 $p_{\mathrm{upper}}=1-0.05^{1/N_{\mathrm{eval}}}.$ 

(11.6)

Correlated trials require an uncertainty analysis that accounts for their dependence. Limited incident-free exposure therefore supports a bounded statement about the tested regime, not a general safety guarantee.

Evidence records should link configurations, observations, actions, interventions, and judgments, with appropriate access controls for private information. Permitted learning experience must remain separate from hidden scoring feedback. Material changes to software, hardware, tasks, or scoring require versioning and targeted re-evaluation, while shared anchor tasks connect successive assessments. This structure supports both a comparable capability profile and an application-specific acceptance decision, keeping each claim tied to observed physical behavior under declared conditions.

## 11.3 Physical Safety and Action Alignment

The capability evidence developed in Section 11.2 must be complemented by constraints on how goals are pursued. In Physical AI, an erroneous decision can become motion, contact, or an environmental change before correction is possible. Safety therefore depends on the evolving relation among human intent, the agent’s decisions, physical feasibility, and permitted consequences. This includes both preventing hazards created by the agent and ensuring that actions intended to reduce existing environmental hazards do not introduce new ones. Detecting danger, possessing the means to intervene, and having authority to act are separate requirements.

This section first explains the transition from content safety to physical action safety, examining separation, contact force, energy, object integrity, persistent environmental effects, and hazardous task interpretations. It then develops multi-layer action alignment from task reasoning through planning, real-time control, and actuator safeguards. Shared action contracts connect intended effects, preconditions, operating bounds, and termination conditions across these layers. The discussion shows why successful task completion can coexist with unsafe or unauthorized behavior, and why warning, clarification, assistance, or safe termination may be appropriate outcomes. These action-level requirements provide the basis for the integrated-system and lifecycle assurance developed in Section 11.4.

11.3.1 Physical Agent Security

The security of a physical agent concerns its ability to maintain the integrity of perception, decision-making, and action under malicious interference. As defined in Chapter 8, a physical agent is a goal-directed system that integrates sensing, computation, physical embodiment, execution, and feedback. Its security cannot therefore be reduced to the robustness of an individual foundation model. An adversary may influence the agent through its observations, instructions, learned components, communication interfaces, or control commands. Unlike attacks on purely digital applications, successful interference with a physical agent may propagate into unauthorized motion, inappropriate contact, or other physical consequences. Security must consequently be considered across the complete perception-decision-execution loop.

Threat Models and Attack Surfaces

Security threats should first be distinguished from ordinary uncertainty and physical failure. For example, a sensor may produce an incorrect measurement because of noise or occlusion, whereas an adversary may deliberately manipulate the observed scene to induce a particular decision. Similarly, a policy may fail on an unfamiliar object without being attacked, while a compromised model may exhibit malicious behavior when a specific trigger appears. The distinction matters because defenses against distribution shift do not necessarily protect against an adaptive adversary. A useful threat model should specify the attacker’s objectives, accessible interfaces, permitted modifications, and intended effects on the agent. Relevant security properties include the integrity of observations and commands, authenticity of instructions, availability of essential functions, and preservation of authorized decision-making. SafeClawArena evaluates system-level security in persistent software agents, including failures arising from interactions among their components (niu2026understanding).

Adversarial Perception Attacks

Perception provides an important attack surface because physical agents depend on observations that may originate outside their trusted computational boundary. Adversarial perturbations can influence learned perception without requiring access to the model’s parameters. eykholt2018physical demonstrate that physical modifications to traffic signs can induce incorrect visual classifications under varying viewpoints and environmental conditions. Such results illustrate how deliberately constructed physical inputs may alter downstream decisions. For a physical agent, the consequences depend on the role of the compromised perception output. An incorrectly identified object may affect grasp selection, while a manipulated environmental feature may influence navigation or task planning. Possible defenses include multimodal consistency checks, temporal verification, detection of abnormal observations, and conservative responses when critical state estimates are unreliable. Their effectiveness must be established against specified attack conditions rather than assumed from improved nominal perception accuracy.

Prompt Injection and Instruction Manipulation

Physical agents increasingly use language models to interpret commands, decompose tasks, and select actions. This creates a security boundary between authorized instructions and information obtained from less trusted sources. Text detected in the environment, retrieved documents, external messages, or tool responses may contain instructions intended to redirect the agent. RoboPAIR (robey2024robopair) and BadRobot (zhang2025badrobot) investigate adversarial attacks against robotic systems controlled by large language models (LLMs), demonstrating that manipulated instructions can induce harmful physical-action decisions under the evaluated conditions. These findings motivate explicit separation between task authority and contextual information. An agent may use external content to understand its surroundings, but such content should not independently authorize new objectives, override operational restrictions, or disable protective mechanisms. Memory adds a temporal dimension to safety risks in LLM agents, as information accumulated during benign interactions can contribute to violations on later, unrelated tasks through temporal memory contamination, even without adversarial input (Al-Tawaha et al., 2026).

Model Backdoors and Supply-Chain Attacks

Security risks also arise before deployment. Physical agents may incorporate pretrained models, third-party skill libraries, training datasets, and remotely maintained software components. An attacker with influence over these resources may introduce hidden behaviors that are difficult to identify through ordinary testing. BadNets (gu2017badnets) demonstrates how malicious training procedures can insert trigger-dependent behavior into learned models while preserving apparently normal performance. This attack mechanism provides a threat model for learning-enabled components in physical agents. Practical safeguards include verifying model and data provenance, restricting component permissions, validating software updates, and testing for suspicious behavior under controlled trigger conditions. These measures should extend to the interfaces connecting learned models with executable robot skills.

Security vulnerabilities may also occur outside the learned models. Sensor spoofing, unauthorized remote commands, communication interference, and compromised middleware can modify the information or control signals exchanged among agent components. A perception model may function correctly while receiving falsified measurements, and a planner may generate valid commands that are subsequently altered before reaching the controller. Protecting the foundation model alone is therefore insufficient. Authentication, integrity checks, access control, interface isolation, and monitoring of command consistency provide complementary safeguards.

The key challenge is that attacks can propagate across layers. A manipulated observation may change a high-level objective, which leads to a plausible plan and is then faithfully executed by an otherwise functioning controller. Security evaluation should therefore examine complete attack-to-action pathways, including whether the agent detects suspicious inputs, preserves authorized objectives, rejects unauthorized commands, and prevents compromised decisions from producing unacceptable actions. Independent physical constraints provide an additional boundary when upstream components fail, but they do not replace protection against unauthorized control. Physical agent security is ultimately concerned with maintaining trustworthy agency. The agent should act according to authorized objectives despite malicious attempts to alter its perception, decisions, or execution.

11.3.2 Layered Environmental Safety and Action Alignment

Physical agents can contribute to environmental safety by perceiving hazardous conditions, selecting appropriate responses, and executing interventions that reduce physical risk. This role extends beyond ensuring that the agent itself is not attacked or compromised. The surrounding environment may contain unstable objects, moving machinery, excessive temperatures, leakage, obstructed pathways, or unsafe interactions among people and equipment. Such hazards can arise independently of the agent’s behavior. Environmental safety therefore concerns whether the agent can recognize relevant physical conditions and influence their evolution without introducing additional risks.

A physical agent’s contribution to environmental safety depends on the coordination of several capabilities. Perception provides evidence about the current state. Foundation models and task reasoning connect observations with safety objectives. Planning identifies feasible interventions. Control and actuation realize those interventions under physical constraints. Feedback determines whether the intended safety improvement has occurred. These functions may be implemented through separate modules or integrated learned policies, but their responsibilities remain distinguishable. The relevant alignment problem is to maintain consistency among human intent, agent decisions, physical feasibility, and environmental safety requirements throughout execution.

Environmental Perception and Hazard Identification

Environmental protection begins with identifying physical states that may lead to unacceptable consequences. Relevant observations include geometry, object stability, contact relationships, human proximity, equipment motion, temperature, pressure, vibration, and other process-specific variables. A single visual observation may reveal an obstruction but provide insufficient evidence about its mass or stability. Likewise, an abnormal equipment image may not establish whether a mechanical failure is developing. Multimodal sensing and temporal state estimation can provide complementary evidence, while uncertainty estimates help determine whether additional observations are required.

AnomalyGPT (gu2024anomalygpt) illustrates how vision-language models can support industrial anomaly detection and localization. Such methods provide a possible perceptual foundation for environmental safety agents, particularly when hazardous conditions have recognizable visual manifestations. However, anomaly recognition is not equivalent to hazard assessment. The system must relate the detected condition to physical consequences, operating requirements, and the potential development of the environment. A physical agent should therefore distinguish observed abnormalities from evidence-supported risks and unresolved conditions that require further inspection.

Foundation-Model Reasoning and Safety Objectives

After identifying a potential hazard, the agent must determine what response is appropriate. This requires connecting physical observations with task objectives, human intentions, operating permissions, and safety priorities. A household agent may detect a spill near electrical equipment, while an industrial agent may observe that a person has entered a machinery workspace. In both cases, the desired response depends on context rather than object recognition alone. Possible responses include warning nearby people, restricting access, delaying the current task, requesting assistance, or initiating an authorized physical intervention.

Foundation models can assist by interpreting safety-related observations and decomposing high-level objectives into executable steps. SayCan (ichter2023saycan) illustrates a mechanism for combining language-based action selection with estimates of robotic skill feasibility. For environmental protection, a related approach can associate safety-oriented skills with explicit preconditions, permitted interactions, and expected outcomes. An agent may identify that an obstruction should be removed while determining that its available manipulation skills are insufficient to move the object safely. In such cases, requesting assistance can be more appropriate than executing a semantically plausible but physically unsupported action.

Human intent and environmental safety requirements must also remain aligned. An instruction to transport an object does not authorize passing dangerously close to a person, exceeding contact-force limits, or disturbing hazardous equipment. Conversely, detecting a hazard does not automatically grant the agent permission to perform unrestricted intervention. A practical implementation can distinguish the requested objective, the agent’s authorized actions, and mandatory environmental constraints. These elements define the permissible scope within which autonomous decisions can be made.

Safety-Constrained Planning

Planning converts safety objectives into physically realizable actions. Candidate interventions should be evaluated for reachability, collision, stability, contact conditions, workspace restrictions, and possible effects on surrounding objects or people. VoxPoser (huang2023voxposer) illustrates how language-level constraints can be grounded in three-dimensional spatial representations to support manipulation planning. Such representations provide one possible mechanism for translating environmental safety requirements into motion-related objectives, although their use does not independently guarantee safe execution. Safe reinforcement learning complements planning by incorporating safety requirements into policy optimization. Constrained Policy Optimization optimizes expected return under bounds on expected discounted cumulative costs (Achiam et al., 2017), with a multi-agent extension for multi-robot control (gu2023safe).

Environmental protection requires considering both intervention and non-intervention. Moving an unstable container may reduce one hazard while increasing the probability of spillage. Similarly, an agent approaching malfunctioning machinery may expose itself or others to additional risk. A safety-aware planner should therefore compare alternative responses according to their expected consequences and uncertainty. Observation, warning, isolation, or human assistance may be preferable to direct manipulation when the available evidence is insufficient.

The admissibility of an intervention can be expressed through constraints on the predicted physical trajectory. Let $b_{t}$ denote the agent’s belief about the joint state, $\mathbf{a}_{t:t+H-1}$ a candidate action sequence, and $C_{i}^{\mathrm{safe}}$ a task-dependent safety constraint. Let $X_{t:t+H}$ denote the predicted random state trajectory under the belief and candidate actions, and let $N_{\mathrm{constr}}$ be the number of safety constraints. One possible joint chance-constrained formulation is

 $\Pr\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{constr}}}\left\{C_{i}^{\mathrm{safe}}(X_{t:t+H},\mathbf{a}_{t:t+H-1})\leq 0\right\}\,\middle|\,b_{t},\mathbf{a}_{t:t+H-1}\right)\geq 1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{risk}},$ 

(11.7)

where $H$ is the prediction horizon and $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{risk}}$ bounds the probability that at least one constraint is violated. This formulation is conditional on the validity of state estimation, dynamics prediction, and uncertainty characterization. It provides a possible planning criterion rather than a universal safety guarantee.

Control and Physical Execution

Even an admissible plan may become unsafe when environmental conditions change during execution. A person may enter the workspace, an object may slip, or the contact dynamics may differ from those assumed during planning. Low-level control must therefore monitor the actual physical state and adjust commands when motion, force, or proximity approaches a safety boundary. Control barrier functions provide one established mechanism for enforcing such constraints. Ames et al. (2017) formulate safety-critical control through barrier functions and quadratic programming, allowing nominal commands to be modified when necessary to preserve a specified safe set. Their guarantees depend on the assumptions concerning system dynamics, state information, and available control authority.

The actuator and hardware layer supplies further physical protection through joint limits, torque limits, compliant mechanisms, braking systems, and protective stops. These mechanisms bound the physical consequences of commands that pass through higher-level decision-making. They also determine which environmental hazards the agent can address. A robot may recognize a high-temperature or heavy object without possessing the mechanical protection, payload capacity, or sensing required for safe manipulation. The ability to identify a hazard should therefore not be confused with the capability to remove it.

Cross-Layer Action Alignment

Environmental safety requires these layers to operate under consistent conditions. One possible mechanism is an action contract specifying the intended intervention, required preconditions, authorized contacts, physical limits, termination criteria, and evidence needed to verify the outcome. Foundation-model reasoning identifies the safety objective, planning establishes a feasible intervention, control constrains its execution, and feedback determines whether the relevant hazard has been reduced.

This organization also clarifies why task completion alone does not establish safe behavior. An agent may remove an obstruction while damaging nearby equipment or exposing a person to another hazard. Conversely, an agent that declines direct intervention because the available evidence is insufficient may be acting appropriately. The objective is not unrestricted autonomous intervention, but the reliable realization of authorized safety objectives under physical and operational constraints.

11.3.3 Predictive Safety and Degradation

Conventional safety mechanisms often respond after a hazardous condition has been detected, for example when a collision occurs, a contact-force threshold is exceeded, or an emergency stop is activated. Such mechanisms remain necessary, but their effectiveness may be limited when physical consequences develop faster than corrective action can be applied. A more capable physical agent should anticipate risks before execution, monitor whether its assumptions remain valid, and modify its behavior while safer alternatives are still available. This progression applies both to preventing unsafe agent behavior and to protecting the surrounding environment from developing hazards.

Risk Prediction

Predictive safety begins with estimating how the physical state may evolve under candidate actions or existing environmental conditions. Geometric checks, dynamic models, contact prediction, and learned representations can assess collision, instability, excessive force, or inadequate stopping distance. The prediction horizon should reflect the relevant physical process rather than only the next control step. A grasp may remain stable during initial lifting but become unsafe during subsequent acceleration, while a navigation trajectory may become hazardous as nearby agents move. Evaluating these possibilities before execution allows the physical agent to compare actions according to their expected consequences.

For environmental protection, prediction also considers how a hazard may develop without intervention. An inspection agent may observe increasing equipment temperature or vibration, while a mobile agent may estimate whether moving objects are approaching a dangerous configuration. The agent can then compare continued observation, warning, physical intervention, and human escalation. Prediction should include uncertainty because physical environments are partially observable and their dynamics are not always known. When uncertainty can be reduced through additional sensing, the agent may change its viewpoint or acquire another measurement. When further observation is insufficient or delay is dangerous, conservative constraints or restricted operation may be more appropriate.

Self-Checking and Execution Verification

Prediction alone cannot establish safety because the predictor may itself be incorrect or compromised. A physical agent should therefore verify critical conditions before, during, and after execution. Before acting, it checks task preconditions, relevant permissions, and the current physical state. During execution, it compares observed motion, contact, and environmental changes with expected behavior. After execution, it determines whether the intended outcome occurred and whether unintended effects remain. Inner Monologue (huang2023inner) demonstrates how environmental and task feedback can inform the revision of language-based robotic plans. This provides one possible route toward closed-loop decision revision, although safety-critical conclusions still require reliable physical evidence.

Self-checking should use evidence that is sufficiently independent of the mechanism generating the action. A policy that proposes a trajectory and then evaluates its own safety using the same potentially incorrect representation provides limited protection against shared errors. Independent geometric checks, force or tactile measurements, redundant state estimates, and separately implemented monitors can expose discrepancies. For security-sensitive agents, these mechanisms can also help detect inconsistencies between authorized instructions, received observations, and executed commands.

A practical runtime process can therefore follow a predict-execute-verify cycle. The agent evaluates a candidate action, executes it while monitoring relevant constraints, and verifies the resulting state before proceeding. For environmental protection, the corresponding process extends to an observe-predict-intervene-verify sequence that identifies a potential hazard, estimates its development, selects a justified intervention, and confirms that the hazard has been reduced. If observations differ substantially from prediction, the agent should revise its plan rather than continue an obsolete action sequence.

Safe Degradation and Fallback Control

When a physical agent cannot maintain its nominal operating conditions, it should reduce its capabilities in a controlled manner instead of continuing unrestricted operation. Possible degraded modes include reducing speed, restricting workspace access, disabling contact-intensive skills, increasing human supervision, or transferring control to a simpler policy. SOTER (desai2019soter) illustrates a runtime-assurance architecture combining an advanced controller with a safety-oriented fallback controller, with switching governed by specified conditions. Such mechanisms provide a possible implementation of controlled degradation, but their guarantees remain conditional on the validity of the safety specifications and controller assumptions.

Degradation must also apply to agents performing environmental safety functions. An inspection agent with unreliable localization may continue collecting local measurements while suspending autonomous navigation near hazardous equipment. An agent that detects a dangerous condition but cannot determine a safe manipulation strategy may issue a warning or request assistance instead of intervening directly. Likewise, when the integrity of critical observations or commands cannot be established, the agent should restrict actions that depend on the affected components. The available operating modes should reflect the information and control capabilities that remain trustworthy.

Importantly, entering a degraded mode must not create a new physical hazard. Immediate stopping may be inappropriate when a manipulator is carrying a heavy load or a mobile system is maintaining dynamic stability. The agent may first need to secure the object, reduce stored energy, or reach a stable configuration. Similarly, an intervention intended to protect the environment should not be abandoned in a state that increases the original risk. Returning to normal operation should require evidence that the conditions responsible for degradation have been resolved.

Experience from near misses, rejected actions, unexpected environmental changes, and unsuccessful interventions can provide evidence about declining safety margins. These observations may reveal weaknesses that are difficult to identify through ordinary task-success measurements. They can inform improvements to risk prediction, sensing, action constraints, and regression testing. The objective is not to assume that a physical agent can prevent every failure, but to recognize emerging hazards before they produce unacceptable consequences, preserve appropriate control under uncertainty, and reduce autonomous capability when safe continuation cannot be established.

## 11.4 System Safety and Risk Governance

Action alignment for a highly intelligent physical agent depends on an integrated physical system whose sensing, computation, communication, control, actuation, and power remain adequate for the task. Even correct AI-model decisions can be undermined by delayed commands, unreliable observations, degraded actuators, or interacting failures across these layers, compromising the constraints developed in Section 11.3. Conversely, an incorrect model output need not cause physical harm if independent safeguards can constrain or prevent unsafe execution. Safety assurance must therefore examine how the complete agent detects faults, contains their propagation, and preserves an appropriate physical state. It must also account for changes in hardware condition, software, task permissions, and operating environments, because evidence from initial testing may no longer describe the deployed agent.

As illustrated in Figure 11.3, system safety and risk governance follow the three connected stages of cross-layer risk analysis, risk-driven assessment, and lifecycle safeguards. Cross-layer failure analysis first investigates how local faults propagate into hazardous physical outcomes and how independent safeguards can interrupt this process. These failure pathways then motivate system-level safety assessment, which examines observable degradation, evaluation indicators, and protective responses across the hardware and software layers of a physical agent. Beyond these immediate risks, lifecycle risk governance connects hazard analysis and pre-release verification with deployment, maintenance, and operational reassessment. Continuous safety assurance is integrated into this lifecycle perspective through runtime monitoring, protective intervention, user-facing fault communication, field feedback, controlled software updates, and physical remediation. As physical agents move toward increasingly autonomous operation in homes, factories, and public environments, these mechanisms shift safety evaluation from a one-time test result toward a continuously maintained body of evidence throughout the product life cycle. They also establish the technical records and responsibilities needed for the broader legal, ethical, and institutional governance discussed in Section 11.5.

Figure 11.3: Risk-driven framework for system safety and risk governance.
(a) Faults in sensing, software, communication, power, and actuation
can propagate through perception, control, and execution into physical hazards.
(b) The corresponding safety assessment maps perception degradation to
sensor-validity and estimator checks. It maps timing and computation faults to
latency, jitter, and command-age tests. It maps actuation or power hazards
to current, thermal, and power-loss verification.
(c) Safety evidence supports pre-deployment verification and
post-deployment monitoring, user warnings, protective intervention,
updates, maintenance, and reassessment.
Solid arrows indicate the progression from identified risks to
assessment and safeguards. The dashed arrow denotes field feedback

11.4.1 Cross-Layer Failures and Cascading Risks

Perception and Timing Cascades

A local fault becomes a physical hazard when it propagates through the perception-planning-control-actuation chain. A mobile robot moving from a dim room into strong illumination, for example, may receive temporarily saturated camera frames while automatic exposure adjusts. Industrial-camera documentation confirms that exposure changes may take effect only after subsequent frames have been acquired (baslerExposureAuto). Benchmarks of visual depth estimation further document sensitivity to lighting, sensor, and data-processing corruptions (kong2023robodepth). If these observations are treated as reliable, obstacle detection may fail and a seemingly coherent navigation decision may increase collision risk. A different cascade begins in real-time scheduling. As a hypothetical example, a controller nominally updated every 10 ms may experience a delay of 100 ms because of thread contention or blocking. Meanwhile, momentum, gravity, and contact continue to change the robot state. Research on control timing explains why execution delays must be analyzed with closed-loop dynamics rather than average processing speed alone (cervin2003timing).

Shared Infrastructure and Physical Actuation

Processor overheating may activate thermal throttling, protecting a chip while reducing the computation available for time-critical decisions (nvidiaJetsonThermal). Communication timeouts and inconsistent timestamps can make feedback stale. The need to detect communication anomalies is also well established in networked control systems (Baglietto et al., 2020). Undervoltage or power interruption may simultaneously disable multiple subsystems, making the robot’s power-loss behavior a distinct safety-verification concern. At the joint level, an unsafe position target is not identical to a motor current. A controller translates tracking error into drive demand, which a motor driver regulates under the actual mechanical load. If a joint is obstructed, persistent error may sustain high demand. Without suitable protection, overheating, transmission damage, or loss of support may follow. Existing drivers demonstrate current regulation, overcurrent protection, and thermal shutdown (tiDRV8874), while surveys of robotic fault-tolerant control document the broader need to detect and accommodate actuator faults (milecki2023faulttolerant). These functions must be verified for the specific actuator rather than assumed universally.

Containment Under Degraded Conditions

The appropriate response depends on the remaining physical capabilities. Command-age checks, watchdogs, current and torque limits, thermal protections, and independent safety supervision can interrupt some cascades, but a generic emergency shutdown may create another hazard. Abrupt removal of joint power can destabilize a balancing humanoid or cause a load-bearing manipulator to drop its payload. Safe intervention may instead require controlled deceleration, support retention, a designed braking mechanism, or an energy-independent mechanical fallback. The appropriate stopping function and residual hazards must be specified for the application, rather than inferred from the existence of an emergency-stop device (iso13850_2015; bi2021assurance). Loss-of-power behavior must be tested before deployment. Fault analysis should therefore record the initiating event, propagation path, physical consequence, and intended protective barrier. System-theoretic accident analysis complements component-oriented methods by identifying hazardous interactions that need not begin with a defective part (leveson2004accident). The resulting failure pathways provide the basis for the risk-driven safety assessment that follows. Each path must be associated with an observable precursor, a protective requirement, and a physically meaningful verification outcome.

11.4.2 Risk-Driven System Safety Assessment

From Failure Pathways to Safety Evidence

Task-success rates, perception accuracy, and tracking errors quantify useful capabilities but do not establish what happens after corrupted observations, missed deadlines, or degraded actuators. A defensible safety claim concerns the complete physical agent, its authorized tasks, the exposure of people and equipment, and the conditions under which protective functions remain effective. It should distinguish an action proposed by the model, the command actually admitted and applied, and the resulting physical state. Surveys of safety-critical robotics and safeguarding of autonomous systems identify the need to state assumptions, adopt suitable safety mechanisms, and examine evidence across heterogeneous application domains (guiochet2017survey; mueller2022safeguarding). Research on testing standards for integrated robots likewise identifies limitations of component-centered performance tests when systems combine multiple functional modules (bi2020testing). Assessment should consequently be derived from the fault pathways described above, with explicit acceptance criteria for both component degradation and end-to-end physical outcomes.

Observable Indicators Across System Layers

Perception cascades motivate tests of image saturation, dropped measurements, timestamp consistency, estimator residuals, and behavior when observations are unreliable. Robust-perception benchmarks explicitly test lighting, sensor, and processing corruptions, although they do not by themselves establish the safety of the complete robot (kong2023robodepth). Fault-tolerant robotics research also addresses failures in sensor information and state estimation (milecki2023faulttolerant). Timing cascades require tail latency, deadline-miss rate, control jitter, and command freshness. Real-time control research relates timing to closed-loop performance, while ROS 2 guidance identifies blocking, memory allocation, and priority inversion as sources of execution-time nondeterminism (cervin2003timing; ros22026realtime). Processor and supply degradation motivate thermal, clock-frequency, voltage, and interruption tests. Hardware thermal-management documentation establishes why computation may degrade under overheating (nvidiaJetsonThermal). Communication assessment should measure latency, loss, and timeout behavior, drawing on networked-control fault-detection research (Baglietto et al., 2020). Actuator assessment must examine current, temperature, joint and torque limits, stall detection, and the resulting physical response. Existing driver protections and robotic fault-tolerance studies provide corresponding engineering foundations (tiDRV8874; milecki2023faulttolerant). Table 11.5 synthesizes these candidate measurements and associated protective responses. Their thresholds and applicability should follow the robot’s risk assessment. Even published safety-related test guidance for personal care robots does not treat every test as universal (isoTR23482_2020; mueller2022safeguarding).

End-to-End Protection Verification

Measurements become safety evidence only when they are tied to the physical response of the integrated system. Fault injection should introduce exposure faults, delayed commands, packet loss, thermal or computational degradation, actuator restrictions, and loss of power under representative tasks. Systematic reviews of robotic testing, validation, and verification, together with research on integrated-robot testing, provide a foundation for selecting complementary test methods and reporting their coverage (Araujo et al., 2023; bi2020testing). Evaluation should measure detection and intervention latency, the ability to isolate a failing component, and whether the robot can enter a state whose residual risk is acceptable. Work on interpretable runtime monitoring demonstrates how predicted unsafe states can trigger corrective replanning, while safety-critical control research develops explicit constraints on admissible system behavior (difranco2020monitoring; Ames et al., 2017). Safety-related control design supplies further principles for protective functions whose effectiveness must be validated independently of the nominal policy (iso13849_2023; bi2021assurance). The goal is a traceable relationship between an identified hazard, a tested safety requirement, and the observed outcome, not a context-free aggregate safety score.

11.4.3 From Pre-Deployment Verification to Post-Deployment Safeguards

Safety-by-Design Before Delivery

Risk governance starts before a product is placed into use. Developers should identify foreseeable operating environments, human proximity, loads, task permissions, misuse, and failure combinations, then translate them into safety requirements and independent protection functions. Recent robotics safety reviews emphasize risk assessment across both design and deployment (Adesiji et al., 2026). Simulation, hardware-in-the-loop testing, cross-module fault injection, environmental stress testing, and controlled physical trials should verify both nominal performance and behavior under degraded conditions, using complementary techniques whose limitations have been surveyed in the robotic testing literature (Araujo et al., 2023). The corresponding evidence must record hardware and software versions, model or policy configuration, operating limits, residual risk, and what was not tested. ISO 12100 and ISO 13849-1 provide established foundations for machinery risk assessment and safety-related control design. ISO 13482 and ISO 10218-1 illustrate additional requirements for particular robot applications, not universal certification rules for every physical agent (iso12100_2010; iso13849_2023; iso13482_2014; iso10218_2025).

Release as an Evidence-Based Transition

Acceptance testing should validate not only whether a robot can complete its assigned tasks but whether its safety monitors, limits, fallback controllers, brakes, and any emergency energy provisions work together when a fault occurs. The need to test the integrated configuration and select risk-dependent test methods is reflected in integrated-robot testing research and application-specific ISO guidance (bi2020testing; isoTR23482_2020). A release record should link the tested product configuration to its operating envelope, protective functions, acceptance criteria, and outstanding hazards. Wear, new payloads, changed environments, repaired components, and updated policies may invalidate the assumptions documented in the release record. Post-deployment safeguards must therefore maintain and revise the evidence created before delivery rather than replace it with an unrelated monitoring process (guiochet2017survey; mueller2022safeguarding).

Runtime Detection and Protective Action

After delivery to the user or operator, the robot should monitor whether observations remain trustworthy, commands are fresh, and control deadlines are met. It should also monitor whether actuator, computing, communication, and power subsystems retain adequate capacity. Where justified by the hazard analysis, an independent safety supervisor should restrict commands or transfer control when the nominal policy is unavailable or wrong. Runtime monitoring and corrective replanning have been demonstrated for autonomous robotic operation, while control-barrier methods illustrate how physical safety constraints can be imposed on control inputs when their modeling assumptions hold (difranco2020monitoring; Ames et al., 2017). Predictive checking and measured feedback should support graduated responses, including limiting speed or workspace, disabling contact-rich actions, reducing payload, requesting confirmation, or moving into a validated protective mode. In an emergency, local protection must act within the required response time rather than wait for a user decision. The chosen safe state must respect the actual mechanics. A dynamically balancing robot or one supporting a heavy load may need controlled motion or braking before torque is removed. Protection must also recognize when insufficient power or sensing makes autonomous recovery impossible.

User-Facing Warnings and Operational Responsibility

A deployed safety system must communicate consequential faults, not merely store engineering logs. Research on human-robot collaboration identifies operator awareness and effective visual, acoustic, and other notification channels as important interface design concerns (grushko2021awareness; bi2021assurance). Operators or household users should receive an intelligible account of the affected capability, the protective action already taken, and the appropriate next step. For example, the account should explain that a joint has overheated, forceful manipulation has been disabled, and servicing is required before that function resumes. Notifications should distinguish informational maintenance advice from an urgent restriction on continued use, without exposing users to raw diagnostics they cannot interpret. In higher-risk settings, a warning may need to be paired with physical isolation, a lockout, or escalation to an authorized operator. Such interaction supports accountable operation but must not substitute for automatic, timely safety intervention.

Validated Updates and Physical Remediation

Some defects can be corrected by over-the-air (OTA) software or firmware updates, but changing perception, scheduling, control logic, or model capabilities may invalidate safety assumptions. Future update processes should verify provenance and integrity, assess hardware-software compatibility, test affected safety functions, stage deployment, and provide recovery or rollback where feasible. The software-update-management principles of UN Regulation No. 156 offer an automotive precedent, not a law automatically applicable to robots (unece2021r156). Other defects require inspection or replacement. Motors, gearboxes, brakes, sensors, batteries, and power electronics can wear or fail in ways software cannot correct. When a common defect affects a product batch, the manufacturer may need to identify affected configurations, contact users, restrict risky operation, provide repairs, or initiate a recall. Automotive recall practice offers a relevant governance analog.1010
 10

 NHTSA, Check for Recalls: Vehicle, Car Seat, Tire, Equipment. OTA maintenance is not a substitute for on-device protection during an unfolding hazard.

Continuous Improvement Across the Product Life Cycle

Incident and near-miss reports, safety-filter interventions, maintenance histories, and configuration records should connect field observations to the original hazard analysis and qualification tests. Comparing evidence across deployed robots may reveal emerging combinations of temperature, wear, environmental conditions, and task behavior that were not covered before release. Data collection should remain proportional to the safety purpose, particularly in private environments. Updated risks must result in reviewed corrective decisions, re-validation of affected configurations, and, where necessary, revised operating permissions or withdrawal from service. Linking risk analysis to subsequent tests is consistent with existing safety-assessment and robotic verification research (Adesiji et al., 2026; Araujo et al., 2023). The objective is not to guarantee the absence of all faults, but to maintain a credible and revisable basis for safe operation as physical agents and the environments in which they work continue to evolve.

## 11.5 Law, Ethics, Standards, and Global Governance

The preceding sections have examined how to evaluate the behavior and competence of physical agents, constrain their actions, and maintain safety evidence throughout operation. These technical foundations inform deployment decisions, but they do not by themselves determine who is responsible, which uses of autonomy are acceptable, or what oversight is required. Because Physical AI connects perception and decision-making to actions in the physical world, governance must address the deployed system rather than the model in isolation. Law, ethics, standards, and international coordination connect technical evidence to obligations and acceptable uses, extending the chapter’s focus from measurable behavior and safety assurance to accountable deployment.

This section first addresses responsibility allocation and traceability, then examines human control, privacy, fairness, and ethical boundaries. It next considers legal and regulatory frameworks from technical, ethical, and application perspectives, connecting these issues to safety standards and the book’s illustrative risk-tiered governance framework. Finally, it explores global cooperation through compatible evaluation evidence, incident records, and investigation procedures.

11.5.1 Responsibility Allocation and Traceability

Learning-based systems may behave in ways that designers and operators cannot fully anticipate, creating difficulties associated with the responsibility gap (matthias2004responsibility). Responsibility consequently extends beyond the person exercising immediate control. Model developers should document capabilities, limitations, and versions. Hardware manufacturers should address mechanical and electrical hazards. Integrators should validate interfaces and operating limits. Operators should maintain safeguards and intervention procedures. Maintenance providers must track safety-relevant updates and configuration changes. These engineering duties support accountability but do not themselves determine legal liability.

This allocation depends on what each party supplies or changes. For example, replacing a model, increasing permitted speed, or changing an end-effector can alter different parts of a safety argument. Documentation should identify who approved the change, which assumptions were reconsidered, and what evidence supports continued operation.

Product-liability law provides a complementary perspective. Directive (EU) 2024/2853 includes software and addresses safety-relevant updates and upgrades. Its rules apply to products placed on the market or put into service after December 9, 2026 (eu2024productliability). The significance for Physical AI is that assessment cannot stop at initial delivery. Subsequent changes may alter the behavior of the deployed system.

Accountability also depends on reconstructing what occurred. A safety-relevant event record should connect system and model identity with perception states, decisions, executed actions, safety settings, and human interventions, together with update, maintenance, and cybersecurity histories. Recording should serve investigation and safety improvement rather than unrestricted surveillance. Data minimization, access controls, encryption, and proportionate retention are therefore part of traceability design, not exceptions to it.

11.5.2 Human Control, Privacy, Fairness, and Ethical Boundaries

Meaningful human control requires more than the presence of a supervisor. A person must understand relevant capabilities and limitations, receive usable information, possess intervention authority, and have sufficient time to act. An override that cannot bring the system into a safe state within the available response time offers little practical control. Human oversight and accountability are also central to the UNESCO and OECD AI ethics frameworks (unesco2021ethics; oecd2019ai).

The appropriate form of oversight depends on the task. A supervisor may authorize a sequence in advance, monitor execution, or intervene when an exception occurs. These roles require different information and response times. Where physical dynamics are faster than human reaction, protective functions must constrain the system without waiting for an operator to diagnose the problem.

Physical sensing extends privacy concerns beyond direct users. A domestic robot may observe visitors or neighbors who have neither purchased nor authorized it. Privacy by Embodiment, used here as a design principle, connects privacy protection to sensing and actuation. Under this principle, systems should process data locally where feasible, minimize raw-data retention, protect sensitive information, and communicate active sensing and remote access. User authorization does not by itself resolve bystander exposure.

Fairness likewise concerns physical outcomes, not only balanced prediction accuracy. Differences in mobility, body characteristics, or speech may change whether users can interact safely or obtain timely assistance. Evaluation should therefore examine accessibility and failure consequences across intended users, particularly children, older people, and people requiring care. Greater autonomy does not remove the need for human judgment where actions threaten safety, dignity, or essential services. Physical AI may also displace workers, while newly created jobs may not benefit those affected. Fair deployment should therefore consider worker participation, retraining opportunities, and the equitable distribution of productivity gains (unesco2021ethics; oecd2019ai).

11.5.3 Legal and Regulatory Frameworks for Physical AI

Technique

Technical regulation connects responsibility allocation, change management, and traceability to legal accountability. The EU AI Act’s high-risk framework addresses risk management, technical documentation, event logging, and cybersecurity, subject to its scope and application dates (eu2024aiact; eu2026aiactconsolidated). Directive (EU) 2024/2853 complements this framework by covering software and addressing safety-relevant updates in product liability (eu2024productliability). As discussed in Section 11.5.1, model replacements or changes in speed and tooling should prompt reassessment, with records identifying who approved each change and what evidence supports continued operation. Event records should connect deployed versions, actions, interventions, and maintenance histories. These engineering duties support accountability but do not themselves establish legal liability.

Ethics

Meaningful human control, Privacy by Embodiment, and fairness require safeguards for people affected by deployment. The EU AI Act’s high-risk framework addresses effective oversight, while practical intervention must remain feasible within the available response time (eu2024aiact; eu2026aiactconsolidated). The GDPR addresses lawful processing, data minimization, and protection by design. China’s Personal Information Protection Law addresses sensitive information and fairness in automated decision-making (eu2016gdpr; china2021pipl). Article 5 of the AI Act prohibits specified manipulative practices and exploitation of vulnerabilities where its statutory conditions are met (eu2024aiact; eu2026aiactconsolidated). Legal compliance does not exhaust the ethical responsibilities identified in Section 11.5.2, including equitable access to safe assistance and support for workers affected by automation (unesco2021ethics; oecd2019ai).

Application

Application-level regulation depends on intended use, system boundaries, and jurisdiction. Industrial robot installations fall under applicable machinery rules, while qualifying medical robots are subject to medical-device regulation (eu2006machinery; eu2023machinery; eu2017medicaldevices). The EU AI Act separately classifies high-risk systems through Article 6 and Annex III, subject to their statutory conditions (eu2024aiact; eu2026aiactconsolidated). Table 11.6 presents the book’s illustrative five-tier framework, considering harm severity, human exposure, tooling, autonomy, safeguard reliability, and user vulnerability (iso12100_2010; pi12_tabassi2023). These tiers are neither legal categories nor an international standard and do not map directly onto the AI Act. Classification must record operating assumptions and be reassessed when conditions change. A guarded robot’s Low placement reflects controlled exposure, not harmless machinery. Lower tiers do not remove legal duties, and higher tiers cannot authorize prohibited uses.

Table 11.6: Illustrative risk tiers proposed in this monograph. Placements depend on task, exposure, and validated safeguards

Supervised, low-energy desktop sorting without sharp, hot, or heavy tooling. Contact harm is at most trivial and is reversible.
